title: The Seated Woman of Çatalhöyük Flanked by Felines
medium: Fired terracotta with traces of burnishing
collection: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
description: Two big cats hold up this woman's seat: their heads, usually identified as leopards, form the ends of the arm-rests, and her hands come down to rest on them like a queen patting her hounds. The group is baked clay, modelled by hand and only about 12 cm high, yet it weighs roughly a kilogram. Treat the head and the right-hand cat with some suspicion: both were missing when the figure came out of the ground, and the ones you see today are modern replacements. The heavy breasts, the belly folding down over the knees and the left-hand cat are the Neolithic part.
context: James Mellaart excavated the figure at Çatalhöyük, in Turkey's Konya Province, in 1961, and it is now in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara. It is usually dated to around 6000 BCE. Mellaart's report puts it in a storeroom of the level he called the 'Hunting Shrine', and a much-repeated detail says it was found in a grain bin, which he read as a sign that she protected the harvest. He saw a fertility goddess giving birth on a throne. Later writers are more cautious, and some suggest that figurines of this kind show older women of high standing rather than a deity. The identity of the cats is not settled either: leopard is the usual reading, while some accounts, including Wikipedia, say lionesses.
feline_symbolism: The paired cats are often read as an early 'Mistress of Animals' motif, a woman who commands wild beasts.
title_eng: The Seated Woman of Çatalhöyük Flanked by Felines
location: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
image_credit: Dosseman · Own work

title: Dagger with Wild Cats Hunting Ducks (the "Nilotic" Dagger)
title_original: Χάλκινο εγχειρίδιο με διάκοσμο παραποτάμιου τοπίου
title_eng: Bronze Dagger with Riverside Landscape: Wild Cats Hunting Ducks
medium: Bronze, inlaid with gold and silver
description: Along a dark bronze blade only 16 cm long runs a river. Papyrus heads bloom in gold, fish jump clear of the water, and ducks scatter in panic while a spotted wild cat in gold and silver has already sunk its claws into one of them, body stretched flat in mid-pounce. Further along, birds flee towards the tip. The colours came from different metals laid into the bronze: yellow gold, pale silver, against a ground that was once black and glossy, so the scene would have glittered like a painting done in jewellery.
context: The dagger was buried in Tomb V of Grave Circle A at Mycenae, the shaft graves Heinrich Schliemann opened in 1876, alongside the gold masks and the rest of the Mycenaean elite's grave goods. Scenes like this are usually called "Nilotic" because papyrus, ducks and hunting cats look Egyptian, but the National Archaeological Museum makes a cheekier point: the Aegean versions actually pre-date the comparable Egyptian pictures, and they echo the wall paintings of Thera and Minoan Crete, where wild cats seem to have been brought very early, probably to keep down the rodents. So this may be less a Mycenaean dream of Egypt than a picture of a riverbank much closer to home.
feline_symbolism: Put on a weapon, the cat seizing its prey is a hunter's emblem: speed, stealth and a quick kill, the qualities a warrior would want his dagger to carry.
image_credit: Gary Todd · Greek Prehistory Gallery, National Archaeological Museum, Athens, 20 July 2016 (CC0)

title: Enthroned Woman Holding a Leopard Cub, from Hacılar
title_original: Hacılar, Leopar Yavrusu Tutan Tahtta Oturan Kadın Heykelciği
title_eng: Enthroned Woman Holding a Leopard Cub, from Hacılar
collection: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
location: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
description: A seated woman, barely the height of a coffee cup, clutches a young leopard to her chest with both arms. She is all curves: heavy thighs folded under her, a broad back, a small pinched head with a pointed chin and eyes made from pressed-on pellets of clay. The cub is a modest lump wedged between her hands and shoulder, so you have to know it is there, but once you see it the pose reads clearly: this is a body built for holding something precious and slightly dangerous.
context: The figure comes from Hacılar, a village mound near Burdur in south-west Turkey that James Mellaart dug between 1957 and 1960, a few years before his far more famous campaign at Çatalhöyük. The museum dates it to the Late Neolithic, around the middle of the sixth millennium BCE, which makes it a few centuries younger than the Seated Woman of Çatalhöyük, also in Ankara, whose throne ends in two cat heads. Hacılar women come with leopards again and again: sitting on them, standing beside them, or, as here, cradling a cub. Mellaart read them all as a mother goddess with her sacred animal; more recent writers prefer to leave the label open and simply note how stubbornly the leopard stays at the woman's side.
feline_symbolism: A woman nursing or holding a wild cat cub suggests a power over nature that is protective rather than violent: the predator raised, not killed.
image_credit: Dosseman (Dick Osseman) · Own work, 3 July 2019

title: Leopard Reliefs from Çatalhöyük
collection: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
location: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
description: Two pairs of leopards, modelled in clay plaster straight onto a house wall and later cut out for display. In the upper pair the cats stand nose to nose, or rather would, since their heads are lost, and their bodies are covered in little black rosettes and crosses: a Neolithic painter's shorthand for spots, done with more enthusiasm than zoology. The lower pair is fatter and smoother, two cats face to face around a pair of round bosses where their heads once were, tails curling up at either end, with only patches of the painted spots still showing through.
context: James Mellaart found the reliefs in the 1960s at Çatalhöyük, the huge Neolithic settlement on the Konya plain, and later reports place pairs of facing leopards on the walls of his building 44 in levels VII and VI. The museum label in Ankara makes the most telling point: the leopard heads carry so many coats of plaster and paint that the reliefs must have stayed on the walls for years, refreshed again and again by people who lived with them. Leopard skins turn up across the site, worn by hunters in the bull and deer murals, and Ian Hodder, who reopened the excavation in 1993, called his popular account of it "The Leopard's Tale". Nobody has ever found leopard bones at Çatalhöyük, though, which makes the animal's grip on the town's imagination all the stranger.
feline_symbolism: The leopard seems to have been the dominant wild animal of Çatalhöyük's imagery, tied to hunting, danger and perhaps the authority of whoever wore its skin.
image_credit: Dosseman (Dick Osseman) · Own work, 3 July 2019

title: Cosmetic Vessel in the Shape of a Cat
title_original: Cosmetic Vessel in the Shape of a Cat
description: This cat sits bolt upright on a flat rectangular base, front legs straight and close together, tail curled forward round its haunch. It is carved in the round from travertine (Egyptian alabaster) and hollowed out to hold cosmetics: look between the ears and you find the mouth of the jar, cut straight into the top of the skull. The eyes are rock crystal set in copper rims, now gone green, so the stare still catches the light like a wet eye would, and traces of paint survive on the stone. Tense and alert, it is more hunter than aloof temple cat.
context: The vessel dates to early Dynasty 12 of the Middle Kingdom, around 1990–1900 BCE. The Met bought it in 1990 with a Lila Acheson Wallace gift and described it as the earliest known three-dimensional representation of a cat in Egyptian art; cats had first appeared in painting and relief at the end of the Old Kingdom, some centuries earlier. Then the story changed. The Met's online record now states that the object was restituted in April 2026 and is no longer in its collection. The record does not say who received it, so its present home should be treated as unconfirmed until a public notice turns up.
title_eng: Cosmetic Vessel in the Shape of a Cat (Middle Kingdom)
submovement: Middle Kingdom stone cosmetic vessels (early Dynasty 12)
medium: Travertine (Egyptian alabaster), copper, quartz crystal, paint
collection: Formerly The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (restituted April 2026; current holder unconfirmed)
location: Restituted (no longer in the Metropolitan Museum of Art's collection)
image_credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Cuff Bracelets Decorated with Cats
artist: Unknown royal goldsmith of Thutmose III
date_display: Reign of Thutmose III, c. 1479–1425 BCE
description: Three little cats lie in a row on the gold spacer at the centre of this cuff, two in gold and one between them in red carnelian, each with ears pricked and forepaws stretched out. The spacer, just over 5 cm across, keeps the rows of tiny barrel beads in order, so the animals do a structural job as well as a decorative one. On either side the beads, each under a centimetre, run in bands of gold, carnelian, lapis lazuli and turquoise-coloured glass. Each cuff of the pair is about 16.8 cm long and 5 cm wide, and the colours would have shifted as the wrist moved.
context: The cuffs come from the tomb of three minor wives of Thutmose III (reigned c. 1479–1425 BCE) in Wadi D of the Wadi Gabbanat el-Qurud, Thebes. The women, Menhet, Menwi and Merti, carry names that most scholars consider non-Egyptian. Local men found the tomb in August 1916 and emptied much of it before archaeologists arrived; the contents went to dealers, and Herbert Winlock later bought back part of the hoard, which is now split between Cairo and the Met. The Met points out that the cat spacers echo royal jewellery from the start of Dynasty 18, and that many pieces from this group are incised with Thutmose III's name, which suggests they were his personal gifts.
title_eng: Cuff Bracelets Decorated with Cats (Tomb of the Three Princesses)
medium: Gold, carnelian, lapis lazuli, turquoise glass
dimensions: L. 16.8 cm; W. 5.1 cm; Th. 2.2 cm; cat spacer 5.2 × 2.9 cm
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
feline_symbolism: The Met links the cats to Bastet, the gentler counterpart of the lioness Sakhmet.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat Eating Fish beneath the Lady's Chair (Tomb of Nakht, TT52)
title_original: Scene from the Tomb of Nakht (TT52)
medium: Tempera on mud plaster over limestone bedrock
collection: Tomb of Nakht (TT52), Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, Thebes, Egypt
description: Look under the chair rather than at it. While Nakht's wife Tawy sits at the banquet, a striped tabby crouches beneath her seat, back humped into an almost perfect dome, head ducked low over a pale fish on the floor. Its ringed tail runs flat along the ground line behind it. It wears no collar and no lead, and nobody in the scene pays it any attention. The painters gave it the same crisp outline and flat colour as the people above, on plaster laid over the rock of the tomb, so the cat reads as part of the household inventory: chair, wife, fish, cat.
context: Tomb TT52 at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, on the west bank at Thebes, belonged to Nakht, a 'scribe and astronomer of Amun', probably under Thutmose IV (c. 1401–1391 BCE). Tawy appears beside him in the offering and banquet scenes. Norman de Garis Davies published the tomb in 1917, and facsimiles by Nina de Garis Davies circulate widely. The cat is often called the most detailed example of the cat-with-fish motif in Theban tombs. One oddity: in March 1915 a statue of Nakht was found thrown down the tomb shaft. It was shipped to New York later that year, and the steamer carrying it, the Arabic, was torpedoed off Ireland, so the statue now lies on the seabed.
title_eng: Cat Eating Fish beneath the Lady's Chair (Tomb of Nakht)
dimensions: Detail approx. 45 × 50 cm; wall mural approx. 1.8 × 2.2 m
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Matthias Seidel, Abdel Ghaffar Shedid: Das Grab des Nacht. Kunst und Geschichte eines Beamtengrabes der 18. Dynastie in Theben-West, von Zabern, Mainz 1991 ISBN 3805313322

title: Cat Amulet
description: A cat sits upright on a small rectangular plinth, head lifted and ears pricked, carved from lapis lazuli and only 1.3 cm long, roughly the size of a fingernail. At this scale the carver could give only the essentials: a rounded haunch, straight forelegs, a blunt muzzle. A tiny hole drilled through a loop behind the head shows it was strung and worn rather than looked at from across a room. Bend close and the deep blue turns out to be shot through with grey-white streaks and glints of golden pyrite, most of them pooled around the base.
context: The Met dates the amulet to Dynasty 18 of the New Kingdom, about 1550–1300 BCE, and it came to the museum in 1915 as part of the bequest of Mary Anna Palmer Draper. It is listed in Gallery 117. In the Met's Egyptian holdings it sits at the small end of a long range of cat objects that runs all the way up to Ptolemaic bronze cats made to hold a mummified animal, such as 56.16.1, which is more than twenty times its size. The museum's catalogue title is about as plain as Egyptology gets: 'Amulet, cat'.
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
image_credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Royal Limestone Sarcophagus of Prince Thutmose's Cat, Ta-Miu
title_original: Sarcophage de la chatte Ta-Miu du prince Thoutmôsis
description: The cat sits upright on a low mat, ears tall and pointed, gazing across at its own offering table, heaped with bread, a jug, plucked geese and a joint of beef, one goose laid flat across the top. A neat band at its neck reads as a scarf. This is a small limestone sarcophagus made for a cat, built like a human coffin box with a lid, and behind the cat stands a mummiform figure, its head seemingly feline too. Isis and Nephthys guard the ends, and hieroglyphs run along the top edge and over the lid, just as they would on a coffin for a person of rank.
context: The coffin comes from Mit Rahina, ancient Memphis, and is in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo (CG 5003, also cited as JE 30172). Its inscription names the owner of the cat: Prince Thutmose, eldest son of Amenhotep III, 'Crown Prince', overseer of the priests of Upper and Lower Egypt, high priest of Ptah at Memphis and sem-priest. Thutmose died before his father, and his brother came to the throne as Amenhotep IV, later Akhenaten. This cat box is one of the few objects that carry Thutmose's name, and without it we would not know he held the title of crown prince. Twist: in a 2014 article Heimo Hohneck questioned whether the sarcophagus is genuine, so treat it as probably, not certainly, ancient.
feline_symbolism: The cat receives exactly the offering-table cult a dead human would, and the inscription places it under the protection of Isis and Nephthys.
title_eng: Royal Limestone Sarcophagus of Prince Thutmose's Cat, Ta-Miu
submovement: Memphite relief sculpture, reign of Amenhotep III
image_credit: Larazoni · https://www.flickr.com/photos/laraz/2063179834/

title: Nebamun Hunting Fowl in the Marshes (Tomb-Chapel of Nebamun)
artist: Unknown Master of the Nebamun Tomb-Chapel
medium: Plaster fragment with tempera painting and gilded cat eye
dimensions: Overall: 81 × 98 cm; cat detail approx. 28 × 35 cm
description: The cat steals the scene. Tawny and striped, it scrambles up a papyrus stem left of centre, one bird clamped in its jaws and more caught in its paws, while Nebamun strides across his small boat with a throw-stick raised. His wife Hatshepsut stands behind him, a cone on her wig, and their young daughter kneels between his feet holding a lotus. Lean close and you will find the cat's eye is gilded with gold leaf, a detail you only catch from a few centimetres away. Around it the marsh is full of lotus flowers, fish and Plain Tiger butterflies, their wings dabbed in with quick, loose strokes.
context: Nebamun was a middle-ranking scribe and grain counter at Thebes around 1350 BCE, in the Eighteenth Dynasty. His tomb-chapel was found around 1820 by Giovanni d'Athanasi, working for the British consul-general Henry Salt, and the British Museum bought the paintings from Salt in 1821 (EA 37977). The tomb itself was then lost: d'Athanasi fell out with the museum over his fee and died without revealing the location, though analysis in 2008–09 points to the area of Dra' Abu el-Naga'. A restoration campaign ended with eleven fragments going on show in 2009. Quoted museum commentary says the gold on the cat's eye is the only such gilding known on Theban tomb-chapel walls.
feline_symbolism: Cats were household pets, but here the cat may also stand for the sun god hunting the enemies of light and order; the gilded eye points to that religious reading.
title_eng: Nebamun Hunting Fowl in the Marshes (British Museum EA37977)
image_credit: anonymous · The Open University

title: Tomb of Sennedjem: Solar Cat Beheading Apep
title_original: Mural from the Burial Chamber of Sennedjem (TT1)
artist_dates: Reigns of Seti I and Ramesses II (c. 1290–1270 BCE)
collection: Tomb of Sennedjem (TT1), Deir el-Medina, Thebes, Egypt
description: A big tabby cat sits back on its haunches beside a leafy tree and cuts off the head of a serpent with a long blade, calm as a cook at a chopping board. One forepaw drives the knife down, and red drops spatter where the severed head lies on the ground. The serpent is Apep, the chaos snake, and the cat is the sun god Ra in the guise of the Great Cat. The yellow ground covers the whole burial chamber, a colour that may be meant to recall papyrus. Opposite the doorway sit the twin lions of the horizon, so the cat gets the better wall.
context: Sennedjem was a 'servant in the Place of Truth', one of the craftsmen who cut the royal tombs, and lived at Deir el-Medina under Seti I and Ramesses II in the early thirteenth century BCE. His burial chamber (TT1) was found intact in January 1886 by Salam Abu Duhi and three companions and was cleared by Eduardo Toda y Güell in about three days, with few photographs and no plan. The finds went to the Bulaq Museum; some were sold, and the Met bought 29 objects. Charles K. Wilkinson painted a full-size facsimile of the cat in 1920–21, now in the Met (30.4.1). Gaston Maspero reportedly hoped the sales would raise 60 or 80 guineas toward work at the Sphinx.
title_eng: Tomb of Sennedjem: Solar Cat Beheading Apep
dimensions: Scene approx. 65 × 85 cm; chamber wall approx. 2.4 × 3.2 m
feline_symbolism: The Great Cat killing Apep shows the sun's nightly victory over chaos, and the Met ties the image to Chapter 17 of the Book of the Dead.
location: Tomb of Sennedjem (TT1), Deir el-Medina, Thebes, Egypt
image_credit: Charles Wilkinson · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Papyrus of Hunefer: The Great Cat of Heliopolis Slaying Apep
title_original: rw nw prt m hrw, Spell 17
medium: Ink and opaque watercolour on papyrus
description: In one small vignette of Hunefer's Book of the Dead, a spotted cat with tall ears and a ringed tail stands over a serpent and saws into its neck with a knife, pinning the head down by its forepaws. The snake of darkness loops twice in black-spotted white. The image is ink and colour on papyrus, in the crisp, outlined manner of a Ramesside royal workshop, and tiny compared with the roll: the whole papyrus is about 40 cm high and some 5.5 m long. The cat turns a calm, almost smiling face toward us, which makes slicing up a snake look like routine administration.
context: Hunefer was a scribe of divine offerings, overseer of royal cattle and steward of Seti I in the Nineteenth Dynasty, and his Book of the Dead is dated to about 1275 BCE. The papyrus is in the British Museum (EA 9901). It is best known for a different scene, the judgement in which Anubis leads Hunefer in, his heart is weighed while the monster Ammit waits and Thoth records the result, and Horus presents him to Osiris. The cat vignette is easy to miss beside that set piece. A Spanish-language caption on Wikimedia Commons names the cat Miuty, the Great Cat of Heliopolis.
title_eng: Papyrus of Hunefer: The Great Cat of Heliopolis Slaying Apep
submovement: Ramesside Illustrated Funerary Papyri (Book of the Dead)
location: British Museum, London (Department of Egypt and Sudan)
feline_symbolism: The cat is the sun god, who in one account defeats the serpent Apophis (Apep) in feline form, a nightly victory of order over chaos.
image_credit: Hunefer · Jon Bodsworth (photographer)

title: Ostracon of a Cat Minding Geese
medium: Ink and pigment on limestone flake (ostracon)
description: A spotted cat walks on its hind legs like a herdsman, a long crook over its shoulder with a small net bag of provisions dangling from the far end, and its ringed tail curling down between its feet. In front of it, in two rows, go six geese or ducks, and above them sits a nest full of eggs. It is drawn and painted on a flake of limestone, the scrap paper of ancient Egypt, in black outline with touches of red on the birds' legs and bills. The joke is the reversal: the predator has become the shepherd, and the birds look entirely unworried.
context: The ostracon comes from Deir el-Medina, the village of the royal tomb-builders on the west bank at Thebes, and is in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo (JE 63801). The craftsmen there used limestone flakes for notes, letters, lists and copies of literature, and some for sketches like this one, where the picture is the point. Scenes of animals acting like people are common, but nobody is sure what they meant: they may illustrate lost fables, poke fun at a rigid social order, or simply be an artist amusing himself between jobs. The date is also debated in the sources, which range from the Eighteenth Dynasty to the Ramesside period.
title_eng: Ostracon of a Cat Minding Geese
feline_symbolism: Several scholars read such scenes as parody of the social hierarchy, an upside-down world where the cat tends what it would normally eat.

title: Ring with Cat and Kittens
title_original: Ring with Cat and Kittens in the Papyrus Marshes
culture: Ancient Egyptian (New Kingdom, Ramesside Period – Third Intermediate Period)
dimensions: Bezel 1.6 × 1.3 × 1.7 cm; inner diam. 1.9 cm; shank (papyrus) L. 6.3 cm
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: The mother cat sits bolt upright on top of this faience ring, while a cluster of kittens crowds around her feet like an audience waiting for a speech. The whole bezel group is less than 2 cm in any direction. The shank is not a plain hoop: it is modelled as papyrus, some 6 cm of it, bound stalks opening into openwork umbels, so the cat family seems to sit in a marsh thicket that wraps around the finger. Faience is a glazed quartz paste rather than true pottery, and its turquoise glaze let workshops turn out small, bright, cheap things like this in quantity.
context: The Met bought the ring in 2017 with gifts from Patricia A. Cotti and the Friends of Egyptian Art, and dates it broadly to about 1300–664 BCE, from the Ramesside Period into the Third Intermediate Period. It is shown in Gallery 125. Kittens point to Bastet: as the Cleveland Museum of Art notes, statuettes of the goddess often show her with basketfuls of kittens. The odd detail is that papyrus shank: at 6.3 cm it is longer than the bezel is wide, so the ring is mostly marsh and only a little bit cat.
feline_symbolism: Cat-and-kitten groups are tied to Bastet, whose statuettes often carry baskets of kittens; a wish for fertility is the usual, if unstated, reading.
submovement: Ramesside to Third Intermediate Period faience rings
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (Gallery 125)
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Ostracon of a Cat Serving an Enthroned Mouse Lady
title_original: Ostracon of a Cat Serving a Mouse Lady (Ramesside Period, c. 1200 BCE)
description: A tabby cat stands upright on its hind legs like a servant, ears pricked, tail hanging straight to the ground, one paw gripping the pole of a half-round feather fan and the other holding out a plucked bird, a napkin over the paw. Facing it, a mouse lady in a long skirt holds court on a folding stool with animal legs, a hide thrown over it with the tail hanging down. She sniffs a flower and holds up a cup. The whole thing is drawn in ink on a limestone flake, with traces of white paint left on the mouse's body.
context: The ostracon was found at Deir el-Medina, the village of the royal tomb-builders at Thebes, and dates to the Ramesside Period, about 1290–1070 BCE. It is in the Brooklyn Museum (37.51E). The draughtsman borrowed the layout of a real banquet scene, where servants fan and feed a seated lady, and then swapped the cast. What it meant is anyone's guess: suggestions include a satire, an illustration of a lost fable, a caricature of the royal family, or a doodle. The comedy rests on the reversal: the cat, the mouse's natural enemy, is waiting on her with a napkin.
title_eng: Ostracon of a Cat Serving an Enthroned Mouse Lady (Brooklyn 37.51E)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (New Kingdom, Ramesside Period, 19th–20th Dynasty)
medium: Black and red ink on smoothed limestone flake (ostracon)
collection: Brooklyn Museum, New York, United States
feline_symbolism: The reversal of predator and prey is usually read as parody of a hierarchical society, a world turned upside down.

title: Tomb of Inherkha: Great Cat of Heliopolis Slaying Apophis
title_original: Mural from the Tomb of Inherkha (TT359)
medium: Tempera on mud plaster and smoothed limestone wall
dimensions: Detail: 70 × 92 cm; burial chamber frieze approx. 1.9 × 3.4 m
collection: Tomb of Inherkha (TT359), Deir el-Medina, Thebes, Egypt
description: In one of the Book of the Dead scenes that cover Inherkha's tomb, a cat attacks the serpent Apophis, one forepaw pinning the snake's head to the ground while the other drives a red-bladed knife into its neck. The cat is the sun god Ra in the form of the Great Cat, oddly long-eared, almost hare-like, tongue out. Behind the action a persea tree spreads blue-grey branches dotted with red fruit, and the spotted snake winds round its trunk. The confident outline belongs to painters who decorated tombs for a living, because in this village that is exactly what the tomb owners and their neighbours did.
context: Tomb TT359 at Deir el-Medina belonged to Inherkha (Inherkhau), 'Foreman of the Lord of the Two Lands in the Place of Truth', who led a gang of the royal tomb-builders under Ramesses III and Ramesses IV in the Twentieth Dynasty. His father Huy was also a foreman. The tomb has an outer and an inner chamber, decorated with offering scenes, the Book of Gates, the Book of the Dead and two rows of kings, queens and princes. Part of it has left Egypt: a doorway scene of Ahmose-Nefertari and Amenhotep I is now in Berlin, and a stela from the tomb is in Chicago. The cat scene stays in situ.
title_eng: Tomb of Inherkha: Great Cat of Heliopolis Slaying Apophis (TT359)
feline_symbolism: The sun god, in the form of a cat, slays the serpent Apophis, the nightly victory of order over chaos.
image_credit: Ismoon ( talk ) 17:37, 5 May 2020 (UTC) · own work, scan from ISBN 978-2-85-088235-7

title: Amulet of Bastet
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
description: A cat 4.4 cm tall sits bolt upright on a low base, neck long, muzzle lifted, ears up. The surprise is underneath the chin: the front legs are carved free in openwork, so you can see daylight between them and the chest, which is a bold thing to attempt in hematite, a heavy, brittle iron ore that polishes to a dark metallic shine. Here the polish is so high that the studio lights slide down the neck and forelegs like water. The base is shaped from hieroglyphs, the tail curls round the left side, and a suspension loop on the back shows it was worn.
context: The amulet dates to Egypt's Third Intermediate Period, about 1069–715 BCE. Cleveland explains that the base combines the hieroglyph for 'ointment jar', which is also used to write the name of Bastet, with the sign for 'protection', so the stand spells out what the cat is for. The provenance is the fun part. The amulet belonged to Howard Carter, the excavator of Tutankhamun's tomb, until his death in 1939, after which it passed to his niece Phyllis Walker. She sold it to an English private collector; it later went through the Sussex Armoury and was bought by the Cleveland Museum of Art in 1973.
feline_symbolism: The cat is Bastet's sacred animal, and the hieroglyphs of the base turn it into a written wish for her protection.
submovement: Third Intermediate Period Hardstone Amuletic Carving
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Amulet of Bastet as a Seated Cat
dimensions: H. 2.93 cm; W. 1.1 cm; D. 2 cm
description: A seated cat less than 3 cm high, cast in copper alloy and striped in gold like a tabby: bands ring its neck and forelegs, and rows of short gold dashes run down its chest and flanks. Even the eyes are rimmed in gold, which gives it a wide-awake stare. It wears a collar, and a scarab sits on its forehead, the same two marks of divinity found on much larger Bastet bronzes, here shrunk to the size of a fingertip. Turn it round and there is a loop on the back for a cord. The metal has darkened almost to black, which makes the gold stand out.
context: The Louvre dates the amulet by style to the Late Period, 664–332 BCE, and identifies the cat as the goddess Bastet. It was bought for the museum at the public sale of the collection of Jean Henri Hoffmann, approved in May 1895, and still carries his sale number, 416, alongside the Louvre's E 10661. Rather than sitting with the gods, it is displayed in Room 334 of the Sully wing among objects chosen to show Egyptian materials and techniques, which suits it: the point of the piece is how much casting and inlay can be fitted onto something the size of a thumbnail.
feline_symbolism: The collar and frontal scarab mark the cat as Bastet herself rather than an ordinary pet.
title_eng: Amulet of Bastet as a Seated Cat
image_credit: Rama · Own work

title: The Gayer-Anderson Cat
title_original: Bronze Statuette of the Goddess Bastet (EA 64391)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (Late Period, 26th Dynasty to Ptolemaic Period)
submovement: Saite & Late Period Monumental Votive Bronzes
description: A bronze cat 42 cm tall sits upright on long, straight front legs, chin raised, and wears its jewellery like a temple official: a gold ring through the nose, another hanging from the ear, a scarab on the head, a winged scarab engraved on the chest and a protective wedjat amulet on a plaque hanging from a finely incised collar. The eyes are empty now and probably once held stone or glass, which gives the face a sleepy, inward look. Look at the tail, too: the stripes there are metal of a different composition, set into the casting to suggest markings. The patina has gone a mottled sea green.
context: The statue was cast in the Late Period, around 664–332 BCE, and is said to come from Saqqara. It is named after Major Robert Grenville Gayer-Anderson, who gave it to the British Museum together with Mary Stout Shaw; a replica stays in the Gayer-Anderson Museum in Cairo. He was a keen amateur restorer, and he chipped away the heavy crust of verdigris and red patina himself. The repair goes deeper than it looks. X-rays show a crack running almost all the way round the body, and only an internal strengthening system keeps the head on. Analysis puts the alloy at about 85% copper and 13% tin, and the gold earrings and nose ring may not be original to the cat.
feline_symbolism: The cat represents the goddess Bastet, and the wedjat amulet on its chest adds a charm of protection.
image_credit: Peter D. Tillman from USA · Gayer-Anderson Cat, British Museum

title: Hollow-Cast Bronze Statuette of a Seated Cat
collection: Brooklyn Museum, New York, United States
description: A cat sits upright on long, straight forelegs, head turned slightly aside, ears tall and finely hatched on the inside. It is cast in bronze as a hollow shell around a core rather than as a solid lump, which saved metal and kept a large figure light enough to carry into a temple. The pose is the formal, upright one used for images of Bastet. Bend close and small incised details appear: whisker lines on the muzzle, a round mark on the forehead, a thin line across the chest. Time has darkened the surface to a deep chocolate brown, which hides how bright it would have been when new.
context: The statuette belongs to Egypt's Late Period, about 664–342 BCE, and is catalogued as an image of the cat goddess Bastet. It came to the Brooklyn Museum as a gift of Alice Heeramaneck and carries the accession number 78.243. Hollow casting was the ambitious option for a bronze of any size, since the founder had to hold a clay core in place inside the mould while the metal flowed around it. A small modern footnote: the cat was photographed in February 2009 for 'Wikipedia Loves Art', a project in which museum visitors shared photographs of collection objects under a free licence, which is why its picture turns up all over the web.
title_eng: Hollow-Cast Bronze Statuette of a Seated Cat (Brooklyn 78.243)
feline_symbolism: As an image of Bastet's animal, the cat stood in for the goddess and carried the donor's request to her.
image_credit: Photographed February 2009 by Wikipedia Loves Art participant " one_click_beyond " Uploaded from the Wikipedia Loves Art photo pool on Flickr. Wikipedia Loves Art at the Brooklyn Museum This photo of item # 78.243 at the Brooklyn Museum was

title: Bronze Statuette of Bastet as a Seated Cat
medium: Solid-cast copper alloy with traces of gilding
description: A small cat sits upright on top of a tall, narrow pillar capped with a projecting cornice, so the whole thing looks like a statue set on a miniature shrine. Around its neck hangs a collar with a wedjat eye, and a scarab sits on its forehead. It is solid-cast in copper alloy, 18.2 cm high, and once had gilding: traces of gold survive on the right eye only, so one eye still catches the light and the other has gone dull. Its tail curls across the cornice top, and the lean neck and long front legs give it the alert outline of Late Period cat bronzes.
context: The Louvre dates the figure by style to the Late Period, 664–332 BCE, and identifies it, cautiously, as Bastet. It came from the collection of Antoine Barthélémy Clot, known as Clot Bey, and entered the museum's inventory in 1852 by purchase. It carries a stack of numbers that record that journey: E 672 today, N 3915 in an older Louvre series, and 'Clot bey C 16 n°23' from his own collection. It is displayed on the first floor of the Sully wing, Room 643. The Louvre's own name for it is just 'figurine'.
feline_symbolism: The wedjat collar and frontal scarab suggest the cat is Bastet, as the Louvre tentatively proposes.
title_eng: Bronze Statuette of Bastet as a Seated Cat

title: Bastet as a Cat Nursing Two Kittens
description: A mother cat lies stretched out on a flat slab while two kittens stand pressed against her belly to nurse. The whole group is only 5 cm high and about 10 cm long, cast in copper alloy, and the low, horizontal composition is unusual next to the upright, formal cats that fill most Egyptian bronze cases. The kittens are reduced to small, rounded shapes, one gone a paler green than the other. Her front legs reach forward, her head lifts and turns straight out at you, ears up, as if keeping an eye on the room while the kittens get on with it.
context: The Louvre dates the group by style to the Late Period, 664–332 BCE, and describes it as the goddess Bastet as a cat, lying down and suckling two kittens. The museum bought it from a Mme Perimony, with the purchase approved on 31 October 1912 (inventory E 11295). Its display spot is a small surprise: it sits in Room 332 of the Sully wing in a case about livestock, hunting and fishing, so a goddess ends up among the farm animals.
feline_symbolism: The nursing mother presents Bastet as a protector of motherhood and young.
title_eng: Bastet as a Cat Nursing Two Kittens
image_credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Ancient Egypt Bronze Nursing Cat

title: Bronze Statuette of a Cat Playing with her Kitten (Chatte couchée, jouant avec son petit)
description: A mother cat lies along a half-round base with her kitten tucked against her chest, and the pair are cast together in copper alloy, about 10 cm across. The Louvre's older French title says she is playing with her young one, and the group has that relaxed, sprawled quality: hind legs stretched out behind, a row of teats along the belly, head lifted and turned toward us. Look for the writing: a hieroglyphic inscription runs on the piece, the kind of text you skip at first glance and that turns out to be the whole reason the object exists.
context: The Louvre dates the group by style to the Late Period, 664–332 BCE, and suggests that the cat may represent Bastet. The inscription is a dedication naming the goddess and a woman called Tadimout (the reading is uncertain), described as 'mistress of the house', so this was a gift paid for by a private person. It belonged to Henry Salt, the British consul-general and collector, and was bought by the Louvre in 1826. It still carries Salt's number 270 and a catalogue number, 'Champollion B. 313', that ties it to Jean-François Champollion, the decipherer of hieroglyphs, who catalogued the Louvre's early Egyptian holdings.
title_eng: Bronze Statuette of a Cat Playing with her Kitten (Louvre N 3930)
submovement: Late Period votive bronzes (dedications to Bastet)
feline_symbolism: A cat with kitten links Bastet to motherhood, and the dedication shows a woman asking the goddess for her favour.
title_original: Chatte couchée, jouant avec son petit
image_credit: Rama · Own work

title: Carved Statuette of Four Seated Cats (Quatre chats assis)
description: Four seated cats share a single block of acacia wood here, a little group only 14 cm high and 27 cm long. They were carved in the round and then painted black, and where the paint has flaked a paler layer shows through in patches, so the surface now looks dusted with gold. Look at how the repetition works: four sets of ears, four upright chests, four pairs of front legs, with the slight unevenness that tells you a hand, and not a mould, made each one. The second cat from the left is noticeably smaller, and the third pricks its ears highest.
context: The Louvre dates this group to the Late Period (664-332 BCE) on stylistic grounds, since nothing about its find-spot was recorded. It came from Antoine-Barthélemy Clot, the French doctor known in Egypt as Clot Bey, who ran the Kasr al-Aini medical school for Muhammad Ali; his old collection number (C 9 no. 15) still travels with it, and it entered the Louvre's inventory by purchase in 1852. Its main number today is E 615, with N 3910 kept as a secondary one. Fun fact: nobody had to guess the timber. Laboratory analysis by the CTFT in 1971 identified the wood as acacia, and in 1994 the cats left Paris for a garden-themed exhibition in Dijon, 'Nil était une fois'.
title_eng: Carved Statuette of Four Seated Cats (Louvre N 3910)
image_credit: Rama · Own work

title: Statuette of cat
dimensions: H. 11 cm; W. 3 cm; L. 6 cm; H. with tang 12 cm
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: A small cast cat in copper alloy, just 11 cm tall, sits bolt upright with its tail swept round the base until the tip lies beside its right forepaw. A short tang under it once slotted it into a separate base, which pushes the full height to about 12 cm; today it disappears into a modern white mount. At this size every feature has to be stated simply: the ears are two firm triangles, the body a single smooth volume, a thin incised line marks the collar. The tang tells you it was a fitted object, set upright in a stand where it could be seen and left.
context: The Met dates this statuette broadly to 664-30 BCE, the long stretch from the Late Period into Ptolemaic rule when Egyptians bought and dedicated huge numbers of cat bronzes, many linked to the goddess Bastet. The museum's own subject tags put it under both 'Cats' and 'Goddess'. It came from Egypt and entered the collection in 1904 as a gift of Darius Ogden Mills, and it is shown in Gallery 130. Oddity worth knowing: catalogue copies of this cat have long carried inflated measurements (nearly 15 cm), but the Met's record gives a much smaller 11 cm body and 3 cm width, small enough to sit in a cupped hand.
feline_symbolism: Cat bronzes of this period are generally read as offerings to Bastet; the Met tags this one with 'Goddess'.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Square Bowl with Pampas Cats
description: Pampas cats stare out from the walls of this squared-off bowl, each reduced to geometry: a frontal face of blocky eyes and a stepped mouth, a body spotted with round dots, a banded tail curving up beside it like a striped horn. On one side two cats sit shoulder to shoulder. The form is unusual for a vessel, a soft square about 18 cm across and only 9 cm deep, so the cats get four flat-ish walls. The ochre, red, grey-green and cream sit on top of the fired clay as post-fire paint, while the inside stays plain dark brown and the base is solid red.
context: The bowl was made on Peru's south coast by Paracas potters around 500-400 BCE. It spent decades in private hands: with Margrith Brenner in Zurich from before the late 1960s until 1994, then with a New York collector, who sold it to the Cleveland Museum of Art in 2021 (J. H. Wade Fund). It now sits in the museum's Andean gallery. Fun fact: Cleveland is specific about the species. Its label names the animal as the pampas cat, a small, reclusive wild feline that lives on the edges of farmland, and argues that Paracas potters kept returning to it because it hunted the rodents that plagued their fields.
feline_symbolism: Cleveland suggests the pampas cat, a hunter of crop pests, was linked with the fertility of nature and, by extension, human prosperity and continuity.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Double-Spout Bridge Vessel with Incised Feline
culture: Peru, South Coast, Paracas (Cavernas) style (700 BCE–1 CE)
medium: Earthenware with incised decoration and post-fire resin-based paint
description: An abstracted feline wraps around this round vessel, which rises to two spouts joined by an arched bridge. Its face sits front and centre under the bridge, a black mask with heavy-lidded eyes and a red mouth, while its body arches away to the left as a red, spotted hump on stepped legs, and a banded crescent curves beneath like a grin. The smoky black firing now shows only on the spouts, bridge and base; the colours came afterwards, as resin-based paint pressed into the incised fields. It is about 14 cm across and 11 cm high. Look at the foot of one spout: a tiny modelled head peers out.
context: Paracas potters on Peru's south coast made this vessel in the Cavernas style, which Cleveland dates broadly to 700 BCE-1 CE. The museum received it as a gift of John Wise. Cleveland is candid that 'little is known' about what these abstracted felines meant, and the double-spout-and-bridge form, common on fine south-coast ceramics, probably carried meaning that is now lost. Oddity: in 1966 this clay pot appeared in a Cleveland exhibition called 'Treasures of Peruvian Gold', a reminder that curators have long hung Paracas pottery beside the metalwork. The museum's identification of the cat is the pampas cat, a small wild hunter of field pests.
title_eng: Double-Spout Bridge Vessel with Incised Feline
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Small Globular Bottle with Feline
culture: Peru, South Coast, Paracas (Cavernas) style (700 BCE–1 CE)
medium: Earthenware with incised decoration and resin-based paint
description: This little bottle, barely 10 cm high and 7.5 cm across, carries an abstracted feline incised into its surface, and it seems to have two faces. One side stares with huge ringed eyes under prong-like ears and pokes out a red tongue; the other is a broader mask with arched, heavy-lidded eyes, a red dot of a nose and a mouth full of blocky teeth. The clay was fired in a smoky kiln that turned it black, still visible on the neck and base, and only then were the incised areas filled with resin-based paint, so the colour sits in the grooves like inlay.
context: Made by Paracas potters on Peru's south coast in the Cavernas style, which Cleveland dates to 700-1 BCE, the bottle was a gift to the museum from John Wise, the same donor behind a larger double-spout vessel with a similar cat (1948.477). It was illustrated in the Cleveland Museum of Art Handbook of 1958. Fun fact: like its sibling, it was shown in Cleveland's 1966 exhibition 'Treasures of Peruvian Gold', despite being made of clay. Cleveland identifies these felines as pampas cats, small wild hunters that live on the edges of fields and eat the rodents farmers hate.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat
culture: Egypt, Late Period, Dynasty 26 or later
dimensions: 9.2 x 2.3 x 5.5 cm; without tang 7.5 cm
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
description: A seated cat in bronze, long-necked and narrow-chested in the classic votive pose, wears jewellery: an embossed pendant hangs at its chest and a gold hoop, almost as big as the ear itself, pierces its left ear. The figure is tiny, 9.2 cm with its tang and 7.5 cm without, so the gold is a bright point against the dark metal. The tang under the base means it was made to stand in a socket or plinth. Turn it round and the collar crosses in an X between the shoulder blades. The earring is what turns a generic cat into somebody's well-dressed one.
context: Cleveland places this cat in Egypt's Late Period, Dynasty 26 or later, with a date range of 664-30 BCE. John L. Severance bought it from R. H. Blanchard's 'Egyptian Museum' in Cairo, an antiquities shop, and it came to Cleveland with his bequest, shown in the 1942-43 exhibition of his collection. Silvia Wunderlich published it in the museum's Bulletin in November 1942. Cleveland describes such figures as votive offerings and connects them to Bastet, goddess of cats and protector of the home. Fun fact: the catalogue entry it replaces doubled its size; the real cat is shorter than a playing card.
feline_symbolism: Cleveland identifies cats as the sacred animal of Bastet, protector of the home, and reads this figure as a votive offering.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Box for a cat mummy inscribed for Bastet
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: A cat crouches on the lid of a long, low metal box, front legs braced, hindquarters tucked, neck stretched forward as if it has just spotted something at the far end of the room. The whole thing runs 34.7 cm from end to end but only 8 cm wide and 17.6 cm high including the figure. The box below is the business end: it held a mummified animal, and the cat on top announces what was inside. An inscription names Bastet, the goddess to whom the offering was made. Look at the cat's body: its whole coat is combed with fine incised lines, a texture the plain box never gets.
context: The Met dates this box to the Late Period-Ptolemaic Period (664-30 BCE). It was purchased through the Rogers Fund in 1912 and is displayed in Gallery 134. Boxes like this were made in cupreous metal to receive small animal mummies offered at temples, and the inscription for Bastet ties it to her cult. Fun fact: it belongs to a whole menagerie at the Met. The museum also holds near-identical boxes topped by a shrew, a falcon, a pair of ichneumons, a coiled snake, and another with two cats, each sized for its own sacred animal.
title_eng: Box for a cat mummy inscribed for Bastet
feline_symbolism: The box is inscribed for Bastet, so the cat on the lid signals both the animal inside and the goddess receiving it.
image_credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Cat Statuette Intended to Contain a Mummified Cat
title_eng: Cat Statuette Intended to Contain a Mummified Cat (Met 56.16.1, Profile View)
dimensions: H. 27.4 x W. 11.9 x D. 23.3 cm; 2.5 kg; H. with tangs 32 cm
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: This seated cat is hollow on purpose. Cast in leaded bronze and standing 27.4 cm high (32 cm with the tangs that fixed it to a base), it was made as a container for a mummified cat, a sculpture and a coffin in one. It sits tall on long, straight forelegs, its tail swept round the base until the tip rests against the front paws. Look at the chest: a thin collar is incised round the neck, with a wedjat eye engraved below it, so faint you need raking light. It weighs about 2.5 kg, and the tangs underneath show it stood on a separate support.
context: The Met dates this statuette to the Ptolemaic Period (332-30 BCE). It came from Egypt and was bought through the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund in 1956; it is shown in Gallery 134. In the Late and Ptolemaic periods, temple workshops sold animal mummies to pilgrims as offerings, and a bronze case like this one was the deluxe option. Cleveland owns a close cousin (1917.998), a 51 cm hollow bronze cat with an open base, which suggests these were a recognised product rather than one-offs. Fun fact: the Met records its weight twice, 2.5 kg for the cat and 3.7 kg with its modern mount.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat Coffin
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
description: A big seated bronze cat, 51 cm tall, sits with its tail curled around its right side, which Cleveland notes is the usual arrangement, the tip running round the base to meet the front paws. Its forelegs are startlingly long and straight, and the small, wide-eyed face looks straight out. It is hollow with an open bottom, because it is a coffin: the body of a sacred cat was meant to go inside. Look at the chest. Faint scratches there trace a necklace that seems to have been incised into the bronze after casting, a small finishing touch that only shows up when the light rakes across the metal.
context: Cleveland dates the coffin to the Ptolemaic dynasty (305-30 BCE) and stresses that it is unusually large. The museum points out that although the cat feels like the most Egyptian of animals, it only became an object of worship late in Egyptian history. The piece was sold by the dealer Dikran G. Kelekian of New York and entered the museum in 1917 as a gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust. It has been in Cleveland exhibitions from the 1941 Silver Jubilee show to 'A Cleveland Bestiary' (1981), and Berman and Bohač catalogued it in 1999. Fun fact: the necklace is so faint that the museum flags it as a 'did you know'.
feline_symbolism: Cleveland describes it as made to hold the mummified remains of a sacred cat, tied to the late flourishing of cat worship.
location: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Papyrus Column with Two Cats
title_eng: Papyrus Column with Two Cats (Louvre E 11204)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (Late Period to Ptolemaic Period)
collection: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C.
location: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution
description: Two cats perch side by side on top of a papyrus column in this faience amulet, only 4.4 cm tall and a centimetre wide, their heads pressed together and barely wider than the capital they sit on. The column is the papyrus-stalk form Egyptians used for amulets: a faceted shaft on a small square foot, rising to a flared head incised with pointed leaves. An eyelet at the top shows it was threaded and worn. At this scale the modelling is summary, two compact bodies and two pairs of ears, and a dark streak in the bright turquoise glaze runs down between the cats like a shared shadow.
context: This is in the Freer Gallery of Art (Smithsonian), not the Louvre. Charles Lang Freer bought it in Cairo in 1908 from the dealer Ali Arabi, and it entered the museum with Freer's gift in 1920. The Smithsonian dates it to 305-30 BCE, possibly the Ptolemaic period, and has shown it in 'A Collector's Eye: Freer in Egypt'. Similar amulets turn up elsewhere: the British Museum has a green-glazed example with 'two cats of Bastet' on a papyrus column, and Penn has one whose shaft is lost. Fun fact: the dealer's name is recorded two ways in Freer's papers, as Ali Arabi and as 'Ali Arabi Jr.', so even this tiny object has a small provenance puzzle.
feline_symbolism: Comparable amulets are described by the British Museum as the cats of Bastet on a papyrus column, so the pair probably invokes the goddess's protection.

title: Etruscan Bronze Incense Burner with Clambering Cat (Thymiaterion)
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
description: Halfway up the fluted shaft of this 61 cm bronze incense burner, a spotted cat or panther clings on with its forepaws, tail dangling, its coat stamped with little ring-shaped spots. Above it a crested bird, perhaps a rooster, perches on the shaft, so the hunt is frozen mid-climb. At the base a youthful nude male, perhaps the wine god Dionysos, shoulders the shaft with one hand on his hip, standing on a tripod with cloven-hoofed feet. At the top a square plate with a shallow circular dip held the incense; holes at its corners once carried more animals or ornaments that are now missing.
context: Etruscan bronze workers made this thymiaterion in the 2nd century BCE. Cleveland describes the type as at least three parts, tripod, shaft and incense bowl, often with a figural support like this one. It once belonged to the Count de Sarzana and was bought through the John L. Severance Fund; John Cooney published it in the museum's Bulletin in 1971, and Laura Ambrosini included it in her 2002 study of Etruscan bronze thymiateria. Oddity: in 1962 this pre-Roman burner was shown in a Cleveland exhibition titled 'Art and Humanism in the Renaissance', presumably as an ancient model, an unusual career move for an incense stand.
title_eng: Etruscan Bronze Incense Burner with Clambering Cat (Thymiaterion)
location: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Parrots Drinking at a Porphyry Basin, with a Lurking Cat
title_original: Mosaico con gatto e pappagalli alla fontana
medium: Opus vermiculatum stone and glass paste polychrome tesserae
collection: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (MANN), Naples, Italy
description: The cat crouches in the lower right corner, a striped and spotted tabby with one forepaw raised and its ears pricked toward the basin above. Up on the rim, two green parrots with long tails and red collars flank a paler, speckled bird bent down to drink (a dove, by some descriptions). That ambush is the whole joke. The basin stands on a red stone pedestal, and a split pomegranate lies on the ground at left. The panel measures 58 x 50 cm and is made in opus vermiculatum, tesserae so small they let the mosaicist shade feathers and fur almost like paint.
context: The mosaic was found in 1855 at Santa Maria Capua Vetere, ancient Capua, where it served as the central emblem of a floor, and it is now in the mosaic section of the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (inv. 9992). Sources date it to the early 1st century BCE; one picture library gives 80-60 BCE. Fun fact: it is a remix. Birds drinking at a bowl was a well-known Hellenistic motif, and the Capua designer swapped in parrots and added a lurking cat, turning a peaceful scene into one with suspense. The emblem was cut from its floor, which is why it now hangs on a museum wall.
title_eng: Parrots Drinking at a Porphyry Basin, with a Lurking Cat
submovement: Campanian Late Republican Floor Mosaics (Opus Vermiculatum)
location: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (MANN), Naples, Italy
image_credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Roman Mosaic: Parrots drinking at the fountain, from Capua Vetere

title: Cat Pouncing on a Partridge (House of the Faun, Pompeii)
title_original: Mosaico con gatto che azzanna una pernice
submovement: Pompeian Hellenistic Mosaic Emblema (House of the Faun)
medium: Opus vermiculatum polychrome limestone, marble, and glass tesserae
collection: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (MANN), Naples, Italy
description: In the top register a spotted tabby has its teeth in a bird, a quail in most descriptions, a partridge in others, pinning it with a forepaw while the victim's wings fly up in a brown-and-white fan. The cat stares straight out of the picture, whiskers splayed, as if daring you to object. Below, the mosaic calms down into a still life of things Romans liked on the table: two ducks (one with lotus buds in its beak), four small birds tied by the feet, shellfish (a mussel, a date mussel, a cockle, a murex) and seven little fish. Fine opus vermiculatum shades fur and plumage tessera by tessera.
context: The panel comes from the House of the Faun in Pompeii (VI.12.2), a grand house built in the 2nd century BCE that also gave Naples the Alexander Mosaic. Like most of the house's floors, it was lifted and moved to the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli, where it is inventory 9993. The date usually given for the mosaic is around 100 BCE, though I found no museum record pinning it down. Fun fact: the bird is still contested. Italian sources say quail, English captions often say partridge, and the catalogue entry here had it as both, so pick your bird and defend it.
title_eng: Cat Pouncing on a Partridge (House of the Faun, Pompeii)
dimensions: Upper register: 45 × 45 cm; full emblema: 85 × 52 cm
location: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (MANN), Naples, Italy
image_credit: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany · Mosaic depicting a cat with a partridge (above) and ducks, fish & shellfish (below), from the House of the Faun, Pompeii, Naples Archaeological Museum

title: Floor Mosaic Emblema with a Cat Attacking a Bird and Two Ducks
medium: Opus vermiculatum polychrome marble and hardstone tesserae
collection: Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Massimo alle Terme, Rome, Italy
description: Up top, a striped tabby crouches low with its teeth in a bird's neck, the prey's brown wings flung up behind its head, while the cat turns wide eyes straight out at us. Below, two ducks rest together, one holding a lotus flower in its beak. The ducks are not the cat's prey, despite the old title; they are a separate, quieter scene. Both bands are worked in opus vermiculatum, tiny tesserae that let the maker shade the cat's coat. The little square sits in the middle of a pale floor, so it reads like a framed picture laid on the ground.
context: The mosaic paved the dining room (triclinium) of a Roman villa on the Via Ardeatina, in the Cecchignola estate, then well outside the city and now part of Rome. It dates to the first quarter of the 1st century BCE and is in the Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Massimo alle Terme (inv. 124137). The emblem was once shown on its own at the Museo delle Terme and was remounted and moved to Palazzo Massimo in 1995. Fun fact: not everyone is a fan. One guide to the museum's highlights calls it 'actually of mediocre quality', then admits that anyone who owns a cat will recognise the scene instantly.
title_eng: Floor Mosaic Emblema with a Cat Attacking a Bird and Two Ducks
submovement: Roman Late Republican Polychrome Floor Mosaics
image_credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen (2009)

title: Rhyton Terminating in the Forepart of a Wild Cat
title_original: Rhyton terminating in the forepart of a wild cat
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: The wild cat bursts out of the lower end of this silver drinking horn, mouth wide open in a snarl, ears up, forelegs flung forward with the toes spread, as if it were leaping out of the vessel. Mercury gilding picks out its collar and eyes, a band of leaves around the rim, and a panel of vine leaves and grape clusters across its chest, which fits a vessel for wine. The rest is bare silver, so gold and silver alternate across the surface. The whole thing is about 28 cm high and 30 cm deep, and it is made in two parts (a and b).
context: Made in Parthian Iran around the 1st century BCE, this rhyton is a horn-shaped drinking vessel of a kind long made in Iran, finished with an animal forepart. The Met acquired it in 1979. Fun fact: the credit line is a small crowd. The purchase combined the Rogers Fund, gifts from Enid A. Haupt, Mrs. Donald M. Oenslager, Mrs. Muriel Palitz and Geert C. E. Prins, the Pauline V. Fullerton Bequest, and several older bequests (Mary Cushing Fosburgh, Edward C. Moore, Stephen Whitney Phoenix) sold off 'by exchange'. In other words, the Met traded parts of its own past to buy this cat.
title_eng: Rhyton Terminating in the Forepart of a Wild Cat (Met 1979.447a, b)
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Shell with Inlaid Feline
medium: Spondylus shell with shell, stone, and gold inlay
description: A pampas cat in inlaid shell and stone stands stiff-legged across this ornament, its dark purple face turned straight at us with round orange eyes and a turquoise mouth. Its pale body carries bean-shaped and crescent spots, its tail is banded dark and light, and in front of its paws floats a gourd or fruit made of gold. The background is a Spondylus shell whose outer surface was carved away to expose a layer of bright orange, so the cat sits on a glowing ground. The piece is about 7.5 cm square. The beans are the clever bit: the cat's spots are also crops.
context: Nasca craftsmen on Peru's south coast made this ornament sometime between 100 BCE and 700 CE. The piece came to Cleveland as a gift from Helen Humphreys in memory of her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Henry Humphreys. It has been reproduced in James Richardson's 'People of the Andes' (1994) and the museum's 2014 'CMA Companion'. Fun fact: Cleveland notes that in both Paracas and Nasca art the small wild pampas cat is strongly tied to beans and other crops, perhaps as a guard against the rodents that raided the fields.
feline_symbolism: Cleveland links the pampas cat in Nasca and Paracas art with beans and other crops, possibly as a protector of fields against rodents.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Veii Floor Mosaic: Cat, Rooster, and Two Ducks (Gatto, gallo, due anatre e mele)
medium: Polychrome marble, limestone, and glass paste tesserae (opus vermiculatum)
collection: Musei Vaticani, Museo Pio Clementino, Sala degli Animali, Vatican City
description: The cat is mid-pounce, a long grey tabby stretched on a diagonal from raised hindquarters down to the forepaw pinning a red-combed rooster, whose dark tail feathers curl up in two hooks behind the cat's head. Its wide violet eyes stare straight at us. Below, two ducks rest on a strip of green ground beside a sprig of apples, and an olive branch floats in between: a farmyard and a fruit bowl in one frame. It is the kind of mixed still life, live animals beside food, that Roman house-owners liked underfoot, worked in small polychrome tesserae so fur and feathers are built from graded stone colours.
context: The panel is shown in the Sala degli Animali of the Museo Pio-Clementino in the Vatican, inventory 420, labelled as Antonine (mid to late 2nd century CE) and as coming from excavations at Veii in 1811-13. The Sala itself is an 18th-century creation: Pope Pius VI set up the two rooms between 1775 and 1799 as a 'stone zoo' of ancient animal sculpture, much of it restored and sometimes reworked. Fun fact: a popular Rome guide claims a near-identical cat-and-chicken mosaic comes from Hadrian's Villa at Tivoli, so the panel's findspot depends on whom you ask; the museum label's Veii provenance is the one to trust.
title_eng: Veii Floor Mosaic: Cat, Rooster, and Two Ducks (Gatto, gallo, due anatre e mele)
location: Musei Vaticani, Museo Pio Clementino, Sala degli Animali, Vatican City
image_credit: Fabrizio Garrisi · Own work

title: Stirrup Spout Bottle with Cat
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A cat crouches with its legs tucked under a compact, loaf-shaped body, and from its back rises the hollow arched handle and single spout that make the Moche stirrup-spout bottle instantly recognisable. The head juts forward, rounded ears pricked, heavy-lidded eyes half shut, as if it has noticed something worth getting up for but not quite yet. The bottle is 21.3 cm tall and only 9.5 cm wide, and its slip finish here is a dark, almost black sheen with brown patches where it has worn. The stirrup doubles as a handle, so the bottle could be lifted and poured without touching the sculpted cat.
context: Moche potters on Peru's north coast made this bottle between the 4th and 7th centuries CE. Moche ceramics are famous for sculpted animals and people, and stirrup-spout bottles were among their most prestigious forms. The Met received it in 1965 as a gift of Nathan Cummings, the food-industry collector whose donations brought a large group of ancient Peruvian ceramics to American museums. Fun fact: the Met calls the animal simply a 'cat', without guessing at ocelot or another wild species, a caution that is worth copying.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Lindisfarne Gospels: Incipit Page of Luke with a Cat (Cotton MS Nero D IV, fol. 139r)
title_original: Lindisfarne Gospels, Luke incipit page (Cotton MS Nero D IV, f. 139r)
medium: Egg tempera, orpiment, red lead, and organic pigments on vellum
description: The cat's head pokes out at the bottom right corner of the frame on the opening page of Luke's Gospel: pointed ears, a pale muzzle, a round eye with a dark pupil, while its long, scale-patterned body runs straight up the right-hand border. According to the British Library's description, this cat has already eaten some birds and is now stalking the ones lined up along the bottom border. Everything else on the page is spirals, interlace, red dotting and a giant initial Q, so the cat is a joke hidden in plain sight. Once you see the head you cannot unsee it.
context: The Lindisfarne Gospels were made on Holy Island around 715-720, almost certainly by one hand, Eadfrith, Bishop of Lindisfarne (d. 721), in honour of St Cuthbert. They are now British Library Cotton MS Nero D IV, and the cat is on folio 139r, the incipit of Luke. The vellum came from roughly 150 calf skins, and Eadfrith mixed his palette from a handful of local minerals and plant extracts. Fun fact: about 250 years later a priest called Aldred squeezed an Old English translation between the Latin lines, and in his colophon he credits Eadfrith, the binder Ethelwald and the metalworker Billfrith, so we know who made this cat.
title_eng: Lindisfarne Gospels: Incipit Page of Luke with a Cat (Cotton MS Nero D IV, fol. 139r)
image_credit: Eadfrith · Lindisfarne evangeliarium

title: Book of Kells: Cat Chasing a Rat with the Host (MS 58, fol. 48r)
medium: Iron gall ink and mineral pigments on vellum
description: The cat sits upright between two lines of text, a plump little body striped blue and yellow, head turned to watch a long, pale rat stretched out in full flight to the right, a round piece of what looks like Eucharistic bread clamped in its jaws. Both are outlined in brown and ringed with red dots; a tiny blue-and-yellow rosette waits at the end of the line. It is a small drama painted in the same pigments as the grand initials. The rat's prize is the sort of detail that gets argued about: a joke, a riddle, or a warning about crumbs in the sacristy.
context: The Book of Kells, a Gospel book now Trinity College Dublin MS 58, was made around 800, probably in a Columban monastery (Iona, Kells, or both; the question is still debated). Its earliest firm mention is in the Annals of Ulster for 1007, when it was stolen from the sacristy at Kells for the sake of its jewelled shrine and later recovered. Trinity's own teaching material illustrates fol. 48r as 'the cat catching the rat', and notes that the cats in the book prowl, hunt and sit among the lines without obvious religious symbolism. Fun fact: the cats are numerous enough that a Trinity MPhil thesis was written on them alone (Henry Byrne, 'Cats in the Book of Kells', 2011).
title_eng: Book of Kells: Cat Chasing a Rat with the Host (MS 58, fol. 48r)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Book of Kells folio 48 recto

title: Book of Kells: Cats and Mice Contending for the Eucharistic Host (MS 58, fol. 34r Chi-Rho Detail)
title_original: Book of Kells, Chi-Rho page (MS 58, fol. 34r)
culture: Hiberno-Saxon / Celtic Christian (Iona, Scotland or Kells, Ireland)
medium: Tempera, orpiment, kermes, and indigo pigments on vellum parchment
description: Two cats sit on a dark red ground near the foot of the giant Greek letters of the Chi-Rho page, the most crowded page in the Book of Kells, and between them two mice tug at a round Eucharistic wafer. More mice perch on the cats' backs, so the much-repeated reading of cats carrying mice is right there to see. Both cats look oddly unbothered, ears up, watching the theft happen under their whiskers. You have to get close: the animals are a few centimetres tall on a page that is otherwise spirals, knotwork and gold-coloured pigment. They are the domestic punchline at the bottom of the sacred monogram.
context: Folio 34r opens Matthew 1:18, the 'second beginning' of Matthew where Christ's life story starts, and the Chi-Rho monogram swells to fill the whole page. Wikipedia, following the specialist literature, calls it the largest and most lavish surviving Chi-Rho in any Insular Gospel book. The manuscript, made around 800 in a Columban monastery and now Trinity College Dublin MS 58, was stolen from Kells in 1007 and recovered. Fun fact: scholars attribute the Chi-Rho to the so-called 'Goldsmith', an artist who used colour to imitate metal, so the cats live inside an imitation of jewellery.
title_eng: Book of Kells: Cats and Mice Contending for the Eucharistic Host (MS 58, fol. 34r Chi-Rho Detail)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Book of Kells folio 34 recto

title: Monkey and Cats (猴貓圖)
description: The cat on the left, white with dark grey patches, has got away: it scampers off with its tail up and twists its head back toward the thief. On the right a tethered monkey sits hunched in a ball of soft brown fur, clutching a second kitten to its chest and gazing upward, looking very pleased with itself. The captive kitten peers out from under the monkey's chin, calm but wary. There is no landscape, just the stake and its looped rope against bare silk, so all the drama is in the bodies. The fur is built from fine hair strokes under ink washes.
context: Yi Yuanji (c. 1000-c. 1064) of Changsha began as a bird-and-flower painter, then, the National Palace Museum says, went into the mountains of Hunan and Hubei for years to watch monkeys and other animals, and even built a garden and pond at home to observe creatures up close. The handscroll (31.9 x 57.2 cm, ink and colour on silk) is in the National Palace Museum, Taipei. It carries a brief title by Emperor Huizong and, on the paper behind, colophons by Zhao Mengfu, Zhang Xi and Bi Long (dated 1790). Fun fact: Zhao Mengfu's colophon reads the scene exactly as a cat owner would, one kitten held, the other frightened, and orders the owner to treasure it.
submovement: Northern Song bird-and-flower and animal painting
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on silk
image_credit: Yi Yuanji · "Grand View: Painting and Calligraphy from the Northern Sung Dynasty", Taipei, National Palace Museum, 2006-12, ISBN 957-562-504-8 Transferred from zh.wikipedia ; transferred to Commons by Acsakw using CommonsHelper

title: Diquís Gold Pendant of a Double-Headed Feline
title_original: Diquís Delta Cast-Gold Feline Pendant (Costa Rica, c. 700–1500 CE)
description: A gold feline struts on stubby legs, its big square head turned toward us with bulging button eyes, rounded ears and a grin full of pointed fangs. The twist is at the other end: the raised tail ends in the head of a second feline, so the animal has a face at each end. The body is cast, with legs and head reduced to compact, rounded forms that would survive being worn on a cord. Look for the second head first, then follow the curve of the tail back to the main animal. Most visitors spot one cat; the pendant has two.
context: The pendant is displayed in the Museo del Oro Precolombino in San José, run by the Banco Central de Costa Rica, and is attributed to the Diquís (South Pacific) region of Costa Rica, 700-1550 CE. Fun fact: the museum's caption is matter-of-fact, 'a gold pendant in the form of a feline whose tail ends in the head of another feline', and leaves the species open; the jaguar identification comes from outside cataloguers.
title_eng: Diquís Gold Pendant of a Double-Headed Feline
submovement: Diquís cast goldwork (South Pacific Costa Rica)
medium: Cast tumbaga (gold-copper alloy) with depletion gilding
collection: Museo del Oro Precolombino, San José, Costa Rica
location: Museo del Oro Precolombino, San José, Costa Rica
image_credit: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz) · Own work

title: Cats at Play (宋人戲貓圖 軸)
artist: Anonymous late Ming court painter (traditionally attributed to a Song artist)
submovement: Late Ming court painting (traditionally attributed to Song)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
description: A big white long-hair grooms a grey kitten on a bench at left, another kitten hides underneath, a white cat balances on top of a green drum-shaped stool while a spotted one sniffs at its base, and a white cat with a dark patch noses about by the bamboo fence at bottom right. The museum counts eight in all, among lake rocks, bamboo, a tree and peonies. The garden is furnished: brocade screens with tassels, a clothes rack with dragon and phoenix finials, and a lacquered table holding vases of coral and lacquer boxes. Check the eyes: thin slit pupils, the museum says, put the hour around midday.
context: This large hanging scroll (139.8 x 100.1 cm, colour on silk) is in the National Palace Museum, Taipei. It has long carried the title 'Song people's cats at play', but the museum argues that the furniture gives it away: the horse-hoof legs are too strained for Song design, so it was probably painted by a late Ming court artist. Its seals track a royal career, including those of Hongzhan and the Prince Guo household, and the Jiaqing and Xuantong emperors; it was listed in the third series of the Qing imperial catalogue Shiqu baoji. Fun fact: the museum featured it in a 1996 exhibition on furniture in painting, which is how the cats lost their Song date.
title_eng: Cats at Play (宋人戲貓圖 軸)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · https://www.shuge.org/meet/topic/91208/

title: Kitten (Song Dynasty Album Leaf, Li-tai Hua-fu-Chi)
title_original: 歷代畫幅集 冊 幼貓
medium: Album leaf; ink and fine mineral color on silk (gongbi)
description: The kitten stands on bare silk and turns its head to look straight at us, white on the chest, muzzle and legs, with grey-brown tabby markings over its back and a striped tail held up behind. The painter laid light grey washes on the head, ears, face, back, tail and hind legs, flicked white specks onto the face and limbs, and used darker ink for the body markings. The pupils were done in three tones of ink so they seem to catch shifting light. Do not skip the paws: soft and round like plum blossoms, they are the most kitten-like thing in the picture.
context: This is the fourth leaf of an album of paintings from various dynasties (Li-tai hua-fu chi) in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, catalogued as anonymous, Song dynasty (960-1279). The description praises the brushwork for making each kind of fur distinct, which is the whole point of a picture this small. Fun fact: the museum's note compares this dappled cat to a pet of Princess Qionghua of the Later Tang, who called her own spotted cat a 'bridle cicada cat'; later poets borrowed 'bridle cicada' as a nickname for cats.
location: National Palace Museum (Li-tai Hua-fu-Chi Album, Leaf 4)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · https://culture.teldap.tw/culture/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=222

title: The Aberdeen Bestiary: The Cat (Musio / Cattus) (Univ Lib MS 24, fol. 23v)
medium: Egg tempera, burnished gold leaf, and iron gall ink on vellum
collection: University of Aberdeen Special Collections, Aberdeen, Scotland
description: Three cats perform on burnished gold: a blue one stalks along a wavy blue hill, a second rears up on a red mound, and between them an orange cat curls into a tight ball, the contortion that the sister manuscript at Oxford shows as a cat licking its own backside. The interesting part is missing: the mice. The text says the cat is called musio because it is the enemy of mice, yet the Aberdeen painter left the mice out, shifting the emphasis to the cat's sharp sight. Nearby on the page a separate mouse carries grain, a detail the text never mentions.
context: The Aberdeen Bestiary (Aberdeen University Library, Univ. Lib. MS 24) was written and illuminated in England around 1200. Its recorded history starts in 1542, when it appears as no. 518, 'Liber de bestiarum natura', in the inventory of Henry VIII's Old Royal Library at Westminster, a collection built partly from monastic books dispersed at the Dissolution. It probably moved to Marischal College in Aberdeen around the time James VI became king of England. Fun fact: the book was never finished, so its pages keep sketches and notes that show how it was planned, and scholars compare it constantly with its near-twin, the Ashmole Bestiary in Oxford.
title_eng: The Aberdeen Bestiary: The Cat (Musio / Cattus) (Univ Lib MS 24, fol. 23v)
feline_symbolism: The bestiary text explains the name musio as 'mouse-catcher' and praises the cat's eyesight, which can pierce the dark.
location: University of Aberdeen Special Collections, Aberdeen, Scotland
image_credit: Я вырезал это изображение из полностраничного изображения страницы Абердинского бестиария, взятого с сайта Абердинского университета: http://www.abdn.ac.uk/bestiary/ · Изображение с описанием http://art.biblioclub.ru/picture_119356_koshki_m

title: The Rochester Bestiary: The Cat Chasing Mice (Royal MS 12 F XIII, fol. 43r)
title_original: The Rochester Bestiary Cat Miniature (England, c. 1230, Royal MS 12 F XIII)
