description: The cat runs flat out over a green hillock, a long ochre body speckled with dots, ears pricked, tail streaming, after two black mice that bolt to the right as silhouettes. As elsewhere in the Rochester Bestiary, the miniature comes at the end of the passage it illustrates, and you can see the handover: the line just below already starts the next animal, 'est pusillum animal ex humore terre natum', the mouse. That passage is the standard entry: cats are the enemies of mice, and their eyesight cuts through the dark. Some pages still carry the scribe's notes telling the painter what to draw.
context: The Rochester Bestiary (British Library, Royal MS 12 F XIII) was made around 1230-40, probably at St Andrew's Priory, Rochester Cathedral. It has 55 finished miniatures; after the vulture (f. 52v) the pictures stop and the spaces stay empty. The painter seems to have worked a decade or more after the scribe, and by adding a fourth lion where three were planned he pushed every later picture after its text. Fun fact: the book was once stolen from the priory. A 14th-century note records its return by 'brother John Malling', and a John Malling was excommunicated in 1387 as an apostate and thief. It reached the royal library by 1542 and the British Museum in 1757.
title_eng: The Rochester Bestiary: The Cat Chasing Mice (Royal MS 12 F XIII, fol. 43r)
medium: Tempera, burnished gold leaf, and ink on vellum
feline_symbolism: The bestiary text presents the cat as the enemy of mice, with eyes that see through the night.

title: The Harley Bestiary: The Cat (Musio) and Mice (Harley MS 4751, fol. 30v)
medium: Tempera and ink on vellum (no gold)
description: Three cats sit squeezed together in a roundel, two grey and one ginger with darker stripes, and only the ginger one is working: it reaches out and holds a grey mouse up in its forepaws while its companions gaze off. In the next miniature on folio 30v the mice are off stealing eggs, so hunter and hunted share the page. The painter of this book used no gold at all, and Payne describes its colours as sometimes sombre; here a starry blue ground and a dark red disc do the work. In the margin: a later hand has squeezed in a doodle of a cat playing a stringed instrument.
context: Harley MS 4751 is a Latin bestiary of the so-called second family, made in England around 1230–1240, possibly at Salisbury. It runs to 74 vellum leaves (about 30.8 × 23.2 cm) with 106 coloured miniatures in square and round frames, each tagged with a red label, and it is a close sibling of Bodleian MS Bodley 764. It came to the British Library with the Harley manuscripts. Fun fact: little notes to the painter still survive in the margins, such as "hic est Ceru" beside the stag, telling him which beast went where. The British Library's bloggers, less solemn, dubbed the fiddling cat on this page an ancestor of Keyboard Cat.
title_eng: The Harley Bestiary: The Cat (Musio) and Mice (Harley MS 4751, fol. 30v)
feline_symbolism: The bestiary text calls the cat musio, the enemy of mice, and credits it with eyes sharp enough to pierce the darkness of night.

title: Luttrell Psalter: Tabby Cat Holding Mouse in Margin (Add MS 42130, fol. 190r)
culture: English (Lincolnshire, commissioned by Sir Geoffrey Luttrell)
submovement: East Anglian High Gothic Manuscript Illumination
medium: Tempera and shell gold on vellum
description: The cat sits upright in the margin of folio 190r, a grey tabby with wavy stripes, ears up and a long ringed tail swept out behind, pinning a small brown mouse under one outstretched forepaw and eyeing it sideways. Around it the Luttrell Psalter's crowd of grotesques, farm workers and hybrids carries on, and because the cat sits outside the text block, the psalm above continues as if nothing were happening. The motif clearly amused the workshop, because a cat and mouse turn up again on folio 204. It is a good reminder that the famous farmyard scenes share their margins with household animals doing ordinary, slightly cruel, things.
context: The psalter was made for Sir Geoffrey Luttrell (1276–1345), lord of the manor of Irnham in Lincolnshire, by one scribe and at least five artists. Its date is argued over: Eric Millar suggested 1335–40, Lucy Sandler 1325–30 and Michelle Brown 1330–45. The book measures about 35 × 24.5 cm and has some 309 vellum leaves. It stayed for generations with the Weld family of Lulworth. Fun fact: when Herbert Weld Blundell sent it to Sotheby's in 1929, British Museum lawyers showed it actually belonged to Mary Angela Noyes, and the museum bought it from her with a loan from J. P. Morgan Jr. It is now British Library Add MS 42130.
title_eng: Luttrell Psalter: Tabby Cat Holding Mouse in Margin (Add MS 42130, fol. 190r)
image_credit: Ioreth · Zuffi, Stephano. Cats in Art. New York: Harry N. Abrams, Inc., 2007.

title: Cats and Flying Butterflies (明宣宗戲貓圖卷)
title_original: 明宣宗耄耋圖真蹟 卷
artist: Emperor Xuanzong of Ming (Xuande Emperor, 朱瞻基)
medium: Handscroll; ink and light color on paper
description: Cats lounge, curl and play along this long handscroll, each little group set alone on bare buff ground with columns of inscription in between, and butterflies flit in the air above them: the sort of picture that is really a pun you can unroll. The Chinese title, maodie tu, plays on sound: mao for cat, die for butterfly, together echoing the words for great old age. Read from right to left, the scroll sets the cats at leisure below with the butterflies overhead, a birthday wish dressed up as a garden afternoon. The image on file is stitched together from photographs of separate sections, so expect the odd seam.
context: The National Palace Museum in Taipei catalogues this handscroll as Ming Xuanzong's Maodie tu, "authentic trace" (明宣宗耄耋圖真蹟 卷), under the donated-paintings number 贈畫000722, which means it reached the museum by gift rather than from the old Qing imperial collection. The Xuande Emperor, Zhu Zhanji (1399–1435), was a serious amateur painter, often compared with the Song emperor Huizong. Fun fact: the museum's records show he liked this kind of visual wordplay, noting on another of his cat paintings that the cat's name sounds like the word for old age. The phrase "authentic trace" is part of an old title, a claim by a past owner rather than a verdict by the museum.
feline_symbolism: Cat (mao) puns on mao 耄, advanced age, so the cat works as a wish for long life; the NPM spells out the same pun for the emperor's Peonies in a Vase.
image_credit: Xuande Emperor · The National Palace Museum Collection

title: Kittens Playing Beneath Flowers (明宣宗畫花下貍奴圖 軸)
title_original: 明宣宗畫花下貍奴圖 軸
artist: Emperor Xuanzong of Ming (Xuande Emperor, 朱瞻基)
description: Two cats share the ground below a pitted Taihu garden rock: a grey tabby crouches with its striped tail wrapped round, and in front of it a white cat with dark patches lies curled in a soft crescent, peering out at us over its own flank. The painter laid in their bodies with soft "boneless" washes first and only then drew the fur and stripes on top, so the animals read as warm, solid bodies with markings floating on them. The rock gets the opposite treatment: hard outlines, then scratchy dry-brush texture. The picture is small, about 41.5 × 39.3 cm, with a big calligraphy panel mounted above it.
context: An inscription dates the painting to the bingwu year, 1426, the first year of the Xuande reign, when Zhu Zhanji (1399–1435) had just taken the throne. The National Palace Museum in Taipei, which holds it among the former Qing imperial paintings (故畫000421), notes that the cats closely follow the manner of the Song academy painter Li Di, and compares the emperor with the painter-emperor Huizong. It is recorded in the Qianlong-era imperial catalogue Shiqu baoji. Fun fact: the emperor turned out this careful little cat study in his first year on the throne, between rather more pressing state business.
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
image_credit: Xuande Emperor · The National Palace Museum Collection

title: Cat with Peonies in a Bronze Pot (壺中富貴圖)
artist: Emperor Xuanzong of Ming (Xuande Emperor, 朱瞻基)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and light color on paper
description: The cat sits at the very bottom of the picture, long-furred and white with ginger patches and a ringed tail, its coat drawn hair by hair, head tipped back to stare up at the bronze vase hanging from a blue cord at the top of the sheet. The vase is stuffed with white peonies: only three blossoms, but the leaves pile up in layers. Off to the right stands a low three-legged basin of the type made at the early Ming imperial kilns, a bit of product placement for the emperor's own porcelain. Above, a long inscription by Grand Secretary Yang Shiqi fills the sky.
context: Painted in 1429, the fourth year of the Xuande reign, by Zhu Zhanji (1399–1435), the fifth Ming emperor, who wrote poetry and painted animals with a seriousness that invites comparison with the Song emperor Huizong. It carries the emperor's library seal "Xuande mige tushu zhi bao" and an inscription by his chief minister Yang Shiqi (1365–1444). It measures about 110.5 × 54.4 cm and passed through the Qing imperial collection, listed in the third Shiqu baoji catalogue, before reaching the National Palace Museum in Taipei. Fun fact: the title, Huzhong fugui, means roughly "riches and rank in a pot", and the cat is a working part of that rebus rather than a pet who wandered in.
title_eng: Cat with Peonies in a Bronze Pot (Wealth and Prosperity in a Pot)
feline_symbolism: The museum explains that the cat's name sounds like mao 耄, old age, so cat plus peony reads as a wish for long life and riches.
image_credit: Xuande Emperor · The National Palace Museum Collection

title: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: The Mice Hanging the Cat
title_original: Misericord: The Mice Hanging the Cat
medium: Carved English oak choir stall misericord bracket
description: The cat hangs in the middle, forepaws up at the gallows beam and its round face staring straight out with an air of mild surprise, while on the left three rodents (rats or mice, depending on whom you ask) haul it aloft. The world turned upside down, carved in oak under a choir seat. An owl perches on each side as a supporter, ear tufts up. The casting is the joke: owls hunt mice too, so the executioners go about their work with the next predators already watching. The carving sits on the underside of a hinged seat and was only on show when the seat was tipped up.
context: Great Malvern Priory's choir keeps a set of medieval misericords, small ledges that let monks half-sit through long services. Wikipedia counts 22 fifteenth-century misericords plus 12 Victorian additions. Older accounts describe two medieval sets, twelve Labours of the Months and twelve miscellaneous subjects, and date the miscellaneous group to the late fourteenth century, about a century before the calendar carvings, so the date of this one is open to argument. The stalls were shuffled after the priory was dissolved in 1539, and their original order is lost. Fun fact: the same carver seems to have worked at Worcester Cathedral and at Ripple, where close cousins of these misericords survive.
title_eng: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: The Mice Hanging the Cat
image_credit: Geograph: Julian P Guffogg · This image was taken from the Geograph project collection. See this photograph's page on the Geograph website for the photographer's contact details. The copyright on this image is owned by Julian P Guffogg and

title: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: Cat Gripping Mouse
title_original: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: Cat and Mouse
medium: Carved English oak wooden seat bracket
description: The cat crouches low on its ledge with a mouse clamped under its forepaws and jaws, round eyes turned out toward us and its tail curled into a neat loop behind. It is carved in oak on the bracket beneath a tip-up choir seat, with the usual order of things restored. Compared with the medieval hanging scene elsewhere in the choir, where the mice take their revenge, this one plays the subject straight. The carver kept to the medieval format of a single scene on the misericord bracket, so it slots in among the older stalls without much fuss until you start comparing the woodwork.
context: Great Malvern Priory has 22 medieval misericords and 12 more from the nineteenth century, when extra stalls were added at the east end of each row. According to the photographer who recorded it, this cat and mouse is one of the modern pieces, carved to replace a lost or damaged original rather than surviving from the fifteenth century. Fun fact: it makes an accidental pair with the priory's genuinely medieval misericord in which three rodents hang a cat, so the choir now tells the story both ways round.
title_eng: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: Cat Gripping Mouse
image_credit: Bob Embleton · Geograph Britain and Ireland

title: The Virgin and Child with a Cat (Recto and Verso Studies)
title_original: Studio per la Madonna del gatto
medium: Pen and brown ink over stylus underdrawing; the other side pen and brown ink with brown wash
description: The cat is not enjoying this. On the pen side of the sheet the Christ Child sits on the Virgin's knee and hugs a cat to his chest, and the cat leans hard the other way, head up, plainly planning its exit. Mary looks down at the pair, the whole group packed into a thin arched frame. On the other side Leonardo went over the same idea in pen and a thin brown wash, with Child and cat now turned to the left. You can still see him changing his mind: there are two heads for the Virgin, one looking out to the left and the one he settled on, looking down to the right. Up in the top left corner sits a small sketch of a clock.
context: Leonardo drew both sides in Florence around 1478 to 1481, while working out a Madonna with a cat that never became a finished painting, or at least none survives; several other sheets on the theme exist, in the British Museum, the Uffizi, Bayonne and a New York private collection. The British Museum's own account shows the working order: he traced the central head of the Virgin through the thin paper from the composition on the reverse, tried her looking left, then settled on her looking down. That turning, pyramid-shaped group became a habit of his mature style. Fun fact: the museum bought the sheet in 1856 from Giovanni Battista Cavalcaselle, better remembered as one of the founders of modern connoisseurship than as a dealer.
title_eng: The Virgin and Child with a Cat (Recto and Verso Studies)
image_credit: Photograph © The Trustees of the British Museum (public-domain artwork), via Wikimedia Commons

title: The Last Supper
description: The cat is down on the chequered floor in front of the table, a grey tabby crouched with its tail curled, squaring up to a dog that snarls back at it. Off to the left a little white dog stands begging on its hind legs beside a man in red. Rosselli seats Christ and the apostles round a horseshoe table in a coffered room, and the white cloth is almost bare: one chalice in front of Christ. Judas sits alone on the near side with his back to us. Gilded and silvered kitchenware stands in the foreground as a little still life, and three windows behind the diners open onto Gethsemane, the Arrest and the Crucifixion.
context: The fresco, about 349 × 570 cm, was painted around 1481–82 on the wall of the Sistine Chapel, where Florentine painters had been sent to Rome as part of a political reconciliation between Lorenzo de' Medici and Pope Sixtus IV. Rosselli brought his son-in-law Piero di Cosimo as an assistant, and some authorities give the window scenes to Biagio d'Antonio. Its frieze reads REPLICATIO LEGIS EVANGELICAE A CHRISTO, pairing it with the Moses scenes opposite. Fun fact: Vasari ranked Rosselli among the weaker painters in the chapel, yet his bright colours reportedly pleased the pope more than his colleagues' work.
submovement: Florentine Quattrocento Wall Painting & Sistine Chapel Fresco Cycle
feline_symbolism: The quarrelling cat and dog next to Judas are usually read as underlining his treachery and the discord he brings to the table.
image_credit: Cosimo Rosselli · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rosselli/cosimo/lastsup"

title: Hortus Sanitatis (Garden of Health): The Cat (Cattus)
title_original: Hortus sanitatis, Tractatus de animalibus, cap. xxv: Cattus
description: Two cats sit on a riverbank beside a stone fountain whose spouts pour into a basin and run off as a stream: a big striped one upright on the left, mouth open as if it has something to say, and a smaller, paler one sitting on the far bank. The woodcut is plain black line, all hatching and no colour, cut so that it could be read at a glance. It stands at the foot of the column that closes the dog chapter and opens the next one. Turn the page and the chapter heading reads Ca. xxv, Cattus. An early owner has written Koth under the picture in brown ink, which looks like the Polish word for cat, kot, in an old spelling.
context: Jacob Meydenbach printed the Hortus sanitatis in Mainz on 23 June 1491, his first book: a fat folio of 454 leaves in five sections (herbs, land animals, birds, fish and stones) plus a treatise on urine, with a woodcut at the head of nearly every chapter. It grew out of Peter Schöffer's Mainz herbals of 1484 and 1485 and is often called the first printed natural-history encyclopaedia. The cat chapter opens with Isidore of Seville's etymologies: the cat is called musio because it is the enemy of mice (mures), and common people say cattus from captura, catching, while others derive it from catat, it sees, because its eyes are sharp enough to beat the dark of night. The copy shown is in the National Library of Poland and belonged to Stanislaus Rubicundus. Fun fact: the same animal section that sensibly covers the cat also has chapters on the unicorn and the dragon.
medium: Woodcut and letterpress on paper (printed book, folio)
submovement: German Incunabula & Early Natural History Printmaking
image_credit: Jacob Meydenbach (printer), Mainz, 1491 · National Library of Poland (SD Inc.F.1074) / Polona

title: Cat, from Album of Sketches from Life (寫生冊 貓)
description: A single cat curled into a ball, done almost entirely in ink wash on paper. Its eyes are wide open and slide diagonally upward, so the animal looks sleepy and alert at the same moment, which anyone who has lived with a cat will recognise. Shen Zhou keeps the outline loose but lets the paws peek out from under the bottom edge of the round body, a small observed detail that makes the shape read as a real animal rather than a fur cushion. There is no setting at all, only paper.
context: The leaf belongs to Sketches from Life (寫生冊), sixteen paintings of plants and animals plus a leaf of the artist's own calligraphy, painted in 1494 when Shen Zhou (1427–1509) was about 67, the founding figure of the Wu school of Suzhou. A colophon by Gao Shiqi records that the album first belonged to Li Zhaoheng of Jiaxing before passing to Gao; it later entered the Qing imperial collection and is now in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, which had it certified a National Treasure in 2014. Fun fact: Shen Zhou's family once had a cat that ran away, and he wrote a poem, The Lost Cat's Journey, recalling its daily habits.
title_eng: Cat, from Album of Sketches from Life
image_credit: 國立故宮博物院 · https://digitalarchive.npm.gov.tw/Collection/Detail/3870?dep=P

title: Adam and Eve
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: The cat lies curled between the two nudes, almost underfoot, eyes narrowed, its long tail snaking out towards Eve's heel. A little way off to the left, beside Adam's foot, sits a mouse with its tail trailing, and nobody pounces. Dürer engraves the forest behind them line by line until it nearly turns black, and the animals keep turning up: an elk's antlered head by the tree trunk, an ox and a rabbit in the undergrowth, a parrot on Adam's branch, a goat on the far crag. A tablet hangs from that branch reading ALBERT DURER NORICUS FACIEBAT 1504.
context: Dürer cut this copper plate in Nuremberg in 1504, after years of measuring live models and studying classical proportion, and the two figures are his demonstration pieces: Adam owes his pose to the Apollo Belvedere, known to Dürer only through prints. The signature tablet announces him proudly as a man of Nuremberg. The Met's impression (19.73.1) was bought through the Fletcher Fund in 1919. Fun fact: two trial proofs survive from before the plate was finished, and they show that the cat was added late in the process, so the star of this catalogue entry was an afterthought.
feline_symbolism: The four animals are usually read as the four temperaments, the cat standing for the choleric; held in balance before the Fall, the cat leaves the mouse alone, a truce that will end with the bite of the apple.
image_credit: Albrecht Dürer · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Penelope with the Suitors
description: The cat sits low on the chequered floor under Penelope's loom, grey, with a dark-ringed tail and pale yellow eyes, one front paw resting on a stray ball of yarn. It looks straight out at us, a domestic extra photographers like to crop out as its own detail. Above it the suitors crowd in, one showing off a falcon, and a man with a staff, probably Odysseus in disguise, steps through the door in the same red and blue as the bow and arrows hanging over Penelope's head. Through the window the Odyssey carries on: Odysseus's ship flying the Petrucci arms, the Sirens, sailors diving and Circe's pigs.
context: Pintoricchio painted this around 1509 as one of eight frescoes for the Siena palace of Pandolfo Petrucci, who ordered them to celebrate his son's marriage to a niece of Pope Pius III. A tale of a wife who stayed faithful for twenty years was a pointed choice for a wedding, and perhaps a personal one for Pandolfo, back in Siena after exile in the late 1490s. The fresco was later transferred to canvas (125.5 × 152 cm) and bought by the National Gallery at the Alexander Barker sale in 1874 (NG911). Fun fact: Circe's pigs are painted as Cinta Senese, the belted local Tuscan breed.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work

title: Studies of Cat Movements and Positions
description: About twenty cats tumble over one sheet: playing, fighting, cringing, hunting, licking themselves, curled asleep and standing stock still, all in pen and brown ink with brushed wash over chalk. One at the left arches its back with its fur puffed out like a bottle brush; two in the bottom row go nose to nose in a scrap. Some bodies twist so far they stop looking like cats and start looking like springs. Just below the middle a small dragon curls among them, drawn with exactly the same supple spine. Two notes in mirror-writing at lower right, del pieghamento and esstendimento (bending and extending), say what he was really after.
context: Leonardo made the sheet very late, around 1517 to 1518 according to the Royal Collection, some thirty-five years after his Florentine studies of the Virgin and Child with a cat. The inscriptions suggest it belonged to his long-planned studies of movement, perhaps for a treatise. Like most of his surviving drawings, it passed through the collection assembled by the sculptor Pompeo Leoni and is now in the Royal Library at Windsor (RCIN 912363), catalogued as Cats, lions, and a dragon; a few of the bigger, heavier bodies are lions, and the rest are house cats. The second image is the back of the sheet, where the drawing shows through in reverse. Fun fact: the dragon is the giveaway to his method. Leonardo built imaginary creatures from real anatomy, so his dragon simply borrows a cat's way of curling.
title_eng: Studies of Cat Movements and Positions
medium: Pen and ink with wash over black chalk on paper
image_credit: Royal Collection Trust (rct.uk), public-domain scans via Wikimedia Commons

title: The Annunciation
collection: Museo Civico Villa Colloredo Mels, Recanati
description: The cat is caught mid-floor between angel and Virgin, a striped tabby bolting with its back arched and tail up, the only creature in the room acting the way a real one would. The angel has dropped to one knee at the loggia's threshold, lily in hand, arm flung up, while God the Father leans out of a cloud above the pergola. Mary swings round to face us with both palms raised, as if we were the intruders. Lotto fills her room with clutter worth checking: a curtained bed, a shelf with a book and a candlestick, and an hourglass on a stool.
context: Lotto painted the canvas (166 × 114 cm) around 1534, probably for the Confraternita dei Mercanti of Recanati, which had moved to a new seat in 1533 and needed an altarpiece. A minority view places it earlier, around 1527, when Lotto was still in Venice and could have sent it to the Marche. The first certain record of the picture dates only from 1601, and it is signed L. Lotus. It is now in the Museo Civico of Villa Colloredo Mels in Recanati. Fun fact: the critic Giulio Carlo Argan set it against Titian's Annunciation, where the Virgin is a queen receiving a messenger in her palace; Lotto's Virgin, he wrote, is a good girl caught by surprise at her prayers, whose gesture is that of someone struck from behind by a sudden call.
feline_symbolism: Italian Wikipedia's account reads the fleeing cat as a sign of evil put to flight by the Incarnation, and also as a gentle touch of irony.
image_credit: Lorenzo Lotto · The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title: The Supper at Emmaus
description: There are two cats here, and neither is interested in the miracle. A white cat with ginger patches sits on the tiled floor at lower left, a few steps from the innkeeper, and a second, grey-and-white one peeks out from under the stool at the far right edge, almost cut off by the frame. Between them Christ raises his hand over the bread, one disciple throws up both palms in recognition, and a servant in a plumed red hat brings in another dish. Bassano paints the cherries on the cloth, the glass of red wine, the carpet under the tablecloth and the flask on the floor with the same attention he gives the saints, which was rather the point of his kind of religious painting.
context: Jacopo Bassano, from Bassano del Grappa in the Venetian mainland, painted this canvas about 1538, early in a career built on putting farmyard and kitchen life into sacred stories. It is oil on canvas, about 100.6 × 128.6 cm, and hangs in the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth (APx 1989.03), acquired with the help of a gift from Mildred Sterling Hedrick. Fun fact: when Veronese crowded his Wedding at Cana with portraits of Venetian painters, he cast Jacopo Bassano as one of the musicians, so the inventor of this table-side cat ended up at another cat-haunted feast.
image_credit: Photograph by FA2010 (Wikimedia Commons), released into the public domain

title: Flowers, Birds, Kittens, and Puppies (花鳥猫狗圖)
artist: Attributed to Yi Am (이암, 李巖)
submovement: Early Joseon animal and bird-and-flower painting (yeongmo)
medium: Pair of hanging scrolls (diptych); ink and light color on paper
collection: Pyongyang Joseon Art Museum (조선미술박물관), North Korea
description: The cats take the high and the low ground: a black-and-white cat clings to a tree trunk at upper left under big red blossoms, while another, also black and white, plants itself at lower right over two small companions. Between them sparrows flit across the open paper, and at bottom left a black-and-white puppy sprawls beside a paler one. Yi Am made his name with these round-faced, guileless native Korean dogs, and the cats share the same soft, flat-coloured manner. It is a small world arranged for gentle comedy: predators and pets lounging where, in nature, someone would be chasing someone else.
context: Yi Am, born in 1499 to the Joseon royal lineage (great-grandson of Grand Prince Imyeong), was celebrated for bird-and-animal paintings. Extant works include the Mother Dog with Puppies (National Museum of Korea) and Flowers, Birds, and Puppies (Leeum Museum, Treasure No. 1392, which contains no cats). This painting, Flowers, Birds, Kittens, and Puppies (Hwajomyogudo), is a pair of hanging scrolls preserved in the Pyongyang Joseon Art Museum in North Korea. Outside North Korea, photographic reproductions of this pair are scarce, typically scanned from 20th-century cultural art volumes.
image_credit: Yi Am · Yi Am

title: Leda and the Swan
description: The cat is almost lost in the shadows at lower left, a dark shape at the foot of a wooden coop with a duck shut inside it, and it is looking out at us rather than at the bird. Above it the maid leans over the coop with one hand on its bars. Leda reclines across the bed, naked but for pearls at her throat and in her hair, her hand on the swan that presses in from the right, and a small white dog scampers along the green cover at her feet. Red curtains sweep behind her, and a parrot sits in a cage in the gloom at the back. Her body runs in one bright diagonal against the maid's opposite lean, a V that keeps the whole picture moving.
context: Tintoretto painted the canvas in Venice in the 1550s, when he was producing erotic mythologies such as Mars and Venus Surprised by Vulcan; restorations in 1988 and 1994 settled earlier doubts about its authorship. It belonged to the Duke of Orléans in Paris in the late eighteenth century, then to the Duke of Bridgewater in London and to Paul Norton in 1857, before Arturo De Noè Walker gave it to the Uffizi in 1895 (inv. 3084). Fun fact: the Uffizi stores a second version, from the Contini Bonacossi collection, which at some point had the maid cut away, leaving only a scrap of her dress; that mutilated canvas is thought to be the prototype for this one.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY 3.0

title: Netherlandish Proverbs (To Bell the Cat)
description: The cat is lying on top of a low brick wall at the left of the village, a striped tabby flattened against the bricks, while a man in full armour leans over it, carefully tying a bell round its neck: to bell the cat, the plan every mouse agrees with and none will carry out. Armour, it turns out, is what it takes. Around him a whole Flemish village has gone mad, acting out roughly 126 proverbs at once. People bang their heads against walls, fill in the well after the calf has drowned, and a woman in red drapes a blue cloak over her husband. Bruegel paints it all in the same brisk, matter-of-fact way, so the cat's predicament gets no more fuss than anyone else's foolishness.
context: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted the panel in Antwerp in 1559; it measures 117 × 163 cm and is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin. Its older title, The Blue Cloak or The Folly of the World, comes from the centre, where a wife hangs a blue cloak on her husband, that is, cuckolds him. Scholars have identified around 126 proverbs and idioms, and more keep being proposed. Fun fact: the Berlin picture's ownership can be traced back only to the late nineteenth century, a short paper trail for a painting this famous.
feline_symbolism: To bell the cat means attempting a dangerous or impractical plan, from the fable of the mice who decide the cat should wear a bell but find no volunteer.
image_credit: Google Arts & Culture, Gemäldegalerie, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (public-domain artwork), via Wikimedia Commons

title: The Wedding at Cana
submovement: Venetian High Renaissance Monumental Decorative Painting
description: The cat has found the one spot nobody is watching: down on the floor at lower right, a small grey shape tangled up with a big pale wine amphora while a servant bends beside it pouring from another jar. Some 130 guests pack the lower half of this canvas, the largest painting in the Louvre, and while the miracle of water into wine plays out at the table, the cat busies itself with the jar that holds the evidence. Two dogs lounge at bottom centre, a dwarf holds a bright green parrot, and in the middle a band of musicians, Veronese himself among them, plays on regardless.
context: The Benedictines of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice commissioned the canvas on 6 June 1562 for the end wall of their Palladio-designed refectory, and Veronese delivered in September 1563. The contract paid 324 ducats, his keep, a barrel of wine and meals in the refectory, and required the best colours, ultramarine included. On 11 September 1797 Napoleon's soldiers cut the canvas horizontally, rolled it up and carried it to Paris; in 1815 Vivant Denon argued it was too fragile to send back. Fun fact: tradition identifies the musicians as Veronese, Tintoretto, Jacopo Bassano and Titian, so Tintoretto and Bassano, who both painted cats of their own, sit in the wedding band.
image_credit: Paolo Veronese · https://artsandculture.google.com

title: Madonna of the Cat (Madonna del Gatto)
description: The cat rears up on its hind legs at the lower left edge, a ginger-and-white cat stretching its forepaws towards the goldfinch that young John the Baptist dangles high above it. A rosy-cheeked, domestic Holy Family crowds the rest of the canvas: Mary nurses the infant Christ, Joseph leans in from the right with a hand on a yellow-draped table, and John's reed cross leans against the wall behind him. Wicker baskets and cushions fill the floor. The figures run on a diagonal up to the right, a restless arrangement that already points towards the Baroque.
context: Barocci painted the canvas (112.7 × 92.7 cm) around 1575 for Antonio Brancaleoni, Count of Piobbico, a village about twenty miles from Urbino. Its small size and domestic subject suggest it was meant for the family's rooms, perhaps the countess's apartments, and it did pass down the female line to her daughter Isabella. Cornelis Cort's engraving of 1577 spread the composition widely, and some thirty-five preparatory drawings survive. A second version at Chantilly is thought to be a workshop replica, since only the London canvas shows changes of mind under X-ray. It came to the National Gallery with the Revd William Holwell Carr's bequest in 1831 (NG29). Fun fact: the Brancaleoni arms show a rampant lion under a cross, so the National Gallery suggests the cat and John's reed cross may be a family pun.
title_eng: Madonna of the Cat (Madonna del Gatto)
feline_symbolism: The goldfinch foretells Christ's Passion, so the cat stalking it brings the threat of that future into a cosy family scene.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY 3.0

title: Montaigne and his Cat
title_original: Quand je me joue à ma chatte
description: The cat sits bolt upright on the table at the left, facing Montaigne across it like an equal in conversation. The philosopher, in ruff and fur-trimmed gown, leans over the tabletop with his hands out, coaxing. Strang worked in a deliberately old-fashioned, linear manner, so the scene looks almost like a sixteenth-century print come back to life, all firm contour and crisp hatching: a carved cabinet behind the cat, a dark archway behind the man, plates on the chimneypiece. His initials W.S. sit in the plate at lower left. The joke underneath is Montaigne's own: who is entertaining whom.
context: William Strang (1859–1921), a Scottish painter-etcher trained under Alphonse Legros in London, made this plate around 1902; the Commons record, drawn from the National Galleries of Scotland, says it was published in London and New York. It illustrates a famous line from Montaigne's Essays, Book II, chapter 12, the Apology for Raymond Sebond, written in the 1570s–80s: "Quand je me joue à ma chatte, qui sait si elle passe son temps de moi plus que je ne fais d'elle". Fun fact: in that chapter the cat is Montaigne's star witness against human vanity, and three centuries later an etcher took the hint.
collection: British Museum, London / National Library of France
feline_symbolism: For Montaigne the cat is a test case for human arrogance: if she may be amusing herself with him, humans cannot claim to be the only minds in the room.
image_credit: William Strang · https://www.nationalgalleries.org/art-and-artists/32723

title: The Annunciation
description: The cat sleeps curled in a tight ball in the lower left corner, nose tucked in, sleeping through the most important announcement in Christian history. Gabriel kneels in gold and rose with a lily, one hand held out, and Mary, standing at her prie-dieu, answers with one palm raised and the other open, a quiet gesture in soft light. A red curtain swags across the top of the room. Through the window behind them Barocci gives a view of the Palazzo Ducale in Urbino, his home town and the seat of his patron, so the miracle happens with a local landmark out of the window.
context: Barocci painted the altarpiece in 1582–84 for the chapel of Francesco Maria II della Rovere, Duke of Urbino, in the Basilica of the Holy House at Loreto. It is oil on canvas, 248 × 170 cm. Taken to Paris in 1797, it came back to Italy in 1815 and was then placed in the Vatican Pinacoteca (cat. 40376). Fun fact: Barocci reproduced the composition in his last and most ambitious etching, which spread the sleeping cat far beyond Loreto.
feline_symbolism: The NGV's essay reads the sleeping cat, with the view of Urbino, as a naturalistic detail that balances the miraculous encounter.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY-SA 3.0

title: Two Children Teasing a Cat
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: The cat crouches on the right edge of the table, a ginger-and-white tabby with its head lowered and eyes narrowed to slits, while a boy dangles a crayfish just above its ear and keeps his other hand on its back. The girl leans in, laughing. A second crayfish lies loose on the tabletop, and nobody has noticed it. Annibale stops the clock one second before trouble, which is the whole joke. The faces are broad and unidealised, the brushwork loose, the background plain brown, so all attention goes to three heads and one claw.
context: Annibale Carracci painted the canvas (66 × 88.9 cm) around 1587–88 in Bologna; with no documents, the date rests on its Venetian-looking brushwork, which fits his known trip to Venice in those years. Once given to his brother Agostino, it was assigned to Annibale by Roberto Longhi, and the Metropolitan Museum acquired it in 1994. The theme borrows from Sofonisba Anguissola's lost Boy Bitten by a Crayfish, known from a drawing. Fun fact: Sofonisba and Caravaggio showed the bite; Annibale shows the moment before, and Bolognese painters liked the idea enough to make several derivatives, including Crespi's Girl Playing with a Cat and a Mouse.
title_eng: Two Children Teasing a Cat with a Crayfish
image_credit: Annibale Carracci · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"c/carracci/annibale/1/children"

title: Sight (One of the Five Senses)
description: The felid is easy to miss: a small lynx peers out from the lower right corner, just under the hand mirror, ears up and eyes wide, the animal that stood for keen eyesight. Above it Sight is played by a fashionable young woman who holds up the mirror but turns her eyes to us, while a man in a floppy hat, wearing a decidedly mischievous look, gets a hand on her breast. The pen-and-brown-ink drawing is worked up with wash and white highlights, and her face alone is touched with red chalk, so it glows warmer than everything around it. Goltzius signed with his HG monogram on the mirror frame.
context: Hendrick Goltzius drew this sheet in Haarlem around 1595–96 as the finished design for one plate of a Five Senses series engraved by his close collaborator Jan Saenredam. The lines are indented for transfer, so the working process is still readable in the paper. Boijmans points out that Goltzius swapped the usual stiff personifications for contemporary flirting couples, closer to genre than allegory, and that the senses' traditional animals (the lynx here, a deer in Hearing) shrink to small corner details. The drawing belonged to F.J.O. Boijmans in Utrecht and came to Rotterdam with his 1847 bequest, so it has been in the museum since it opened in 1849.
medium: Pen and brown ink, brown wash, white heightening, red chalk, indented for transfer
feline_symbolism: The lynx was the classic emblem of sharp sight, which is why it turns up as Sight's attribute, even if Goltzius makes it a footnote to the flirtation.
image_credit: Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam (public-domain artwork), via Wikimedia Commons

title: Tibert the Cat Summons Reynard the Fox
title_original: Tibert de kat dagvaardt Reinaert de vos
description: Tibert the cat stands at the left with tail raised high, head lowered towards the foxes as if reading out the king's summons. Four foxes gather in front of a rocky den, two sitting up, one lying at ease and one peering out from behind, Reynard among them. It is a small etching, under ten centimetres high, that plays like a scene from a courtroom drama. Everdingen was a landscape man first, so the animals act out their story in a proper outdoor setting, with overhanging rock, scrubby trees and a wicker basket on its side at lower right, and they look like real animals rather than people in costume.
context: Allaert van Everdingen (1621–1675) of Alkmaar etched a series of 57 plates on the adventures of Reynard the fox, which Stedelijk Museum Alkmaar dates to around 1670; the Rijksmuseum gives this sheet 1665–1675. In the medieval story the king sends Tibert to fetch Reynard to court, and the fox repays him by luring him into a trap. The plates had a long afterlife. They illustrated Gottsched's 1752 German Reineke edition, and in 1843 Henry Cole, writing as 'Felix Summerly', published forty of them in London after acquiring the original coppers. He grumbled that someone had since added ruled skies, and tried to recover the early look through lithographic transfers.
title_eng: Tibert the Cat Summons Reynard the Fox
submovement: Dutch Golden Age etching (Everdingen's Reynard the Fox series)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum · http://hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.collect.70690

title: Still Life of Fish and Cat
title_original: Stilleven met vis, kaars, artisjokken, krab en kat
collection: National Museum of Women in the Arts, Washington, DC
description: A tabby cat crouches at the left edge of the table with its paws clamped on two small fish, ears up and eyes fixed on us, as if daring anyone to take them back. Behind it a big carp lies across a perforated ceramic colander, scales glinting, with a smaller fish tucked underneath. In front, a tangle of red crayfish crawls towards the edge, and at right a heap of oysters and shells ends in one opened oyster, wet and pearly. Peeters lines up the textures like a sampler: fur, slime, glazed clay, crayfish armour, rough shell. The cat is the only thing on the table still breathing.
context: Clara Peeters, active in Antwerp from about 1607, was one of the earliest painters to specialise in still life and the only Flemish woman known to do so that early. The National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington dates this panel to after 1620; it came as a gift of the museum's founders, Wallace and Wilhelmina Holladay. NMWA reads it as plain household abundance, without the moral subtext still lifes often carry. Fun fact: her biography is slipperier than her fish. A 1594 baptism record may be hers, but some scholars push her birth back into the 1580s, since otherwise her accomplished 1607 pictures would be the work of a 12- or 13-year-old.
title_eng: Still Life of Fish and Cat
image_credit: Clara Peeters · Bridgeman Art Library : Object 51954

title: The Cardinal's Leisure
description: The cats have taken over the floor: a big ginger-and-white cat lies on the unrolled map like a paperweight, while four kittens tumble across it, one white kitten flipped onto its back near the hem of the Cardinal's red robe. Richelieu leans sideways out of his chair, quill still in hand, to look down at them, while a bearded friar behind the desk keeps reading his papers. Delort paints what academic history pictures did best, heavy red silk, a carved high-backed chair, ship models, an embroidered wall hanging, and sets against it the soft disorder of cats. France's most feared man is upstaged by animals playing with his paperwork.
context: Charles-Édouard Delort (1841–1895) specialised in costume pieces set in the age of musketeers and cardinals. This canvas, signed 'C. DeLort', was sold in New York in 1885 with George I. Seney's collection and is now in the Detroit Institute of Arts as The Cardinal's Leisure, a gift of Mrs. Helen L. DeRoy. It also circulated as a photogravure titled Richelieu and his Cats. The picture leans on a famous story that Richelieu kept fourteen cats with names like Lucifer and Soumise. His biographer Françoise Hildesheimer (2004) finds no documents for them. The one solid trace is money he settled on the writer Marie de Gournay for her cat and its kittens.
feline_symbolism: The cats are companions and comic relief, a 19th-century way of giving a feared statesman a private soft spot.
image_credit: Charles Édouard Delort · https://www.dia.org/art/collection/object/cardinals-leisure-42360

title: A Boy and a Girl with a Cat and an Eel
title_original: Twee kinderen met een kat en een aal
description: A boy in a fashionable hat clamps a cat against his chest and dangles an eel just out of its reach, grinning at someone we cannot see. The cat is not enjoying the game: it stares out at us, ears up and wary, hind legs braced against his arm. His little sister looks straight at us with a warning finger raised, which would be more convincing if her other hand were not gripping the cat's tail, ready to pull. Leyster sets the two clean faces and crisp white collars against a dark ground, so the trouble reads instantly. The ebony frame is a 17th-century Dutch one, fitted in 2011.
context: Judith Leyster painted this panel in Haarlem around 1635, a couple of years after she entered the city's painters' guild and set up a workshop with apprentices of her own. The National Gallery links it to the proverb 'he who plays with cats gets scratched': entertainment with a warning attached. Unusually, the culprits are well-off middle-class children, when naughty children in Dutch pictures were more often poor. It came to the gallery in 1943 with the bequest of C.F. Leach. Leyster's own reputation had a rough ride. Her works were long credited to Frans Hals or to her husband Jan Miense Molenaer, until her monogram turned up under a false Hals signature in 1893.
title_eng: A Boy and a Girl with a Cat and an Eel
feline_symbolism: The cat is the trouble waiting to happen: under the proverb, whoever torments it is about to get scratched.
image_credit: Judith Leyster · National Gallery, London (official image, via Wikimedia Commons)

title: Young Man with a Cat
collection: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Museumslandschaft Hessen Kassel
description: The cat is clamped against the young man's chest at the bottom edge of the panel, a tabby with its ears back and mouth open in a pink protest, while his hand presses down on its head. He hardly seems to notice. Under a broad black hat with a white plume, he turns a flushed, half-smiling face to us. This is a half-length genre head of the Haarlem type, on an oak panel very nearly square, about 45 by 43 centimetres, where the point is the sitter's mood and the quick handling. The Kassel cataloguer singles out that face: its modelling is restless, more agitated than in Leyster's secure pictures.
context: The Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister in Kassel bought this panel in 1962 from the Basel dealer H. F. Fankhauser and catalogues it as Judith Leyster, attributed. Frima Fox Hofrichter, author of the Leyster catalogue raisonné, dates it 1635, the year before Leyster married Jan Miense Molenaer. Not everyone is convinced. Bernhard Schnackenburg's 1996 Kassel catalogue notes how the restless face departs from her secure work, yet finds no grounds to hand it to anyone else, such as one of Frans Hals's sons. Commons metadata even files it under 'follower of Frans Hals'. Fittingly for Leyster, whose pictures spent two centuries passing as Hals's, the argument still runs in both directions.
image_credit: Judith Leyster · http://altemeister.museum-kassel.de/32783/

title: Nemuri-neko (Sleeping Cat Architectural Relief Carving)
title_original: 日光東照宮 眠り猫
artist: Attributed to Hidari Jingorō (左甚五郎)
description: The cat sleeps curled among peonies, a soft grey body with its eyes shut and head lowered onto its forepaws, one ear chipped where the pigment has flaked away. It sits in a kaerumata, the frog-leg bracket over a beam of the shrine's eastern corridor near the Sakashita Gate, framed by gilded blossoms, green leaves and a turquoise cloud band. It is tiny, about 15 by 20 centimetres, and painted in mineral pigments, so most visitors find it by the crowd standing under it. Round the back sparrows play among bamboo. After a dispute about whether the eyes were half open, restorers repainted them shut in 2017.
context: The carving belongs to the lavish rebuilding of Nikkō Tōshō-gū, the shrine to Tokugawa Ieyasu, enlarged under the third shōgun Iemitsu and completed in 1636. It sits on the route up to the Okusha, Ieyasu's tomb. Tradition credits Hidari Jingorō, a carver so legendary that some scholars doubt he existed; the real hand is unknown. The east and west corridors became a National Treasure in 1951, and the shrine is part of the UNESCO site Shrines and Temples of Nikkō (1999). Readings pile up. The sleeping cat plus carefree sparrows means peace; peony plus cat is a Chinese pun for wealth and long life; or the cat is a guard against mice on the path to the tomb.
medium: Carved wood painted with mineral pigments
submovement: Early Edo shrine carving (Tōshō-gū, Kan'ei rebuilding)
feline_symbolism: A cat asleep while sparrows play on the other side is read as an image of peace under Tokugawa rule; the peony-and-cat pairing also puns on wealth and longevity.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Cats Fighting in a Larder, with Loaves of Bread, a Dressed Lamb, Artichokes and Grapes
title_original: Dos gatos riñendo en una despensa
collection: Galerie Pierre Birtschansky, Paris (sold Christie's New York, 27 April 2017, lot 40A)
description: The cats have broken into the larder and gone for each other instead of the food. One launches itself down from the window ledge, claws out and mouth open, while two more lock together on the tabletop at left, one flipped on its back and snarling up at the attacker. A fourth, ginger, peers in over the sill to watch. Around the scrap Snyders piles the goods: an overturned basket spilling loaves and oranges, scattered knives and forks, a dressed lamb draped over a copper cistern, artichokes, asparagus, grapes. It is a big panel, more than 90 by 100 centimetres.
context: Frans Snyders (1579–1657), master in the Antwerp guild from 1602 and later its dean, made his name with market stalls, larders and animal fights, and supplied animals and still-life passages for Rubens. He often dropped live animals, cats especially, into still lifes to set the living against the inert. This panel's recorded history is short. It was probably with D.A. Hoogendijk in Amsterdam in 1932, sold in Stockholm in 1942 to a family who kept it for generations, and was auctioned at Christie's New York on 27 April 2017. Commons now lists it with Galerie Pierre Birtschansky. Snyders signed few pictures, and variants of kitchen scenes from his studio circulate widely.
title_eng: Cats Fighting in a Larder, with Loaves of Bread, a Dressed Lamb, Artichokes and Grapes
image_credit: Frans Snyders · Christie's , LotFinder: entry 6068925

title: Peasant Family in an Interior
title_original: Famille de paysans dans un intérieur
description: The cat is the one to look for: a small white cat with grey patches peeping out beside the copper cooking pot on the floor, anxiously keeping an eye on the viewer. Its opposite number is a little pop-eyed dog at lower left that seems lost in its own thoughts. Above them three generations of a peasant family sit by the hearth, staring out at us more than at each other. A barefoot boy plays a recorder, the grandmother holds a glass of wine, and bread, wine and salt sit on the table. At 113 by 159 cm, this is the largest and most ambitious of the brothers' peasant interiors.
context: The Louvre gives this canvas to Louis Le Nain (c. 1593–1648), with his brother Antoine as a possible partner, and dates it about 1642. The three Le Nain brothers worked together in Paris and rarely signed individually, so the 'which brother' question never quite goes away. The picture came from the dukes of Marmier at Ray-sur-Saône, sold in Paris in 1914, passed through George Demotte and was bought for the Louvre in 1915 with Arthur Pernolet's bequest. Fun dispute: scholars including Cuzin and Dickerson have read the bread and wine as a hint at the Eucharist and an act of charity. The Louvre's notice calls that reading 'very fragile' and sees studio props, the animals included.
image_credit: Attributed to Louis Le Nain / Antoine Le Nain · https://www.panoramadelart.com/Le-nain-famille-paysans-interieur

title: Head of a Cat (small size)
description: A cat's head and nothing else: a striped tabby seen dead on, round eyes with bright catchlights fixed on us, ears pricked, whiskers fanning out past the jaw in single hair-thin lines. It is etched on a plate about 7 centimetres square, small enough to cover with a palm, and signed W Hollar fec 1646 at lower left. No body, no setting, no story, just the specimen-like attention Hollar paid to shells, insects and fur muffs. The catalogue title adds (small size), which tells you a larger plate of the same subject exists. At this scale the print works like a page from a naturalist's notebook.
context: Wenceslaus Hollar (1607–1677), from Prague, worked mostly in London and, during the Civil War years, in Antwerp, and etched almost anything put in front of him: cities, costume, maps, animals. The University of Toronto's Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library holds an impression in its Hollar collection, classed under natural history and filed as plate P2108, catalogued as Head of a cat (small size). Hollar's best-known cat is a different and odder print entirely: Le vray portrait du chat du grand duc de Moscovie, attributed to him and dated 1663, an impression of which is in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
image_credit: Wenceslaus Hollar · Artwork from University of Toronto Wenceslaus Hollar Digital Collection Scanned by University of Toronto High-resolution version extracted using custom tool by User:Dcoetzee

title: Peasant Court with an Old Woman and a Cat
description: The cat sits in the old woman's lap at lower left, a ginger-and-white cat held steady while she parts the fur on its head with her fingers. The panel is modest, 49 by 64 centimetres, and painted on oak, which suits Teniers's quick, silvery handling: a few strokes for a wheelbarrow, a smear of light for a copper basin, a white cloth dropped by a tub. Thatched houses, a tall plank fence and a well with a copper jug fill the yard under a grey sky. The woman and the cat are the only living company here, and the cat turns farmyard clutter into a household.
context: David Teniers the Younger (1610–1690) of Antwerp, court painter to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm in Brussels, made his fortune with small scenes of Flemish peasants, sold to collectors who never set foot in such yards. This panel belongs to the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest, which received it in 1953 when the holdings of the Budapest Municipal Gallery were transferred to it. The museum's title, Peasant Court with an Old Woman and a Cat, does most of the iconographic work; Teniers turned out these yard scenes in quantity, and most of his figures are types, not portraits.
title_eng: Peasant Court with an Old Woman and a Cat
title_original: Boereninterieur met oude vrouw en kat
image_credit: David Teniers the Younger · Own work , Yelkrokoyade , 20 July 2011

title: The Virgin and Child with the Cat and Snake
description: The cat crouches at lower left on a cushion by the step, one paw out to play with the hem of Mary's skirt, and from under that same skirt, near the bottom centre, a small snake slides out, trodden under her foot. The Holy Family has moved into a Dutch living room. Mary sits low by the fireplace cradling the Child, cheek to cheek, with a chair behind her, while Joseph peers in through the window from outside. The leaded panes behind her head line up into a makeshift halo. The signed plate is small, under 15 centimetres wide.
context: Rembrandt etched this plate in Amsterdam in 1654 and signed it 'Rembrandt f. 1654'. The V&A notes that he based the group partly on an engraving of the Virgin and Child by Andrea Mantegna, then dressed it in contemporary clothes. The National Gallery of Art in Washington owns an impression given by Philip Hofer in 1941. Fun fact: the copper plate itself survives. It passed from the dealer Clement de Jonge (1679) through Basan and later owners, was last printed in 1906, and was bought by the V&A in 1993 with Art Fund support, then varnished so no one could print from it again.
title_eng: The Virgin and Child with the Cat and Snake
feline_symbolism: The snake under Mary's foot casts her as the new Eve defeating sin; the cat, toying at her hem, keeps the scene firmly domestic.
image_credit: Rembrandt van Rijn · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Barbershop with Monkeys and Cats (Barbierstube mit Affen und Katzen)
description: A barber's shop run by monkeys, with cats among the clientele: this is the singerie, the genre in which animals act out human trades. Abraham Teniers paints it on a small copper plate, about 24 by 30 centimetres, a support that lets the brush lay down crisp, enamel-smooth detail, ideal for fur, whiskers and the gleam of a razor. The joke depends on the cats, who make the most reluctant possible customers for a shave, in a room full of busy, self-important monkeys in human dress.
context: Abraham Teniers (1629–1670), younger brother of David Teniers the Younger, worked in Antwerp and helped his brother develop the monkey-and-cat satires that collectors loved in the mid-1600s. The Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna dates this copper to the second third of the 17th century (inv. GG 1786). It has a long imperial pedigree: it is recorded in the Habsburg Schatzkammer in 1747/48 and in the picture gallery by 1781. The theme travelled widely in print. A Coryn Boel engraving after David Teniers, The Monkeys' Barber Shop, is in Washington, and the Rijksmuseum has a print simply titled Een aap scheert een kat, 'a monkey shaves a cat'.
feline_symbolism: In singeries cats and monkeys parody human vanity and pretension; the cat as unwilling customer sharpens the satire.
image_credit: Coryn Boel after David Teniers the Younger · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Interior with a Sleeping Maid and her Mistress (The Idle Servant)
description: The cat has climbed onto the cupboard above the sleeping maid and is helping itself to the raw goose, a grey tabby flattened over the dish with its jaws in the bird. The National Gallery notes, unkindly, that Maes seems to have had only a vague idea of what a cat's teeth look like. Below, the maid has dropped off on a stool, head propped in her hand, sleeves rolled after cooking. Her mistress, in a crisp white apron, turns to us with an open palm, smiling. Pots and pans litter the floor, and up a few stairs a proper family dinner goes on in the room beyond.
context: Nicolaes Maes (1634–1693), a former pupil of Rembrandt, painted this signed and dated panel in 1655, soon after going home to Dordrecht. The maid's slump borrows the traditional pose of Acedia, Sloth, though the mistress looks amused rather than outraged. The picture may play on a Dutch saying that a kitchen maid should keep one eye on the pan and the other on the cat; this one manages neither. Its view through to a second room is among the first of its kind, a device Maes kept using. Richard Simmons bequeathed it to the National Gallery in 1847, and it hangs today in a 17th-century Italian frame.
title_eng: Interior with a Sleeping Maid and her Mistress (The Idle Servant)
feline_symbolism: The thieving cat is the cost of idleness, the proverb's warning made literal.
image_credit: Nicolaes Maes · http://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/nicolaes-maes-the-idle-servant

title: Old Woman Saying Grace, Known as 'The Prayer without End'
title_original: Oude vrouw in gebed, bekend als 'Het gebed zonder end'
description: The cat has run out of patience. In the lower right corner it rears up on its hind legs and hooks its claws into the tablecloth, while the old woman bows over her folded hands with her eyes shut. She is saying grace, and she is taking her time. Bread, a salmon steak on a pewter plate and a stoneware jug sit one good tug from the floor. On the shelf behind her stand an hourglass and a funnel, keys hang below, the props of a careful household and of time running out. Maes paints her nearly life-size on a big canvas, 134 by 113 centimetres.
context: Maes painted this in Dordrecht around 1656 and signed it with a monogram. Its Dutch nickname, Het gebed zonder end ('the prayer without end'), is the cat's point of view. The Rijksmuseum puts the virtue in her self-control and sense of duty to God: the begging cat does not distract her. The picture went from A. Lacoste in Dordrecht to the Amsterdam society Felix Meritis, which gave it to the city of Amsterdam in June 1889. The city lent it to the Rijksmuseum that November, and it has stayed on loan ever since.
title_eng: Old Woman Saying Grace, Known as 'The Prayer without End'
feline_symbolism: The cat stands for worldly appetite and distraction, set against the old woman's patient devotion.
image_credit: Nicolaes Maes · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"m/maes/old_pray"

title: The Large Cat (De grote kat)
description: A tabby cat crouches at rest and fills almost the whole plate, eyes narrowed to sleepy slits, forepaws tucked, nose towards a few leafy plants at lower right. Visscher engraves every stiff whisker and builds the striped fur from fine, soft lines until you can almost feel the nap. Behind the cat, at far left, a mouse has squeezed through the bars of an arched window and peers out. The cat does not care. That is the joke, and maybe the sermon: a guard animal dozing while the thief walks in. Even the signature joins the scene, written on a scrap of paper lying on the ground at lower left.
context: Cornelis Visscher (1629–1658) of Haarlem, praised by Houbraken for his drawing from life, engraved this plate in 1657, a year before he died young; a stone at lower left is inscribed 'Corn. Visscher fecit', and his relative Claes Jansz. Visscher published it. Two states are known, and impressions are in the British Museum, Rijksmuseum, National Gallery of Art and elsewhere. It was popular enough to be copied: the Rijksmuseum's RP-P-1904-722 is an anonymous copy after it. The Leiden Collection compares it with Gerrit Dou's cat on a ledge, painted the same year, though it thinks a direct link unlikely. The preparatory drawing sold in 1883 and is now lost.
feline_symbolism: The sleeping cat ignoring the mouse may allude to Proverbs 19:15, where sloth leads to hunger.
image_credit: Rijksmuseum · http://hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.COLLECT.191123

title: Las Hilanderas (The Spinners / The Fable of Arachne)
description: The workshop cat is easy to miss: a grey shape curled on the floor at bottom centre, among tufts of fleece and a ball of yarn, right by the old spinner's bare foot. Around it the weaving workshop is in full swing: an older woman at the spinning wheel on the left, a young one in a white blouse winding yarn on the right, helpers bending over the wool. Up a step at the back, in a bright alcove, elegant ladies stand before a finished woven hanging copied from Titian's Rape of Europa. Velázquez paints with startling economy; the spinning wheel's spokes dissolve into a blur.
context: Velázquez painted this canvas around 1657 for Pedro de Arce, a royal huntsman, whose 1664 inventory calls it a 'Fábula de Aracne'. For centuries it was read as a view of Madrid's Santa Isabel weaving works, until Diego Angulo showed in 1948 that it stages Ovid's story of Arachne, who out-wove Athena and was turned into a spider; the old woman is the goddess in disguise. It passed to the Medinaceli family and the royal Alcázar, probably survived the palace fire of 1734, and reached the Prado in 1819. Somewhere along the way strips were added, about 50 cm on top and 37 cm at the sides, now hidden behind a double wall.
title_eng: Las Hilanderas (The Spinners / The Fable of Arachne)
image_credit: Diego Velázquez · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"v/velazque/09/0901vela"

title: Cat Crouching on the Ledge of an Artist's Atelier
title_original: Kater op een vensterbank van een schildersatelier
description: A ginger-and-cream striped cat crouches in profile on a stone ledge, front paws stretched forward, eyes alert, watching something just outside the picture to the right while its long banded tail trails off the left end of the sill. Dou built the fur from countless tiny strokes with a brush of only a few hairs. A red curtain with violet highlights hangs from rings in the arched niche, and deep in the dark room behind, a painter works at his easel with a violin on the table beside him. The cat looks like a particular animal rather than a generic one; an 1859 catalogue went ahead and called it 'Master Dou's Housecat'.
context: Gerrit Dou of Leiden signed and dated this panel 'GDou 1657'. It is one of only three known animal paintings by him and the only picture in which he shows an artist actually at work. The Leiden Collection reads the cat as Sight, following prints like Goltzius and Saenredam's Visus, and the curtain as a nod to Parrhasius, whose painted curtain fooled a rival; Dou was praised as the 'Dutch Parrhasius'. X-rays reveal a different first idea underneath: a young woman pouring from a jug, perhaps a mousetrap. The panel is reused Baltic oak. It was in the Dresden royal collection by 1722, returned to the House of Wettin in 1924, and bought by the Leiden Collection in 2006.
title_eng: Cat Crouching on the Ledge of an Artist's Atelier
feline_symbolism: The keen-eyed cat stands for Sight, the sense on which a painter of Dou's illusionism depends.
image_credit: Gerrit Dou · Leiden Collection

title: Old Woman Eating Porridge
title_original: Oude vrouw die pap eet met een kat
collection: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (Eijk and Rose-Marie van Otterloo Collection)
description: The cat lies curled on the floorboards at lower right, a grey-brown tabby that looks straight out at us instead of up at the spoon, while an old woman in a white cap and blue apron eats her porridge. Metsu paints it small, on a panel only 35.5 by 28 centimetres, the size of a page, so the figure, bowl and cat are close and intimate. A tipped-over copper pot, a stray slipper and a wedge of cheese on the white cloth fill the corners. Pictures like this belong to the early Metsu, before his glossier Amsterdam interiors: plain people, plain food, and a domestic animal to make the scene feel lived in.
context: Gabriël Metsu (1629–1667) was born in Leiden and moved to Amsterdam around 1657. The RKD dates this panel to about 1654–57. Its documented history begins with the Secretan sale in Paris in 1889. It is now part of the Eijk and Rose-Marie van Otterloo collection, which the couple have pledged to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, where it is registered under a loan number. The painting is not the Dresden picture the old record claimed.
image_credit: Gabriel Metsu · https://rkd.nl/explore/images/246721

title: Cats with a Still Life of Marine Animals, Fruit and Vegetables
title_original: Katten bij een stilleven in een voorraadkamer
artist: Workshop of Jan van Kessel the Elder
submovement: Antwerp cabinet painting on copper (van Kessel workshop)
description: A white kitten peeks over the rim of a red earthenware pot, paws hooked on the edge, while a black-and-white cat at right makes off with a long silver fish clamped crosswise in its jaws. The French sale title, Deux chats jouant avec du poisson, gets straight to the point. Around them spill eels, red mullet, a spiny red crab, oysters, a salmon steak hung on the wall and a basket of pale grapes. It is painted in oil on a small copper plate, 23.5 by 31 centimetres, the hard, smooth support that van Kessel's shop favoured because it let fine brushwork stay crisp: individual scales, wet shell, single hairs of fur.
context: Jan van Kessel the Elder (1626–1679), grandson of Jan Brueghel the Elder, ran a busy Antwerp studio producing small, jewel-like animal and still-life pictures on copper for collectors' cabinets. The RKD catalogues this one as a workshop product of about 1665–79, which means assistants carried out a composition the master devised. It is not in a museum: its last public appearance was a Paris auction on 29 March 1994, and its present owner is unknown. The uploader to Wikimedia Commons credited it to 'Jan van Kessel III', a mix-up of the family's many Jans that the RKD record corrects.
title_eng: Cats with a Still Life of Marine Animals, Fruit and Vegetables
image_credit: Workshop of Jan van Kessel the Elder · Auctioned in Paris on 29 March 1994

title: Allegory of Night
title_original: Alegoría de la noche: El concierto de gatos y búhos
collection: Private collection (sold Lempertz, Cologne, 16 November 2019, lot 1070)
description: Two cats work the night shift: a grey tabby stalks along a root at the top, hissing at a passing bat, and a second, half hidden at the left edge, opens its mouth over a fallen one. Night, van Kessel style, is a crowd of the animals that come out after dark: cats, bats, a weasel and a pair of polecats, packed onto a copper plate barely 17 by 23 centimetres. At the centre a big bat spreads its veined wings with two pink young clinging to its chest. Fur and leathery wing are rendered hair by hair. The signature, 'I. VKESSEL' with the V and K joined, sits at lower left.
context: Jan van Kessel the Elder (1626–1679) worked in Antwerp and specialised in small natural-history pictures on copper, often grouped by theme (the elements, the continents, times of day) and sold as sets for collectors' cabinets. This Allegory of Night is signed and was auctioned at Lempertz in Cologne on 16 November 2019 (lot 1070); its present location is not public. Dating within his career is open; the Commons record gives only his working span.
feline_symbolism: Cats belong to the night animals here, alongside bats, as creatures of darkness and nocturnal hunting.
image_credit: Jan van Kessel the Elder · https://www.lempertz.com/en/catalogues/lot/1141-1/1070-jan-van-kessel-the-elder-1.html

title: Cat Musicians
artist: Anonymous, style of David Teniers the Younger
description: Five cats, two of them kittens, crowd a pink-draped table around an open songbook, and a grimacing tabby at the back is plainly going for the high note. An owl perches on the book like a conductor, a monkey in a feathered hat blows a shawm at lower left, and one more cat peers in through a slot in the wall. The table stands on carved fish, a snack the singers cannot reach. The cat concert was a running joke in Flemish painting, since cats yowl all night. This painter borrows Teniers's monkey-and-cat formula for an 18th-century market, on a small panel about 25 by 31 centimetres.
context: The National Trust catalogues this panel at Erddig, near Wrexham, as an anonymous work in the style of David Teniers II (1610–1690), dating it to the 18th century, around 1750. Pictures like it were turned out long after Teniers's death to satisfy demand for his singeries, which is why the old 'Teniers' label on so many cat concerts in country houses deserves a raised eyebrow. Erddig is famous for the Yorke family, who kept nearly everything, which helps explain how a modest decorative panel like this survived.
feline_symbolism: Singing cats were a stock image of cacophony and folly, mocking human music-making.
image_credit: anonymous · Art UK

title: Merry Company in a Pergola (The 'Cat Family')
description: The cat family sits at the left, not the centre: a young woman leans over the table where a striped mother cat sprawls with her kittens, two small faces peering up beside her. That cluster is why the Budapest picture is nicknamed 'The Cat Family'. Around it a merry company crowds under the pergola: a man hoists a glass high, a youth plays the flute, a little boy saws at a fiddle, a spotted dog yaps and a crow struts past the barrel. Steen paints it big, about 150 by 148 centimetres, so the party fills the canvas at almost life size, with the feline family mirroring the human one.
context: Jan Steen (1625/26–1679) painted this canvas around 1660. It belongs to the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest (inv. 337), where it is titled Merry Company in a Pergola (The 'Cat Family'). Hofstede de Groot listed it as no. 525 in his 1908 Steen catalogue. Fun fact: it spent June 1945 to December 1946 at the Munich Central Collecting Point, the Allied depot where looted and displaced art was sorted after the Second World War, before going back to Hungary.
title_eng: Merry Company in a Pergola (The 'Cat Family')
image_credit: Jan Steen · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/s/steen/page2/m_party"

title: Woman Eating, Known as 'The Cat's Breakfast'
title_original: Het ontbijt van de kat (Vrouw die een kat voert)
description: A grey tabby rears up on its hind legs at lower left, forepaws against the woman's skirt, reaching for the scrap she dangles from her plate. Her breakfast is herring and bread, and she is sharing it. Look closely and there is trouble: a fish bone has caught in the cat's throat, hence the title. A water pump stands at the left, a dead hen lies over a barrel in the foreground, and a vase of tulips and white blooms sits on a little table at right. The stems and leaves now look blue because the yellow in the original green has faded.
context: Gabriël Metsu painted this panel in Amsterdam around 1661–64 and signed it 'G. Metsu' at the top. Herring with bread, washed down with beer, was an everyday 17th-century breakfast, which the Rijksmuseum notes is exactly what the woman is eating. The painting belongs to the city of Amsterdam, which lent it to the Rijksmuseum in March 1892; it has since travelled to Leiden (1966), Tokyo (2007) and the Metsu retrospective in Dublin and Washington (2010–11). Its nickname, Le Déjeuner du chat, has made the cat the star of a picture officially titled Woman Eating.
title_eng: Woman Eating, Known as 'The Cat's Breakfast'
image_credit: Gabriel Metsu · www.rijksmuseum.nl : Home : Info : Pic

title: Children Teaching a Cat to Dance, Known as 'The Dancing Lesson'
title_original: De dansles (Kinderen leren een kat dansen)
submovement: Dutch Golden Age Comedic Genre & Moral Didacticism
description: The household cat, mostly white, dangles by its forepaws from the hands of a grinning boy in a red hat, made to step to the tune. A gang of children has decided it should learn to dance. A girl in a blue skirt plays the shawm, the loud, reedy ancestor of the oboe, and a spotted dog leaps up at the cat. A man looks down on the whole business from a small window above, and a lute hangs on the wall at right. Steen keeps the scale domestic, on a panel 68.5 by 59 centimetres, and the cat, unwilling dancer, is the only one not laughing.
context: Jan Steen (1625/26–1679), the great comic narrator of Dutch genre, painted this panel sometime between 1660 and 1679 and signed it 'JSteen'. The Rijksmuseum calls it simply a mischievous prank, which is fair. The picture came to the museum in 1880 with the bequest of Jonkheer J.S.H. van de Poll of Amsterdam. Fun detail: the museum's own Dutch and English texts do not quite agree, since the Dutch description also has a dog barking at the scene, while the English says nothing about it.
title_eng: Children Teaching a Cat to Dance, Known as 'The Dancing Lesson'
feline_symbolism: Teaching a cat to dance was a byword for useless effort and childish folly, the kind of misbehaviour Steen loved to stage.
image_credit: Jane023 · Own work

title: Concert of Cats
collection: Private collection (sold Artcurial, Paris, 23 March 2022, lot 72)
description: A dozen cats crowd around an open songbook, mouths wide, and the score itself is the joke: the notes on the right-hand page are tiny mice, with a whole mouse drawn below them. A grey cat in spectacles bellows at right, another blows a brass trombone at the back, and a black cat lurks in the shadow at lower left. A recorder, a violin and a lute lie abandoned on the floor. It is all painted in oil on a copper plate about the size of a postcard, 13.5 by 16.5 centimetres, made to be held and peered at, and the smooth copper lets every whisker stay sharp.
context: Jan van Kessel the Elder (1626–1679), of the Antwerp Brueghel dynasty, specialised in small animal pictures on copper for collectors. This one is dated to about 1650–60 and is not in a museum: it was sold at Artcurial in Paris on 23 March 2022 (lot 72). Concerts of cats were a favourite Flemish joke, often teamed with owls or monkeys, and van Kessel and the Teniers circle returned to them repeatedly.
feline_symbolism: A cat choir is a stock image of discord and noise, a parody of human music-making.
image_credit: Jan van Kessel the Elder · https://www.artcurial.com/fr/lot-attribue-jan-van-kessel-amsterdam-1641-1680-le-concert-des-chats-huile-sur-cuivre-4171-72#popin-active

title: A Cat Overturning a Vase of Flowers
title_original: Le Chat renversant un vase de fleurs
description: The cat has a strangely human face, eyes wide and mouth open in a yowl, and it pops up at lower left with one paw on a wooden mousetrap. It went for a mouse, and the bouquet it was meant to ignore is on the brink: a honeysuckle sprig and an ear of wheat have already slipped over the stone ledge, and water splashes at the foot of the vase. Striped tulips and roses burst out of the dark above. Everything is painted with Mignon's hard, petal-by-petal clarity, so the accident lands on a picture built to look perfectly still. The canvas is about 89 × 70 cm.
context: Abraham Mignon (1640–1679) came from Frankfurt and worked in Utrecht, where he followed his master Jan Davidsz. de Heem but gave his flowers firmer form and colour. This canvas belongs to the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon, which hangs it among its golden-age flower pieces. The Rijksmuseum owns a close variant, The Overturned Bouquet (SK-A-267), signed 'A. Mignon: fe.', with the same cat, trap and toppled vase. Fun fact: Lyon has made this alarmed, human-nosed cat its online mascot.
