The museum also points out that the cat-and-mousetrap motif has been compared to an emblem in the Emblemata amatoria, where the mouse stands for a man who can live neither with love nor without it.
title_eng: A Cat Overturning a Vase of Flowers (The Mousetrap)
submovement: Dutch Golden Age flower still life (circle of Jan Davidsz. de Heem)
feline_symbolism: Lyon reads the spilled water and falling blooms as a last vanitas allegory, with the cat as the bringer of the disorder that ends all earthly beauty.
image_credit: Abraham Mignon · Œuvre appartenant au Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon

title: Children Teaching a Cat to Read
description: A grey-and-white cat is being taught to read, which goes about as well as you would expect: a boy in a feathered cap pins it in his arms while a girl on a low seat holds the open book up to its face and lifts her other hand like a schoolmistress. Another boy grins from behind the table at right, and an older girl looks on, smiling. Steen stages the lesson on a small panel, about 45 × 35.5 cm, and the joke works because the cat stays entirely a cat while the children treat it as a pupil. Children playing at school are, at that moment, skipping the real thing.
context: Jan Steen (1625/26–1679), the Leiden painter of noisy households, painted this oil on panel around 1665–1668. It is in the Kunstmuseum Basel (inv. G 1958.39), not the Rijksmuseum. Steen returned to the idea of children drilling a cat more than once: the Rijksmuseum's Children Teaching a Cat to Dance (SK-A-718) has a girl playing a shawm while the cat screeches, a dog barks and an old man scolds from a window. Fun fact: a Sotheby's note on a painting by a follower of Steen proposes that its composition was conceived as a pendant to this Basel cat-reading picture, which shows how quickly the subject was copied.
title_eng: Children Teaching a Cat to Read
image_credit: Jan Steen · http://sammlungonline.kunstmuseumbasel.ch

title: Cat and Rock (猫石图卷)
artist: Bada Shanren (Zhu Da, 八大山人 / 朱耷)
description: The plump, sleepy cat is tiny in this view of the whole scroll: a soft ink shape curled on top of a rock left of centre, while the rest of the paper fills with broad dark leaves, flowers and grasses, punctuated by red seals. The scroll is 34 cm high and about 2.18 m long, made to be unrolled an arm's length at a time from right to left, so the cat arrives as a surprise somewhere along the way. Bada Shanren builds fur and stone from washes of different density, pale under dark, so the animal and its perch share the same soft weight.
context: Bada Shanren (Zhu Da, 1626–1705) was a descendant of the Ming imperial house who became a monk after the dynasty fell and later one of the great individualist painters of the early Qing. This handscroll is in the Palace Museum, Beijing (新00077585). In 2026 the Palace Museum lent a group of his late works, including a Cat, Rock and Flowers handscroll, to Nanchang for the 400th anniversary of his birth. Fun fact: a China Daily reading of the cat calls it 'chubby and sleepy' and sees in it both a leisurely life and a painter looking for inner peace after years of anger and worry.
image_credit: Bada Shanren · https://minghuaji.dpm.org.cn/paint/detail?id=fe46cad67fd84873bff14d6bbf16e207

title: Still Life of the Remnants of a Meal with a Lunging Cat
title_original: Nature morte aux restes de repas avec chat à l'affût
description: A tabby-and-white cat has crept onto the tablecloth and is caught mid-lunge, one front leg stretched out so its paw lands on a slice of ham on a pewter plate (the French title calls it 'chat étendant la patte'). The meal is over, and Desportes paints its remains on a canvas about 74 × 92 cm: a dish of peaches, a cut ham on the bone, a pie, and glass carafes of water and red wine on a stand. That single stretched leg turns a still life into a small crime scene. A signature and date sit faint at lower left, the last digits of the year no longer readable.
context: Alexandre-François Desportes (1661–1743) made his name painting hounds and game for Louis XIV, and turned the same eye on kitchens and tables. This canvas is in a private collection and was offered at Sotheby's New York in the 2024 sale A Scholar Collects. It is catalogued in the Desportes catalogue raisonné by Georges de Lastic and Pierre Jacky (2010) as P 662bis. Fun fact: its early history is a 'perhaps': Sotheby's suggests it may have belonged to the Paris collector François Abraham Mouchard and sold in his 1782 posthumous sale, before it resurfaced with the critic and historian Jean Locquin in the twentieth century.
title_eng: Still Life of the Remnants of a Meal with a Lunging Cat
submovement: French court animal and still-life painting (Louis XIV to Régence)
collection: Private collection (Sotheby's New York, A Scholar Collects, 2024, lot 26)
image_credit: Alexandre-François Desportes · https://www.sothebys.com/en/buy/auction/2024/a-scholar-collects/still-life-of-the-remnants-of-a-meal-with-a

title: Nightlight in the Form of a Cat (One of a Pair)
description: Two black cats curl into neat ovals, tails wrapped round their flanks, and poke out small pale tongues at each other; this entry is one of the pair, photographed here side by side. Each is a porcelain cat about 12.4 cm tall, coated in black enamel so that it reads as a sleek black animal, and the two were made as matching ornaments. The round, goggling eyes are not original: the museum records them as a modern plastic repair, so the stare is a twentieth-century replacement. The body is otherwise Jingdezhen porcelain under its dark enamel coat, and one cat has an opening in its back.
context: The figure was made at Jingdezhen, the great porcelain centre of Jiangxi province, in the eighteenth century under the Qing dynasty. It came to the Metropolitan Museum in 1931 with the Friedsam Collection, the bequest of Michael Friedsam, together with its partner (32.100.423). Fun fact: hollow porcelain cats of this period were often made as nightlights, with a candle inside shining through the eyes, and the Rijksmuseum has one that works this way. The Met, however, does not call this pair nightlights, so that function stays a possibility, not a fact.
title_eng: Nightlight in the Form of a Cat (One of a Pair)
medium: Porcelain painted with famille verte enamels on the biscuit
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Still Life with Cat and Fish
title_original: Nature morte au chat et aux poissons
description: A calico cat, white with ginger and black patches, crouches on a stone ledge with one paw pinning a cut fish on a dish, and looks straight at us as if caught. Above, two fish hang head-up from a single hook against the wall. Chardin lets those hanging fish cut down through the horizontal shelf, so the eye drops from scales to fur. A brass mortar and pestle, an onion and a spring onion sit at right. The paint is laid on thickly and in rich colour; Thyssen notes that later painters admired how he handled the fish scales and the cat's coat. The canvas is 79.5 × 63 cm, signed and dated 1728.
context: Chardin (1699–1779) painted this and its companion, Still-Life with Cat and Rayfish, in 1728, the year the Académie admitted him as a painter of fruit and animals. The pair first appears in the 1778 sale of Rémond, a former royal maître d'hôtel, and later passed through the Beurnonville and Rothschild collections before the Thyssen-Bornemisza collection acquired it in 1986. Variants of the pair are in the Nelson-Atkins Museum and the Burrell Collection. Fun fact: for decades the date was misread as 1758, which would have made it a late work; Pierre Rosenberg corrected it to 1728 for the 1979 Chardin exhibition, which fits the style much better.
title_eng: Still Life with Cat and Fish
image_credit: Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin · https://www.museothyssen.org/en/collection/artists/chardin-jean-baptiste-simeon/still-life-cat-and-fish

title: The Ray (La Raie)
description: To the left, a white-and-tabby cat with arched back and tail straight up picks its way over a heap of opened oysters, ears back, half thief and half alarmed by the sight above it. The ray hangs gutted from a hook in the middle of the wall, and its pale underside reads like a face with a grin. On the white cloth to the right sit a copper pan, a dark stoneware jug, a bottle and a knife balanced over the edge. The canvas is large, 114 × 146 cm, and the cat is small, which makes its nerves all the funnier.
context: Chardin showed The Ray at the open-air Exposition de la Jeunesse on 3 June 1728, and on 25 September that year the Académie royale accepted it, with The Buffet, as his reception pieces, admitting him the same day. It stayed with the Académie until the Revolution and then entered the Louvre (INV 3197). Fun fact: it has collected strong opinions ever since. Diderot found it disgusting, Matisse admired it, and Proust compared the opened skate to the nave of a polychrome cathedral.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work

title: The Cat and the Two Sparrows
title_original: Le Chat et les deux moineaux
submovement: French Rococo book illustration (Oudry's La Fontaine Fables)
description: The cat crouches on the tiled floor with a sparrow clamped in its jaws, tail hooked up behind, while a second bird lies at lower left. Above it the birdcage on the console table stands empty, its little door open. This is the engraved plate for La Fontaine's fable of the cat who grew up beside a sparrow, ate a stranger sparrow, and then his old friend. A tablet at the bottom names it 'LE CHAT ET LES DEUX MOINEAUX. Fable CCXV.', and the lines below credit 'J. B. Oudry inv.' at left and 'J. Duret sculp.' at right. Burin over etching turns Oudry's wash drawing into crisp lines and cross-hatching.
context: Between about 1729 and 1734 Jean-Baptiste Oudry, painter of royal hunts and animals, made a long series of drawings illustrating La Fontaine's Fables. They were engraved only much later and published by Desaint & Saillant in Paris in four folio volumes, 1755–1759; this plate, engraved by Pierre-Jacques Duret, illustrates book XII, fable 2, in volume IV. The Bibliothèque nationale de France holds a copy (Rés. YE 116), and the Louvre's Rothschild collection has an impression dated 1759. Fun fact: Oudry died in 1755, the year the first volume appeared, so he never saw this cat in print.
title_eng: The Cat and the Two Sparrows (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: In La Fontaine's fable the cat stands for appetite dressed up as loyalty: it avenges its friend and then eats him too.
image_credit: Pierre-Jacques Duret / After Jean-Baptiste Oudry · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k1049446f/f147

title: La Toilette (Woman Fastening Her Garter)
description: At the young woman's feet, a small ginger cat sprawls on its side and looks straight out at us, one paw near a ball of wool or twine stolen from the blue sewing bag hanging on the fire screen, the thread trailing across the floor. Above, the young woman ties her garter while her maid, seen from behind, offers her a cap. The room is a pile-up of yellow silk walls, a gold Chinese screen with birds, a fan, bellows, a brush and loose fabric, with a fire going in the grate. The cat is the only figure making more mess than the sitter.
context: Boucher painted this small canvas (52.5 × 66.5 cm) in 1742 for Count Carl Gustaf Tessin, Swedish ambassador in Paris, who paid 648 livres; it reached Stockholm that June. After Tessin's death it was auctioned in 1771 and passed through Swedish and then Viennese Rothschild collections before appearing in New York in 1967 and joining the Thyssen-Bornemisza collection. Fun fact: the woman was once identified as Boucher's own wife, Marie-Jeanne Buzot. The Thyssen notes that her known portraits look nothing like this figure, and that a painter was unlikely to show his wife in such a state of undress for a foreign client.
image_credit: François Boucher · Musée du Louvre

title: The Graham Children
description: Behind the chair at right, a grey tabby hauls itself up over the back, claws hooked on the top rail, and fixes its eyes on the goldfinch in the gilded cage above. The bird flinches. Below, the four Graham children perform for us: Richard Robert turns a little bird organ painted with Orpheus and grins up at the cage, Anna Maria lifts her flowered silk skirts to dance, and Henrietta dangles a bunch of cherries toward baby Thomas in his little carriage. A clock topped by a cherub with scythe and hourglass reads about 1.45. Life-size, 160.5 × 181 cm.
context: Hogarth painted the children of Daniel Graham, apothecary to George I and George II, at their home at 11 Pall Mall, signing and dating the canvas 1742. It is one of the largest pictures he made. The National Gallery suggests the portrait was commissioned because the baby, Thomas, had already died; Hogarth based his face on a chalk study made after death, now in the British Museum. The picture passed through the Graham and Watson Taylor families and the Earls of Normanton before Lord Duveen gave it to the Gallery in 1934. Fun fact: the cat is the picture's quiet threat, the reminder that death can spring into even a comfortable house.
feline_symbolism: The National Gallery reads the cat stalking the caged goldfinch as a hint of how suddenly death took one of the Graham children from their prosperous home.
image_credit: William Hogarth · The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title: A Girl with a Kitten
medium: Pastel on blue paper, mounted on canvas
description: A grey-and-white kitten with round amber eyes peeps up from the girl's hands at lower left, and both of them have plainly been told to sit still. The girl turns her head to the left in near profile, a striped blue bow at her throat. The sheet is pastel on blue paper, later laid down on canvas, 59.1 × 49.8 cm. The face is blended with the stump instead of drawn with the point of the crayon, and it has none of the white highlights you would expect from Perronneau, which gives the girl a soft, slightly unfocused look. The kitten is the most alert creature in the picture.
context: The National Gallery catalogues the pastel as 'probably by' Jean-Baptiste Perronneau (1715/16–1783), and dates it 1743, although it bears a signature and the date 1745. Its owners were the Nevill family until Sir Joseph Duveen bought it and gave it to the Gallery in 1921. The sitter is unidentified; the Gallery thinks it is probably an idealised portrait, not a genre scene. Fun fact: the doubts are technical. The anatomy is weak for an artist who won an Académie drawing prize in 1734, the signature looks wrong, and if genuine it would be his earliest dated pastel, yet the materials are certainly eighteenth-century and there is no sign of later reworking.
feline_symbolism: The National Gallery notes that cats in children's portraits sometimes stand for the wildness of nature pressing in on childhood innocence.
image_credit: After Jean-Baptiste Perronneau · Copy of a painting of Jean-Baptiste Perronneau .

title: Knife Handle (Kozuka)
medium: Copper-silver alloy (shibuichi), iron, gold, silver, copper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A plump cat lies curled on this narrow strip of metal, under 10 cm long and 1.4 cm wide, front paws tucked forward and eyes on a small gold butterfly hovering out of reach at left. Beside it blooms a silvery-blue peony with gold and copper leaves. The ground is shibuichi, the grey copper-silver alloy Japanese metalworkers prized for its soft, matte tone, split by a diagonal into a pale upper field and a dark russet lower one; the picture is built up in iron, gold, silver and copper, each metal chosen for its colour. At this scale the cat is a few millimetres of inlay. It weighs 28 grams.
context: A kozuka is the handle of the small utility knife that slides into a pocket on the side of a sword scabbard, and owners swapped and collected them as miniature pictures. This one is unsigned and dated by the Met only to the Edo period, ca. 1615–1868. It came to the museum in 1929 with the bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, part of a large group of Japanese sword fittings now in the Arms and Armor department. Fun fact: the Met catalogues a sword fitting like this as arms and armour, so a cat with a butterfly lives in the same department as plate armour.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat
description: A small seated cat, 12.7 cm high, lifts its plain cream head to one side with two dark dot eyes and big upright ears, while its body is swirled with chocolate-brown stripes like a marbled tabby. That marbling is agateware, the trick of wedging clays of different colours together so the pattern runs right through the body, and the Met's catalogue links this cat with it. It is salt-glazed stoneware from around 1745: salt thrown into the kiln at full heat vaporises and fuses with the clay, leaving a thin, faintly pitted skin of glaze. It weighs about half a kilo, so it sits firmly wherever it is put.
context: English potters of the 1740s made little salt-glazed animals alongside their teapots and jugs, and most of these figures were never marked. The Met owns three cats of this kind, all dated about 1745 (34.165.18, .19 and .20), given in 1934 by Carleton Macy; this is the middle one in size. Fun fact: the three are 11.4, 12.7 and 15.4 cm tall, yet the museum records each as weighing about one pound, so the smallest cat is, proportionally, the most solid of the set.
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Magdaleine Pinceloup de la Grange, née de Parseval
title_original: Magdaleine Pinceloup de la Grange, née de Parseval
collection: The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
description: Madame Pinceloup sits bolt upright, back parallel to her chair without touching it, and cradles a large grey-blue cat in the crook of her arm. The cat looks straight at us with mild bemusement, round yellow eyes and all, which is more than its owner manages; she gazes off to the left. Her dress is trimmed with flowers and blue ribbons, and the little gold bells on the cat's collar answer the pearls at her throat. The Getty identifies the cat as a Chartreux from its size and colour. Perronneau's signature and date sit at right, level with her ribbon. Oil on canvas, 65.1 × 52.4 cm.
context: Jean-Baptiste Perronneau, better known for pastels, signed and dated this oil '1747/ Perroneau'. It has a companion portrait of the sitter's husband, Charles-François Pinceloup de la Grange, in which he looks a good deal more relaxed than she does. The Getty bought the picture in 1984 from the Matthiesen Gallery, London. Fun fact: Perronneau put cats into several portraits of women and girls, including Marie-Anne Huquier with a kitten (Louvre), and the Getty argues the cats were there to underline the sitters' elegance. Here the matching bells and pearls suggest that cat and woman are both on display.
title_eng: Magdaleine Pinceloup de la Grange, née de Parseval
feline_symbolism: The Getty reads the Chartreux, one of the oldest French breeds, as a mark of refinement, its collar bells rhyming with the sitter's pearls so that both appear as elegant objects for looking at.
image_credit: Jean-Baptiste Perronneau · http://www.getty.edu/art/collection/objects/747/

title: The Trapped Cat and the Frightened Mouse (Rat ?), Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
title_original: صورة السنور في الشبكة والجرذ يخاطبه
culture: India, Gujarat (probably after an Egyptian original)
submovement: Gujarat Sultanate manuscript painting (Arabic Kalila wa Dimna)
medium: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; ink and opaque watercolor on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: The cat stands caught inside the hunter's net, drawn as a neat brown grid: a pale animal with dark spots, an orange collar and a curled tail. Just outside the mesh a dark, long-eared creature in a matching collar faces it, a blue animal slinks under the tree, and a big-eyed owl perches at top right. The Met hedges the rodent as mouse or rat with a question mark. The painting shares the page with Arabic text, a line of it in red; the leaf is 31.8 × 22.6 cm, with a text block of about 21.9 × 12.4 cm. The style is flat, all clear outlines and solid colour.
context: The folio comes from an illustrated Arabic Kalila wa Dimna, the book of animal fables descended from the Indian Panchatantra, painted in the second quarter of the sixteenth century. The Met attributes it to Gujarat, probably after an Egyptian original, which places it in the Gujarat Sultanate's lively trade with the Mamluk world. It entered the Met in 1981 with the Alice and Nasli Heeramaneck Collection, along with many other leaves from the same manuscript. Fun fact: the Met's own title keeps the zoological doubt on record, 'the Frightened Mouse (Rat ?)'.
title_eng: The Trapped Cat and the Frightened Mouse (Rat ?), Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
image_credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Myojakdo (Cats and Sparrows)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and light color on silk
description: Two cats and a tree full of sparrows. A grey tabby with white paws clings halfway up the trunk, claws splayed on the bark, and turns its face out toward us with round yellow eyes, tail swinging free; a black-and-white cat sits in the grass below, head tipped straight up. In the branches above, half a dozen sparrows chatter at them. Byeon paints it in ink and light colour on silk, 93.7 × 42.9 cm, a tall, narrow format that lets the climb run from the bottom of the scroll to the top. The fur is built from fine, close brushstrokes, the kind of detail that earned him his reputation.
context: Byeon Sang-byeok was a painter in the Dohwaseo, the Joseon royal painting bureau, active in the mid-eighteenth century. He helped paint King Yeongjo's portraits in 1763 and 1773 and was praised as a 'national hand' for portraiture, yet posterity remembers him for animals: his cats and chickens earned him the nicknames 'Byeon Cat' and 'Byeon Rooster'. Myojakdo ('Cats and Sparrows') is in the National Museum of Korea. Fun fact: the man who was paid to paint a king is now best known for a cat halfway up a tree.
image_credit: 국립중앙박물관 · https://www.emuseum.go.kr/detail?cateClass=&cateListFlag=&keyword=%EB%B3%80%EC%83%81%EB%B2%BD&pageNum=8&rows=9&reltRows=10&sort=&highQualityYn=&isImgExistOp=&mckoglsvOp=&isIntrstMuseumOp=&filedOp=&detailFlag=&dq=&ps01Lv1=&ps01Lv2=

title: The Cat of Kazan (Kot Kazanskiy)
description: A big striped cat sits bolt upright and stares straight out with round green eyes, whiskers fanned wide like a moustache, posed like a dignitary in a state portrait. The caption block at top left gives him his titles: 'Cat of Kazan, mind of Astrakhan, reason of Siberia', a mock string of honours in the manner of a tsar's style. His coat is dense black hatching that coils into a spiral on the haunch. Colourists often painted him yellow, but this impression spends its colour on the flowers and a little bird around him. It is a cheap popular print, made to be pinned to a cottage wall and laughed at.
context: Part of the vibrant tradition of Russian lubok folk prints—cheaply printed broadsheets hawked at Moscow marketplaces and pinned to peasant izba walls—this single portrait of the Cat of Kazan is an eighteenth-century spin-off of the older lubok The Mice Are Burying the Cat, and both name the cat 'Alabrys'. The historian S. F. Faizov reads Kazan, Astrakhan and Siberia as the khanates Muscovy conquered in the sixteenth century, and the cat as a composite figure of a Tatar ruler or of Peter the Great. The print is best known today through D. A. Rovinsky's catalogue Russian Folk Pictures (1900). Fun fact: Faizov points to the spiral ornament on the cat's coat, absent from earlier versions, as a coiled serpent, hinting at the Old Believers' view of Peter as the Antichrist.
location: State Historical Museum / Pushkin Museum, Moscow
feline_symbolism: Scholars read the cat as a mock ruler, either a conquered Tatar khan or Peter the Great, with titles that parody the tsar's own.
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Ровинский, Д. А. Русские народные картинки / собрал и описал Д. Ровинский ; посмертный труд печатан под наблюдением Н. Собко. — СПб .: Изд. Р. Голике, 1900. — Т. 1. — 370 с.

title: The Four Stages of Cruelty: First Stage of Cruelty
title_original: The Four Stages of Cruelty: First Stage of Cruelty (Plate 1)
collection: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven (impression shown); other impressions in the British Museum and elsewhere
description: Cats get the worst of this street. Over the wall at left, two cats hung by their tails from a lamp bracket claw at each other while a crowd of boys jeers. In the bottom left corner a dog is set on a cat whose entrails spill onto the cobbles. High up at the back, another cat, tied to a pair of bladders, is flung from a garret window. In the centre Tom Nero forces an arrow into a dog while a better-dressed boy offers his tart to make him stop, and the verses below spell out the moral. The line work is deliberately coarse.
context: Hogarth published The Four Stages of Cruelty on 21 February 1751, with verses by the Rev. James Townley, to shame the casual torment of animals he saw on London streets. He wanted the prints cheap enough for 'men of the lowest rank', so he kept the engraving rough, and even had the last two designs cut as woodcuts, which proved too expensive to issue. The image here is an impression in the Yale Center for British Art; the British Museum and many others hold impressions too. Fun fact: the kind boy with the tart has long been said to stand for the young Prince George, later George III.
title_eng: The Four Stages of Cruelty: First Stage of Cruelty
image_credit: William Hogarth · ewEJT9oTA1U1_A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Cat and Mouse (scent bottle)
title_original: Scent Bottle in the Form of a Cat
description: A grey-striped white cat sits up on its haunches and clutches a mauve mouse to its chest with both forepaws, green eyes turned skyward as if nothing happened. The whole animal is a scent bottle, small enough to close a hand around at 6.6 × 5.1 cm, with gold mounts at the necks of bottle and stopper, so the perfume came out of a cat that had just made a kill. It is glassy soft-paste porcelain painted in enamels and gilding on a scalloped gold rim. Turn it over and the domed base carries a bouquet in iron-red, blue, rose, yellow and green, a private flourish for the owner alone.
context: The Chelsea porcelain factory in London made these toys in the 1750s for a fashionable market that collected scent bottles, étuis and seals. This one is in the Gardiner Museum, Toronto (G83.1.971.1-.2), a gift of George and Helen Gardiner. When a similar cat-and-mouse bottle came up at Sotheby's in 1965 the model was called unrecorded; at least two more have surfaced since. Fun fact: that Sotheby's example has a collar mount enamelled with the motto 'CRUELLE ET BELLE', cruel and beautiful, which could describe the cat or the woman who carried it.
medium: Glassy (frit) soft-paste porcelain with overglaze enamels and gilding; gold mounts
feline_symbolism: On a sister bottle the motto 'Cruelle et belle' turns the cat with its prey into a flirtatious emblem of a beautiful, heartless lover.
image_credit: Chelsea porcelain factory · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: The Mice are Burying the Cat
collection: State Historical Museum, Moscow / The State Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg
description: The cat lies flat on its back on a sledge, broad, almost human face turned up and paws bound across its belly, while a long procession of mice hauls it off to the graveyard. Each mouse has its own job and its own joking caption: musicians, mourners, drink-bearers, a mouse urging the team on. Here they march in numbered rows above and below the bier, coloured in quick dabs of red and brown. In some versions a mouse still sits in the dead cat's mouth. The number of mice grew over the years, up to sixty-six, and some editions set the funeral in winter and others in summer.
context: A cornerstone of the Russian lubok movement, this carnival burlesque inverted feudal hierarchies by setting up an army of joyful rodent gravediggers to inter their mortal feline oppressor. This is one of the oldest and most reprinted Russian popular prints. The earliest surviving versions are woodcuts usually placed at the end of the seventeenth century; eighteenth-century editions were mostly engraved on copper, and nineteenth-century ones were lithographed. Nineteenth-century scholars, Rovinsky and Stasov among them, read it as an Old Believer satire on Peter the Great's funeral. M. A. Alekseeva later argued that this was anachronistic for the early versions, which she saw as carnival parody, not political attack. Fun fact: Stasov called it 'capital in the history of Russian popular development', high praise for a joke about mice.
title_eng: The Mice are Burying the Cat (Funeral of the Cat of Kazan)
feline_symbolism: Long read as a satire on a dead tyrant, usually Peter the Great, although recent scholars prefer to see a carnival parody in which the oppressor is mocked by the oppressed.
image_credit: Anonymous Russian painter (1670s-1917) Public domain image (according to PD-Russia-expired ) · http://philologos.narod.ru/lotman/lubok.htm

title: The Painter's Daughters with a Cat
title_original: The Painter's Daughters with a Cat
description: The cat is barely there: a ghostly ochre head with two dark eyes floats against the elder girl's yellow sleeve, a few strokes never taken further. Margaret, in front, cradles it while her older sister Mary wraps her arms around her, partly to help hold the squirming animal and, it seems, to pull its tail. The girls' faces are finished, Margaret's lips pursed as she eyes us sideways; almost everything else is not. Feathery gold, blue and grey strokes around them suggest storm clouds, sun and trees. Loose drawn lines still show in the unfinished hands and dress, laid in over a pinkish-brown ground. Oil on canvas, 75.6 × 62.9 cm.
context: Gainsborough painted his daughters Mary and Margaret around 1760–1, probably in Bath, a year or so after the family moved there. The picture stayed in the family: Margaret, then Mary, then the heirs of Gainsborough's sister Susannah Gardiner, until it was sold at Christie's in 1923 and bought by the National Gallery from Knoedler the same year. Fun fact: the cat was partly painted out in a yellow that does not match Mary's dress, perhaps because Gainsborough knew he would never finish it. When Richard Lane made a lithograph of the picture around 1827, titled The Orphans, he left the cat out entirely.
title_eng: The Painter's Daughters with a Cat
image_credit: Thomas Gainsborough · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/g/gainsbor/03daught"

title: Gukjeong chumyo: Autumn Cat in a Garden with Chrysanthemums
medium: Ink and light color on paper
description: A spotted cat crouches in an autumn garden beside a spray of chrysanthemums, ears up, gazing hard at something off to the left that we cannot see. Its coat is grey tabby stripes broken by big black patches, every hair laid in with a fine brush, and its yellow eyes are the brightest note on the sheet. Tucked and coiled, it could be wary or a second from pouncing. The painting is small, 29.5 × 23.4 cm, in ink with light colour on paper, and the rusty-pink flowers and grasses stay loose and airy so the attention goes to the solid little animal beneath them.
context: Byeon Sang-byeok, a court painter of the Joseon royal painting bureau active in the mid-eighteenth century, was so associated with animals that he was nicknamed 'Byeon Cat' and 'Byeon Rooster'. Gukjeong chumyo, 'Autumn cat in a garden with chrysanthemums', is in the Kansong Art Museum, Seoul, the collection built by Jeon Hyeong-pil to keep Korean art in Korea. Fun fact: Byeon was also a sought-after portraitist who helped paint King Yeongjo twice, in 1763 and 1773, yet his surviving reputation rests mostly on cats like this one.
title_eng: Autumn Cat in a Garden with Chrysanthemums
image_credit: Byeon Sang-byeok or Hwajae (Byeon's pen name) · [1] Image scanned from a pamphlet published from Gansong Art Museum.

title: White Angora Cat Chasing a Butterfly
title_original: Un chat angora blanc guettant un papillon
description: A white Angora cat, all plume and ruff, stops mid-stride and stares straight up. The title promises a butterfly, but what flutters over its head in this picture is a small grey-and-white bird, wings spread against dark foliage. Bachelier makes the long coat the real subject, building the fur in soft white masses, while the tail rises behind like a feather duster held up in alarm. The pink nose and upturned gaze make the cat's concentration look faintly absurd. This is a small cabinet picture of the kind an Académie painter of animals and flowers sold to private collectors, and the cat gets the attention a portrait sitter would.
context: Jean-Jacques Bachelier (1724–1806) was a painter of flowers and animals who also ran the decoration workshop at the Sèvres porcelain factory. At the Salon of 1761 he showed 'Un chat Angola qui guette un oiseau', an Angora cat watching a bird, a canvas of about 25 × 35 cm now in a private collection. The Musée Lambinet in Versailles owns a very close picture, a white Angora cat watching a butterfly, which is the one catalogued here. Fun fact: the Salon booklet spells the breed 'Angola', a common eighteenth-century confusion with Angora (Ankara).
title_eng: White Angora Cat Chasing a Butterfly
submovement: French animal painting of the Académie and Salon
image_credit: Jean-Jacques Bachelier · pic

title: Beautiful Woman Playing with a Cat
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
collection: Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities (Östasiatiska museet), Stockholm
description: The cat is tiny and very busy: a white kitten with a red ribbon rolls on the veranda boards at lower left, clawing at a flowered ball. A young woman in a long-sleeved furisode kimono, red over a pale robe sprinkled with blue irises, steps from a doorway, dangling the red string that leads to it. That is the whole drama, painted at the scale of a person: the scroll is about 179 cm tall. Ink and bright colours on silk. Beyond the veranda sit low stones and bamboo, painted in the manner of the Kano school, a polite nod to the official style framing a very unofficial game.
context: Tsukioka Settei (1710–1786) was the leading painter of beautiful women in Osaka, working in hand-painted scrolls instead of prints. This scroll dates from the 1770s and is in the Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities, Stockholm (OM-1984-0020), acquired through the London dealer David Newman with help from the museum's Friends. Fun fact: Settei signs it 'Hokkyō Tsukioka Settei gisha', which the museum translates as 'playfully painted by Tsukioka Settei of Hokkyō', using his honorary Buddhist rank to sign a picture of a woman teasing a cat.
title_eng: Beautiful Woman Playing with a Cat
submovement: Edo Period Kamigata School Bijin Painting
image_credit: Tsukioka Masanobu Settei (1710 - 1786) Details on Google Art Project · xgHA8xy1UPu5vQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Figure of a Girl with Cat
artist: Nymphenburg Porcelain Factory, model probably by Dominicus Auliczek
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
description: The cat has the high ground. It perches on top of a rococo scroll arch, one paw raised, peering across at a girl in a broad-brimmed hat who stands by a column and gazes straight up at it. The group, 24.5 cm high, was made at the Nymphenburg factory outside Munich around 1770 and left in plain white glaze, so everything reads through light and shadow. It is modelled in the round, the cat still legible from behind, meant to stand on a table or mantel where people would pick it up and turn it. Hard-paste porcelain lets the modeller pinch details very fine, down to the cat's tail.
context: The Cleveland Museum of Art credits the model, probably, to Dominicus Auliczek (1734–1804), who worked as a modeller at Nymphenburg in the generation after Franz Anton Bustelli. Before coming to Cleveland the figure belonged to Dr. Kurt Rossacher in Salzburg, from whom Severance and Greta Millikin acquired it in 1962; it came to the museum with Mrs. Millikin's bequest. Fun fact: Nymphenburg, founded in 1747, is still making porcelain today, so the factory that produced this girl and her cat has outlived almost every one of its eighteenth-century rivals.
title_eng: Figure of a Girl with Cat
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Nekomata: The Fork-Tailed Monster Cat (Gazu Hyakki Yagyō)
title_original: 画図百鬼夜行: 猫股 (ねこまた)
description: Three cats on one page, and they read like a before-and-after. At lower left an ordinary cat pokes its face out by the lattice of a shōji screen. On the right a cat with a hand towel over its head rests its front paws on the veranda, not quite able to stand. In the middle a striped third cat, also toweled, rears fully upright on two legs, forepaws up as if mid-dance. Above them hangs a round ornament sprouting a spray of leaves. Black ink only, cut into a woodblock and printed, so the drama comes from line and from the bare white paper.
context: Toriyama Sekien published Gazu Hyakki Yagyō ('The Illustrated Night Parade of a Hundred Demons') in 1776, a picture encyclopedia of yōkai in three volumes, Yin, Yang and Wind; the nekomata, the old cat that grows a forked tail and supernatural powers, appears in Yin. Sekien drew heavily on Sawaki Sūshi's 1737 painted scroll Hyakkai Zukan, but his innovation was to put the monsters into a cheap, reprintable book. Fun fact: one reading of this page sees it as a sequence, an ordinary cat, a cat still too young to walk upright, and an old cat that has fully turned nekomata.
title_eng: Nekomata: The Fork-Tailed Monster Cat (Gazu Hyakki Yagyō)
medium: Woodblock-printed book illustration; ink on paper
collection: Tokyo National Museum / National Diet Library
feline_symbolism: The nekomata stands for the fear that a cat kept too long will grow uncanny; folk belief linked such cats with stealing corpses.
location: Tokyo National Museum / National Diet Library
image_credit: Toriyama Sekien · http://www.linet.gr.jp/

title: Kasha (from Gazu Hyakki Yagyō)
title_original: 今昔画図続百鬼: 火車
description: The kasha comes out of a storm cloud to steal a corpse, and in Sekien's hands it is a shaggy cat-demon, wild-maned and wide-eyed, rearing on clawed hind feet. Sekien draws it in black ink for a woodblock-printed book, so everything depends on contrast: the dark, boiling cloud built from stippled dots, ribbons of flame trailing off to the right, and the white of the paper around it. A bushy tail swings down between its legs. It is a single page from a cheap illustrated encyclopedia of monsters, and it shows how a fear about funerals could be fixed into one memorable image.
context: The kasha ('fire cart') was a Buddhist-folklore demon that snatched the bodies of the wicked from funerals. Toriyama Sekien included it in the second volume, Yang, of his Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, published in 1776. Earlier pictures showed the corpse-thief as a hell warden or thunder god; by the late seventeenth century tales were giving it a cat's form, merging it with the nekomata, and Japanese scholarship credits Sekien's book with fixing the cat-shaped kasha in pictures. Fun fact: in Yamagata a 'kasha-cat' tail, said to be left behind when a priest drove the monster off a rich man's coffin, is shown once a year at the Hase Kannon hall in Nan'yō.
medium: Woodblock-printed book illustration; ink on paper
collection: Tokyo National Museum / National Diet Library
feline_symbolism: The cat-kasha draws on the belief that cats were drawn to corpses, making the cat the thief that robs the dead of a proper funeral.
image_credit: Toriyama Sekien · scanned from ISBN 4-0440-5101-1 .

title: Woman with a Cat
title_original: بانویی با گربه (Zand Dynasty Woman with a Cat)
collection: Shangri La Museum of Islamic Art, Culture & Design (Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art), Honolulu, Hawaii
description: The cat sits at the woman's feet in the lower right corner, pale and round-faced, with huge eyes fixed on us and a thin tail curling over the carpet. A full-length figure fills a canvas more than one and a half metres tall and not even ninety centimetres wide, a proportion that makes sense once you know Zand painters cut canvases to slot into palace wall niches; the pointed arch at the top still traces one. She raises a wine glass beside a bowl of red fruit and a glass flask. Shangri La catalogues the picture simply as Woman with a Cat, and the cat earns the billing.
context: The painting was made in Iran in the late eighteenth century, under the Zand rulers (c. 1751–1794), when large oil paintings decorated palace walls. Sotheby's notes on a comparable Zand canvas that paintings were cut to fit wall niches and that this shape was common in Zand royal residences. Doris Duke acquired it for Shangri La, her Honolulu house, now a museum of Islamic art, where it carries accession number 34.8. Fun fact: the picture lives a double life online. The museum's Google Arts & Culture record calls it Woman with a Cat, while Wikimedia Commons titles the same canvas Cupbearer with a Cat, a reminder that the androgynous beauties of Persian painting regularly confuse cataloguers.
image_credit: Anonymous Unknown author · https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/woman-with-a-cat-unknown/gwG4RAuhI5R8WA

title: Portrait of Julia Manteuffel née Duhamel with a Cat
description: A fluffy white cat lies cradled in Julia Duhamel's arms, head tipped back to gaze up at her, one pink-padded paw resting on her forearm. She smiles out at us under a blue-ribboned cap. The oval is a compact oil on canvas, about 65 by 52 cm, and the cat made it into the Polish title: Portret Julii z Duhamelów Manteuffel z kotem, 'with a cat'. A pet in a young sitter's arms was a standard trick for loosening up a formal portrait, and the 2018 Warsaw exhibition press photo simply captioned it Julia Duhamel with a Cat.
context: Marcello Bacciarelli (1731–1818), the Rome-born painter who became court painter to Stanisław August, Poland's last king, signed and dated a run of portraits of the Duhamel family around 1780–81; a companion portrait of Marianna Duhamel belongs to the same group. This one is now in the Raczyński Foundation collection at the National Museum in Poznań (FR 722). In 2018 it travelled to the Royal Castle in Warsaw for 'Marcello Bacciarelli. Najpiękniejsze portrety', a 44-work show marking two hundred years since the painter's death. Fun fact: the castle sourced the online image, which is likely why the catalogue entry had wrongly parked the painting in Warsaw.
title_eng: Portrait of Julia Manteuffel née Duhamel with a Cat
title_original: Portret Julii z Duhamelów Manteuffel z kotem
image_credit: Marcello Bacciarelli · www.zamek-krolewski.pl

title: The Angora Cat
description: A long-haired white Angora is the star, and it is busy: up on its hind legs on a rug-draped table, paws pressed to a glass gazing globe, ready to attack its own reflection. Around it the studio piles on textures for contrast: the young woman's pale yellow satin rendered fold by fold and a brightly coloured, long-fringed Turkish rug spilling off the table edge. She rests one hand on the globe and holds a fan in the other. Check the shadows: a man peers round the door, and a little spaniel scampers in at lower left. The canvas is a modest 65 by 53.5 cm.
context: The Wallraf-Richartz-Museum in Cologne dates the canvas c. 1783–85 and credits it to Jean-Honoré Fragonard (1732–1806) together with Marguerite Gérard (1761–1837), his young sister-in-law and pupil, who lived with the Fragonards in their lodgings at the Louvre from 1775. The city of Cologne gave it to the museum in 2011 for its 150th anniversary (WRM 3652). Fun fact: the joint attribution is fairly recent. The painting surfaced on the London dealer Colnaghi's stand as a Gérard alone, and only then was Fragonard's hand proposed, which is why some sources still list it under her name or date it 1780.
feline_symbolism: Angoras, the first long-haired cats known in Europe, were favourites at the French court from Louis XIII to Louis XVI, so the breed itself signals luxury.
image_credit: Jean-Honoré Fragonard / Marguerite Gérard · Rheinisches Bildarchiv Köln/Wallraf-Richartz-Museum&Fondation Corboud/Foto:Britta Schlier

title: Hwangmyo nongjeop: Yellow Cat Frolicking with a Butterfly
description: An orange-and-white cat crouches on the right of the sheet, body pulled tight, head twisted round to track a black swallowtail flapping above. On the left a rock is built up with soft, dry strokes, and red pinks (dianthus) grow beside it over a carpet of pale green grass. The butterfly's wing pattern gets the sharpest brushwork in the picture, as if Kim wanted it to be the thing the cat, and we, cannot stop looking at. The cat's tail stretches out straight behind, the one part of it not yet committed to the chase. Colour on paper, 30.1 by 46.1 cm.
context: Kim Hong-do (1745–c. 1806), known as Danwon, painted for the Joseon court for decades; King Jeongjo said he had let him do all the major court paintings for thirty years. An inscription at upper right gives his title as county magistrate and his name as Danwon, which ties the picture to his years as magistrate of Yeonpung in the 1790s. The leaf is now in the Kansong Art Museum, Seoul, and was shown in its 2015–16 exhibition at Dongdaemun Design Plaza. Fun fact: Kansong curator Baik In-san has suggested it may have been a birthday present.
title_eng: Yellow Cat Frolicking with a Butterfly
medium: Album leaf; ink and light color on paper
submovement: Late Joseon court painting (Dohwaseo painter, animal and flower subject)
feline_symbolism: Following Chinese wordplay, the cat stood for age seventy and the butterfly for age eighty, so together they wish the recipient a long life.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: The Cat's Lunch
description: A big long-haired cat, white with brown and black patches, sits on a red tasselled stool and is already lapping from the plate a young girl holds out. She half kneels at left in grey satin, turned to the right and smiling. The French inventory lists every prop as if taking stock of a kitchen: stool, drapery, ewer, bowl, spoon, and here they all are, green drapery under the cat, pewter ewer and spoon-filled bowl on the floor. A small black-and-white spaniel sits between girl and stool, staring up at the plate, presumably wondering why the cat gets served first. Fur and pewter get equal patience.
context: Marguerite Gérard (1761–1837) was born in Grasse and trained in Paris under her brother-in-law Jean-Honoré Fragonard, with whom she lived at the Louvre for about thirty years. The canvas (61 × 50 cm) went back to her home town: it belonged to Léon Chiris and was given to the town, which keeps it in the Musée Fragonard (inv. 2010.0.369). Fun fact: the French national database still dates it only loosely, to somewhere between the end of the eighteenth and the start of the nineteenth century, so the 'c. 1785' label is a guess.
image_credit: Marguerite Gérard · https://www.flickr.com/photos/repolco/7167210055/sizes/l/in/photostream/

title: Cat Fight (Riña de gatos)
description: Two cats square off on top of a brick wall, and that is the whole picture: no people, just two arched backs and a lot of sky. On the left a black cat bristles, tail low; on the right a grey tabby bares its teeth, one forepaw lifted. Ivy trails over the bricks, and a little weed sprouts between them. The canvas is about 56 cm high and nearly two metres long, a strip shaped to hang above a door. Goya studies the animals closely rather than prettily. The paint surface is softer than in his other cartoons, damage from decades rolled up under weight in damp storage.
context: Goya painted this cartoon between May 1786 and late 1787 as a full-size design, or cartoon, to be woven for the royal palace of El Pardo; sources disagree on the room, the Fundación Goya naming the king's conversation room and others the Prince of Asturias's dining room. It was listed in the 1834 inventory by Vicente López, reached the Prado in 1870 and then disappeared into the basement. Mercedes Águeda identified it in 1984 and it joined the displayed collection in 1986 (P006323). Fun fact: scholars still argue over it. Janis Tomlinson flatly rejects Goya's authorship, while Arnaiz finds it entirely in keeping with his style.
submovement: Tapestry cartoons for the Royal Tapestry Factory of Santa Bárbara
image_credit: Francisco Goya · http://www.museodelprado.es/es/pagina-principal/coleccion/galeria-on-line/galeria-on-line/zoom/1/obra/rina-de-gatos/oimg/0/

title: Felina with a Kitten
description: A white kitten is hugged up against a girl's shoulder, narrowed eyes and pink nose peering out of the crook of her arm, and the title does the joking: 'Felina' turns the child into a cat-girl before the kitten gets a look in. She grins at us from under russet curls in a pale gold dress, dark trees behind. The Detroit Institute of Arts records it as an oil on canvas of 1788. Holding a small animal kept a young sitter busy and gave the painter a second face to work with. Watch where fur meets skin: in late Reynolds those soft edges are where the paint loosens up.
context: Sir Joshua Reynolds (1723–1792) had been the first President of the Royal Academy since its founding in 1768 when he painted this canvas in 1788. Within a year his working life was effectively over: in 1789 he lost the sight of his left eye and retired. The picture is now in the Detroit Institute of Arts (F71.68). Fun fact: the catalogue ID for this entry points to Kenwood House in London, but every record I could open puts this canvas in Detroit, so either the ID inherited an old error or a second version is hiding in the files.
image_credit: Joshua Reynolds · https://www.dia.org/art/collection/object/felina-kitten-58340

title: Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zuñiga (1784–1792)
title_original: Don Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zúñiga
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: This photograph is a detail, and arguably the best part: three cats lurking behind the magpie. A calico, white with black and ginger patches, crouches with wide amber eyes; a grey tabby sits beside it, staring straight out; a black cat behind is nearly lost in the dark except for two round eyes. The magpie on its string holds Goya's visiting card in its beak, and the boy's white satin shoe peeks in at the right edge. Elsewhere on the 127 by 101.6 cm canvas a small boy holds that string beside a cage full of finches. Nobody in the picture has noticed the cats except us.
context: The sitter is Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zúñiga (1784–1792), son of the Count of Altamira, who commissioned the portrait; Goya painted it in 1787–88, and the boy died aged eight. The picture sold in Paris in 1878, belonged to the playwright Henri Bernstein, passed to the dealer Joseph Duveen in 1925 and was bought by Jules Bache in 1926 after his daughter Kathryn Bache Miller fell for it. It came to the Met with the Bache Collection in 1949 (49.7.41), yet hung periodically in Miller's apartment until her death in 1979. Fun fact: Goya slipped his signature into the plot by handing his card to the bird.
feline_symbolism: Commentators often read the caged birds as the innocent soul and the cats as a lurking evil force, a reading sharpened by the boy's early death.

title: A Lady with Her Cat
description: A large white cat with ginger patches on its head and a ginger tail sits on the table at left, head slightly tilted, fixing us with yellow-green eyes. Beside it a young woman in white muslin and a starched ruff rests her arm on a blue shawl and holds a small ring-shaped object, curls pinned up, a little gold earring catching the light. The cat's direct gaze mirrors its owner's composure, as if the two had agreed to pose together, and its tail hangs over the table edge like a bell-pull. The picture is small, 32.4 by 24.5 cm, and signed 'Mle Gerard' at lower left.
context: Marguerite Gérard (1761–1837) trained informally under her brother-in-law Jean-Honoré Fragonard and became one of France's leading women painters in the late 1780s, specialising in the private world of wives and mothers, with their children, servants and pets. Christie's, which offered the painting at auction, calls it a characteristic example of her mature style, with a cool, silvery palette and precise finish. Fun fact: the sale catalogue described it as oil on panel, and a saleroom notice then had to correct it to canvas, which is why online copies still disagree about its support.
feline_symbolism: Christie's reads the cat, like its mistress, as a charming example of comfortable domesticity.
image_credit: Marguerite Gérard · [1] [2]

title: Portrait of Marguerite Gérard with Her Cat
collection: Private collection (sold Ader, Hôtel Drouot, Paris, 3 November 2022, lot 28)
description: The cat peeps over the sitter's shoulder, a fluffy, dark-masked face with round eyes pressed against her cheek. This is a portrait of Marguerite Gérard, not by her: a roundel in black chalk, only 17.3 cm across. Her face is fully worked up, frank and faintly amused, while bonnet, kerchief and dress dissolve into loose outline, so the eye travels from her face straight to the cat's. On the original mount, outside this photograph, a four-line verse praises the sitter as formed by Love and the Arts, then grumbles that a cat is an odd companion and she ought to be holding the bird of Venus instead.
context: The drawing is attributed to Jacques-Augustin-Catherine Pajou (1766–1828) and dated to the end of the eighteenth or the start of the nineteenth century. It probably stayed in the Pajou family for generations, passing from Augustin-Désiré Pajou (1800–1878) down to Louise Marie-Saint-Germain, née Pajou (1855–1940), and appears as no. 117 in P. Nusbaumer's 1997 catalogue of the artist. It sold at Ader, Hôtel Drouot, Paris, on 3 November 2022 (lot 28) for €4,864, against an estimate of €3,000–4,000. Fun fact: the poet on the mount scolds Gérard for her choice of pet and offers Venus's dove as the proper accessory, a swap she evidently ignored.
title_eng: Portrait of Marguerite Gérard with Her Cat
title_original: Portrait de l'artiste avec son chat
feline_symbolism: The verse sets the cat against Venus's dove, so the cat reads as Gérard's own choice over the conventional emblem of love.
image_credit: Attributed to Jacques Augustin Catherine Pajou · Ader

title: A Woman and a Cat
title_original: 風俗美人時計 未の刻 (猫と遊ぶ女)
medium: One sheet of a triptych of woodblock prints; ink and color on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: The cat is the troublemaker at the bottom of the sheet: a white kitten with black patches and a red collar has tangled itself in the hem of a sheer robe, paws in the air, mouthing the fabric. Above, a woman kneels and lifts the gauzy garment, biting one edge to hold it, eyes lowered toward the culprit. A black lacquer sewing box with a pincushion stands behind her and scissors lie at lower left, so this was meant to be quiet needlework. The sheet, 38.4 by 25.9 cm, was once part of a woodblock triptych, each colour printed from its own carved block in register.
context: Kitagawa Utamaro (c. 1753–1806) designed this print around 1793–94, in the years when his pictures of beautiful women dominated Edo print publishing. The Met holds it as one sheet of a triptych (JP1672), from the H. O. Havemeyer Collection bequeathed by Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer in 1929. Fun fact: the catalogue entry had linked a different Met print, Utamaro's 'Woman and Child' (JP2812), whose subject tags list a woman, a child and fruit but no cat at all; the cat lives on JP1672.

title: Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat (Design 9)
title_original: The Poems of Thomas Gray, Design 9
description: Selima is half woman, half cat: she reclines in a pink gown, cat's ears poking up beside her bonnet, while a striped tabby tail curls up behind the printed page in an S. Below, her reflection floats upside down in faint pencil on the water among bellflowers and dusky fish. Blake's design 9 is built around this inlaid letterpress page of Gray's poem, worked in watercolour, pen, ink and graphite. Yale titles it from the lines 'The pensive Selima, Her ears of jet, and emerald eyes, She saw; and purr'd applause'. The sheet is 41.9 by 32.4 cm.
context: William Blake (1757–1827) made his illustrations to the poems of Thomas Gray in 1797–98, painting around pages of printed text. Gray wrote the ode in 1747 about Selima, a cat belonging to Horace Walpole that drowned in a tub of goldfish. The sheet is now in the Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Collection (B1992.8.11(5)), and appeared in 'William Blake: Burning Bright' at Yale in 2025. Fun fact: the leaf is double-sided, and its back carries design 10, 'Still had she gaz'd', so Selima's fatal lean continues over the page.
title_eng: Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat, Drowned in a Tub of Gold Fishes
medium: Watercolor with pen and black ink and graphite, with inlaid letterpress page
collection: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven

title: The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters (Los Caprichos, Plate 43)
title_original: El sueño de la razón produce monstruos
submovement: Los Caprichos satirical etching and aquatint (Goya)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A large cat, usually read as a lynx, sits on the floor at lower right with tufted ears and wide eyes, the one creature not fussing over the sleeper. A second, dark cat crouches behind the artist's back, only its glowing eyes picked out. The artist slumps over a desk, head buried in his arms, while owls and bats pour out of the dark; one owl pushes a chalk holder at him. Etching gives the crisp lines of feathers and fur; aquatint lays down the grainy night. The desk front carries the title, 'El sueño de la razon produce monstruos'. The plate measures 21.2 by 15.1 cm.
context: Goya worked on the image between 1797 and 1799 and published it as plate 43 of the 80 aquatints of Los Caprichos in 1799. A preparatory drawing of 1797 carries his note that his only purpose is to banish harmful, vulgar beliefs. The Met's impression (18.64(43)) was a gift of M. Knoedler & Co. in 1918. Fun fact: the art historian Philip Hofer argued that Goya first meant this image as the frontispiece of the whole set, then tucked it into the middle as number 43.
title_eng: The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters
feline_symbolism: Owls are often read as folly and bats as ignorance; one critic has Goya borrowing the lynx's piercing sight to expose such vices, which casts the wakeful cat as the clear-eyed exception.
image_credit: National Library of Medicine - History of Medicine · https://www.flickr.com/photos/nlmhmd/4379551324/

title: Figure of a Cat
description: A cat small enough to sit in two cupped hands: 10.2 cm high, 13.3 cm long and 7.6 cm deep, made in hard-paste porcelain at Meissen around 1800. It lies with front paws stretched out and tail curled round its flank, head up, staring straight ahead. Its patches are painted as fine hatched strokes, so the fur looks drawn rather than coloured, and the whisker pads are pricked out in dots. Hard paste is the dense, glassy porcelain fired at very high temperature, so body and glaze fuse into one skin. Figures like this were made for cabinets and mantelpieces, to be turned in the hand.
context: The Meissen manufactory in Saxony, founded in 1710, was the first in Europe to make true hard-paste porcelain. This cat dates from about 1800, well after the factory's famous mid-century animal sculpture, when small domestic subjects were steady sellers. It came to the Brooklyn Museum as a bequest of Dr. Grace McLean Abbate (81.53.6). Fun fact: the catalogue ID credits Johann Joachim Kändler, but Kändler died in 1775, a generation before this figure was made, so whoever modelled this cat, it was not him.
image_credit: Brooklyn Museum · Brooklyn Museum

title: Trompe-l'œil with a Cat and a Log through a Canvas
title_original: Trompe-l'œil avec un chat et une bûche de bois à travers une toile
description: A grey, fluffy cat pushes through a rip in a canvas, its face peering out above a sawn log lying across the hole. Everything is painted, the tear included, and we are looking at the back of a picture: bare canvas, wooden stretcher bars and wedged corners. Fish hang from a string on the upper right, and through a second tear at lower right sits a plate with something dark on it. Boilly lays out the props of a kitchen still life, log and fish, then lets the cat break the frame to get at them. At 85 by 96 cm the trick works from across a room.
context: Louis-Léopold Boilly (1761–1845), born in La Bassée and active in Paris, is credited with the first use of the term 'trompe-l'œil' for a painting: at the Salon of 1800 he showed layers of prints and papers under broken glass, titled 'Un trompe-l'œil'. Critics mocked it, the public admired it, and the word became the name of a genre. This cat picture is undated and in a private collection in Paris. Fun fact: in a genre built on fooling people, Boilly gives the cat the most believable motive in the picture, which is the fish.
title_eng: Trompe-l'œil with a Cat and a Log through a Canvas
image_credit: westudio.fr · Own work

title: A Cat in a Cage
description: A tabby cat crouches inside a gilded birdcage, body hunched, staring out through the bars, and the margins explain why: mice everywhere. They scurry over the sandy ground, sit up on a broken tree stump, nibble in pairs and peer from holes, a whole town out to enjoy the jailing of the enemy. Mind worked in watercolour, building fur from small strokes of thin colour over a light drawing, and the cage's thin gold bars cut across the cat's striped coat like ruled lines. Crumbling ruins and a blue mountain turn the joke into a landscape. Wikimedia Commons files the sheet under 'cats and mice in art', with good reason.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) was born and died in Bern. Apprenticed at about fourteen to the Swiss painter Sigmund Freudenberger, he learned drawing and watercolour, carved small wooden animals that sold as local decorations, and spent long hours at the city's bear pit. This sheet is dated about 1800. Fun fact: his nickname, 'the Raphael of Cats', is often credited to Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, who passed through Bern in 1807, though the attribution is shakier than the name's popularity suggests.
image_credit: Gottfried Mind · scanner

title: Cat and Three Kittens
medium: Print (copy of plate 2 of Mind’s Katzengruppen)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: A big mother cat, white with brown patches, crouches in a loaf with paws tucked in, eyeing a dish of spilled food and a ball of wool trailing its thread. Three kittens keep to the right, one curled behind her and two huddled in front. The Library of Congress catalogues this as a copy of plate 2 of Mind's Katzengruppen ('cat groups'), a published set of plates that spread his drawings far beyond Bern. The lettering below names Ch. Fenderich of Philadelphia and Childs & Inman's lithographic press, and the soft stippled grain, lightly tinted, shows how the printmaker translated Mind's watercolour fur.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) spent his life in Bern, where his cats, and his bears from the city bear pit, made him a local celebrity; in 1831 George Fairholme gathered his work into a collection called Mindiana. Prints after his drawings kept him in circulation long after his death. This sheet belongs to the Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts, pga.10607). Fun fact: the shelflist card names 'Fenderich', probably Charles Fenderich, a Swiss-born lithographer who worked in America, which would make this cat family an emigrant.

title: Cat Eating While Kittens Play
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: The mother cat is eating, and the kittens have decided this is the perfect moment to play. She crouches at left, eyes squeezed shut, gnawing a scrap at her paws, her big patched body ending in a tail that sweeps up in a curl. Behind her hind legs two kittens tussle, one pawing at the other's face. The digitiser describes it exactly so: a domestic cat eating while kittens play. It is a lithograph after Mind, drawn on stone with greasy crayon and printed in ink, so his washes become grainy tone. Head-down absorption against tangled young is the everyday cat behaviour Mind made his name on.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814), the Bern artist nicknamed 'the Raphael of Cats', drew and painted cats in watercolour; lithographs like this one, credited to Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), carried his compositions to buyers who would never own an original. The image comes from the Library of Congress and was digitally enhanced by rawpixel. Fun fact: Mind was not only a cat man. He spent so long at Bern's bear pit that his bear portraits were also highly regarded.

title: Cat Napping While Three Kittens Play
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: The mother naps, eyes closed, a broad patched cat lying low at the centre; her three kittens refuse to. One sits alert at far left, one stretches out to bat a crumpled ribbon, and the third clambers up her flank to peer over her back. Anyone who has lived with a litter knows the arrangement. The digitiser describes a domestic cat napping while three kittens play, and the saucer from the keywords sits off to the right, empty. The lithographic crayon turns sleeping fur into a soft, even grey, while the kittens' movement is carried by outline and placement. Mind's gift was noticing that rest and play need different drawing.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) learned drawing and watercolour as an apprentice to the Bern painter Sigmund Freudenberger, then spent his career on animals, above all cats. After his death, lithographs such as this one, linked to the lithographer Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), kept his designs in circulation. This image comes from the Library of Congress, enhanced by rawpixel. Fun fact: modern writers often call Mind an autistic savant, while nineteenth-century accounts described him in the harsher medical language of their day.

title: Domestic Cats
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: The mother cat has claimed the stool, a padded seat edged with studs, and leans over its rim to touch paws with a kitten below. Three kittens play around the legs: one sits under the seat looking up, one sprawls on its side tugging a string, and a patched one rears against a leg on the right. The digitiser's keywords pick out a soft chair and a stool, cats and play. Mind liked to set his animals on real objects, which gives the print a floor and a scale; a kitten beside a stool leg reads as small in a way it never would on blank paper.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) of Bern drew cats so persistently that the nickname 'Raphael of Cats' stuck to him; it is often credited to Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, who visited Bern in 1807. Lithographs after his designs, associated with Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), spread them in the decades after his death. This sheet is from the Library of Congress, enhanced by rawpixel. title: Cat and Puppy
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Not two cats, as the catalogue once claimed, but a cat and a puppy. The cat stands on top of a rough stone block, back arched and fur up, glaring down; the shaggy puppy rears against the side with front paws on the stone and mouth open, barking up at her. The digitiser describes a domestic cat and a playful puppy, with a block and a rock in the keywords, plus 'fighting', which is generous to the puppy. Broken chips of stone litter the ground. Interspecies scuffles were a favourite joke of animal printmakers, and here the cat wins on dignity and on altitude.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) is remembered as a cat specialist, but he drew other animals too, from the bears of Bern's bear pit to dogs like this one. He was apprenticed young to Sigmund Freudenberger and never left the orbit of his native city. This print after his design, linked to the lithographer Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), comes from the Library of Congress via rawpixel. Fun fact: the catalogue entry had renamed it 'Alert and Recumbent Felines', quietly turning the dog into a cat.

title: Cat and Three Playful Kittens
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: The mother cat strides off to the right, tail out straight, looking back at us with wide, faintly startled eyes, while three kittens tumble behind her. They are fighting over a length of wool: one rolls on its back with the thread in its mouth, one grips a scrap from above, and the ball has rolled away at lower left. The digitiser's description and keywords call it a wool rope. A loose cord is a draughtsman's gift: one curving line ties the group together and gives every kitten something to do. In lithograph it reads as a crisp dark line against the soft grey fur.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) worked in Bern, first as an apprentice to Sigmund Freudenberger and then on his own as a specialist in animals. His cats, mothers with kittens above all, became his signature, and lithographs after them, associated with Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), reached a wide buying public. This impression is in the Library of Congress, digitally enhanced by rawpixel. Fun fact: before his drawings sold, Mind carved small wooden animals that were popular as local decorations.

title: Cat with Three Newborn Kittens
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: The mother cat is a great round loaf of fur, crouched with paws tucked under, staring off to the left with wide eyes. The digitiser describes a domestic cat with three newborn kittens, and the keywords mention a saucer of food, toys, a wool rope, 'attention' and 'looking'. Here they all are: a dish with food spilling out, a ball of wool trailing thread, and three tiny kittens on the right, one creeping behind her and two huddled nose to nose. Newborns are hard to draw, little more than blunt heads and folded legs, and the lithograph has to make three near-identical lumps read as three animals.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814), born and died in Bern, drew mother cats with litters so often that it became his trademark subject. Prints after his designs, linked to the lithographer Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), carried that subject well beyond Switzerland after his death. The Library of Congress holds this sheet, here digitally enhanced by rawpixel. title: Cat and Kittens Drinking Milk from a Saucer
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: A big patched mother cat and a single striped kitten drink from the same saucer, heads almost touching, the kitten's front paw on the rim. The digitiser speaks of kittens, but this impression has only one. A saucer is the oldest trick in the cat painter's book: it pulls every animal toward one point, so even this mismatched pair becomes a composition. The mother's heavy body nearly dwarfs the kitten, and her tail flicks out behind. In the lithograph the milk is just untouched white paper, and the darker fur around it does the work of making it look wet.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814), the Bern artist known as 'the Raphael of Cats', drew this kind of everyday scene over and over, and lithographs after his designs, associated with Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), made them affordable after his death. This sheet is in the Library of Congress and was digitally enhanced by rawpixel. Fun fact: the Library also holds a near-identical subject, 'Domestic cat and kitten drinking milk from a saucer', signed 'CF' and numbered 3, so this cat and her saucer may appear twice in the catalogue.

title: Cats
description: Count them: three cats, a mother and two kittens, just as the old title promised. Commons titles this simply 'Cats', a watercolour by Gottfried Mind of about 1800. The tortoiseshell-and-white mother sits upright on a low wooden bench, one forepaw lifted, staring straight out with round amber eyes. Below, a ginger kitten wrestles a bench leg and a calico kitten guards a scrap on the floor. Watercolour suited Mind: thin, layered strokes build a coat hair by hair, and the bare paper stands in for a pale belly.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) was born and died in Bern and trained as a youth under the Swiss painter Sigmund Freudenberger, who taught him drawing and watercolour. His cats earned him the nickname 'the Raphael of Cats', often credited to Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun after her 1807 visit to Bern, and in 1831 George Fairholme compiled his work as Mindiana. Fun fact: modern writers frequently describe Mind as an autistic savant, a retrospective diagnosis that replaced the cruder labels nineteenth-century writers used.

title: Sword Guard (Tsuba)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: The cat is not hiding at all: it rears up on its hind legs at lower left, a gold cloth draped over its head and shoulder, tongue poking out, front paws raised as if mid-dance. Across the plate a grinning, balding old man in copper leans in, long gold-tipped nails curled over the rim. The guard, the plate between blade and grip, measures only 8.6 by 7.9 cm and 6 mm thick, yet weighs 164 grams of mostly iron. Gold, silver and copper glint against the near-black ground. The Met's tags name a man and a cat; the reverse is bare iron with incised rays.
context: Japanese, eighteenth century. In the long peace of the Edo period, sword fittings became a field for small-scale virtuosity, with metalworkers turning the guard into a picture surface for any subject a client fancied. This one came to the Metropolitan Museum of Art as part of the bequest of Edward G. Kennedy in 1932 (33.40.43). Fun fact: the Met record lists no maker and no school, and its tags pair a man with a cat, which is not the 'sleeping cat among peonies' the old catalogue text promised.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Le Chat mort (Study of a Dead Cat)
collection: Musée du Louvre, Paris (Département des Peintures)
description: A dead cat, grey-and-white, sprawled across a plain wooden block with its head hanging over the near edge and one foreleg dangling toward the floor. Géricault paints it in oil on a canvas 50 by 61 cm, close to the size of the animal itself, and gives the corpse the same attention he gave his human studies: no props, no owner, just the body and a hard light raking from the left against a near-black ground. Watch the ears and closed eyes droop downward, and how fast 'a cat' turns into weight, slackness and fur that no longer lies right.
context: Théodore Géricault (1791–1824), born in Rouen and dead in Paris at thirty-two, painted this study around 1820, though a Louvre caption reproduced on Commons gives 1824, the year of his death. The Louvre bought it in 2003 (RF 2003 6), and it hangs in the Department of Paintings in the Sully wing, room 941 at last report. Fun fact: the catalogue entry had placed the picture in the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Rouen with a 1938 bequest, an easy slip given the painter's birthplace, but the Louvre's own record shows a purchase in 2003.
title_eng: The Dead Cat (Study of a Dead Cat)

title: Domestic Cat and Kitten Drinking Milk from a Saucer
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: A stout tabby-and-white cat and her tiny striped kitten bend over a saucer of milk, two heads lowered to the same point and nearly touching. The mother is a broad, rounded mass with dark patches across her back; the kitten, front legs braced, stands on the far side with its tail curled up. The Library of Congress catalogues it as a lithograph, so Mind's watercolour becomes grainy greys and dark accents. A small '3' in the upper right marks it as one plate in a series, and 'CF' sits at lower right, beside the kitten. The sheet is 23 by 31.4 cm.
context: The design is by Gottfried Mind (1768–1814), the Bern artist nicknamed 'the Raphael of Cats'; the lithograph is credited to Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862) and dated between 1820 and 1860, so it postdates Mind's death. It belongs to the Popular Graphic Arts collection of the Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division (LCCN 2012645540). The Library's own staff devised the title. Fun fact: the 'CF' signature does not match either credited name, so a third hand, perhaps the draughtsman who copied Mind onto the stone, signed the print.

title: Domestic Cat Eating While Two Kittens Play
title_original: Katze frisst, während zwei Kätzchen spielen
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: A heavy-bodied tabby-and-white cat crouches at left with her head down over her food, a small rectangular scrap on the floor, eyes squeezed shut in concentration and tail curling up behind her. Tucked under her hindquarters, two kittens get on with the more important business of play, one pawing at the other's face. The sheet is black lithographic ink on paper about 23 by 32 cm. Check the corners: a printed 10 sits at upper right, the initials 'CF-' at lower right, and the cataloguers read a partial watermark, 'LHEU...', at bottom right.
context: The design goes back to Gottfried Mind (1768–1814), the Bernese draughtsman who spent his working life in the studio of the painter Sigmund Freudenberger and, after 1801, of Freudenberger's widow, drawing cats, bears and children. The stone was drawn by Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a lithographer and publisher born in Überlingen who worked in Zürich and Schaffhausen and died in Basel. The Library dates the sheet loosely to 1820–1860 and keeps it in its Popular Graphic Arts collection.
