Fun fact: Mind's nickname, “the Raphael of Cats”, is usually credited to Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, but the Public Domain Review points out that no primary record of her saying it survives; Champfleury seems to be the one who spread the story.
title_eng: Domestic Cat Eating While Two Kittens Play
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645552 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05443v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat Napping with Three Playful Kittens
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: The mother is nearly out for the count, eyes half shut, her bulk settled in the centre of the sheet; her three kittens are not. One sits upright at far left like a sentry, one sprawls in front of her batting a curl of ribbon, and the third clambers onto her back from the right, mouth open. An empty saucer waits at the right edge. The sheet measures 23 × 31.7 cm, carries a printed 6 at upper right and is initialled 'C.F.' at lower right. On the back someone pencilled '1227 U 5 D 57', a code that turns up on several sheets from the same group.
context: Brodtmann's lithographs carried Mind's cats well beyond Bern, where the artist died in 1814. Mind had been apprenticed at about fourteen to Sigmund Freudenberger, and his first job there was colouring his master's etchings of peasant life; animals took over only later. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a Swiss lithographer best known for natural-history plates such as Schinz's illustrated books on birds and fishes, put the drawing on stone. The Library of Congress dates the print between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: in the much-told studio story, the teenage Mind looked at a cat in one of Freudenberger's compositions, declared “That is no cat!”, and drew a better one, after which his master let him finish the figure.
title_eng: Domestic Cat Napping with Three Playful Kittens
title_original: Schlummernde Katze mit drei spielenden Kätzchen
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: https://lccn.loc.gov/2012645542 Image download: https://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05433v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc

title: Domestic Cat on a Stool Playing with Three Kittens
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: The adult cat has taken the high ground. She crouches on a padded, stud-trimmed stool and hooks one paw down over the edge toward the three kittens below, so the action runs up and down the sheet instead of across the floor. One kitten sits under the stool looking out at us, one lies flat beneath it, and the third stands on its hind legs at right, reaching up. A shallow dish sits at left. It is a lithograph in black on paper of 23 × 31.8 cm, with a 4 printed at upper right and 'C.F.' at lower right. Library of Congress staff supplied the title.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) made his cat drawings in Bern, in the studio first of Sigmund Freudenberger and then of Freudenberger's widow, who kept him on after 1801. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a lithographer and publisher active in Zürich and Schaffhausen, translated a run of them into numbered lithographs; the Library of Congress dates this impression between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: Mind's English biographer George Fairholme, in his 1831 Mindiana, described the artist at work with a favourite cat sitting “in the hollow formed by his neck & shoulders” while other cats warmed his knees.
title_eng: Domestic Cat on a Stool Playing with Three Kittens
title_original: Katze auf einem Schemel mit drei Kätzchen
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645541 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05432v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat Sleeping with Three Kittens Resting
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: Nobody is playing in this one, or almost nobody. A big tabby-and-white mother sleeps curled at right, eyes shut, with one kitten draped asleep across her neck like a scarf. At left, two more kittens rest in a heap, though one of them is wide awake and stares straight out of the sheet. The sheet is 23 × 27.1 cm, narrower than the numbered plates, and has no plate number. Instead a small round stamp at bottom centre reads 'im Museum zu Basel', which the Library records without explanation.
context: The design is Gottfried Mind's (1768–1814); the lithograph is by Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), the Überlingen-born printmaker who worked in Zürich and Schaffhausen and died in Basel. The Library of Congress holds the sheet in its Popular Graphic Arts collection and dates it between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: Mind's reputation came wrapped in the medical language of his day. Engravings published after his death called him “the Swiss cretin”, Fairholme's Mindiana (1831) used “cretin imbecile”, and later psychiatrists cited him as a case of preserved talent; modern writers often reclassify him as an autistic savant, a diagnosis nobody can now confirm.
title_eng: Domestic Cat Sleeping with Three Kittens Resting
title_original: Schlafende Katze mit drei ruhenden Kätzchen
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645539 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05430v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat Standing on a Block with a Playful Puppy
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: A cat stands on a rough stone block with its back arched high, ears flattened and head lowered, glaring down at a shaggy puppy who has planted both front paws on the block and gazes up hopefully. Broken chips of stone litter the ground beside them. The lithograph is printed in black on a sheet of 23.2 × 32 cm, with the number 7 at upper right and a pencil inscription on the back. Among the Mind cat plates the Library holds, it is the one where a dog gets a look in.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) was known in Bern for cats, but he also drew children at play and, above all, the bears of the city's bear pit, the Bärengraben, where he was said to get on unusually well with the animals. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862) turned a set of his animal drawings into numbered lithographs, and the Library of Congress dates this one between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: as a boy Mind passed through Pestalozzi's school for poor children, where the famous educator noted him down as “a strange creature, full of artist-caprices”.
title_eng: Domestic Cat Standing on a Block with a Playful Puppy
title_original: Katze auf einem Holzblock mit einem spielenden Welpen
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645549 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05439v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat with Three Newborn Kittens Beside a Saucer
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: A round, hunched mother cat sits in the middle of the sheet with her chin low and eyes wide, as if daring anyone to approach the three newborn kittens behind and beside her. One curls up at her back; two huddle in front at right, still blunt-faced and tiny. To the left lie a saucer of spilled food and a ball of yarn. The print is a lithograph on a sheet of 23.2 × 31.5 cm. A printed 2 at upper right marks one of the earliest plates, the paper is watermarked 'Basel', and the verso carries the code '1227 U 5 D 57'.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) drew cats in Bern for most of his adult life, working in the studio of Sigmund Freudenberger's widow after the painter died in 1801. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a lithographer who also produced natural-history plates for books on birds, reptiles and fishes, put this design on stone; the Library of Congress dates the impression between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: the Public Domain Review singles out Brodtmann's lithograph of a mother cat with three kittens as one of the ways Mind's cats reached a public far beyond the Bernese studio where, as one obituary put it, he “spent his whole life on the selfsame stool”.
title_eng: Domestic Cat with Three Newborn Kittens Beside a Saucer
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645547 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05435v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat with Three Kittens at Play
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: A mother cat strides off to the right, tail out straight and face turned to us with a wary look, while her three kittens roll in a knot behind her, tangled in a length of yarn with two little balls spilling loose. One kitten paws at a scrap of ribbon on its sibling's head. The sheet is a lithograph on paper measuring 22.7 × 27.2 cm, narrower than most numbered plates and without a plate number. A small round stamp at bottom centre reads 'im Museum zu Basel', and the credit 'Brodtmann nach Mind' is printed at lower right, keeping draughtsman and lithographer neatly apart.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) spent his career in Bern drawing cats, bears and children; Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862) made lithographs after him, and a Brodtmann sheet in the Swiss National Library carries the same “Brodtmann nach Mind” signature. The Library of Congress dates this impression between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: Mind's fame peaked half a century after his death, when the critic Champfleury used one of his drawings as the frontispiece of his 1868 book on cats, the same book Édouard Manet advertised with the poster known as “The Cats' Rendezvous”.
title_eng: Domestic Cat with Three Kittens at Play
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645538 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05429v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat with Two Kittens Inspecting the Ground
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: Three heads go down together. A broad tabby mother and two kittens nose at something small and dark on the ground, a scrap the Library of Congress cataloguers sensibly declined to name. One kitten creeps in from the left with its tail up; the other is pressed so close to its mother that their faces almost merge. A saucer of milk sits to the right. The lithograph is printed on a sheet of 23.1 × 31.8 cm with the number 8 at upper right. The paper is watermarked 'in Basel', and the verso carries the code '1227 U 5 D 57' shared with companion plates.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) worked in Bern, first as an apprentice to the painter Sigmund Freudenberger and later in the studio run by Freudenberger's widow, producing watercolours of cats grooming, hunting and playing. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a Swiss lithographer and publisher, put a numbered run of them on stone; the Library of Congress dates this impression between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: even Mind's admirer George Fairholme conceded that the artist “had not studied the anatomy of animals”, yet praised his accuracy all the same, and he noted visible corrections in Mind's drawings, a sign that the famous facility was worked for.
title_eng: Domestic Cat with Two Kittens Inspecting the Ground
title_original: Katze mit zwei Kätzchen bei der Untersuchung
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645550 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05440v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat with Two Kittens Playing with a Ball of String
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: A mother cat sits upright in profile, looking down at a striped kitten crouched in front of her with a ball of string trapped under its paws, the loose thread snaking off to the right. A second kitten peeks out from behind her back, watching the game with round eyes. The lithograph is printed on paper 23.6 × 32 cm, the largest sheet in this group, with the number 5 at upper right and a watermark reading 'in Basel' at bottom centre. The verso carries the pencilled code '1227 U 5 D 57' found on several sister plates.
context: The drawing behind this plate is by Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) of Bern; the lithograph is by Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), who also produced natural-history plates for Heinrich Rudolf Schinz's books on birds, reptiles and fishes. The Library of Congress dates the impression between 1820 and 1860 and holds it in its Popular Graphic Arts collection. Fun fact: Mind left a self-portrait, reproduced in an 1816 lithograph by Johann Heinrich Lips, in which he draws with a cat on the desk beside him and, for reasons nobody has explained, a dead frog in a jar.
title_eng: Domestic Cat with Two Kittens Playing with a Ball of String
title_original: Katze mit zwei Kätzchen und einem Wollknäuel
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645548 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05438v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Sleeping Cat
medium: Porcelain with overglaze color enamel and gold (Hizen ware)
description: A porcelain cat sleeps curled up, small enough to sit in two hands at 9.5 × 14.6 cm, chin resting on folded front paws and tail wrapped along its flank. It wears a red collar patterned in white, tied in a bow behind the ears, with a gold bell, the standard accessory for these models. The fur is the clever part. The Cleveland Museum of Art notes that very fine lines were incised into the clay and thin strokes of orange and gold brushed over the glaze, so the orange patches read as soft fur. Look at the closed eyes: two curved orange slits that make the nap look smug.
context: The cat was made in Japan in the early to mid-1800s, late in the Edo period, as Hizen ware, the porcelain of north-western Kyushu. Cleveland notes that sleeping cats with collars and bells were popular decorative objects, and that some were made to work as incense burners or hand warmers; this one was purely for display. It belonged to the Cleveland industrialist John L. Severance (1863–1936), passed to his relatives Severance and Greta Millikin, and came to the museum as their gift in 1964. Fun fact: in 2001 this little cat travelled to Australia for the exhibition Monet & Japan at the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra and the Art Gallery of Western Australia in Perth, where it appeared as catalogue no. 129.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Koma-neko (guardian cats) of Kijima-sha, Kotohira Shrine
title_original: 金刀比羅神社 狛猫
artist: Unknown stonemason (donated by Tango silk merchants)
description: Only one of the two stone cats makes it into this photo: the open-mouthed one, lichen-mottled grey granite, ears pricked, round eye fixed ahead and whiskers carved as fine grooves on the muzzle. Behind it hang a straw rope and paper streamers, and a wooden signboard names the Kijima shrine (Kijima-sha) inside the precinct of Kotohira Shrine in Mineyama. The pair follow the komainu script: facing the shrine, the left cat opens its mouth on 'a' and holds a kitten against its body; the right cat keeps its mouth shut on 'un'. A Kyotango photo archive reads them as mother and father.
context: Kotohira Shrine was founded in 1811 by the lord of the Mineyama domain on the Tango peninsula, a district that lived by silk and is still known for Tango chirimen crepe. The deity of the Kijima sub-shrine is a god of sericulture, and cats earned their place by keeping rats and mice away from silkworms and cocoons. According to the Kyotango photo archive, the statues were donated in 1832 by silk merchants and wholesalers, among them the Tonomura family and Komuro Rishichi of the Sanyaya house in Iwataki. Fun fact: the local tourism office calls this the only shrine in Japan with koma-neko in place of koma-inu, a claim not independently tested here; since a 2011 local project the grounds have also filled with some 400 ceramic cats.
title_eng: Koma-neko (guardian cats) of Kijima-sha, Kotohira Shrine
collection: Kijima-sha, Kotohira Shrine (金刀比羅神社), Mineyama, Kyōtango, Kyoto Prefecture
submovement: Late Edo Shinto Stone Shrine Sculpture
feline_symbolism: The cats are working guardians: the sub-shrine's deity protects sericulture, and the statues honour the animals that kept rodents away from the silkworms.
image_credit: Asturio Cantabrio · Own work

title: Girl in Red Dress with Cat and Dog
title_original: Girl in Red Dress with Cat and Dog
collection: American Folk Art Museum, New York
description: The white cat lies stretched across the girl's red lap, held in both her hands, its tail hanging down in an S-curve against the dress and its pink-rimmed eyes turned toward us. After the dress it is the brightest thing here. The girl wears a coral necklace and lace-trimmed sleeves. A brown-and-white dog lies on the floor at lower left. The painting is oil on canvas, about 30 by 25 inches. Of four similar Phillips portraits of children in red with a dog on the floor, this is the only one where a cat gets in.
context: Ammi Phillips (1788–1865), born in Colebrook, Connecticut, was an itinerant portrait painter who moved between towns such as Troy, Rhinebeck and Amenia in New York and New Marlborough in Massachusetts; more than 800 portraits are attributed to him, but only eleven are signed. This one dates to about 1830–1835, when he lived in Dutchess County, New York. It was bought for the American Folk Art Museum in 1985, reportedly for about a million dollars (a contemporary report gives a $682,000 bid), and appeared on a 1998 US postage stamp. Fun fact: Phillips was lost for decades. His 1830s portraits were credited to an anonymous “Kent Limner”, named after a 1924 antiques show in Kent, Connecticut, until Barbara and Larry Holdridge showed in 1958 that Phillips had painted the anonymous groups.
title_eng: Girl in Red Dress with Cat and Dog
image_credit: Ammi Phillips · Collection American Folk Art Museum, New York, Gift of the Siegman Trust, Ralph Esmerian, trustee, 2001.37.1, Photo by John Parnell, New York

title: The Peaceable Kingdom
collection: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (de Young museum)
description: Hicks's leopards are why this painting is here, and there are two: one prowls across the lower left with its mouth open, the other lies below it with its chin down and a wide-eyed stare. Following Isaiah 11:6–9, the animals of the prophecy gather in the foreground with children, everyone suspiciously calm, a white-faced ox and a heavy-maned lion at the centre, a lamb and a wolf at lower right. In the distance William Penn makes his 1682 treaty with the Lenape, a ship at anchor behind them. This late version, around 1846, is oil on canvas, 63.5 × 72.4 cm.
context: Edward Hicks (1780–1849) apprenticed with coach makers in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, worked as a coach, house and tavern-sign painter, and was recorded as a Quaker minister in 1812. He painted about sixty versions of The Peaceable Kingdom from around 1820 until his death. This one, of about 1846, was given to the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco by Mr. and Mrs. John D. Rockefeller 3rd and is shown at the de Young. Fun fact: the series ran alongside a church quarrel. In 1827 the Friends split into Hicksite and Orthodox factions, and the conflict discouraged Hicks from preaching, while painting, which had become his main income, kept repeating the same message of peace.
feline_symbolism: In Isaiah's prophecy the leopard lying down with the kid marks the end of predation in God's kingdom, and Hicks uses the big cats as the hardest test case for that peace.
image_credit: Edward Hicks · tAHzgNBfxNbfkw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Embroidered Carpet (the Caswell Carpet)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Find the blue cat: it sits in a square on the bottom row, deep blue with a white bib, amber eyes and stitched whiskers, set against a striped ground. It has company. Two squares to the left, a pair of grey cats lounge on another striped panel, and in the left column two puppies cuddle in a third. The Met's tags list birds, flowers, plants and a dog, and the blue cat later got a children's book of its own. The whole carpet is wool worked in chain stitch, 396.2 × 373.4 cm, made for walking on. The initials 'ZHG' and '1835' are stitched along the top edge.
context: Zeruah Higley Guernsey (1805–1899; Caswell after her marriage) embroidered the carpet in Castleton, Vermont, between 1832 and 1835. The Metropolitan Museum received it in 1938, a gift of Katharine Keyes in memory of her father, Homer Eaton Keyes, and catalogues it plainly as Embroidered Carpet. Fun fact: in 1946 the writer Catherine Coblentz visited Castleton, and the librarian Hulda Cole told her about a local girl whose embroidered carpet now hung in the Metropolitan Museum. Its blue cat became the hero of Coblentz's The Blue Cat of Castle Town (1949), a Newbery Honor book in 1950.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Self-portrait (frontispiece to vol. 2 of Chinpen shinkeibai)
description: The cat gets the cushion. A black-and-white cat sprawls asleep on the patterned floor cushion at right, a tabby curled against it, while two more cats doze at lower left. Kuniyoshi pictures himself from behind, kneeling by his desk of books, having given up his seat, a domestic joke his readers would have caught at once. His robe, swirling with flames and dragon scales, was his personal emblem, which is how buyers knew this was the artist although the book is signed with a pseudonym. A long pipe (kiseru) lies at lower right. It is a woodblock-printed book page, so the self-portrait came in every copy.
context: The book is Chinpen shinkeibai (枕辺深閏梅), an erotic illustrated book (enpon) written by the fiction writer Hanagasa Bunkyō and illustrated by Kuniyoshi; the self-portrait is the frontispiece of its second volume, and the Commons copy dates it 1839. Because the book was erotic, Kuniyoshi signed with a joke name, Ichimyōkai Hodoyoshi, and let the cat and the clothes identify him. Fun fact: his cat habit is well documented. He is said to have kept anything from a few to more than a dozen cats and to have worked with them tucked inside his kimono; dead cats were buried at the temple Ekō-in, and the household kept memorial tablets and a death register for them.
title_eng: Self-portrait (frontispiece to vol. 2 of Chinpen shinkeibai)
title_original: 枕辺深閏梅 下巻口絵 (自画像)
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat on the cushion works as a signature: it stands in for Kuniyoshi himself, letting readers recognise the artist behind the pseudonym.
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · http://visipix.com/search/search.php?userid=1616934267&q=%272aAuthors/K/Kuniyoshi%201797-1861%2C%20Utagawa%2C%20Japan%27&s=23&l=en&u=2&ub=1&k=1

title: Cats' Lesson (Neko no keiko)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e, uchiwa-e format); ink and color on paper
description: Three cats in kimono take a lesson, and the clothes carry the jokes. At right a black-and-white cat in blue robes plucks a shamisen, mouth open mid-song; at left a pupil in a blue-and-white robe leans over a text set on a wooden stand, and behind them an orange-and-white cat squints at a songbook. The teacher's robe is said to be patterned with bells, gold koban coins and pawprints, the pupil's with cat treats. A red lantern hangs above. It is a fan print (uchiwa-e): the pale rounded cut-out at the bottom marks the fan's outline, so it was made to be waved and worn out.
context: Kuniyoshi designed this comic print (giga) in 1841 (Tenpō 12). The date matters: the Tenpō Reforms of 1841–1843 banned prints of actors and beauties and put Kuniyoshi under the magistrates' eye, and he answered with workarounds such as giving fish the faces of actors. Anthropomorphic cats were part of the same sly repertoire, though whether this sheet hides particular real people is not recorded. Fun fact: Kuniyoshi's cats were famous enough in their own right that the comic writer Kanagaki Robun worked them into a passage of one of his humorous books.
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Unknown source Unknown source

title: Series of Proverbs (Tatoe-zukushi no uchi), right sheet of a triptych
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: Four cats on one grey sheet, each acting out a saying. Top left, a calico sits with its back to us, gazing up; top right, a ginger cat folds into a perfect loaf, eyes shut, a red spotted collar round its neck, next to a pair of dried fish. Below, a white-and-black cat stretches with its head ducked under its own body, and a calico at bottom right sits up licking a raised paw. A rice cracker and a wooden ladle lie on the floor. This is the right-hand sheet of a triptych in which Kuniyoshi illustrates proverbs with cats, so this is a third of the joke book.
context: Tatoe-zukushi no uchi (From a Collection of Proverbs) was published in the 4th month of 1852 by Kagaya Yasubei, late in Kuniyoshi's career; the Kuniyoshi Project's series list sums it up as “Proverbs illustrated by cats”. By then he had been putting cats to work for over a decade, from comic fan prints to the c. 1842 Neko no ateji, in which cats contort themselves into the kana of fish names. Fun fact: Kuniyoshi is said to have had a particular weakness for spotted cats and to have pushed his pupils to draw cats too, which may explain why calicoes keep turning up in his sheets.
title_eng: Series of Proverbs (Tatoe-zukushi no uchi), right sheet of a triptych
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · http://visipix.com/search/search.php?userid=1616934267&q=%272aAuthors/K/Kuniyoshi%201797-1861%2C%20Utagawa%2C%20Japan%27&s=15&l=en&u=2&ub=1&k=1

title: Cat and Mice (Neko to nezumi), from Shingaku osanae toki (Moral Philosophy Illustrated for Children)
artist: Utagawa Kuniyoshi (Ichiyūsai Kuniyoshi, 歌川国芳)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
collection: Private collection, Japan (exhibited at the Osaka Museum of History)
description: A grey-headed cat in a dark patched robe sits cross-legged at lower left, grinning with its fangs out and reaching toward a white mouse in blue robes with a pair of chopsticks. The mouse sips calmly from a cup beside a tray of food and sake. The verse above reads osoroshii mono o nyan to mo omowazaru kokoro kara mi o tsui ni toraruru, rendered on Commons as 'anyone so ignorant as not to fear the danger would lose his life anytime soon.' Read the fourth word again: where the sense needs nan to mo, the poem says nyan.
context: Kuniyoshi published the series Shingaku osanae toki around 1842 (Tenpō 13) with the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi; the Kuniyoshi Project translates the title as “Moral philosophy illustrated for children” and lists it among his comic prints. The impression shown here belongs to a private collection and was lent to an exhibition of cats in ukiyo-e at the Osaka Museum of History. Fun fact: the cat gets into the grammar. Swapping nan to mo (“not at all”) for nyan to mo turns a sober warning about danger into a miaow, so the predator is audible in the very line that warns about it.
title_eng: Cat and Mice (Neko to nezumi), from Shingaku osanae toki (Moral Philosophy Illustrated for Children)
title_original: 心学稚絵得 猫と鼠
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat is the danger the careless mice fail to respect, a predator used as a warning for children.
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · https://kyobashi.keizai.biz/photoflash/4224/ 京橋経済新聞

title: Emma Homan
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: The cat is climbing the rose bush. A grey tabby stands on its hind legs on the rim of a terracotta pot at lower left, front paws hooked into the branches, yellow eyes turned toward us among the pink roses. Beside it, a small girl in a frilled white bonnet, coral necklace and brown dress picks a rose. She was about two when John Bradley painted her, around 1844, and he gave her the full formal portrait anyway, on a canvas of 86.4 × 68.9 cm. Bradley's manner ran to rich colour, light outlines and plenty of detail: look for the fallen rose on the patterned carpet.
context: John Bradley was a British-born painter who worked in New York in the 1830s and 1840s; city directories list him as a portrait painter from 1836 to 1847 at addresses on Hammersley and Spring Streets in today's SoHo, after which he vanishes from the record. The sitter, Emma Homan (1842–1908), daughter of the businessman George W. Homan, grew up to be Emma Homan Thayer, botanical artist and author of Wild Flowers of Colorado (1885), so the flowers in her toddler portrait turned out to be a forecast. The Met received the painting in 1966 from Edgar William and Bernice Chrysler Garbisch. Fun fact: Bradley could not spell his homeland; five portraits are inscribed “Drawn by I. Bradley from Great Britton”.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Kamada Matahachi Slaying the Monster Cat of Mount Suzuka
title_original: 鎌田又八勢州松坂の人無双強力なり同国鈴鹿乃山中にてとしふる大猫を殺す (inscription)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: The cat is enormous, which is the whole point. Its white, orange and black-spotted body fills the sheet, claws splayed at the corners, yellow eyes wide and fangs bared, while Kamada Matahachi crouches on top of it and drives his sword down toward its head. His robe is patterned with blue dragons; pink begonias and broad leaves spill up from the bottom. The inscription says Kamada Matahachi of Matsusaka in Seishū (Ise Province) was a man of matchless strength who killed a great cat grown old with years in the Suzuka mountains. The sheet is a vertical oban woodblock print, 36.2 × 25.2 cm.
context: Kuniyoshi designed the print in the mid-19th century; the British Museum, which holds this impression (2008,3037.21219), dates it no more closely and points readers to B. W. Robinson's 1982 supplement to his catalogue of Kuniyoshi prints. Matahachi was a local hero of legend from Matsusaka, and his fight sits within the Edo taste for monster-cat stories on stage and in print. Fun fact: the inscription's toshifuru ōneko, “great cat grown old”, explains the monster in two words. Folk belief across Japan held that aged cats turned into bakeneko, with tales from Ibaraki and Nagano naming twelve years as the tipping point.
title_eng: Kamada Matahachi Slaying the Monster Cat of Mount Suzuka
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat is a bakeneko-type monster: in Edo folklore great age turned a house cat into something supernatural, and the hero's victory restores order.
image_credit: Print artist:Utagawa Kuniyoshi (歌川国芳) · https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/A_2008-3037-21219

title: Ō itai (Ouch! That Hurts!), No. 7 from Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: A cream-coloured cat in a red collar squirms upside down against the woman's chest, front paw on her collar and mouth clamped on her fingers, and the title tells you how that is going: Ō itai!, 'Ouch! That hurts!'. She looks down at it with a surprisingly calm face. The British Museum describes the main scene simply as a woman playing with a cat. In the inset above, a fisherman in a small boat wrestles the big octopus of Namerikawa in Etchū Province named in the cartouche. It is a vertical oban woodblock print, 36.9 × 25.2 cm, number 7 of its series.
context: The series is Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated), published in the 8th month of 1852. Each sheet pairs a half-length woman with an inset of a famous regional product, and according to the British Museum's notes the insets were done by Kuniyoshi's pupils; Commons also lists Utagawa Yoshitori among the hands. Fun fact: the titles riff on the series' medetai (“auspicious”) by ending in -tai, so this sheet is ō itai, no. 19 is hayaku kimetai (“I want to settle it quickly”) and no. 2 is hayaku mitai (“I want to see it soon”).
title_eng: Ō itai (Ouch! That Hurts!), No. 7 from Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated)
title_original: 山海愛度図会 ヲゝいたい 越中滑川 大蛸 七
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · http://visipix.com/search/search.php?userid=1616934267&q=%272aAuthors/K/Kuniyoshi%201797-1861%2C%20Utagawa%2C%20Japan%27&s=19&l=en&u=2&ub=1&k=1

title: Hayaku kimetai (I Want to Settle It Quickly), No. 19 from Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: While the woman reads a printed fortune, the cat behind her shoulder has decided the future can wait: a cream cat with black patches on its head and back, curled into a ball with eyes shut and chin tucked down. That is the British Museum's own description of the scene, and the title on the sheet, Hayaku kimetai ('I want to settle it quickly'), supplies her side of the mood. The inset shows fishermen on the shore with baskets, harvesting the octopus of Takasago in Harima Province. It is a vertical oban woodblock print, 35.2 × 25.2 cm, number 19 in its series.
context: This is no. 19 of Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated), published in the 8th month of 1852, a series pairing half-length women with insets of regional products drawn by Kuniyoshi's pupils. The British Museum holds this impression (2008,3037.02115). Fun fact: the series title on the sheet writes medetai as 愛度, with the characters for “love” and “degree”, instead of the usual 目出度, a small bit of wordplay that turns “auspicious” into something closer to “degrees of affection”.
title_eng: Hayaku kimetai (I Want to Settle It Quickly), No. 19 from Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated)
title_original: 山海愛度図会 はやくきめたい 播州高砂 蛸 十九
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Sheet from Myōdensu jūroku rikan (Sixteen Wonderful Considerations of Profit)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: A white cat with orange patches burrows into the hem of the woman's striped robe, tail up, teeth bared on the fabric, while she kneels over a bowl at her toilette. A Buddhist holy man with a halo watches from a hanging scroll at upper right. The British Museum's records show that Kuniyoshi slipped a cat into at least two of the sixteen designs: one beside a woman at her toilette, another crawling into the outer robe of a woman seated at a stove. Here the cat seems to do both jobs at once.
context: The series, Myōdensu jūroku rikan (Sixteen Wonderful Considerations of Profit), was published around 1845 by Enshūya Matabei. Its title is a pun: rikan (利勘), reckoning profit, stands in for rakan (羅漢), the Buddhist arhats, so the Sixteen Arhats become sixteen object lessons. Each woman's sheet carries a mock-arhat name; the National Diet Library copies include Asane sonja, the late riser, and Tanki sonja, the short-tempered one. Fun fact: those names write sonja with 損, the character for “loss”, so the venerable ones become, roughly, the venerable losers.
title_eng: Sheet from Myōdensu jūroku rikan (Sixteen Wonderful Considerations of Profit)
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Okabe, from Tōkaidō gojūsan tsui (Pairs for the Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: The cat fills the whole upper left of the picture: a huge, ghostly grey head with pricked ears, glowing yellow eyes and bared teeth, rising like smoke behind the old woman. She leans forward, white hair streaming, toward a young girl who flinches away at lower left. The station is Okabe on the Tōkaidō, and the print turns on a belief recorded with it: a girl who reached a temple after dark might be offered lodging by an old woman, who would become a witch, take the shape of a cat and devour her. It is a large vertical oban print published by Ibaya Kyūbei.
context: The print belongs to Tōkaidō gojūsan tsui (Pairs for the Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō), published between 1844 and 1847, in which each post station on the road from Edo to Kyoto is paired with a story. The Japanese notes on the Commons copy tie this one to a kabuki play by Tsuruya Nanboku IV, Hitori tabi gojūsan-tsugi (独道中五十三駅). Fun fact: the cat may have been borrowed from down the road. The scene those notes cite is the play's “bakeneko of Okazaki”, a different station, while Okabe had its own hook: a cat-shaped rock said to sit on Mount Utsu.
title_eng: Okabe, from Tōkaidō gojūsan tsui (Pairs for the Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō)
title_original: 東海道五十三對 岡部
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat here is a shapeshifter: Edo folklore credited old cats with turning into bakeneko that could take human form, and the old woman who is really a cat is one of its stock figures.
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · http://visipix.com/search/search.php?userid=1616934267&q=%272aAuthors/K/Kuniyoshi%201797-1861%2C%20Utagawa%2C%20Japan%27&s=23&l=en&u=2&ub=1&k=1

title: The Favorite Cat
dimensions: Image: 31 × 22 cm; image and text: 33.7 × 22.1 cm; sheet: 35.3 × 25.6 cm
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A tabby cat sits for its portrait, square to the viewer, head and broad chest filling the frame, round yellow-green eyes wide open and a pink nose the only other touch of colour. The forehead is splashed with dark leopard-like spots, the whiskers are long fine lines, and the chest fur is built from soft curved bands. The title, The Favorite Cat, does the sentimental work in three words, lettered beneath with Currier's imprint. The Met catalogues it as a hand-coloured lithograph, the picture 31 × 22 cm, the printed area 33.7 cm high with lettering. The colour went on by hand, so no two impressions match exactly.
context: Nathaniel Currier, credited by the Met as publisher, ran his New York shop alone as “N. Currier, Lithographer” from 1835 until 1856; his bookkeeper James Merritt Ives became a full partner in 1857, when the name Currier & Ives first appeared. The Met dates this print 1838–48, squarely in the solo years. It came to the museum with the bequest of Adele S. Colgate in 1962. Fun fact: the colouring was an assembly line. A dozen or more women, often German immigrants with some art training, each added one colour and were paid six dollars per hundred prints; small prints sold for between five and twenty cents.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Onoe Kikugorō III (Baijū), Ichimura Uzaemon XII and Sawamura Sōjūrō V in Onoe Kikugorō ichidai banashi
title_original: 尾上菊五郎の鍋島の化猫
artist: Utagawa Kunisada (Toyokuni III, 歌川国貞)
description: The cat looms across the top of the right and centre sheets: a giant spotted head with glowing yellow eyes and a red, fanged mouth, floating behind the actors, while ghostly red flames burst from the middle panel. Below it, Kikugorō, the centre figure under his new retirement name Onoe Baijū, plays the cat spirit of the Okazaki story as a wild-haired old woman, crouched in a heap of patterned robes. Ichimura Uzaemon XII and Sawamura Sōjūrō V flank him, swords at the ready. Kunisada, signing as Toyokuni on each sheet, gives the actors their stage likenesses in full nishiki-e colour across three sheets, one stage.
context: The print advertises a real event: the programme Onoe Kikugorō ichidai banashi, staged at the Ichimura theatre in the seventh month of 1847 as Kikugorō III's farewell run of greatest hits. Kunisada (1786–1865), the most prolific actor-print designer of his day, worked these names into the cartouches so buyers could collect the show. His rival Kuniyoshi made his own triptych of the same programme, with Kikugorō as Usugomo and a giant cat-ghost looming in a ruined temple; a copy of that one is in the Worcester Art Museum. Fun fact: the cat-ghost role was already old by 1847. Kikugorō had first made the Okazaki cat famous at the Ichimura theatre in 1835, and the farewell show brought it back one more time.
title_eng: Onoe Kikugorō III (Baijū), Ichimura Uzaemon XII and Sawamura Sōjūrō V in Onoe Kikugorō ichidai banashi
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
submovement: Late Edo Kabuki Actor Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: In the Okazaki plays the cat is a bakeneko, an aged cat that has turned into a shape-shifting demon and disguises itself as an old woman.
image_credit: Utagawa Kunisada · Internet

title: Scene at Okazaki: Onoe Kikugorō III as the Spirit of the Cat Stone (Gojūsan-tsugi no uchi Okazaki no ba)
medium: Woodblock print triptych (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: A giant cat face fills the smoke behind the centre sheet, all whiskers and saucer eyes. Below it sits Onoe Kikugorō III as the Neko-ishi no kai, the spirit of the cat stone, cat ears poking from grey hair, conjuring the monster against the samurai Shirasuga Jūemon, played by Mimasu Gennosuke I on the right. Ichimura Uzaemon XII, as the young lord Inabanosuke, holds the left sheet beside a lantern that shows a cat's shadow. Two small cats in headscarves dance on their hind legs. It is an actor print first: three tall ōban sheets, the cast of the season's hit play for Edo fans to buy.
context: Kuniyoshi designed the triptych in 1835 for a kabuki production at Edo's Ichimura theatre, usually titled Ume no haru (or Ume no hatsuharu) gojūsan-tsugi, a Tōkaidō travel play whose Okazaki scene introduced a cat that turns into a demon. The British Museum's impression (2008,3037.19408) catalogues it as 'Gojūsan-tsugi no uchi [Okazaki no ba]', and the Japan Society showed another from the Hiraki Ukiyo-e Collection. Fun fact: the role stuck to Kikugorō for the rest of his career. When he retired in 1847, the cat came back on stage for his farewell run, and Kuniyoshi and Kunisada both made new prints of it.
title_eng: Scene at Okazaki: Onoe Kikugorō III as the Spirit of the Cat Stone (Gojūsan-tsugi no uchi Okazaki no ba)
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat here is a bakeneko, a cat grown old enough to become a shape-shifting demon; in the Okazaki story it disguises itself as an old woman.
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · scanned from ISBN 978-4-336-04139-5 .

title: Cats Suggested as the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō
title_original: 其のまま地口・猫飼好五十三疋
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
medium: Woodblock print triptych (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: Fifty-five cats sprawl across three sheets, each one standing in for a stop on the Tōkaidō road from Edo to Kyoto, plus the two ends. Some catch rats, some eat fish, one squeezes out of a basket. Each cat sits beside a station name in a red cartouche, and the joke is that the pose rhymes with it. Miya, the 41st station, sounds like oya, 'parent', so a mother cat lies with two kittens. Ishibe sounds like mijime, 'miserable', and gets a scrawny, scruffy cat in the bottom left. Look for the lone all-black cat in the middle sheet and the mice scampering along the top edge.
context: Utagawa Kuniyoshi (1797–1861), the Edo print designer best known for warriors and for his own crowded cat-filled studio, published this parody around 1847–50; dates in the literature range from 1847 to 1850. It sends up Hiroshige's best-selling Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (1833–34) by turning landscape into puns. Even the title is a joke, swapping Tōkaidō for 'Myōkaikō', roughly 'fondness for keeping cats'. Fun fact: animal parodies like this flourished because the Tenpō reforms of the early 1840s banned prints of actors and courtesans, so Kuniyoshi learned to slip people, and jokes, into cats.
title_eng: Cats Suggested as the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō
image_credit: 歌川国芳 (Utagawa Kuniyoshi, 1798 - 1861) · http://visipix.com/search/search.php?userid=1616934267&q=%272aAuthors/K/Kuniyoshi%201797-1861%2C%20Utagawa%2C%20Japan%27&s=22&l=en&u=2&ub=1&k=1

title: Inumura Daikaku Stabbing the Monster Cat, from Kyokutei-ō seicho Hakkenshi zui-ichi
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: A giant calico cat, orange and black patches on white, sprawls upside down across the sheet while Inumura Daikaku, one of the eight dog-warriors of the Hakkenden, drives his blade in near its throat. The cat's head lies at bottom left, fangs bared and whiskers flying, and its clawed paws grip the warrior from both sides. The cat is far bigger than the man, which is the point: Kuniyoshi's warriors always fight something oversized. Notice the long scroll looped over Daikaku's shoulders and across the cat's body, a paper-and-ink joke on a print series that advertises itself as 'the best of refined authors'.
context: This sheet comes from Kuniyoshi's series Kyokutei-ō seicho Hakkenshi zui-ichi (The One and Only Eight Dog History of Old Kyokutei, Best of Refined Authors), which the British Museum dates to about 1835. It illustrates Kyokutei Bakin's enormous novel Nansō Satomi Hakkenden, published over 28 years (1814–42) in 106 booklets, about eight heroes whose names all contain the character for 'dog'. A dog-hero killing a cat demon is about as on-brand as Edo fiction gets. Fun fact: Bakin went blind before he finished the novel and dictated its last parts to his daughter-in-law, Michi Tokimura.
title_eng: Inumura Daikaku Stabbing the Monster Cat, from Kyokutei-ō seicho Hakkenshi zui-ichi
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat is the villain, a monstrous cat demon that the dog-named hero must destroy.
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · http://www.britishmuseum.org/research/search_the_collection_database/search_object_image.aspx

title: The Famous and Unrivalled Hidari Jingorō (Meiyo migi ni teki nashi Hidari Jingorō)
medium: Woodblock print triptych (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
collection: British Museum / Waseda University Theatre Museum
description: A white cat with black patches sits at bottom left, twisted round to lick its leg, the only figure in the room ignoring the sculptor. The left-handed Hidari Jingorō kneels on a cushion stamped with Kuniyoshi's own kiri (paulownia) seal, chisels and a whetstone tub at his knees. Behind him crowd his creations, so lifelike they wear the faces of kabuki stars: a bearded sage, a veiled lady, a red-robed Daruma, two masks on the floor. Commons metadata identifies the faces as Morita Kan'ya XI, Onoe Kikugorō IV, Ichikawa Danzō VI, Ichimura Uzaemon XII and Matsumoto Kōshirō VI. By legend, Jingorō's best-known work was a cat.
context: Kuniyoshi published Meiyo migi ni teki nashi Hidari Jingorō (The Famous and Unrivalled Hidari Jingorō) with Ebisuya Shōshichi around 1847–50, judging by its censor seals. The title puns on hidari (left) and migi (right): Jingorō is unmatched 'on the right', though he carves with his left. The Kuniyoshi Project lists the print among the artist's disguised self-portraits, reading the sculptor as Kuniyoshi himself. Fun fact: Jingorō may never have existed. Tradition credits him with the Nemuri-neko, the sleeping cat carved above a gate at Nikkō Tōshō-gū, and with a carved woman who came to life before a mirror.
title_eng: The Famous and Unrivalled Hidari Jingorō (Meiyo migi ni teki nashi Hidari Jingorō)
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Netsuke of Cat
title_original: 象牙彫 眠り猫根付 (懐玉斎正次)
description: A cat, carved from a single piece of ivory and small enough to close a fist around: 2.5 cm high, 3.2 cm wide, 2.2 cm deep. It crouches low with its tail wrapped forward along its side, head turned and tipped up as if someone just said its name. Dark staining picks out the ears, brows and the line of the haunch, and the honey-coloured ivory has a glassy shine. That compact shape is practical: a netsuke had to sit snugly against a man's sash without snagging. The Met photographs it from every side, because on a netsuke the underside, where the cord ran, is part of the design.
context: Netsuke were toggles. Men's kimono had no pockets, so pouches and inrō boxes hung on cords from the obi, and a carved netsuke held the cord in place. Cats were a natural subject for a compact katabori (carved-in-the-round) piece, usually one to three inches tall. This one came to the Met in 1910 as a gift from Mrs. Russell Sage. Fun fact: the Met cannot say which century's fashion it served. Its record gives the period as 'Edo or Meiji', and Meiji is exactly when Western dress put netsuke out of work and sent so many to Western collectors.
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Portrait of a Court Lady with a Cat
medium: Oil on canvas in arched gilt frame
collection: Private collection (sold Roseberys, London, catalogue 481, lot 143618)
description: A fluffy white cat sits upright in a Qajar lady's lap, cradled by her right hand, its pink-tinged face turned aside. She rests her head on her other hand, a green jacket open over a full pale-blue skirt, legs crossed at the ankle. At her feet a white swan curls its neck, easy to miss. The painting, about 145 cm high, sits in a pointed-arch gilt frame against a soft blue sky. Look at her face before you look back at the cat: a small diamond-shaped mark between her eyebrows, which the cataloguer reads as a tattoo, a practice once common across the Middle East and North Africa.
context: Qajar painters took up oil on canvas under European influence and favoured heavy paint and dark, saturated colour, with life-size figures and women holding mirrors, fruit or wine as stock themes. This portrait is catalogued simply as Iran, circa 1850, early in the reign of Naser al-Din Shah (1848–96). It is not a museum object: it passed through the UK auction house Roseberys (catalogue 481, lot 143618), and the image on Wikimedia Commons comes from that sale, with a note that it was acquired in Paris on 2 December 2015. Fun fact: the cataloguer compares the lady's forehead mark to a Timurid painting in the Metropolitan Museum, linking a 19th-century fashion to one four centuries older.
title_eng: Portrait of a Court Lady with a Cat
image_credit: Roseberys.co.uk · https://auctions.roseberys.co.uk/m/lot-details/index/catalog/481/lot/143618?url=%2Fm%2Fsearch%3Fpage%3D5%26view%3Dgrid%26key%3Dqajar%26sale%3Dundefined%26catm%3Dany%26order%3Dtimeleft%26live%3Dno%26timed%3Dno%26regular%3Dn

title: Cat quilt
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Cats sit bolt upright all over this red-and-green cotton quilt, small appliqué silhouettes with pricked ears and tiny stitched faces, tilted at angles so they seem to orbit the spoked wheel at the centre. Around them grow tulips, hearts, birds and odd palm-like trees on vines that wind out to the corners. The maker cut the shapes from paper templates and stitched them down, so every cat has the same flat, cookie-cutter outline, a bit like a stencil that learned to purr. It is a big bed quilt, 227.3 by 197.5 cm, and pictorial quilts like this were uncommon at the time, when most makers stuck to repeating geometric blocks.
context: An unknown woman made this quilt around 1850, probably in New York State, where the Met notes the paper-template technique was common. The museum calls it a charming example of the creativity of some nineteenth-century American quilt makers and suggests the motifs were her favourite things: cats, plants and love. Allison L. Reddington gave it to the Met in 2020 to mark the museum's 150th anniversary. Fun fact: cats turn up on many New York appliqué quilts of about 1840–70, and the quilt historian Barbara Brackman has floated, very tentatively, a link to New York 'wildcat' banking politics, or to fraternal symbols, before admitting nobody knows.
feline_symbolism: The Met reads the cats as personal favourites of the maker rather than symbols; a political or fraternal meaning has been suggested for cats on New York quilts but remains unproven.
submovement: New York State pictorial appliqué quilt
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Figure of a Baby in a Cradle Holding a Kitten
title_original: Figure of a Baby in a Cradle Holding a Kitten
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A kitten curls on the baby's chest, so small and so white that it reads only as a soft lump with two ears. The baby lies in a hooded, basket-weave cradle on stubby feet, curly head on the pillow, eyes closed, all in unglazed white Parian porcelain small enough for a mantel shelf: 11.1 cm high, 16.5 cm long, 7.9 cm deep. Little raised beads stud the rim and the hood. Parian was made to look like carved marble, so baby, kitten and wickerwork share one matte, sugary white. That is the charm and the joke: a cheap, mould-cast ornament dressed as sculpture.
context: The Met lists the figure as American, dated broadly 1830–70, with no maker named. Parian ware was introduced in England by Copeland and Minton around 1845 and named after the white marble of Paros; because it could be cast in moulds, it put marble-looking busts and figurines within reach of middle-class parlours. American potteries followed, and the United States Pottery Company of Bennington, Vermont (1847–58) made several child-and-cat figures. Dr. Charles W. Green gave this one to the Met in 1947. Fun fact: Copeland and Minton both claimed to have invented Parian, and even the Great Exhibition judges could not settle it.
title_eng: Figure of a Baby in a Cradle Holding a Kitten
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: The Awakening Conscience
description: Under the table at left, a tabby cat crouches over a bird it has caught, a tiny scene of predator and prey that most people only spot after the main event. Above, a young woman rises from her lover's lap, eyes lifted, while he lounges back in his chair beside the piano, mouth open mid-song. The room is crammed with new, glossy things: a gilt clock under a glass dome, a tangle of wool on the red carpet. Hunt paints every surface hard and bright in oil, and the sheet music on the piano is Thomas Moore's 'Oft in the Stilly Night', a song about lost happier days.
context: Holman Hunt painted the picture in 1853, a few years into his Pre-Raphaelite career, for the Manchester industrialist Thomas Fairbairn, who paid 350 guineas. Annie Miller, then engaged to Hunt, sat for the woman. Fairbairn found her original expression too painful to live with and asked Hunt to soften it; Hunt reworked the face and retouched it again in 1864 and 1886. The painting stayed in the Fairbairn family until an anonymous Christie's sale in 1946, and Sir Colin and Lady Anderson gave it to the Tate in 1976. Fun fact: Ruskin defended it in The Times in 1854, insisting that not a single object in the room was without meaning, which rather puts pressure on the cat.
feline_symbolism: The cat playing with a bird under the table mirrors the woman's situation as a kept mistress, caught and toyed with.
image_credit: William Holman Hunt · https://www.flickr.com/photos/gandalfsgallery/5626470779

title: The Painter's Studio: A Real Allegory (L'Atelier du peintre)
title_original: L'Atelier du peintre: Allégorie réelle déterminant une phase de sept années de ma vie artistique et morale
description: In a canvas almost six metres wide, the cat is easy to miss. It is a white cat sprawled playfully on the floor at Courbet's feet, right beside the small boy who stands watching him paint a landscape, while a nude model clutches a white sheet to her chest and looks over his shoulder. To the left crowd figures from every corner of French society, behind them a lay figure slumped like a crucified body; to the right stand Courbet's friends and supporters, one of them reading at a table. The cat is the one figure in the middle with no opinion about art.
context: Courbet painted the picture in Ornans in 1855 and gave it a deliberately odd subtitle, 'a real allegory' of seven years of his artistic life. The jury of the Exposition Universelle accepted eleven of his works but not this one, so he built his own 'Pavilion of Realism' beside the fair, with help from his patron Alfred Bruyas, and showed it there. The canvas, 361 by 598 cm, is now in the Musée d'Orsay. Fun fact: one of the friends on the right is the critic Champfleury, who in 1869 published Les Chats, a book of essays on cats that collected cat images by contemporary artists.
title_eng: The Painter's Studio: A Real Allegory Summing Up Seven Years of My Artistic and Moral Life
image_credit: Gustave Courbet · Unknown source Unknown source

title: Girl with Cat (Girl with Kitten)
description: A grey tabby rides on the girl's shoulder, slung against her right side with its head pressed up by her cheek, its fur nearly melting into the dark background. The canvas is large, just over a metre tall (107 × 84.7 cm), a lot of oil paint to give a child and a pet. Hunt painted it in 1856, fresh from two years at Barbizon beside Jean-François Millet: an ordinary subject, plain colour, a sitter doing nothing grand. She looks down, in a pink dress with braided trim, lace cuffs and black bows, hands folded under the cat. The cat is the reason the girl is holding still.
context: William Morris Hunt (1824–1879), a Vermonter, trained in Paris with Thomas Couture and then fell under the spell of Millet after seeing The Sower at the 1851 Salon. He returned to America in 1855 and became Boston's leading portraitist, and he talked Boston collectors into buying Millet and other French painters, which is a big reason the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (accession 00.504) is so rich in Barbizon pictures. Fun fact: the Great Boston Fire of 1872 destroyed many of Hunt's own paintings and five large Millets he had brought home, so early canvases like this one are the survivors.
image_credit: William Morris Hunt · https://www.mfa.org/collections/object/girl-with-cat-31115

title: Asakusa Ricefields and Torinomachi Festival (One Hundred Famous Views of Edo)
title_original: 名所江戸百景 浅草田甫酉の町詣
description: A white cat sits on the sill of a Yoshiwara room, back to us, looking out through the lattice across the Asakusa rice fields toward Mount Fuji. Birds cross the evening sky. Out in the fields a line of tiny pilgrims heads to the Tori no machi (rooster festival) at the Ōtori shrine of Chōkoku-ji, carrying good-luck rakes. Nobody human appears in the room, but there are clues: a towel and bowl on the sill, and on the floor a folded paper with bear's-paw hairpins that rhyme with the pilgrims' rakes. The cat is the only one left at the window, which is exactly the point.
context: This is print 101 of Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, dated the eleventh month of 1857, when the festival fell. The series ran from 1856 to 1859, published by Sakanaya Eikichi, and was completed by Hiroshige II after Hiroshige died in 1858. The familiar image of this sheet comes from the Brooklyn Museum's impression. Fun fact: the festival is never shown head-on. Hiroshige hints at it through the hairpins, which echo the rakes the pilgrims carry, and the cat stands in for the courtesan, who has just finished her work.
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
submovement: Late Edo Landscape Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking
feline_symbolism: Scholars commonly read the white cat as a stand-in for the absent courtesan resting after work.
image_credit: Utagawa Hiroshige · Online Collection of Brooklyn Museum

title: Kittens Playing (Spelende katjes)
description: A long-haired grey-and-white mother cat with green eyes keeps watch from the right while four kittens wreck a wicker basket: one hangs over its rim, a ginger one pounces on a white sibling rolling on its back, and a dark tabby peers out from the shadows at far left. One paw has already landed in the saucer of milk. The canvas is modest, 49 by 61 cm, and the Boijmans dates it to about 1890, when she was nearly seventy and at the height of her cat fame. Her trick: chaos caught in the act, on a stage of red drapery.
context: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) learned to paint from her father, Joseph August Knip, and supported the family when he went blind. After marrying in 1850 she moved to Brussels, narrowed her subjects to dogs and then cats, and from about 1870 built an international market for playful long-haired cats in comfortable interiors. She kept her models at home, studied them in the studio, and even made paper sculptures of the poses she wanted. Mrs. Ch. and Mrs. E. Jossmann gave this painting to Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in 1939, and the museum lent it to the 2017 exhibition Kattenliefde. Fun fact: she was the first woman admitted as an active member of the Amsterdam artists' society Arti et Amicitiae.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen

title: A Cat Curled Up, Sleeping (Un chat endormi)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A cat curled into a sleeping ball, drawn in graphite on a sheet smaller than a postcard: 11.7 by 10.8 cm. The back is a loose cloud of grey hatching, while the darkest strokes go to the patched head, tucked down on the right with a white blaze and one ear just showing. A few wavy lines underneath suggest a cushion or cloth. This is Manet with nobody watching, no Salon jury and no scandal, just a pencil working out how a coil of fur and a tucked head make one rounded shape. A sleeping cat is the most cooperative model a painter can hope for, until it wakes.
context: Manet made the drawing in 1861, two years before Olympia put a black cat at the centre of a public row. The Met acquired it in 1995 (Bequest of Clifford A. Furst, by exchange), together with a companion sheet from the same year, A Cat Resting on All Fours, Seen from Behind (1995.494), so the two studies now sit side by side in the Drawings and Prints department. Fun fact: cats kept coming back in Manet's graphic work. In 1869 he contributed the etching Cat and Flowers to his friend Champfleury's book Les Chats, a collection of essays and artists' cat images.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Vase
title_original: Vase à pieds léonins et félins
artist: Firm of Ferdinand Barbedienne (made by); Louis-Constant Sévin (designer)
description: Three gilt cats hold up this vase, each a long slim leg ending in a neat paw at the floor and a small alert cat head at the shoulder, with a tall loop handle rising behind it. Paws, not lion feet: the Cleveland Museum names them as cat legs and reads them as a borrowing from ancient Egypt. The amphora-shaped body, 78.7 cm tall, is gilt bronze with champlevé enamel in turquoise, blue and red, with red cabochons set in the gold band where the cats meet. Greek shape, Egyptian feet, Islamic-style scrolls: the vase is a whole museum survey in one object.
context: The Paris firm of Ferdinand Barbedienne made the vase around 1862, to a design by Louis-Constant Sévin, Barbedienne's leading ornamental designer. The model was introduced at the International Exhibition in London in 1862 and sold well enough to come in several colour and shape variations. This example descended in the Barbedienne line (Gustave Leblanc-Barbedienne) and was bought by Cleveland in 1996 through the Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund. Fun fact: it went back on the road in 2012–14 for the touring exhibition Inventing the Modern World: Decorative Arts at the World's Fairs, 1851–1939, which seems fair for an object born at a world's fair.
submovement: French Second Empire Historicism & Champlevé Enamel
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Olympia (The Black Cat at the Foot of the Bed)
description: At the far right end of the bed a black cat stands with its back arched and tail straight up, almost lost against the dark green curtain until you catch its yellow eyes. Manet put it exactly where Titian's Venus of Urbino has a small sleeping dog. Olympia, modelled by Victorine Meurent, lies on white sheets with an orchid in her hair and a black ribbon at her throat, and looks straight out; the maid, modelled by a woman known as Laure, brings a paper-wrapped bouquet from an admirer. The cat is the only figure that reacts to the arrival.
context: Manet painted Olympia in 1863 and showed it at the Salon of 1865, where critics called it immoral and vulgar, and according to Antonin Proust the administration had to take precautions to keep the canvas from harm. After Manet's death Claude Monet organised a subscription to buy it for France, with Winnaretta Singer the largest donor, and the state bought it from Suzanne Manet in 1890 for 19,415 francs. It went to the Luxembourg, then to the Louvre in 1907 on Clemenceau's order, and to the Musée d'Orsay in 1986. Fun fact: Meurent, the model, later became a painter herself and exhibited at the Salon in 1876, 1879, 1885 and 1904.
feline_symbolism: Swapping Titian's dog of fidelity for a black cat with an arched back pointed to night-time promiscuity, helped along by the French slang sense of 'chatte'.
image_credit: Édouard Manet · Google Arts & Culture — ywFEI4rxgCSO1Q

title: Woman with a Cat
description: A fluffy white cat lies belly-up in a young woman's arms, eyes shut in bliss, one front paw pressed to her collarbone and both hind paws pedalling in the air. She tilts her head down at it with a half smile, a ruffled lace cap on her dark hair and a white wrap slipping off her shoulders. Courbet painted the modest canvas, 78.3 by 57.2 cm, in 1864, the same years he was turning out landscapes and nudes for a growing market. Here the scale is domestic. Notice how the dark ground swallows the edges, so that flesh, fabric and fur carry all the light.
context: Gustave Courbet (1819–1877), the self-declared Realist who had shown The Painter's Studio in his own pavilion in 1855, painted La Femme au chat in 1864. It is now in the Worcester Art Museum, Massachusetts (accession 1940.300), and it appears in the standard Courbet catalogues, including Tout l'œuvre peint de Courbet. Fun fact: cats recur at the edges of Courbet's world. A white cat sits at the centre of The Painter's Studio, and his early champion Champfleury, painted into that same picture, went on to write a whole book about cats, Les Chats (1869).
image_credit: Gustave Courbet · Self-photographed , 28 April 2010

title: My Little White Kitties – Into Mischief
title_eng: My Little White Kitties – Into Mischief
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Two white kittens have tipped over a cup on a green tablecloth and are now lapping up the evidence, pink tongues in the spreading puddle of milk, tails up like exclamation marks. A heavy red drape hangs behind them and the carved wooden table edge runs along the bottom. It is a hand-coloured lithograph sold by the sheet: the image is 20.7 by 31.5 cm on a sheet of 28.4 by 35.7 cm, a size made for framing over a parlour table. The colour was laid on by hand over a black lithographic drawing, so each impression differs slightly, and here the colourist kept the kittens almost bare paper.
context: Currier & Ives, the New York lithographic firm active from 1857 to 1907, sold cheap decorative prints in enormous numbers, and cute animals were steady business alongside news scenes and landscapes. The Met dates this sheet broadly to 1857–71, the firm's first fourteen years, and catalogues it simply as a hand-coloured lithograph. It came to the museum in 1962 with the bequest of Adele S. Colgate, part of a large group of the firm's prints numbered in the 63.550 series. Fun fact: the Met's accession number for this sheet is 63.550.479, so it is one of at least several hundred prints in that single bequest.
title_original: My Little White Kitties – Into Mischief
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cats (recto); Sketch of Two Figures Embracing (verso)
medium: Black ink applied with pen (reed) and brush on medium beige laid paper
description: Three cats sit side by side on a beige laid sheet, 23.5 by 17.1 cm: one on the left fully worked up, facing us with a heavy black shadow behind it, and two to the right left as bare outlines seen from behind, one barely more than a curved back and an ear. A reed pen gives a thick, uneven line that catches and splutters, so fur comes out as quick strokes rather than careful hatching, and the brush adds pools of shadow. Turn the sheet over and the mood changes completely: the verso, in graphite, is a sketch of two figures embracing. Ribot clearly used every inch of paper.
context: Théodule Ribot (1823–1891) came to painting late, after working as a bookkeeper and as a foreman in Algeria, and made his name at the 1861 Salon with dark kitchen scenes. His early biographers claimed the inky backgrounds came from painting by lamplight in his evenings, a story Cleveland repeats with a raised eyebrow. He belonged to the circle around François Bonvin and was admired by Courbet. The drawing came from the Shepherd Gallery, New York, in May 1977, and entered the Cleveland Museum of Art in 2010 with the bequest of Muriel Butkin. Fun fact: in 1884 fellow artists including Monet, Rodin and Puvis de Chavannes gave him a medal inscribed 'To Théodule Ribot, the independent painter'.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Le Chat Botté (Puss in Boots)
title_original: Le Maître Chat ou le Chat botté
description: Puss in Boots strides down a riverbank with both paws flung in the air and mouth wide open in a shout, plumed hat askew, cape flying, a dead rat dangling from his belt beside a drawstring sack. Behind him, half hidden in the reeds, a man's head bobs in the water. Doré drew it for the 1862 edition of Perrault's fairy tales, and one of the professional block-cutters who translated his drawings cut it into wood. The cat gets the swagger Doré gave his knights. Up close the image is built from tiny parallel cuts that turn into fur, leather and shadow once you step back.
context: Doré (1832–1883) illustrated Les Contes de Perrault in 1862, and an expanded edition followed in 1863; at the height of his career some forty block-cutters turned his drawings into printing blocks, usually signing the image beside him. The tale is older than Perrault, whose Le Maître chat ou le Chat botté appeared in 1697. The earliest written version is Straparola's 'Costantino Fortunato' in The Facetious Nights (c. 1550–53), and Giambattista Basile retold it in 1634 as 'Cagliuso'. Fun fact: in Straparola the clever cat is a fairy in disguise, helping a poor boy from Bohemia to dupe a king and win a princess.
feline_symbolism: Puss is the classic trickster helper, a cat whose wit wins his poor young master a fortune and a princess.
image_credit: Gustave Doré · http://www.veranijveld.com/gustave-doreacute-a-multitalented-visual-artist.html

title: The Cats' Rendezvous (Le Rendez-vous des chats)
medium: Lithograph in black on ivory wove paper, laid down on ivory cloth
collection: Art Institute of Chicago (impression also in New York Public Library)
description: Two cats meet on the rooftops among chimney pots, one black and one white. The black cat stands with its back to us, tail hooked up in a big question-mark curl, head turned toward the other; the white one faces away, tail curled at the tip, playing it cool. A big lithograph for its day: the image alone is 43.9 by 33.4 cm. Manet keeps the black cat almost solid and lets the white one exist mostly as blank paper: ink against no ink. The flattened shapes owe a debt to the Japanese prints Paris was collecting in the 1860s.
context: Manet drew the image on the stone in 1868 as a poster for Champfleury's book Les Chats, published in 1869 by J. Rothschild as a set of essays on cats with images by contemporary artists. Manet also contributed an etching, Cat and Flowers, to the book itself. The Art Institute of Chicago's impression (1987.15, John H. Wrenn Fund) is printed on ivory wove paper laid down on cloth, a sign it was meant to survive being displayed. Print scholars know it as Harris 58, Guérin 74 and Moreau-Nélaton 80, each recording only one state. Fun fact: Champfleury had been painted into Courbet's Painter's Studio fourteen years earlier, beside its own white cat.
image_credit: Édouard Manet · https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/search/index?filters%5BnamePart_mtxt_s%5D%5B%5D=Manet%2C%20%C3%89douard%2C%201832-1883&keywords=&layout=false#/?scroll=81

title: Champfleury: Les Chats (Poster / Illustrated Edition)
title_original: Champfleury - Les Chats: Histoire, Mœurs, Observations, Anecdotes
submovement: French Realist lithography and early Japonisme
medium: Lithograph with lettering (affichette); printer Lith. du Sénat, Barousse
description: Two cats meet on a Paris roof among chimney pots: a black tom seen from behind, tail hoisted in a tall hook, head turned in profile, and a white cat that stands its ground with its back half to him. Manet keeps them almost flat, black shape against bare tan paper. This is the advertising state, with red letters framing the image, 'Champfleury - Les Chats' on top, 'Deuxième édition avec 52 dessins' up both sides, and 'Prix 5 francs, en vente ici' below, with the printer's line 'Lith. du Sénat, Barousse' in the corner. It measures about 33 × 43 cm, about the size of a shop-window card.
context: Manet drew "Le Rendez-vous des chats" in 1868 to sell Champfleury's best-selling book Les Chats, a cultural history of the cat by the critic who had championed Courbet and Realism. The design went out in several forms: as a lithograph, reproduced in the paper La Chronique illustrée, and as this lettered affichette. The Bibliothèque nationale de France owes its impression to the collector Étienne Moreau-Nélaton, whose legacy was registered on 1 August 1927. Fun fact: the Courtauld notes that Champfleury's book reused single cat motifs from Hokusai's sketchbooks, so Manet's flattened rooftop pair sits in a volume already looking hard at Japan.
feline_symbolism: The rooftop tryst trades on the Parisian image of the cat as a night-time free spirit, which suited a book that presented the cat as the artist's and writer's animal.
image_credit: Manet, Édouard (1832-1883). Lithographe · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cat and the Flowers (Le Chat et les fleurs)
description: A dark cat with a white stripe from belly to chin rears up at a wooden ledge and pushes its nose into a pot of flowers. The pot stands on little clawed feet that echo the cat's own, a joke you notice only on the second look. Behind it are a second pot, without feet, and an iron lattice railing, with some of the flowers poking through the grid. Manet combines etching and aquatint, yet the cat itself is built from dense, rippling lines that follow the lie of the fur. The plate is small, about 17.5 × 13 cm.
context: Manet made the plate in 1869 for an expanded 1870 edition of Champfleury's Les Chats, published in Paris by J. Rothschild. The plate was also sold as a stand-alone print before it went into the deluxe edition, which is why impressions turn up in many collections, with states recorded by Harris (no. 65). The accession number 1979.194 belongs to the Baltimore Museum of Art's impression. Fun fact: sources cannot agree which edition this was. The San Francisco museums call it the second edition, while the Courtauld calls the 1870 printing the fourth.
medium: Etching and aquatint on laid paper
image_credit: Édouard Manet · https://collection.artbma.org/people/5742/edouard-manet

title: A Flood
description: Hunched on the foot of a drifting wooden cradle, a small black cat stares down at the brown floodwater, very much aware of what the baby is not. The baby lies inside under a flowered quilt, wide awake, hands raised, gazing up at raindrops on a bare branch where a small bird perches. A cream jug bobs alongside. Behind them a little bridge is nearly under water, a haystack and a house stand flooded to their lower edges, and men in a boat are pulled along by the current at top right. The canvas is big, about 99 × 145 cm, so the cat is close to life-size.
context: Millais signed and dated the canvas with his monogram, "18 JM 70", and Manchester Art Gallery bought it from Thomas Agnew and Sons in 1891 (accession 1891.7). His son John Guille Millais, in the biography of his father, connected the picture to the Great Sheffield Flood of March 1864, when the Dale Dyke dam burst and roughly 250 people died. Fun fact: newspaper reports of that night included a baby carried off in its cradle, which seems to be the seed of the picture. Millais turned it into a comedy of mismatched reactions, and visitors still argue over whether it is charming or grim.
image_credit: John Everett Millais · Manchester Art Gallery

title: Woman Churning Butter (La Baratteuse)
description: A peasant woman stands at a tall wooden churn, both hands on the dasher, head bent to the work. At her feet a cat presses against her skirts, angling for a spill or a treat, and she ignores it completely. Behind her, sacks of grain lean in the shadows of the dairy, which is where the cat ought to be on mouse duty. Millet builds the figure with dense hatching on a plate under 18 × 12 cm, so the cat is a small warm smudge of lines against her heavy hem.
context: Millet etched La Baratteuse in 1855–56, at Barbizon, as one of a small group of prints of rural labour that spread his peasant subjects far beyond the Salon. Impressions are common in museums. This one, in the British Museum (1865,1209.798), is pencilled 'St ii/iii' at lower right, the second of three states; the MFA Boston and the National Gallery of Victoria hold others. Fun fact: Millet returned to the subject for a life-size pastel around 1866 (Musée d'Orsay, RF 1578, about 122 × 85 cm), and the cat comes along in that version too.
