feline_symbolism: The National Gallery of Victoria reads the cat as a gentle joke about duty: it begs at the churn when its real job is guarding the grain sacks from mice.
image_credit: Jean-François Millet · © The Trustees of the British Museum, shared under the museum's open terms via Wikimedia Commons

title: Cat and Her Kittens in a Painter's Studio (Dans l'atelier)
description: A mother cat and her kittens have the run of a painter's studio, the room where Ronner-Knip spent her working life watching exactly these animals. Her cats are always built from close, directional strokes that follow the lie of the fur, with eyes given a glassy highlight, and the setting is there to give them things to climb, hide behind and knock over. The joke is at the artist's own expense: in this studio the models are in charge, and the painter is absent.
context: Ronner-Knip (1821–1909), born in Amsterdam and settled in Brussels, began with dogs and other animals but after 1870 painted mostly cats, selling them to a middle-class public that liked pets on expensive furniture. The image comes from the Ede dealer Simonis & Buunk; their recorded studio picture, 'Cat and her kittens in a painter's studio', is oil on panel, 54.5 × 72 cm, signed at lower right (and catalogued by Simonis & Buunk as dated 1878), ex-Paris private collection, now in a Dutch private collection, and was shown at the Kunsthal Rotterdam in 1998. Fun fact: she reportedly built a glass-fronted box in her studio so the cats could play and sleep undisturbed while she sketched them.
title_eng: Cat and Her Kittens in a Painter's Studio
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://www.simonis-buunk.nl/kunstwerk/

title: A Cat with Three Kittens (Een kat met drie jongen)
collection: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed (RCE), Dutch state art collection
description: A black-and-white mother cat with a tabby back bends to touch noses with a fluffy white kitten that stands on its hind legs to reach her. A calico kitten peeks over a red cloth draped across a wicker basket, and a tabby kitten creeps out underneath, close to a loose thread. All this on a small oil panel, only about 24 × 19 cm. At this scale Ronner-Knip's method shows best: fur built up in short strokes that follow the direction of growth, eyes picked out with a single wet highlight, and the kittens' poses giving the eye a route around the family.
context: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) was born in Amsterdam, settled in Brussels and from the 1870s painted cats almost exclusively, for buyers across Europe. This panel is in the Dutch state art collection managed by the Cultural Heritage Agency (RCE) under number NK2003 and is kept in the RCE depot. Fun fact: the NK prefix marks works recovered from Germany after the Second World War and placed in the 'Nederlands Kunstbezit' collection, whose origins are still being researched, so even a harmless kitten picture has a wartime file.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://wo2.collectienederland.nl/doc/nk/NK2003

title: The Mask: Children and Frightened Cats (La Maschera)
date_display: undated (variant close to The Boogey Man, 1891)
description: Four cats and kittens share the kitchen floor while a boy in a battered feathered hat leans in wearing a grinning, long-nosed mask. A grey kitten laps from a bowl of milk with a tabby beside it, a ginger-and-white kitten scrambles off to the right, and another cat sits by the fire. The real fright lands on the little girl, mouth open, clinging to the older boy who sits laughing with a jug in his hands. Chierici's prank pictures run on a reliable engine: one grinning disguise, a startled audience, and a kitchen painted so smoothly the brushwork vanishes. Copper, broom and brick get the same care as fur.
context: Gaetano Chierici (1838–1920) of Reggio Emilia built an international market for comic scenes of peasant children, selling especially well in Britain and Austria. The mask joke was one of his most repeated compositions: Christie's sold a signed version dated 1874 (75.5 × 108 cm) that it compared to a version in the Pinacoteca di Brera, and another 1874 canvas was at the Corcoran Gallery in Washington in 1888. The image attached to this record, though, is listed by Wikipedia as an undated variant of unknown location, close to his 1891 'Boogey Man'. Fun fact: Christie's credits his near-invisible brushwork to many thin layers of paint and glaze.
title_eng: The Mask: Children and Frightened Cats
image_credit: Gaetano Chierici · https://wooarts.com/gaetano-chierici/

title: The Unexpected Guest
description: A silver tabby mother lies on a folded rug in a straw-strewn barn, eyes half shut, while her striped kitten nuzzles in at her chest beside a sleeping white creature with pink ears, plausibly the guest of the title, tucked in as if it always belonged. A red earthenware dish and a blue-and-white plate sit in the straw behind. As in most of Couldery's pictures the animals are small and the fur is worked almost hair by hair, the finish Ruskin said could hardly be seen properly without a lens. The comedy is in the mother's face, half dozing, half deciding whether to object. No humans required.
context: Horatio Henry Couldery (1832–1918; many sources wrongly give 1893 as his death year) was born in Lewisham, trained as a cabinetmaker, then studied at the Royal Academy and showed there from 1861, as well as at the British Institution and Suffolk Street. He illustrated children's books and greeting cards and specialised in mischievous cats and dogs. This canvas, dated 1874, is known from an artnet auction record and is in private hands. Fun fact: the largest public group of his work, 42 paintings, is not in Britain but at Glanmore National Historic Site in Belleville, Ontario, given by his brother's family.
image_credit: Horatio Henry Couldery · www.artnet.com/artwork/424061469/196/horatio-henry-couldery-the-unexpected-guest.html

title: Persian Cat and Two Dogs (The Standoff)
description: A long-haired white Persian holds the high ground on a flowered cushion, blue eyes fixed on us, while two small dogs, catalogued on Commons as a miniature pinscher and a terrier, hold the carpet below. The pinscher lies in profile, nose pointed away; the shaggy blond terrier sits up and stares straight out like the cat's deputy. A Persian is a gift to a painter of texture, and Dolph sets its soft, broken-edged coat against the pinscher's tight, glossy black hair. The canvas is about 55 × 75 cm (21½ × 29½ in.), generous for a pet picture, and the three share it like sitters in a group portrait.
context: John Henry Dolph (1835–1903) began as a carriage painter in Ohio, worked as a portraitist in Cleveland and Detroit, and moved to New York in 1864, showing at the National Academy of Design for decades. He studied in Antwerp in 1870–73 and in Paris in 1880–82, and afterwards specialised in cats and dogs, becoming a full Academician in 1898. This painting passed through LiveAuctioneers and is privately owned. Fun fact: he lived in the Sherwood Studio Building on 57th Street, the first New York apartment house built for artists, and was billed as 'the Landseer of America'.
title_eng: Persian Cat and Two Dogs (The Standoff)
image_credit: John Henry Dolph · Live Auctioneers ( Gallery )

title: Cats by a Fishbowl
description: Three tabbies crouch on a red-draped ledge, chins low, every eye locked on a glass bowl at the far left: the oldest suspense plot in pet painting. The big cat in front flattens into a hunting crouch, a second kitten peers round its shoulder, and a third, wearing a pink ribbon bow, watches from behind like a junior apprentice. Couldery's speciality was fur in tiny strokes, and the bowl hands him the opposite problem, clear water and curved highlights, so the canvas doubles as a contest between two surfaces. Two goldfish drift past, unbothered. The fish have the glass on their side; the cats have time.
context: Couldery (1832–1918), a Lewisham-born cabinetmaker turned Royal Academy exhibitor, made his name with cats caught in minor crimes; his first RA picture of 1861 showed two tabby kittens discovering a table with fish. This canvas is signed 'Horatio H. Couldery' and measures 45.5 × 61 cm. It was offered at Bukowskis' Autumn Classic Sale in Stockholm in 2012 (lot 249, estimate 50,000–60,000 SEK) and did not sell. Fun fact: John Ruskin, reviewing a Couldery cat in 1875, said it could not rightly be seen without a lens.
image_credit: Horatio Henry Couldery · https://www.bukowskis.com/en/auctions/571/249-horatio-henry-couldery-katter-vid-fiskskal

title: Cat and Mouse Jug
description: The jug is the cat: a white cat with brown tabby patches sits upright on a green mossy base, head bowed, and its own striped tail curls round to make the handle. The pouring lip opens out of the top of its head, lined in turquoise. A small grey shape between its front paws is presumably the mouse, which is the sort of joke Victorian dining rooms adored. The body is moulded earthenware dipped in Minton's translucent coloured lead glazes, which pool thicker and darker in the hollows so the modelling reads across a table. Every time it pours, the cat looks down at its catch again.
context: Minton's of Stoke-on-Trent developed coloured-glaze 'majolica' in the late 1840s under the French chemist Léon Arnoux and launched it as 'Palissy ware'; by the 1870s naturalistic and humorous designs were selling to the new middle classes alongside grand exhibition pieces. This jug is dated 1875 and is known from a photograph by a private collector, used on Wikipedia to illustrate the 'naturalistic style'. Fun fact: Victorian 'majolica' borrowed its name from Italian tin-glazed maiolica, which it does not resemble at all, and Minton made both, keeping the confusion in the family.
image_credit: Davidmadelena · Own work

title: Woman with a Cat (Femme au chat)
description: A brown tabby, eyes squeezed shut, is hugged against a young woman's shoulder, one forepaw draped over her arm like a stole. Renoir paints the pair as one soft mass: fur, piled-up hair and white blouse are built from the same loose, feathered strokes, so it is hard to say where the animal ends and the sleeve begins. She looks down, half smiling, a green-stoned ring catching the light on the hand that holds the cat. The canvas is modest, 56 × 46.4 cm, against a minty green wall, and it is signed 'Renoir.' at lower left. Nothing happens except closeness, which is the point.
context: Renoir painted this around 1875, the year after the first Impressionist exhibition. Its first known owner was Ernest Hoschedé, the department-store magnate and early Impressionist collector, and it was sold at his bankruptcy sale in Paris on 6 June 1878 (lot 75), bought by the Count de Rasty. Paul Rosenberg had it in 1925–26; Benjamin E. Levy owned it by 1932 and, with his wife, gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1950 (1950.12.1). Fun fact: the NGA lists it as possibly shown at Durand-Ruel's 1899 Monet, Pissarro, Renoir and Sisley exhibition, and it was certainly in the 1900 Exposition universelle.
image_credit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir · https://www.nga.gov/collection/art-object-page.37637.html

title: The Cat and the Rat (Le Chat et le Rat)
description: A striped cat lounges on a stump at the foot of a huge hollow tree, paws tucked, looking pleased with itself, while the rat sits up on its haunches at the far left and keeps a sensible distance. This is La Fontaine's fable of the uneasy deal: the cat, caught in a hunter's net, needs the rat to gnaw the cords. Lambert, who painted almost nothing but cats and dogs, skips the trap and shows the awkward afterwards. Look up into the trunk's dark split: a round-eyed owl peers out. The engraving after his drawing is sized to sit with the text of a family edition.
context: Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900), a pupil of Delacroix and Delaroche, was known at the Salon as 'Lambert des chats' or 'the Raphael of cats'. He drew the animals for an edition of La Fontaine's Fables published in Paris by J. Hetzel in the 'Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation'; the Bibliothèque nationale de France copy (Gallica bpt6k5461375p) is dated 1870 on Commons. 'Le Chat et le Rat' is fable 22 of Book VIII. Fun fact: Lambert went to stay with George Sand at Nohant in 1844 for a month and stayed fourteen years.
title_original: Le Chat et le Rat (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: La Fontaine's moral is that a pact with a natural enemy should not be trusted: the rat accepts the cat's thanks from a safe distance.
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f470

title: The Cat and the Fox (Le Chat et le Renard)
description: The cat has already used its one trick: it peers down from the fork of a pale, split old tree, ears up, safe and smug. Below, the fox rears on its hind legs at the trunk, mouth open, while the hounds' heads push out of the undergrowth at left. This is La Fontaine's pair of pious pilgrims: the fox boasts a sackful of tricks, the cat admits to just one, and when the dogs arrive, up the tree is the one that works. Lambert, a specialist in cats and dogs, gets to draw both his favourite animals in one fable, and the cat wins by altitude.
context: This vignette comes from the La Fontaine published in Paris by J. Hetzel for his 'Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation', with animals drawn by Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900); the BnF copy (Gallica bpt6k5461375p, folio 512) is dated 1870 on Commons. 'Le Chat et le Renard' is fable 14 of Book IX. Lambert had trained with Delacroix, debuted at the Salon in 1847, and was made a chevalier of the Légion d'honneur in 1871. Fun fact: his Salon nickname, 'Lambert des chats', stuck so firmly that it outlived most of his paintings.
title_original: Le Chat et le Renard (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: The fable makes the cat the patron saint of one good idea, against the fox's cleverness: 'Le trop d'expédients peut gâter une affaire.'
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f512

title: The Cat and the Two Sparrows (Le Chat et les deux moineaux)
description: A tabby cat crouches on a kitchen floor with a sparrow already in its jaws, tail up, while the second sparrow stands on its outstretched paw, apparently unaware of how this ends. The cat was raised from kittenhood alongside a pet sparrow; a second sparrow turns up, a quarrel starts, and the cat sides with its friend by eating the intruder, then enjoys the taste enough to eat its friend too. Lambert's vignette for one of La Fontaine's darkest fables gives the cat the starring role, beside an empty dish and the half-open door of a cupboard.
context: The illustration belongs to J. Hetzel's La Fontaine for the 'Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation', with animal drawings by Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900); the BnF copy (Gallica bpt6k5461375p, folio 621) is dated 1870 on Commons. 'Le Chat et les deux Moineaux' is fable 2 of Book XII, the last book of the Fables. Lambert, a Delacroix pupil nicknamed 'Lambert des chats' at the Salon, was the obvious man for the job. Fun fact: a family-education publisher still printed this one, cannibalised best friend and all.
title_eng: The Cat and the Two Sparrows
title_original: Le Chat et les deux moineaux (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: Here the cat is nature that cannot be trained out: friendship lasts exactly as long as appetite allows.
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f621

title: The Cat and an Old Rat (Le Chat et un vieux rat)
description: Rodilardus, the terror of the rats, hangs head-down from a rope among strings of onions, front paws dangling, playing dead. Below, a crowd of mice and rats rears up on a ledge in a little dance of relief, one sniffing at an upturned bowl. His second con, rolling in flour and lying in a meal tub, is still to come; this vignette catches the first. An old rat, tailless from earlier campaigns, keeps his distance and knows a cat is still a cat. Lambert's drawing, cut by the engraver A. Jourdain, turns the beam into a stage and the rodents into an audience.
context: The vignette is from J. Hetzel's La Fontaine in the 'Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation', animals by Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900); the BnF copy (Gallica bpt6k5461375p, folio 202) is dated 1870 on Commons. 'Le Chat et un vieux Rat' closes Book III. Lambert, nicknamed 'Lambert des chats' at the Salon, had studied with Delacroix, who helped fund his early work. Fun fact: La Fontaine borrowed the cat's name, Rodilardus ('gnaw-bacon'), from Rabelais.
title_eng: The Cat and an Old Rat
title_original: Le Chat et un vieux rat (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: The cat stands for disguised danger; the fable's moral praises the caution that comes with age.
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f202

title: The Cockerel, the Cat and the Young Mouse (Le Cochet, le Chat et le Souriceau)
description: The cat sits curled on the straw at right, eyes half shut, paws neatly together, the picture of modesty, while a cockerel stands on the rim of an upturned tub, beak wide open in mid-crow. Between them, tiny at the bottom left, the young mouse looks up at the noisy one. On its first outing the mouse decides the loud, red-crested, flapping bird is terrifying and the soft-furred, gentle-eyed creature lovely; its mother explains it the other way round. Lambert puts the real menace in the role of the charmer, which suited an artist who spent his career painting cats at their most appealing.
context: This illustration comes from the La Fontaine published by J. Hetzel in the 'Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation', with animals by Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900); the BnF copy (Gallica bpt6k5461375p, folio 309) is dated 1870 on Commons. The fable is in Book VI. Lambert, a Delacroix pupil, made his Salon debut in 1847 and was a member of the Société d'aquarellistes français from 1879 to 1896. Fun fact: his works ended up as far afield as the Brooklyn Museum and the Cincinnati Art Museum, which is a long reach for a man known mainly as 'Lambert des chats'.
title_eng: The Cockerel, the Cat and the Young Mouse
title_original: Le Cochet, le Chat et le Souriceau (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: The moral, 'Garde-toi, tant que tu vivras, de juger des gens sur la mine', makes the cat the textbook case of a pleasant face hiding a predator.
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f309

title: Dog and Cat: Animal Studies (Chien et chat)
medium: Pen and black ink on paper
collection: Private collection (ex-Galy collection; sold by Le Manuscrit Français)
description: A cat stalks in from the lower left, head down, tail hooked straight up like a question mark; a dog sits on the right, head bowed, its head worked up while its body stays a rough outline. The cat gets the more confident, finished line, and the pen moves fast and economically, already recognisably Lautrec's hand. On the back someone else wrote an English exercise about Cromwell, and its ghostly lines show through the browned paper. There are small losses at the upper and lower margins, a tiny stain on the right, and a red monogram stamp (Lugt 1338) in the lower left corner.
context: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec (1864–1901) probably drew this between about 1876 and 1880, while he was a pupil at the Lycée Fontanes (now Lycée Condorcet) in Paris. It is catalogued as D.447 in M.G. Dortu's catalogue raisonné (1971, as 'Croquis à l'encre') and was cited by Maurice Joyant in 1927. It came from the Galy collection and was sold by the Paris dealer Le Manuscrit Français with a Toulouse-Lautrec Committee certificate dated 12 November 2024. Fun fact: the same unknown hand wrote an English 'thème' on the back of Dortu D.449, so the boy was apparently sketching on a classmate's homework.

title: Cat and Lantern (Neko to Chōchin)
description: A white cat with brown tabby patches, red collar and little bell, has knocked a paper lantern on its side and shoves its head and forepaws into the open end, hindquarters up, tail flicked. Kiyochika builds a domestic drama from a cat, a lantern and a mouse that has presumably bolted inside. The lantern is unlit here, a pale ribbed drum with a family crest, its bamboo handle rolled out across a deep blue ground. The colour is laid in soft, graded impressions rather than crisp outlines, shading the lantern's curve the Western way. It is a horizontal ōban-size sheet, roughly 24 × 36 cm.
context: Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847–1915), a former retainer of the shogunate, began publishing his kōsen-ga, prints of Tokyo built on Western-style light and shade, in 1876. Cat and Lantern (Neko to chōchin) is dated 1877 and is one of his best-known animal subjects of those years. Fun fact: the Japanese caption on the Commons file, taken from a Tokyo ukiyo-e gallery, says the print needed 35 separate woodblocks, far more than a standard colour print of the time, which is how Kiyochika got those soft gradations.
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
collection: The British Museum, London / Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
image_credit: Kobayashi Kiyochika · https://ukiyo-e.gallery/current_event/

title: A Monster
description: A tabby cat peeks over the back of a wicker chair at upper right, eyes wide, front paws hooked on the rim, keeping well clear of the action. The 'monster' is the little girl herself: she crawls out from under a draped table wearing a whole tiger skin, its head pulled over her curls as a hood, while a pug squares up to her on the carpet. Alphabet blocks lie scattered at the bottom edge. Barber's speciality was fur of every kind, and here he gets three textures in one picture: the child's hair, the coarse striped pelt and the pets' coats.
context: Charles Burton Barber (1845–1894), born in Great Yarmouth, trained at the Royal Academy Schools and exhibited there from 1866 to 1893. He was the favourite painter of children with pets in late Victorian Britain, working for Queen Victoria and the Prince of Wales, and many of his pictures were sold as photogravures. A Monster is dated 1877; its present location is not recorded on Commons. Fun fact: his final commission, in 1894, was to paint the Queen with her grandchildren in her pony carriage, and he died soon afterwards.
submovement: Victorian sentimental genre painting (children and pets)
image_credit: Charles Burton Barber · Source not provided by Perkwus ( talk ) " Own work "

title: Cat with a Fish
description: A bright yellow cat with big black spots sits curled on itself, face turned square to us with huge turquoise eyes and a worried, scalloped brow, and a fat blue-grey prawn clamped in its mouth, red tail fan draped over its back. Kalighat painters worked fast on cheap paper, and it shows in the best way: one swelling outline for the body, flat washes of watercolour inside it, and black patches that read as both fur pattern and pure graphic design. Even the ears get red stripes. The sheet is 45.7 × 28 cm, and on the back someone wrote, in English, the bluntest possible caption: 'Cat caught a fish'.
context: Painters from rural Bengal settled around the Kali temple at Kalighat in Calcutta (now Kolkata) by the 1830s and sold quick, colourful pictures of gods, myths and city life to pilgrims and residents. This one dates from about 1890 and was given to the V&A by M. N. Varvill in 1955 (IS.261-1955). Fun fact: the cat-with-fish was one of the most repeated Kalighat subjects, and the V&A notes it is often read as an illustration of a Bengali proverb.
feline_symbolism: The V&A reads the cat as satire on a false ascetic: a creature that has supposedly renounced the world but cannot control its appetite, with the fish as the giveaway.
image_credit: GIF IT UP India · https://www.flickr.com/photos/189116622@N04/50058561063/ , https://gifitup.net/dag-museums/

title: Kittens
description: Four silver tabby kittens have broken into a jewel box on a lace-edged table, and the evidence is everywhere: a string of pearls trails off the edge, a bangle, a cross and a brooch lie abandoned, and one kitten rolls on its back batting at the loot. Kittens is what the Atkinson calls this canvas, and what Couldery did better than almost anyone in Victorian London. His method was a miniaturist's, tiny strokes laid in the direction of the fur, so the stripes are built hair by hair. Ruskin said one of his cat pictures could not rightly be seen without a lens, and this is the surface he meant.
context: Horatio Henry Couldery (1832–1918), born in Lewisham, gave up cabinetmaking for the Royal Academy Schools and showed at the RA from 1861, specialising in cats and dogs and illustrating children's books and cards. This painting belongs to The Atkinson in Southport (Sefton Council), catalogued as SOPAG-135. Fun fact: Couldery's death is usually given as 1893, the year his career faded, but the death registration found by researchers puts it at 4 February 1918; the Atkinson's own label gives yet another date, 1910.
image_credit: Horatio Henry Couldery · Art UK

title: The Cat (Pisica)
medium: Oil on canvas laid on metal
collection: National Museum of Art of Romania (Muzeul Național de Artă al României), Bucharest
description: A young grey-and-white cat lies twisted on its back, white belly up, paws flung in every direction, head turned toward us mid-play. It is a small study, oil on canvas glued down onto a metal support, painted while Grigorescu was learning from the Barbizon painters, and the handling shows it: broad, quick strokes, a dark muted ground, and the animal treated as a mass of light and shadow rather than a portrait of individual hairs. Only the face and the white chest get any finish; the hind legs dissolve into the brown. The metal backing is the detail most people miss.
context: Nicolae Grigorescu (1838–1907), the founding figure of modern Romanian painting, went to Paris in 1861 and soon gravitated to Barbizon, painting alongside the forest-of-Fontainebleau landscapists. This cat is dated 1864–1867 and is listed among his works made in France. It is in the Modern Romanian Art Gallery of the National Museum of Art of Romania, Bucharest, and was shown in the museum's 2007 centenary retrospective 'Grigorescu pictor al naturii'. Fun fact: the museum's centenary album, which supplied the Commons image, is also the source for the oil-on-metal support.
image_credit: Nicolae Grigorescu · Grigorescu - Album comemorativ la 100 de ani de decesul lui artistului, editat de Muzeul Național de Artă al României cu ocazia expoziției retrospective „Grigorescu pictor al naturii” desfășurată la Galeria de Artă Româ

title: Cat and Butterfly (耄耋圖)
artist: Xugu (Zhu Huairen, 虛谷 / 朱懷仁)
submovement: Late Qing Shanghai School (Haipai) Literati Painting
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A white cat, drawn only as a broken, dotted outline with two blazing orange eyes, stands in the lower half of a tall hanging scroll, tail up, staring straight out, while a flutter of butterflies drifts above it past a bank of pale green chrysanthemums. Xugu painted with the side of the brush in dry, angular strokes, so the cat looks almost cut from paper, and a slatted fence and blue-tipped leaves frame it at right. A column of bold calligraphy runs down the upper right. The image is about 134 × 65 cm on ink and colour on paper, and the mounted scroll is over two metres tall.
context: Xugu (c. 1823/24–1896), born in She County, Anhui, was a Qing army officer who became a Buddhist monk and later sold paintings in Shanghai and Yangzhou, among the most individual of the late-Qing Shanghai painters. This scroll came to the Metropolitan Museum in 1986 as a gift of Robert Hatfield Ellsworth, in memory of La Ferne Hatfield Ellsworth (1986.267.52), as part of a large Ellsworth gift of modern Chinese painting. Fun fact: cat-and-butterfly pairings were standard birthday pictures in China, because the words for cat (mao) and butterfly (die) sound like maodie, 'great old age'.
feline_symbolism: Cat and butterfly together make the rebus maodie (耄耋), meaning a person of seventy or eighty, so the picture wishes the owner a long life.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Woman with a Cat (Portrait of Madame Manet)
title_original: Femme au chat (Portrait de Madame Manet)
collection: Tate, London (purchased 1918), on loan to the National Gallery, London
description: A black-and-white cat sleeps curled in a woman's lap, a dark island in a sea of pink, its white muzzle and chest the sharpest notes in the picture. She sits at three-quarter length, head propped on one hand, looking past us, and her dress dissolves into long, slashing strokes that go soft and unfinished at the edges, as Manet often let them in these late domestic pictures. A blue-white curtain flickers at the left edge. The canvas is upright, 92.1 × 73 cm, so the cat sits right at its centre, the anchor everything else orbits.
context: Manet painted this around 1880, near the end of his life. The sitter is traditionally identified as his wife, Suzanne Manet (née Leenhoff), the Dutch pianist he married in 1863. Tate bought it in 1918 (N03295), and it is currently lent to the National Gallery, London (L675). Fun fact: the Tate number is still N03295, but the picture currently hangs in Trafalgar Square, lent to the National Gallery as L675.
title_eng: Woman with a Cat: Portrait of Madame Manet
image_credit: Édouard Manet · http://www.tate.org.uk

title: Interior with a Lady and a Cat
description: A black-and-white cat lies stretched out on the bare floorboards by an open doorway, a small dark shape that is easy to miss on first look. The woman, in a long white dress, stands with her back to us at a sunlit window. This is the Danish interior Holsøe painted over and over: pale panelled walls, a gilt console with a vase and a tall mirror, and a second room glimpsed through the door with a rush-seated chair. The panel is 45.5 × 50 cm, almost square, and signed 'C. Holsöe' at lower left. The cat anchors a room that is otherwise all air and reflection.
context: Carl Holsøe (1863–1935) trained at the Royal Danish Academy and became, with his friend Vilhelm Hammershøi and Peter Ilsted, one of the painters of the hushed Copenhagen interior. This panel was in a private collection by 1988 and went to auction at Sotheby's London twice in June 2006 (13 June, lot 125; 27 June, lot 415). Fun fact: the same panel came up at Sotheby's twice in two weeks, so its 2006 owner clearly wanted it gone.
title_eng: Interior with a Lady and a Cat
image_credit: Carl Holsøe · sothebys.com .

title: Flowers and Cats (Fleurs et chats)
description: Two cats share the bottom of this flower still life: a brown tabby asleep on a red table, head tucked down, and a grey cat peering out of a wicker basket tied with a red ribbon, a white ball of yarn beside them. Above, a huge bank of red and pink geraniums spills from a painted jardinière, which is rarer than it sounds: Renoir usually kept his cats on people's laps. The canvas is 92.7 × 73.7 cm, signed 'Renoir' and dated '81' at lower right, and petals and fur are made with the same soft, feathery strokes, so the animals read as part of the arrangement.
context: Renoir signed and dated this canvas in 1881. The picture is in a private collection and is reproduced in Gilles Néret's Renoir: Painter of Happiness (Taschen, 2001, p. 147), the source of the Commons image. Its earlier ownership is not recorded on Commons or Wikidata, and the record's Durand-Ruel provenance could not be confirmed. Fun fact: Commons files it under both his still lifes of flowers and his paintings of cats, one of the few Renoirs that straddles the two.
image_credit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir · Renoir, peintre du bonheur : 1841-1919 , de Gilles Néret, Köln, Taschen, 2001, p. 147. ISBN 9783822857410

title: Cat in Summer Greenery (Katt i sommargrönska)
collection: Private collection (sold Bukowskis, Stockholm, auction 653, lot 604A)
description: A tabby-and-white kitten stands square in a summer thicket and looks straight up at us, big round eyes, pink nose, white bib and two white front socks, its striped tail swinging out to the right. The picture is barely bigger than a postcard, 22 by 15.5 cm, upright, painted in oil, and the greenery gets as much paint as the cat: long, wiry streaks of green, rose and dry brown, with a few pale leaves sliding in at the bottom. Look for the inscription at lower left, 'Bruno Liljefors Qvarnbo -84', which pins the picture to a specific place and summer.
context: Liljefors, born in Uppsala in 1860, trained at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts from 1879 to 1882 and then travelled through Düsseldorf, Italy and Paris before coming home. He was still living around Uppsala in 1884, and the inscription names Kvarnbo, a spot near the city, as the place where this small study was made. The painting is in a private collection and surfaced at Bukowskis in Stockholm, the source of the photograph now on Wikimedia Commons. Fun fact: Liljefors was a lifelong hunter who preferred to paint predators and prey, so a kitten in long grass, ears and eyes on something just out of frame, is closer to his usual subject than it first looks.
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Bukowskis

title: White Cat, Black Cat (Chat blanc, Chat noir)
description: Some thirty small cats tumble across this sheet in loose rows, read top to bottom like a film strip: a white cat sniffs at a mousehole, pounces, rears up with the mouse dangling from its paws, and then a black cat slinks in. The two arch their backs, square off and end in a boxing match on hind legs while the mouse scuttles off. There are no words at all, as the record notes, so Steinlen's line does every bit of the storytelling, with only his signature near the bottom. It is a photomechanical print, his pen drawing transferred photographically to a plate and run off with a weekly paper.
context: Steinlen, born in Lausanne, settled in Paris in 1881 and began frequenting Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret in 1884. Salis also ran a weekly paper of the same name, launched in 1882, and Steinlen drew for it between 1884 and 1895, mostly stories in pictures starring cats. The BnF dates this sheet to 1884, lists it as no. 649-153 in Crauzat's catalogue of Steinlen's prints, and has digitised it on Gallica. Fun fact: these strips are usually called histoires sans paroles, stories without words, and this one obeys the label more strictly than several neighbours from the same year, which the BnF records as carrying French text.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
feline_symbolism: The cabaret was named, so the story goes, after an old tomcat that moved in during building work, so any cat in its paper doubled as a house mascot.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: How Love Comes to Cats (Comment l'amour vient aux chats)
description: A white cat lounging by a chimney lunges at sparrows, slips off the roof and lands in the street at the feet of a black cat. Hissing turns into wrestling, wrestling into a moonlit stroll, and the last row delivers the punchline: a long line of kittens, black, white and patched, sitting in order of size. That, according to Steinlen, is how love comes to cats. The BnF classes the sheet as a humorous composition, and the only French text is the printed title at the bottom. It is a photomechanical print, a pen drawing photographed onto a plate for Le Chat Noir.
context: Steinlen came to Paris from Lausanne in 1881 and was drawn into the Chat Noir circle from 1884, the year the BnF gives for this print. Rodolphe Salis's cabaret had its own weekly, launched in 1882, and Steinlen supplied it with drawn stories, most of them starring cats, until 1895. The sheet is no. 649-116 in Crauzat's catalogue of Steinlen's prints, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France has published it on Gallica. Fun fact: Steinlen's reputation as the cat specialist of Montmartre, the one who drew them playing, sleeping and furious, started in these cheap weekly pages more than a decade before his famous 1896 Tournée du Chat Noir poster.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Horrible End of a Goldfish (Horrible fin d'un Poisson rouge)
description: A black cat, drawn as a flat silhouette, works its way through eight scenes around a goldfish bowl on a stemmed stand: it stares, paws at the glass, climbs up, fishes from the rim, falls in with a splash of hatching, and finally bolts, soaked, from the toppled bowl while the goldfish lies stranded in a puddle. The sheet, headed 'Le Chat Noir', comes from that weekly, and the only French text is the title along the bottom. It is a photomechanical print, so the line you see is Steinlen's pen drawing reproduced by photography, and a reader could get the joke before the coffee cooled.
context: Dated 1884 by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, this is one of the first batch of cat stories Steinlen drew for Le Chat Noir, the weekly paper of Rodolphe Salis's Montmartre cabaret. Salis launched the paper in 1882; Steinlen, in Paris since 1881, contributed from 1884 to 1895. The BnF catalogues the print as Crauzat 649-121 and has digitised it on Gallica. Fun fact: the goldfish's grim fate belongs to a long Steinlen habit of letting the cat win, whether the victim is a fish, a mouse or a crow, which is partly why he became known in Montmartre as the specialist of cats.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cat and the Crow (Le Chat et le Corbeau)
description: A white cat naps on an upholstered chair while a black crow perches on the chair back above it, and the rest of the sheet is pure escalation. The crow pecks, the cat wakes and swipes, the crow yanks its tail from under the seat, and the chase spills outdoors and up a tree, where the cat ends up dangling upside down from a branch while the crow looks on. The title puts the cat first, but the crow seems to get the last laugh. The BnF files it as a humorous composition; it is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, Steinlen's pen drawing photographed onto a plate.
context: The Bibliothèque nationale de France dates this print to 1884, the year Steinlen, a Swiss illustrator living in Paris since 1881, began frequenting Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret. The cabaret's weekly paper, launched in 1882, carried his drawn stories from 1884 to 1895, and cats were the leading actors in most of them. This one is no. 649-111 in Crauzat's catalogue of Steinlen's prints, the lowest number among the cat stories in this group, and the BnF has digitised it on Gallica. Fun fact: Rutgers' French department adopted Steinlen's Chat Noir cats as an informal mascot and decorates its website with images from these stories.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Avenging Nail (Le Clou vengeur)
description: A black cat chases a mouse to a row of barrels, climbs and dives in head first, leaving only its tail and back legs sticking out. Then a rabbit bursts out of a barrel instead, and in the last scene the cat perches on the rim while the rabbit bolts away, trailing a long wiggling line snagged on a nail: the avenging nail of the title. The BnF's subject headings list cats, a rabbit, mice, barrels and nails, and a printed dedication at bottom right addresses a lady surprised that rabbits have no innards. It is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, Steinlen's own pen line reproduced by photography.
context: Steinlen drew this story in 1884, according to the Bibliothèque nationale de France, during his first year in the orbit of Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret in Montmartre. Salis's weekly, launched in 1882, printed Steinlen's picture stories from 1884 to 1895, and cats starred in most of them. The BnF catalogues the sheet as Crauzat 649-134 and has published it on Gallica. Fun fact: Steinlen had arrived in Paris in 1881 after studying theology in Lausanne and industrial ornament design in Mulhouse, a training that does not obviously predict a career spent making Parisians laugh at cats and barrels.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Ancestors of Maigriou (Les Ancêtres de Maigriou)
description: Some thirty cats sprawl across a grey-toned sheet, and almost all of them are asleep: curled into rings, flat on their backs with paws in the air, stretched full length, or reduced to a single heavy black head at the corners. A couple wake up to stretch. Maigriou, a name that sounds like a cross between maigre (skinny) and a miaow, gets a family album rather than a tree, and the BnF's only subject heading is 'cats'. It is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, Steinlen's pen line photographed onto a plate and printed on cheap paper, the format in which most Parisians first met his cats.
context: The Bibliothèque nationale de France dates this sheet to 1884 and catalogues it as no. 649-132 in Crauzat's list of Steinlen's prints, next door to 'Le Clou vengeur' (649-134). Both appeared in Le Chat Noir, the weekly that Rodolphe Salis launched in 1882 to promote his Montmartre cabaret, where Steinlen, in Paris since 1881, became a regular from 1884. He drew stories for the paper until 1895, mostly with cats in the lead. Fun fact: Steinlen kept drawing cats long after the paper folded and even modelled them in sculpture, among them a seated Angora now in the Musée d'Orsay.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Shashthi, Goddess of Children, Standing on a Cat
description: A big white cat with black spots crouches flat under Shashthi, goddess of children, its round eyes and almost human brows giving it a look of mild alarm. She has yellow skin and a red sari edged in white dots and carries a baby on her hip, while a second child stands on the cat's head, holding her hand. The cat takes the weight with the patience of divine transport. The painting is opaque watercolour on paper, done in the quick, broad strokes that made Kalighat pictures cheap and fast to produce, and her name, 'shashthi', is written by hand at the bottom.
context: Painted in Kolkata around 1885 by an unrecorded artist working for the pilgrim trade near the Kalighat Kali temple, where patuas from rural Bengal sold bright, simplified pictures of gods and city life. The V&A, which holds the largest Kalighat collection anywhere, acquired this sheet (IS.574-1950) from Miss M. Steele, part of a group she inherited from her mother. Fun fact: in the Jamai-Shashthi tale a greedy daughter-in-law blames the cat for food she ate herself; the cat, being Shashthi's mount, complains to the goddess and steals the woman's babies until she apologises. Worshippers in Bengal still shape dough images of the goddess and her black cat for the rite.
title_eng: Shashthi, Goddess of Children, Standing on a Cat
feline_symbolism: The cat is Shashthi's vahana (mount); in Bengali folklore it acts as her enforcer, so mothers who wrong a cat risk the goddess's protection of their children.
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O71571/painting-shashthi-goddess-of-children-standing/

title: Mother Cat with Three Kittens
title_original: Chatte et ses chatons aux cerises
description: A long-haired ginger-and-white mother cat leans over a blue-rimmed plate with two kittens, one grey-and-white and one brown-and-white, all three noses down at the same scraps, while the third kitten, a calico, has made off to the right with a pink morsel in its jaws. A china cup lies tipped over in the foreground, the only casualty so far. The canvas is small, 25 by 33.5 cm, and the Wikimedia cataloguers file it under 'cats eating in art', fair enough given that nobody here is posing. It is oil on canvas, signed 'Brunel Neuville' at lower left, and the photograph comes from the Dorotheum auction house.
context: Alfred-Arthur Brunel de Neuville (1852–1941) was a French painter who returned to cats often enough for Wikimedia Commons to keep a whole category of his cat paintings, this one included. The canvas has no firm date: the only available record, a Dorotheum sale of nineteenth-century paintings and watercolours, does not supply one, and Commons can only say 'by 1941'. It is in a private collection. Fun fact: Commons also files the picture under 'Three Little Kittens', the nursery rhyme about the kittens who lost their mittens, which says more about the cataloguers' sense of humour than about the painter's intentions.
image_credit: Alfred-Arthur Brunel de Neuville · https://www.dorotheum.com/en/auctions/current-auctions/kataloge/list-lots-detail/auktion/12881-19th-century-paintings-and-watercolours/lotID/238/lot/2308722-alfred-arthur-brunel-de-neuville.html?currentPag

title: The Butterfly
description: A fluffy tabby kitten sits with its back to us on a wooden ledge, tail hanging over the edge, head tipped up at a dark butterfly that has landed in a spray of pink-and-white apple blossom. The blossom rises from a blue-and-white vase painted with a bird on a branch, which raises the stakes nicely: one kitten, one butterfly, one breakable object. Dolph painted it in oil on an upright canvas, 71 by 41 cm, and the tall format lets the blossom climb while the kitten stays put, for now. The picture is known as 'The Butterfly', and it is signed at lower left.
context: John Henry Dolph (1835–1903) started as a carriage painter in Ohio, worked as a portrait painter in Cleveland and Detroit, and moved to New York in 1864, where he showed every year at the National Academy of Design. After study in Antwerp (1870–73) and Paris (1880–82) he specialised in pets, and a reviewer later dubbed him 'the Landseer of America'. The Butterfly is recorded only through the Athenaeum database, which dates it to about 1870; its present owner is not known. Fun fact: Dolph lived and worked in the Sherwood Studio Building on West 57th Street, often called the first New York apartment house built specifically for artists.
image_credit: John Henry Dolph · The Athenaeum

title: Apotheosis of the Cats of Montmartre (L'Apothéose des chats à Montmartre)
submovement: Montmartre cabaret decoration (Le Chat Noir circle)
description: A horde of cats pours over the rooftops of Paris under a full moon, and at the very top of the heap one black cat sits silhouetted against the yellow disc like a king on a throne. Numéro describes the felines as invading the roofs, perhaps on their way to besiege the whole city. The canvas is huge, three metres wide and more than one and a half high, so the cats work as a frieze of silhouettes and attitudes: gingers and tabbies scrambling over a chimney at left, a black cat on the gutter, a tangle of orange cats at right. Windmills crown the hill in the distance.
context: Steinlen, a Swiss illustrator who joined the Chat Noir crowd in 1884, painted this canvas around 1885, and Numéro reports that it hung in the downstairs room of Rodolphe Salis's cabaret. It now belongs to the Petit Palais in Geneva, which owns some 630 paintings, drawings and prints by the artist; it was lent to the Musée de Montmartre for the centenary exhibition of 2023–24. Fun fact: the date is contested. Wikimedia and coverage of the Montmartre exhibition give c. 1885, while Numéro prints 1905, a date that sits awkwardly with its own story of the canvas hanging in Salis's cabaret, whose weekly paper had stopped by 1895.
title_eng: Apotheosis of the Cats of Montmartre
feline_symbolism: Cats were the cabaret's emblem, named after an old tomcat said to have moved in during building work, so an apotheosis of cats is also an apotheosis of the house.
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · LeTemps.ch [1]

title: Cat Watching a Spider
medium: Album leaf; ink and color on silk
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A grey-and-white cat with a black cap of fur crouches at the corner of a folding screen and stares down at a spider in the lower left, and the spider has, so far, not noticed the cat. The cat wears a bright knotted cloth around its neck, orange and turquoise patterned, the only loud colour on the leaf. Painted in ink and colour on silk, 37.5 by 27.9 cm, its Japanese title, Neko ni kumo zu, simply pairs the two animals. The fur is built from fine strokes and soft washes, while the spider needs only a few hard lines. It is an album leaf, meant to be held.
context: Ōide Tōkō (1841–1905) painted this leaf in Japan in about 1888–92, during the Meiji period. It belongs to the Charles Stewart Smith Collection, given to the Metropolitan Museum in 1914 by Mrs Charles Stewart Smith and her sons Charles Stewart Smith Jr. and Howard Caswell Smith in memory of the collector. Tōkō was about fifty when he painted it, an established artist working in the decades when Japan was busy absorbing Western art. Fun fact: the same 1914 gift brought the Met Kawanabe Kyōsai's 'Cat Catching a Frog', so two Meiji cats with very different hunting results now sit a few accession numbers apart (14.76.61.20 and 14.76.61.73).
image_credit: Ōide Tōkō · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: The Cat and the Fox (Katten och räven)
description: A tabby-and-white cat clings to a branch at the top of the picture and peers down, white paws gripping the bark and striped tail hanging below. At the bottom a red fox tips its head back, mouth open, eyes fixed on the prize above. The canvas is absurdly tall and thin, 40.5 by 12.5 cm, closer to a Japanese hanging scroll than a Swedish salon picture, and it stacks the two animals into a vertical standoff. Between them only pale umbels of cow parsley and scratchy brushwork. Liljefors signed it in red at lower right and dated it 1885.
context: Liljefors (1860–1939) trained at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts from 1879 to 1882, travelled through Germany, Italy and Paris, and then settled back around Uppsala, where he lived until 1894. Foxes were already a favourite subject; his 'Foxes' is also dated 1885. This little painting is in a private collection and was sold through Uppsala Auktionskammare in 2019, whose photograph is reproduced here. Fun fact: Liljefors was influenced by Japanese art, which Nationalmuseum sees in his pared-down compositions and in his habit of mounting several narrow paintings in one frame; a strip this slim may well once have had neighbours.
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Uppsala Auktionskammare

title: Cat and Dogs Belonging to Queen Victoria
collection: Royal Collection Trust (Horn Room, Osborne House)
description: A tabby kitten perches on a wooden kitchen chair draped with a brown cloth, and three royal dogs stand below and stare up at it: a dachshund, a smooth fox-terrier and a pug in a studded collar. The kitten holds the high ground, literally, and looks down with calm suspicion. Apple blossom drifts over the orchard, a cottage wall closes the background, and a besom broom leans against the chair at right. Barber signed and dated the canvas 1885. It measures 35.5 by 53.5 cm, the scale of a picture meant for a private room rather than a gallery wall.
context: Charles Burton Barber (1845–1894) painted many of Queen Victoria's animals, and the Royal Collection believes this one was painted for her, though it cannot be matched with certainty to the pictures she paid him for in 1885. It is probably the work recorded at Osborne House in 1886 as 'a cat with Paul, Vic and Princess'; Vic was the fox-terrier. The painting still hangs at Osborne, in the Horn Room, and is catalogued by Oliver Millar in The Victorian Pictures in the Collection of Her Majesty The Queen (1992). Fun fact: the dogs get names in the royal records, while the kitten, the obvious star, stays anonymous.
title_eng: Cat and Dogs Belonging to Queen Victoria
title_original: Cat and Dogs Belonging to Queen Victoria
image_credit: Charles Burton Barber · Royal Collection

title: The Little Patient (Der kleine Patient)
description: A black and white kitten is 'the little patient', propped on a striped yellow cushion with one front paw wrapped in a bandage and its mouth half open in complaint. Beside it stands a corked medicine bottle with a red label, the cure placed exactly where the invalid can resent it. The panel is tiny, only 16.5 by 12 cm, painted in oil on wood, and the smooth support lets Adam work the white bib and whiskers with a fine finish. Panels this small were his stock in trade. The signature and date, 'Jul. Adam 85', sit at upper right.
context: Julius Adam (1852–1913) came from a Munich dynasty of painters that ran to four generations. He worked as a photographic retoucher in Rio de Janeiro as a teenager, studied at the Munich Academy from 1873, and settled as a painter in 1882; after a picture of two cats brought him his biggest success, he turned almost entirely to cats and became known as 'Katzen-Adam', or the 'Raphael of Cats'. This panel, signed and dated 1885, is in a private collection; the photograph comes from the auction house Galerie Bassenge. Fun fact: his cats sold especially well in the United States.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · http://www.bassenge.com/

title: Tales for Sara: The Cat and the Ball of Yarn (Contes à Sara: Le Chat et la Pelote)
medium: Photomechanical print (impression photomécanique); engraved by Charles Gillot
description: A black cat meets a ball of wool, and the sheet tells the rest in sixteen small scenes read like a comic strip. The cat paws the ball off a shelf, dangles from the edge by the thread, stalks it, leaps, wrestles it, and then gets wound up so thoroughly that by the bottom row it has turned into a ball of yarn itself, with knitting needles still sticking out. There is no text at all, so the comedy lives in the cat's body language. It is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, and the plate carries the credit 'Gillot sc.' for the firm that made the printing block.
context: The Bibliothèque nationale de France dates this sheet to 1885 and credits it to Steinlen as illustrator and Charles Gillot (1853–1903) as engraver; it is Crauzat 649-196. Gillot's photomechanical relief process made it cheap to print line drawings next to type, which is how a weekly like Le Chat Noir, launched by Rodolphe Salis in 1882, could fill its pages with Steinlen's picture stories from 1884 to 1895. The series title 'Contes à Sara' (Tales for Sara) frames it as a bedtime story. Fun fact: Steinlen's Chat Noir strips were gathered later into an album of wordless cat drawings, Des chats, so pages like this got a second life as a book.
title_eng: Tales for Sara: The Cat and the Ball of Yarn
title_original: Contes à Sara: Le Chat et la Pelote
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur Gillot, Charles (1853-1903). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cat and the Guinea Pig (Le Chat et le Cochon d'Inde)
medium: Photomechanical print (impression photomécanique); engraved by Charles Gillot
description: A black kitten, a guinea pig and some tinned goods: the BnF's subject headings (cats, guinea pig, canned food) read like an inventory from a slapstick prop room. Across four loose rows the kitten sniffs, bristles, arches its back and bats at the plump white-and-patched guinea pig, which keeps escaping into toppled tins and finally pokes out of one at the far right. There is no text, so Steinlen makes it funny with line alone. The sheet is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, with the credit 'Gillot sc.' for the engraving firm that converted his drawing into a printing block.
context: The Bibliothèque nationale de France dates the print to 1885, catalogues it as Crauzat 649-183 and names two makers: Steinlen as illustrator and Charles Gillot (1853–1903) as engraver. It ran in Le Chat Noir, the weekly that Rodolphe Salis launched in 1882 to accompany his cabaret, where Steinlen published drawn stories from 1884 to 1895, most of them led by cats. Fun fact: Gillot's name on the plate is a reminder that these 'drawings' are really industrial products; his firm's photo-relief process is what made Steinlen's cats affordable enough to be read, laughed at and thrown away every week.
title_eng: The Cat and the Guinea Pig
title_original: Le Chat et le Cochon d'Inde
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur Gillot, Charles (1853-1903). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: A New Arrival
collection: Private collection / location unknown (image from an Invaluable auction listing)
description: A tricolour cat laps milk from a shallow green-rimmed bowl that a girl holds on her lap, its white muzzle dipped and eyes half closed. She looks down at it in a pale blue pinafore, and behind her a long-case clock, a jug, a teacup and a glass of daffodils fill a plain grey room. The 'new arrival' is being welcomed with food. Osborne dated it 1885. The treatment is unsentimental: Osborne painted children and their pets with a realist's eye and a gentle mood rather than with the syrup of much Victorian genre painting.
context: Walter Osborne (1859–1903) trained in Antwerp, where he won the Taylor Prize in 1881 and 1882, then painted in Brittany from 1883 and in England, at Walberswick and elsewhere, before returning to Dublin; he was elected to the Royal Hibernian Academy in 1886. His models included Jules Bastien-Lepage's plein-air realism. A New Arrival is singled out among his pictures of children with pets, and the art historian Julian Campbell notes that Osborne 'eschews the overly sentimental or literary quality of much Victorian genre painting'. The painting's current owner is unrecorded; the known photograph comes from an auction listing on Invaluable.
image_credit: Walter Osborne · http://www.invaluable.com/auction-lot/walter-frederick-osborne,-r.h.a.-1859-1903-179-c-sm3i282das#

title: Quilt Top, Crazy pattern
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A crazy quilt is a patchwork with the rules removed: irregular scraps of silk, satin and velvet fitted together like broken crockery. Here the scraps are corralled into forty-two square blocks, seven rows of six, each edged with feather-stitch embroidery in yellow and red. The Met's tags list a cat, birds, fans and horses among the shards, and fans and horseshoes are easy to spot, while the cat is a small treasure hunt across 154 by 132 cm of shine and nap, perhaps among the black velvet appliqués. This is a quilt top only, never backed or quilted, so it was made for show rather than warmth.
context: An unrecorded American maker assembled this top around 1885, at the height of the crazy-quilt fashion, from silk, satin, velvet and cotton. The maker never got as far as backing and quilting it, so what survives is the decorated face alone. It entered the Met's American Wing in 1989 as a gift of Tracey Blumenreich Zabar (1989.66). Fun fact: the Met's cataloguers tag only four motifs on the whole top, cats, birds, fans and horses, so in a sea of fabric scraps the cat made the official shortlist.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Figure Dish
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A cat lies curled on the lid of this little covered dish, head up and ears pricked, tail wrapped neatly around its haunch. The base is moulded as a woven basket with a rope-twist rim, so the cat looks as if it has settled into its own bed. It is pressed from opaque white glass, the material collectors call milk glass, and stands only 10.8 cm high and 14 cm long. Pressed glass is formed in a mould, so every whisker-less detail was fixed by the mould-maker before a single dish was made. It comes in two parts, base and lid, hence the Met's 'a, b' number.
context: McKee and Brothers, a Pittsburgh glass firm, made this dish between 1880 and 1890. The Met catalogues it simply as a 'Figure Dish', its maker's trade category for dishes topped with a modelled figure. It came to the museum in 1946 as a gift of Mrs. Emily Winthrop Miles and sits in the American Wing as 46.140.755a, b. Fun fact: that accession number means this was at least the 755th object logged from Mrs Miles's 1946 gift alone, so the cat arrived in very large company.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: A Frieze of Cats and Moons (Une frise de chats et de lunes)
title_original: Une frise de chats et de lunes
collection: Weisman & Michel Collection (David E. Weisman and Jacqueline E. Michel), private
description: Cats of every coat, black, tabby, calico and long-haired white, parade along a golden band and pick fights with full moons that all have faces. In the upper strip a white cat rears up and claws a pale moon that scowls and grimaces, while a piebald cat sniffs it from the other side; a pink moon looks on, appalled. A black cat arches its back at the far right like a punctuation mark. Painted in oil on canvas, this is a frieze of cats and moons, and the photograph shows it as intended: two long strips hung one above the other on a wall.
context: Steinlen painted 'Une frise de chats et de lunes' in 1885, a year after he joined the circle around Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret. It belongs to the American collection of David E. Weisman and Jacqueline E. Michel, nearly 200 works by artists who lived or worked in Montmartre, in which Steinlen holds a major place. The Musée Toulouse-Lautrec in Albi showed the collection, frieze included, in 'Montmartre, fin de siècle' from 4 May to 5 September 2021. Fun fact: the museum's own press release spells the artist 'Steinlein' under its illustration of this very picture, a slip the Rutgers French department also makes once on its Steinlen page.
title_eng: A Frieze of Cats and Moons (Une frise de chats et de lunes)
submovement: Montmartre cabaret decoration (Le Chat Noir circle)
image_credit: Jl FilpoC · Own work

title: Cat Catching a Frog
description: A tabby cat catches a frog in this album leaf, pinning it under one forepaw while the frog flails its legs and gapes. The cat comes in low out of a stand of reeds, tail flung up in a high curve, round yellow eyes fixed on its prey. Kyōsai gets two very different bodies to play with: one all fur and coiled spring, the other slick, splayed and out of luck. The leaf is ink and colour on silk, 35.9 by 27 cm, and the reeds are dashed off in quick wet strokes. It was meant to be seen close, one page of an album at a time.
context: Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831–1889) studied briefly as a boy with the ukiyo-e master Utagawa Kuniyoshi and then trained formally in the Kanō school, a double education that shows in his mix of polish and mischief. He painted this leaf around 1887, two years before his death. It is part of the Charles Stewart Smith Collection, given to the Metropolitan Museum in 1914 by Smith's widow and sons (14.76.61.20); the same gift includes Ōide Tōkō's 'Cat Watching a Spider'. Fun fact: one of Kyōsai's most devoted pupils was the British architect Josiah Conder, who studied with him for ten years, until the painter died.
medium: Album leaf; ink and color on silk
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Julie Manet with Cat (L'Enfant au chat)
description: A white-and-tabby cat lies curled in Julie Manet's lap with its eyes squeezed shut and a grin that looks almost smug, the happiest face in the picture. Julie, eight going on nine, sits in three-quarter view in a pale yellow smocked dress, hair cut in a fringe, one hand resting on the cat's back. A pink floral wallpaper and a red chair-back frame her. Renoir signed and dated the canvas at upper right: 'Renoir 87'. It is oil on canvas, 65 by 54 cm, and the cat takes up nearly as much of the composition as she does.
context: Julie Manet (1878–1966) was the only child of the painters Berthe Morisot and Eugène Manet, and Renoir, a close friend of the family, painted her often. This portrait dates from 1887. It stayed with the sitter for the rest of her long life, then passed to Julien Rouart, and in 1999 it entered the Musée d'Orsay by dation, the French scheme that lets heirs settle inheritance tax with works of art (RF 1999 13). Fun fact: Julie married the painter Ernest Rouart in 1900 and their first child, Julien, was born in 1901, so the cat very probably went from the girl in the picture to her son before reaching a museum.
image_credit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir · KQGO9bsplWZeCg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Cat on a Flowerbed (Katt på blomsteräng)
description: A black-and-white cat sits low in the bottom right corner of a summer meadow, half hidden by stems and dandelion clocks, ears pricked and gaze turned off to the right. Liljefors gives the flowers almost as much attention as the animal: yellow daisies, pink clover and silver seed heads crowd the whole canvas. Nationalmuseum calls the composition starkly pared down, and there is almost no horizon, only a sliver of red farm building in the top left corner. It is oil on canvas, 61 by 76 cm. Originally it shared a frame with a painting of red-backed shrike nestlings, the two composed to balance each other.
context: Liljefors painted this in 1887, while living near Uppsala, as part of an ambitious set of six paintings mounted together; the backs of the frames record how they hung. The set was split up at some point. Nationalmuseum acquired 'Nestlings of Red-Backed Shrike' and 'Four Bird Studies' in 1992 and bought the cat painting in 2013 (NM 7128), then reunited them in one frame, as the artist intended. Fun fact: Nationalmuseum reads the whole arrangement as Japanese-inspired, both the pared-down compositions and the very idea of mounting several small paintings in a single frame, a fashion Liljefors picked up when Japanese art was all the rage in Europe.
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Stockholms Auktionsverk

title: Mother Cat with Three Kittens (Katzenmutter mit drei Jungen)
description: A striped tabby mother lies stretched across a rug with her chin up and her eyes on us, while her three kittens spread out around her: one perched on a wooden step at right, one peering over the rim of an upturned basket with a pink-striped cushion, one sitting at her front paws with a white bib. A pale blue brocade curtain falls behind them all. It is a small oil on wood panel, 16 by 21 cm, signed 'J. Adam 1887'. The kittens supply the movement and the mother the calm, and the smooth panel lets Adam paint fur with a fine finish.
context: Julius Adam (1852–1913) belonged to a Munich family of painters that stretched over four generations. He settled in Munich as a painter in 1882 and, after a picture of two cats became his greatest success, devoted himself almost entirely to cats, earning the nicknames 'Katzen-Adam' and the 'Raphael of Cats'. This panel was offered by Lempertz in Cologne in March 2013 and is in a private collection. Fun fact: before he ever painted a cat, Adam spent nearly six years in Rio de Janeiro as a teenager, retouching photographs, a training in patient small-scale detail that his kittens seem to have inherited.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · lempertz.com

title: Three Cats in the Straw (Drei Katzen im Stroh)
description: Two kittens, one black-and-white and one tabby, rear up on a crumpled blue-grey cloth and wrestle in a full embrace, while a third peeks out from under an overturned wicker basket at left, paws on the rim, waiting for its turn. A heap of straw rises behind them in a dark barn. The panel is small enough to hold in two hands, about 20 by 15 cm and taller than it is wide. Adam painted it in oil on wood, so fine strokes of fur sit crisply against the scratchier stalks. The signature and date, Julius Adam 1887, are tucked into the upper left corner.
context: Julius Anton Adam (1852-1913) came from a Munich dynasty of painters that began with his grandfather Albrecht Adam. His father was mainly a lithographer and photographer, and the son worked in landscape photography, including for the family business in Rio de Janeiro, before settling in Munich as a genre painter. He started his cat pictures in 1882, and they sold so well internationally that the rest of his output was, as one biography puts it, somewhat overlooked. This panel surfaced at the German auction house Mehlis. Fun fact: his grave lies next to his grandfather's in Munich's Alter Suedfriedhof, yet the cemetery registers contain no record of his burial.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · Auktionshaus Mehlis

title: Mark Twain with Kitten
description: A tabby kitten sits cupped in both of Mark Twain's hands, and he bends his white head to look down at it with a cigar clamped in his mouth. He sits on a small boulder in his white suit on a sloping lawn under trees. The kitten is the small grey knot at the centre of a picture that is otherwise all white cloth and white hair. It is a press photograph, not a studio confection: a commercial firm made it to be reproduced in newspapers, and it worked.
context: Underwood & Underwood, the New York photographic agency, took this portrait in 1907, three years before Twain's death. A dealer's listing says it became known as 'I Always Had a Fondness for Kittens' after the New York Times ran it that year; the copy on Wikimedia Commons came from the Times photo archive. Twain liked the image enough to sign prints: one sold at RR Auction carries the inscription 'To Mrs. Kate D. Riggs, with the love of Mark Twain, Jan. 14/08'. Fun fact: his cats had names like Sour Mash, Apollinaris, Zoroaster and Blatherskite, which he claimed were chosen to give children practice with hard words.
collection: Mark Twain House & Museum, Hartford, Connecticut / Library of Congress
image_credit: Underwood & Underwood · The New York Times photo archive, via their online store, here

title: Self-Portrait with Cats for 'Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui', No. 349
description: Black and grey cats crowd in around Steinlen as he sits on a rush chair before a blank canvas: one arches on top of the easel, another rubs against his hand at left, and kittens tumble and fight at his feet. He looks away in profile, bearded, in a grey work jacket and pink shirt. The masthead credits the drawing to Jean Caillou, a pseudonym, and the corner inscription dedicates it 'à Steinlen son meilleur ami'. Each issue of the series profiled one personality, usually drawn by a colleague, so here the subject quietly does the job himself and disguises the byline.
context: Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui was a French series of illustrated portraits, one personality per issue; Steinlen's turn came with no. 349 in 1889, when he was thirty and still making his name in Montmartre's humorous papers. French Wikipedia notes that he represented himself here under the pseudonym Jean Caillou, and that he was 'the specialist of cats, which he drew without tiring'. The Bibliotheque nationale de France holds a copy and has digitised it on Gallica. Fun fact: Steinlen also used pseudonyms in his political drawings, reportedly to stay out of trouble, so the caillou (pebble) disguise fits a habit.
title_eng: Self-Portrait with Cats for 'Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui', No. 349
title_original: Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui, n° 349: Steinlen par Jean Caillou
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b53188733z

title: Jacquard-woven Picture
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A small white cat sits at the lower right corner beside a saucer, entirely unbothered by history, while a woman in a bonnet and fichu sews a large starred flag on a porch. The woven caption reads 'Betsy Ross making the first United States flag', and a spinning wheel fills the left side. The picture is pocket-sized, 20.6 by 12.4 cm, and woven rather than painted: every tone comes from silk threads lifted and dropped by a punched-card Jacquard loom. Picture weaving like this turned the factory loom into a printing press, producing the same image hundreds of times.
context: Anderson Brothers worked in Paterson, New Jersey, the centre of American silk manufacturing, and the Met dates this piece between 1887 and 1890. Woven pictures were a sideline for mills that otherwise made ribbons and dress silks, sold as framable souvenirs. The museum bought it through the Friends of the American Wing Fund in 1984, and it sits in the American Wing rather than with European textiles. Fun fact: the Met catalogues the object only as 'Jacquard-woven Picture'; the cushion in the catalogue's old title is not in the museum record.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Pierrot and the Cat (Pierrot et le chat)
description: A black cat hangs stretched to full length in the arms of a small child dressed as Pierrot, hind legs reaching the floor and tail curling up at the bottom right. Black against the white costume is the one sure way to make a black cat as visible as possible. The child, in a black skullcap, looks off to the left rather than at the cat. Steinlen painted it in oil on cardboard, a cheap, absorbent support he used often, and at 79 by 59 cm it is larger than its sketchy surface suggests. The cat endures with the long-suffering patience of an animal that has been carried before.
context: Steinlen, Swiss-born and settled in Montmartre, painted this in 1889, the year his daughter Colette was a baby and his reputation was still built on drawings for the humorous press. Wikimedia Commons, following WikiArt, records it in the Musee du Petit Palais in Geneva under inventory 14383, a private museum built around the collection of Oscar Ghez. Fun fact: the picture is sorted on Commons among full-length standing children holding animals, which is more accurate than the catalogue's old story of an adult mime sharing supper with a cat at a tavern table.
image_credit: Musée du Petit Palais, Geneva (Inv. 14383, Ghez Collection) · Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen

title: Portrait of Elizaveta Yaroshenko with a Cat
title_original: Портрет Елизаветы Платоновны Ярошенко с кошкой
description: A white cat sits upright in Elizaveta Platonovna Yaroshenko's lap with its back to us, ears pricked toward her, while she smiles down at it and rests her left hand on its shoulders. In her right hand she holds not a fan but a paper knife, halfway through cutting the pages of an open book. The two props split the picture's duties neatly: the book is about her mind, the cat about home. The white cat also works as a light reflector, throwing brightness into a portrait otherwise built from dark dress and interior shadow, with only lace cuffs and collar to answer it.
context: Nikolai Yaroshenko (1846-1898), an artillery officer who became one of the leaders of the Peredvizhniki (Wanderers), is better known for social subjects and portraits of writers and scientists. This portrait of a family member belongs to the Kaluga Museum of Fine Arts, whose Yaroshenko holdings were painted and kept at his brother's estate of Pavlishchev Bor in Kaluga province, then confiscated and handed to the museum. Fun fact: the image circulating online came from a Russian art-reproduction site, and even Commons gives the picture no firm date.
title_eng: Portrait of Elizaveta Yaroshenko with a Cat
image_credit: Nikolai Yaroshenko · https://smallbay.ru/artrussia/yaroshenko_pictures.html

title: Cat and Kittens / after Henrietta Ronner
artist: After Henriëtte Ronner-Knip; published by W. Schaus, New York
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts), Washington, D.C.
description: A big black-and-white mother cat crouches behind a green bowl of milk while three kittens drink and squabble around it: a black one at right, a patched one lapping with its tongue out, and a white one at the back mewing open-mouthed. A wicker basket and straw fill the background. Printed in colour from a stack of lithographic stones, the result passes at a distance for a small oil painting. The sheet measures 31.6 by 22.3 cm, and its yellow label announces 'Cat and Kittens, after Henrietta Ronner' from W. Schaus of Broadway. On the back is a pencilled stock number, 5341.
context: William Schaus, a dealer at 749 Broadway in New York, published this in 1867 as part of a series of facsimiles of watercolour drawings and oil paintings by eminent artists, and the date comes from the copyright label stuck to it. It now sits in the Library of Congress's Popular Graphic Arts collection. Henriette Ronner-Knip was by then working in Brussels and had narrowed her subjects mainly to cats and dogs. Fun fact: the print predates the famous late Ronner cat pictures of the 1870s and after, so American buyers met her cats early, through a reproduction.
title_eng: Cat and Kittens / after Henrietta Ronner
image_credit: Schaus, W. (William), publisher; Schaus, W. (William), copyright claimant; Ronner, Henriette, 1821-1909, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2017650796 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/12600/12657v.jp

title: Budding Artists
collection: Private collection (sold Bonhams, London, 26 September 2019, lot 19)
description: A calico mother cat sits on a heavy old book in front of a battered portfolio and looks down at a tabby kitten gazing up at her. On the floor a ginger kitten and a black-and-white one tussle beside a dropped paintbrush, and another kitten scrambles through the legs of a carved chair at upper left. The joke is in the title, Budding Artists: the animals are the apprentices, and the studio clutter is theirs to inspect. The canvas is fairly large, 68.6 by 95.6 cm, signed and dated lower right, 'Ch. Van den Eycken. 1907', painted well after the cat-painting boom of the 1880s.
context: Charles van den Eycken (1859-1923) was born and died in Brussels and made a career as an animal painter, chiefly of cats and dogs, in the same city where Henriette Ronner-Knip had set the market for such pictures. This canvas passed through the Willow Gallery in London to a private collector in France, who bought it on 31 December 2003, and it sold at Bonhams in London on 26 September 2019 for 16,937.50 pounds including premium. Fun fact: the catalogue had it as 1890; the signature itself says 1907.
