image_credit: Charles van den Eycken · https://www.bonhams.com/auctions/25444/lot/19

title: Mother's Pride
description: A grey-and-white mother cat lies on the red velvet seat of a fringed armchair, one paw hanging over the edge, and keeps a narrow-eyed watch on kittens who are treating the furniture as a climbing frame. One tabby sits beside her; below, a ginger-and-white kitten scales the chair leg, two more wrestle in the folds of the yellow curtain, and a fifth tugs at loose sheets of music. It is a modest panel, 32.7 by 45 cm, painted in oil and signed 'Henriette Ronner' at bottom left. The yellow curtain is a warm backdrop against which pale fur and quick legs read clearly.
context: Henriette Ronner-Knip (1821-1909), born in Amsterdam, married and moved to Brussels in 1850 and, after 1870, painted the long-haired, playful middle-class cats that made her famous. In later life she posed her animals with props and even made paper models in the poses she wanted before painting. This panel is in a private collection; it sold at Sotheby's Amsterdam on 7 June 2011 (lot 37) and appeared again at Sotheby's New York on 9 May 2013 (lot 35). Fun fact: Walter Shaw Sparrow wrote in 1905 that she caught 'the heavy laziness of the mature animal, and the frolicsomeness of the kitten'.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Sotheby's, New York, 9 May 2013, lot 35

title: Playing Cat and Mouse
description: A striped tabby mother crouches flat on the floor with two kittens beside her, and all three stare at a small brown mouse in the lower left that has wandered far too close. The mother's white forepaw is already stretched toward it, and one kitten copies her pose exactly, a lesson in progress. Behind them stand a brass kettle and a wicker basket, and an empty saucer sits at right. The picture sold under the title Playing Cat and Mouse and measures 35.5 by 55.8 cm, a wide, low format with plenty of floor for the chase. The auction record gives oil on cardboard, a lightweight parlour support.
context: John Henry Dolph (1835-1903) started as a carriage painter in Ohio, moved to New York in 1864 and built a career as a landscapist before study in Antwerp and Paris turned him to pets, especially cats and dogs. He lived in the Sherwood Studio Building on 57th Street, one of the first New York apartment houses built for artists, and became a full National Academician in 1898. This picture is known from an online auction listing. Fun fact: critics called him 'the Landseer of America', and one compared his cats to John George Brown's street urchins.
image_credit: John Henry Dolph · Live Auctioneers ( Gallery )

title: View of a Roof with a Cat (Vue d'un toit avec un chat)
title_original: Vue d'un toit avec un chat
collection: Musée du Louvre, Département des Arts graphiques, Paris
description: A cat on a roof, so small you could miss it: a pale little shape on the tiles just right of centre, sitting among the ridged roof tiles below a row of chimney pots. Redon sets it down as a view rather than a portrait, and the Louvre title, Vue d'un toit, avec un chat, puts the roof first and the cat second. Most of the sheet is empty sky and blank paper, with tall chimney stacks at left and a gabled building at right, initialled 'Od. R.' below. The inventory marks this side as the recto, so the sheet has something on its back as well.
context: The drawing belongs to the Louvre's department of graphic arts, inventory RF 40644. Neighbouring Redon sheets in the same RF 406xx-408xx range came from the donation of Ari Redon, the artist's son, and his wife Suzanne, which suggests this one arrived the same way. Redon (1840-1916) is best known for his charcoal 'noirs' and lithographs of floating eyes and spiders, so a plain observation of a cat on a rooftop shows the other side of him: the draughtsman who looked hard at ordinary things. Fun fact: the same donation includes a sheet that mixes a profile head, a hooded figure and sleeping cats.
title_eng: View of a Roof with a Cat
image_credit: Odilon Redon · https://arts-graphiques.louvre.fr/

title: Daubigny's Garden
title_original: Le Jardin de Daubigny (avec chat noir)
collection: Kunstmuseum Basel (on long-term loan from the Rudolf Staechelin Family Foundation)
description: A black cat, painted in a few strokes of dark blue, slinks across the bottom left corner of Daubigny's garden toward the left edge, a small dark shape on a lawn of swirling greens and yellows. Van Gogh used a double-square canvas, 56 by 101 cm, the stretched format of his final months, and filled it with a table and chairs, flower beds, a pale fence and a woman in black standing by the house. A church tower rises at right under a choppy green sky. The cat is the smallest figure and the easiest to miss, and it is the detail that tells this version apart from its twin.
context: Van Gogh painted the garden of the late landscapist Charles-Francois Daubigny at Auvers-sur-Oise in July 1890, weeks before his death. This version (F777, JH2105) is in Basel, on long-term loan to the Kunstmuseum from the Rudolf Staechelin Family Foundation. A second double-square version, in the Hiroshima Museum of Art (F776), shows the same garden without the cat. Fun fact: that cat-less canvas once belonged to Emile Schuffenecker, a painter known for copying van Gogh, and its history has fed authenticity doubts; Berlin's National Gallery friends still paid 240,000 reichsmarks for it in 1929.
image_credit: Vincent van Gogh · ArtDaily.com

title: Stalking Cat (Smygande katt)
description: A black-and-white cat creeps out of a snowdrift, body pulled flat and long, eyes locked on two small mice at the lower left. The whole picture is painted almost in grisaille, white snow, grey shadow and dry black weed stems, so the cat's patches and the dark mice are the strongest marks on the canvas. It is an upright canvas of 57.5 by 40.5 cm, a tall shape for a horizontal animal, which squeezes the stalk into a tight diagonal from upper right to lower left. The signature sits at lower left, 'Bruno Liljefors -90', the year shortened to two digits.
context: Bruno Liljefors (1860-1939), from Uppsala, became Sweden's great painter of animals in their surroundings; Wikipedia's summary is that he never exaggerated the ferocity of the predator or the pathos of the prey. He joined the Artists' Union in 1886, the group that set itself against the Royal Academy, and Japanese prints left a mark on his work around this time. This canvas is in a private collection and was offered at Uppsala Auktionskammare in December 2014. Fun fact: he painted domestic cats with the same hunter's eye he turned on foxes and hawks.
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Uppsala Auktionskammare

title: Pin Holder
title_original: Pin Holder: Anthropomorphic Cat at Brinsmead Piano
collection: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York
description: A grey tabby cat sits upright on a tiny piano stool, tail stuck out behind, and plays a grand piano with both front paws, head tipped back as if lost in the music. It is posed like a human player but wears nothing. The piano is a wood-grained grand with an open music stand and turned gilt legs, and its maker's name, BRINSMEAD, is lettered on the side: a tiny bit of brand placement in a sewing-table toy that doubles as a pin holder. Cooper Hewitt describes it as cast brass, gilt and then cold-painted, meaning the colours were applied without firing and can wear off with handling.
context: The museum dates it to the late nineteenth century and does not name a maker. Small cold-painted animal novelties of this kind are usually associated with Viennese workshops, but the record itself stops at 'unknown'. It entered Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum in 1949 as a gift of an anonymous donor and sits in the Product Design and Decorative Arts department, accession 1949-49-33. Fun fact: Brinsmead was a real London piano firm, so the cat is playing a recognisable product rather than a generic instrument.
image_credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist · Catalog Photo

title: Little Girl with a Grey Cat (Jeune fille au chat)
medium: Drypoint etching and pastel on paper
collection: Private Collection, Paris / Musée Marmottan Monet study
description: A grey cat lies across a girl's lap at the lower right, its green eyes half shut and its head just under her arm, while she leans back against a pink cushion and looks straight out at us. She wears a white ruffled dress and a pearl necklace, her fair hair pinned up. This is La jeune fille au chat, which Morisot dated to 1892, and the cat is painted in the same quick blue-grey strokes as the shadows of the dress, so it almost dissolves into her. Morisot, late in her career, liked exactly this sort of unposed household moment.
context: Berthe Morisot (1841-1895) painted it three years before her death, in the period when she often worked with young models at home in Paris and at Mesnil. The image comes from a Christie's sale record, so the work was in private hands when it last appeared on the market. Morisot was one of the founding exhibitors of Impressionism and showed in all but one of the group's exhibitions. Fun fact: she signed and exhibited under her maiden name even after marrying Eugene Manet, Edouard's brother.
title_eng: Little Girl with a Grey Cat
image_credit: Berthe Morisot · https://www.christies.com/

title: Curiosity
description: Three silver tabbies, a mother and two kittens, crouch on a tiled floor and stare at a small green box-cage at the left, where a bird peers back through the bars of a tiny window. The mother is closest and lowest, chin almost on the floor; one kitten presses beside her and the other watches from a ledge behind. A larger cage stands empty above. The canvas is a good size, 60 by 83 cm, and signed 'Horatio H. Couldery' in the lower left. Couldery's speciality was fur painted almost hair by hair, best seen in the bold stripes along the mother's back.
context: Horatio Henry Couldery, born in Lewisham in 1832, trained as a cabinetmaker before studying at the Royal Academy Schools and first showed at the Academy in 1861. The painting appeared at Bonhams. Couldery was long thought to have died in 1893, but his death was registered in Sydenham on 4 February 1918. Fun fact: John Ruskin called one of his cat pictures of 1875 'quite the most skilful piece of minutiae' in the exhibition and said it could not rightly be seen without a lens. The largest public group of his work, 42 paintings, is at Glanmore National Historic Site in Belleville, Ontario.
image_credit: Horatio Henry Couldery · Bonhams

title: The Black Cat: The Cat on the Corpse
title_original: The Black Cat (Illustration for Edgar Allan Poe)
medium: Pen and black India ink on paper
description: The black cat of Poe's story sits planted on top of the corpse's head, claws spread over the hair, one eye shut and the other a white slit glaring straight out. Beardsley gives it the full treatment: pure black ink against blank paper, a habit he took partly from Japanese woodcuts. The cat merges with the black ground, picked out only by a thin white contour and a speckled white blaze on its chest. Below, the dead woman's face is all white paper, eyes closed, earrings still on. The creature will not stay hidden.
context: Aubrey Beardsley (1872-1898) drew a set of illustrations for tales by Edgar Allan Poe in 1894-95, the same years he was art editor of The Yellow Book. Wikipedia names The Murders in the Rue Morgue, The Fall of the House of Usher and The Masque of the Red Death alongside The Black Cat, and this drawing is the standard illustration on the story's own Wikipedia page. Fun fact: the high-resolution scan that circulates online came from a Russian multimedia disc of Beardsley's work published in 2003, which is why its origin is so vague.
title_eng: The Black Cat: The Cat on the Corpse
feline_symbolism: In Poe's tale the cat exposes the narrator's crime, so here it stands for guilt that cannot be walled up.
image_credit: Aubrey Beardsley (1872 - 1898) · Aubrey Beardsley

title: Cat with her Kittens
description: A long-haired cream-and-ginger mother sprawls on her side in the grass at the foot of a leafy bank, eyes half shut, while a ginger kitten stretches out flat against her flank and a tabby-and-white kitten props its front paws on her back to look over the top. It is a small canvas, 19 by 29 cm, the size of a book, in oil, signed 'Jul. Adam' in red at upper right. Adam's cat pictures were built from a family repertory of poses, and the lounging mother surrounded by small busy bodies is one of his staples.
context: Julius Anton Adam (1852-1913), known in Munich as 'Katzen-Adam', came from a family of painters and photographers and began his cat pictures in 1882; they sold internationally and overshadowed his other work. This canvas is in a private collection and appeared at Dorotheum in Vienna in a sale of nineteenth-century paintings and watercolours. Commons dates it only as 'by 1913', the year of his death. Fun fact: a 2017 episode of the German antiques programme Lieb & Teuer featured his cat paintings, a measure of how steadily they still turn up in German attics.
image_credit: Julius Adam · Dorotheum, Vienna (sale photograph, via Wikimedia Commons)

title: The White Cat (Le Chat blanc)
description: A white cat with ginger patches on its head and back arches into an impossible hump, legs stretched long and thin like a table on stilts, eyes squeezed shut and tail curling up behind. Bonnard paints it in oil straight onto cardboard, 51.9 by 33.5 cm, and the brown of the support does much of the work in the sandy ground. Behind, dark green foliage and an orange tree trunk close off the space. The tall, narrow format is an odd choice for a horizontal animal, so the cat stretches upward to fit, which is half the joke.
context: Bonnard painted Le Chat blanc in 1894, during his Nabi years, and showed it at Durand-Ruel in Paris in 1896. It later belonged to the English collector Sir Michael Sadler, whose collection was exhibited at the Leicester Galleries in London in 1944, and then to M. and Mme Jacques Spreiregen in Nice. The French national museums bought it in 1982 and assigned it to the Musee d'Orsay. Fun fact: the number 74 in its inventory, RF 1982 74, coincides with its catalogue number in that 1944 Sadler exhibition.
image_credit: Pierre Bonnard · https://cdn.mediatheque.epmoo.fr/link/3c9igq/xvm189jq06ocbxc.jpg

title: Exposition Steinlen à La Bodinière
description: Two cats sell the show: a black cat sits upright in profile at the right, whiskers fanned against the pink paper, while a calico curls in front of it, eyes half closed and tail wrapped round. Steinlen advertises his own exhibition, and the lettering spells out the offer in orange and grey: 'A La Bodiniere, 18 rue St Lazare, Exposition de l'oeuvre dessine et peint de T. A. Steinlen', running from 10 April to 15 May 1894. It is a colour lithograph printed in Paris by Charles Verneau, whose credit runs up the right edge.
context: La Bodiniere, at 18 rue Saint-Lazare, was a small Paris theatre and exhibition space, also called the Theatre d'Application. Steinlen held a solo exhibition there in April-May 1894, his first big showing of drawings and paintings together, and designed this poster for it. The Bibliotheque nationale de France holds an impression, digitised on Gallica. Fun fact: Steinlen, French Wikipedia says, drew cats 'without tiring', so putting one on the poster for his own retrospective was less a branding decision than a reflex.
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b53074482g

title: New Tenants
description: A tabby-and-white mother cat lies on top of a wooden crate fitted with wire bars and peers down at the kittens who have moved in underneath. New Tenants (Nouveaux Locataires) shows cats taking possession, as cats do, of a space meant for something else: a white kitten looks out between the bars, another rolls on its back below, and a black-and-white kitten stalks in from the left past an open fan. The original is a small oil, 34.2 by 46.3 cm, signed and dated 'Henriette Ronner 1883' with 'Bruxelles'. These tenants have clearly read the lease more carefully than the landlord.
context: Ronner-Knip painted it in Brussels in 1883, in the decade when her cat pictures made her name. The Paris firm Braun, Clement & Co. owned the reproduction rights and issued it as a carbon print, and from that print it was reproduced in Walter Shaw Sparrow's Women Painters of the World (London, 1905). Sparrow called her 'the painter of cats' and praised how she caught 'the heavy laziness of the mature animal, and the frolicsomeness of the kitten'. The painting itself is in a private collection. Fun fact: in old age she posed her models with props and even made paper sculptures of the poses she wanted.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · http://www.gutenberg.org/files/39000/39000-h/39000-h.htm

title: Compagnie Française des Chocolats et des Thés
title_original: Compagnie Française des Chocolats et des Thés
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A single dark tabby cat sits at the bottom left with its back to us and stretches its nose toward the girl's bowl, the only one in the poster not drinking yet. Steinlen sells chocolate and tea in 1895 for the Compagnie Francaise des Chocolats et des Thes by putting the family at the table: a dark-haired woman in red sips from a cup with her eyes closed, while the red-haired child bends over her bowl, spoon in hand, beside an open tin of tea. Wikipedia's caption says Steinlen put his wife and daughter into the picture, so the scene is domestic in the literal sense.
context: Steinlen, Swiss-born and based in Montmartre, made this advertising poster in 1895 for a Paris company selling chocolate and tea. His daughter Rene Germaine (1888-1969), called Colette, appears often in his work and would have been about seven; she later married the conductors and composers Desire-Emile Inghelbrecht and then Roger Desormiere. The Bibliotheque nationale de France holds an impression, digitised on Gallica. Fun fact: Steinlen died in 1923 at his home at 73 rue Caulaincourt, in the same Montmartre streets where he had drawn cats for more than thirty years.
title_eng: Compagnie Française des Chocolats et des Thés
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b9004763g

title: Playtime
medium: Oil on paper laid down on panel
description: A ginger-and-white kitten peeps out of a tipped-over red workbasket, one paw on a pink ball of wool, while a black-and-white kitten sits beside it and looks down at the loot. Kittens at play are the entire subject of this small picture, roughly 25.5 by 33.5 cm, painted in oil on paper later laid down on a panel to keep it flat. Paper takes oil quickly and lets the brush move loosely, which suits models that refuse to hold a pose. A cotton reel and a knitting needle lie in the foreground, and the signature, 'Henriette Ronner', sits upper left, well out of the way.
context: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip was born in Amsterdam in 1821 into a family of painters, married Feico Ronner in 1850 and moved to Brussels, where she narrowed her subject matter almost entirely to dogs and cats. After 1870 she became best known for long-haired, playful cats in comfortable bourgeois rooms. This sheet is known only through a sale at Christie's, and its date is not recorded. Her working method was less spontaneous than the results suggest: after watching her animals in the studio, she made paper sculptures of them in the poses she wanted and arranged these with furniture and fabrics before painting.
image_credit: Creator:Henriette Ronner · https://www.christies.com/lot/lot-1752466

title: Cat Study
description: Two kittens, and nobody is leaping: a tortoiseshell-and-white kitten dozes in front with its eyes shut and a pink tongue-tip showing, while a black kitten with a white muzzle peers out over its back. This is a tiny oil sketch, 11 by 10 cm, about the size of a coaster, painted on canvas in 1895. The fur goes down in quick, scratchy strokes against a pink ground, the working note of a painter checking how an ear turns. The signature 'Henriette Ronner' is underlined at top left. Art UK lists it simply as 'Cat Study'.
context: Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) was 74 when this study was dated, living in Ixelles near Brussels, where she had worked since 1850 and where she kept cats, hunting dogs and a parrot as models in a house with a large garden. Hartlepool Museums and Heritage Service holds this sketch and a companion study (HAPMG 1947.5.5) under consecutive numbers, which suggests they came in together, probably in 1947. Small studies like this fed her finished parlour pictures, which by then were famous enough for M. H. Spielmann to publish a whole book on her as 'the painter of cat life and cat character' in 1893.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: Cat Study
description: Two fluffy kittens lie side by side on a red cushion: a black-and-white one on the left with its eyes half lowered, and a tabby on the right staring straight out with wide green eyes, white front paws tucked neatly in front. A cat study in oil on canvas, 11.5 by 15 cm, small enough to hold in one hand. Ronner-Knip signs it 'Henriette Ronner 95' at top left, above a pale pink ground. The museum catalogues it with no more than the title 'Cat Study' and the date 1895, so the kittens do the talking.
context: Hartlepool Museums and Heritage Service owns two 1895 cat studies by Henriëtte Ronner-Knip, numbered 1947.5.4 and 1947.5.5, which suggests they entered the collection together, probably in 1947. By 1895 Ronner-Knip, born in Amsterdam in 1821, had spent more than four decades in Brussels and Ixelles and had won the Order of Leopold (1887). One detail of her practice explains why studies like this matter: she did not paint her cats purely from life, but made paper sculptures in the poses she wanted and staged them with furniture and fabric, using sketches of the real animals to keep the result convincing.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: Cat with a Cigar
medium: Pen, black ink, watercolor, and gouache on paper
description: A brown tabby stands upright against a washy blue ground, a round glass lens over each eye, a broad grey collar at its neck and one paw pressed to its chest like a gentleman about to make a speech. The smoke is not in its mouth: it holds a short, stubby cigar up in its other paw, a curl of smoke rising beside its ear, so the title wins over the upload's 'cigarette'. Wain keeps the animal a real cat, stripes, whiskers and flattened ears, while handing it one adult human vice. The signature 'Louis Wain' sits at bottom right.
context: Louis Wain (1860–1939) sold his first cat drawings to The Illustrated London News in 1884 and became famous after his 1886 Christmas spread there, A Kitten's Christmas Party, his first drawing of cats behaving like people. By 1890 he was a household name and president of the National Cat Club. This image circulates online without a collection, a dimension or a secure date: the Commons upload, taken from a fan website, dates it 1879, which is almost certainly too early because Wain's cat career only began in the mid-1880s. Treat both the date and the title as provisional.
image_credit: Louis Wain · http://www.lilitu.com/catland/gallery/cigar.shtml

title: Pussy at the Brighton Cat Show
medium: Pen, black ink, and zinc process engraving on newsprint
description: Four cat heads crowd one newspaper block, and the biggest, top left, is labelled 'Sam Woodiwiss's Champion Xenophon', a heavyweight brown tabby and one of the most decorated show cats of the decade. Around him sit a pale cat, a long-haired 'Persian Tabby Dick' and a Persian labelled 'Shazada'. The printed caption reads 'The Premier Cats of England (By Louis Wain)'. It ran in the South Wales Daily News on 21 November 1895. Wain drew for the press in pen and ink, so everything is line and hatching, made to survive cheap newsprint and fast presses.
context: Wain earned a living in the 1880s and 1890s reporting on agricultural and pet shows, and as president of the National Cat Club he also judged cat shows, so he drew the fancy from inside. Xenophon, the likely sitter, was a big blotched brown tabby, reportedly found as a wild kitten in 1892 and weighed at 25 lb in 1895. He passed through four owners, among them a bulldog breeder, Sam Woodiwiss, who took up cats after spotting Xenophon at a dog show, and Lady Decies, who bought him in 1898 and renamed him Fulmer Xenophon. One 1898–99 magazine writer credited him with eight championships and more than twenty first prizes.
title_eng: Pussy at the Brighton Cat Show
image_credit: Louis Wain · messybeast

title: Cat and kitten Figure
collection: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York
description: A pale tabby with green eyes stands up on its hind legs, a darker striped kitten clamped face-down under one arm, and raises a stick high over the kitten's backside. The kitten's mouth is open in a red mew of protest and its legs dangle every which way. The whole drama is 6.8 cm tall: cast in brass and then painted, so the tabby stripes are brushwork laid over metal. The parent's face stays calm, almost smiling, which makes the raised stick read as a perfectly legible sentence.
context: Cooper Hewitt catalogues the figure as late 19th to early 20th century, maker unknown, probably made in Austria, and it came to the museum in 1949 as the gift of an anonymous donor (1949-49-35). Painted miniature animals of this kind are usually associated with Vienna and its trade in small cabinet and mantelpiece figures. The museum's own catalogue entry is unusually frank about the plot: it describes the tabby holding a stick 'as if about to spank' a 'mewing kitten', which is about as much narrative as a design museum ever commits to an object label.
submovement: Austrian cold-painted miniature figures (Vienna bronze type)
image_credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist · Catalog Photo

title: Tournée du Chat Noir de Rodolphe Salis
title_original: Tournée du Chat Noir de Rodolphe Salis
submovement: Montmartre cabaret poster (Art Nouveau colour lithography)
description: A black cat sits with its body in profile and its head swung round to fix us with two yellow eyes, whiskers sprouting right through a red halo lettered 'Montjoye Montmartre'. The motto parodies the medieval French war cry 'Montjoie! Saint-Denis!', so the cat is both a saint and a battle standard. Its tail drops over the red band below and curls into the R of 'Rodolphe Salis'. The text could hardly be shorter: 'Prochainement Tournée du Chat Noir', which is to say 'coming soon'. The Rijksmuseum sheet is a full-size colour lithograph, 140 by 99 cm, printed by Charles Verneau, whose credit runs up the right edge.
context: Rodolphe Salis opened Le Chat Noir in Montmartre in 1881; it is often called the first modern cabaret. Its shadow plays were the big draw, and from 1892 Salis took the troupe on tour, mostly around France in summer, as far as Tunis, Algeria and Belgium. Steinlen, a Lausanne-born artist introduced to the Chat Noir crowd by Adolphe Willette, designed this poster in 1896. Salis died in March 1897 and the cabaret closed soon after, but the poster did not: it has become one of the most reproduced images of Paris, turning up on tin boxes and kitchen trays, in Breakfast at Tiffany's and on a neon sign at 68 boulevard de Clichy. The Rijksmuseum's copy was a gift from a Mr Van Bergen of Zwolle in 1969.
title_eng: Tour of the Chat Noir with Rodolphe Salis
location: Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University (Gift of Susan Schimmel Goldstein); Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (RP-P-1969-78); Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam; Musée de Montmartre, Paris
feline_symbolism: The cabaret took its name from the stray black cats of Paris; the halo and mock war cry turn the cat into a tongue-in-cheek patron saint of Montmartre.
image_credit: Rijksmuseum · http://hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.COLLECT.418236

title: Laziness (La Paresse)
medium: Woodcut printed in black on ivory wove paper
description: A small white cat stands at the lower right of the bed, tail up, while a nude woman sprawls face-down across the covers, her face buried in the crook of one arm and the other hand lazily reaching to stroke it. Vallotton cuts it in pure black and white with no grey in between: the bedding becomes a riot of checks, lattices, zigzags and dots, the body and the cat are bare white shapes cut out of the black. The image is only 17.8 by 22.2 cm, with 'La Paresse' lettered at lower left and the FV monogram at right. Nobody here is getting up.
context: Félix Vallotton (1865–1925), Swiss-born and working in Paris, revived the woodcut at a time when it had fallen out of use as an art form, exploiting its hard contrasts of black and white. He designed, cut and printed blocks like this himself. La Paresse dates from 1896, during his years with the Nabis, two years before his famous Intimités series for La Revue blanche. Impressions are held by several museums, including the Art Institute of Chicago (1947.454) and the Bibliothèque nationale de France. His prints caught attention early: the writer Octave Uzanne hailed his work as 'the renaissance of the woodcut', and by the mid-1890s his blocks were appearing in periodicals in Paris and as far afield as The Chap-Book in Chicago.
image_credit: Vallotton, Félix (1865-1925). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: National Cat Show at the Crystal Palace
medium: Pen, black ink, and mechanical engraving on newsprint
description: Cats in roundels and cats in a heap: this double-page spread captioned 'The Crystal Palace Cat Show', printed in the Bromley & District Times on 23 October 1896, sets a black-and-white long-hair, a black cat and a fluffy 'Blue Russian' in framed medallions, with four Siamese crowded together at lower left. The tabby labelled 'Champion Xenophon' peers in at top centre. Wain's show drawings are portraits of real, named animals, done in pen line that could be reproduced cheaply, and they reward a magnifier: the set of the ears, a fold of a cheek, a tail that could only belong to one cat.
context: The Crystal Palace stood at Sydenham in south London, a short trip from Bromley, which explains why a local weekly wanted a cat-show page of its own. Wain, who served as president of the National Cat Club and judged at shows, drew the same autumn 1896 event for The Illustrated London News the following day. Xenophon, a brown tabby shorthair supposedly found as a wild kitten, was among the most decorated short-haired cats of the period and turns up again and again in Wain's show drawings.
title_eng: National Cat Show at the Crystal Palace
image_credit: Louis Wain · messybeast

title: The Cat Show at the Crystal Palace (Illustrated London News)
collection: British Library, London / Victoria and Albert Museum
description: A huge long-haired tabby, 'Birkdale Ruffie', fills the middle band of the page, glaring out from a dark ground, while a frieze of show cats lines up above and a striped shorthair labelled 'Champion Xenophon' strides across the bottom left. This is The Illustrated London News for 24 October 1896, given over to Wain's prize winners from the Crystal Palace. Zaida sits top right among Persians and a Siamese. These are portraits, not caricatures: Wain is reporting which cat won and making each one recognisable to owners and breeders. Long Persian coats and dense short ones are rendered entirely in black line.
context: The Illustrated London News was where Wain's career started: he sold it his first cat drawings in 1884, and its 1886 Christmas number carried A Kitten's Christmas Party, the drawing that made him famous. He also rented a house in Westgate-on-Sea from the paper's managing director, Sir William Ingram. By 1896 he was an established authority on cats and a show judge. The same show appeared a day earlier in the Bromley & District Times, also drawn by Wain, and Xenophon, the brown tabby here, recurs in his drawings for The Queen, the South Wales Daily News and the Harmsworth London Magazine.
title_eng: The Cat Show at the Crystal Palace
title_original: The Cat Show at the Crystal Palace
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Illustrated London News

title: Cats (Chats)
description: Three cats pile up in the dark: a black cat sits upright at the back, a second black cat rests its chin on a flowered cushion with one pale eye open, and a tabby sprawls across the front with its paws stretched out like a dropped scarf. This lithograph measures 63.6 by 81.5 cm, the size of a small window. The BnF catalogues it simply as 'Chats' and transcribes the inscription 'Steinlen 96', which you can find at lower left. Here Steinlen works almost entirely in black and brown crayon tones, rubbed and smudged, so the black cats nearly dissolve into the shadows around them.
context: Steinlen, born in Lausanne in 1859, settled in Montmartre in the early 1880s and drew cats throughout his career, in posters, illustrations, a wordless picture album and even small sculptures. This sheet was issued in 1896 under the imprint 'Estampe murale' ('wall print') and is number 182 in Ernest de Crauzat's catalogue of Steinlen's prints. The Bibliothèque nationale de France keeps it among the large-format sheets in its Steinlen holdings. The BnF's copy came from the collection of Atherton Curtis (1863–1943), and the library still files it among the 'pièces de grand format', the outsize sheets that do not fit in the ordinary print boxes.
submovement: Art Nouveau decorative wall lithograph (Estampe murale)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Lithographe · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Sleeping Woman with Cat (Śpiąca kobieta z kotem)
description: A black cat arches its back and lifts its tail at the lower right, one yellow eye glinting as it rubs against the hem of a sleeping woman. She lies curled on a sofa of acid green, red hair spread over the cushion, hands folded under her cheek, her black dress a single heavy mass. The canvas is a full metre wide (66 × 100 cm), signed 'W. Ślewiński' at top left. His habits, learned from Gauguin, are all here: forms laid down in flat areas, edges closed with contour, earthy darks lifted by one loud green. The cat is the smallest flat shape, and the only one awake.
context: Władysław Ślewiński (1856–1918) came late to painting. He inherited family estates in Poland in 1886, was ruined within two years and fled to Paris, pursued, so the story goes, by Russian tax collectors, and only then decided to become a painter. He studied at the Académie Colarossi and Académie Julian, befriended Paul Gauguin in 1889 and spent much of the following years at Le Pouldu in Brittany with the Pont-Aven circle. He showed at the Salon des Indépendants in 1895 and 1896, the year of this picture. It is known today through an auction sale; the photograph on Wikimedia comes from the Polish auction house Rempex.
image_credit: Władysław Ślewiński · rempex.com.pl

title: Poster Design with Cat (From 'Posters in Miniature')
medium: Halftone reproduction in the book Posters in Miniature (New York: R. H. Russell, 1896)
description: A Steinlen cat poster shrunk to pocket size: the La Bodinière exhibition poster, its black cat sitting tall in profile behind a curled calico, reproduced with the caption 'STEINLEN' beneath. This is page 235 of Posters in Miniature, a small New York book of 1896 that reproduced posters from France, England, Germany and America in black and white for collectors. The orange lettering of the original turns to pale grey here, nearly vanishing, while the black cat survives untouched, which is a useful test of a poster design: Steinlen's cat still reads at a few centimetres high.
context: Posters in Miniature was published in 1896 by Robert Howard Russell in New York, at the height of the poster-collecting craze. Edward Penfield, the leading American poster designer, wrote the introduction and Percival Pollard the foreword; Pollard pitched it as a handy pictorial survey for the amateur collector. The book also included what it called the most complete set of portraits of poster designers yet published. Penfield's introduction contains a line that suits Steinlen's cats rather well: 'A poster should tell its story at once; a design that needs study is not a poster, no matter how well it is executed.' The scanned copy belongs to the Getty Research Institute.
title_original: Dessin d'affiche au chat (Posters in Miniature)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Cover for 1897 Calendar
medium: Color lithograph and commercial relief process
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A tortoiseshell cat curls on the drawing table with its back to us, chin resting on a yellow sheet of paper, black and orange patches broken up by flecks of pink and green. Above it a man in an orange cap bends over his work, pipe clamped in his mouth, pen in one hand and ink bottle in the other, with three little ink pots lined up beside the cat. The Met's record tags a man, smoking and a cat. The sheet is 14 by 10 3/16 inches, colour lithograph with a commercial relief process, lettered 'Poster Calendar 1897' and 'Published by R. H. Russell & Son'.
context: Edward Penfield (1866–1925), often called the father of the American poster, designed this cover in 1896 for a poster calendar for the year 1897. He was then art director at Harper's, and his posters there helped bring the European poster craze to the United States. The Met acquired the sheet in 1965 through the Elisha Whittelsey Fund (65.658.40(1)); the '(1)' marks it as the first part of a multi-sheet set. Penfield's own rule of thumb, printed the same year in Posters in Miniature, explains the economy: 'A design that needs study is not a poster, no matter how well it is executed.'
image_credit: Edward Penfield · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Preparations for the Journey
description: A white-and-tabby mother cat lies on an embroidered stool and looks down, unbothered, at the wreckage her four kittens are making of somebody's packing. No piano here: this is Ronner-Knip's 'Preparations for the Journey'. One kitten scrambles up the inside of an open trunk, another balances on an overturned blue hatbox, and a black-and-white one pounces on the straw hat that has rolled out of it, feathers and pink roses and all, while a white kitten peeks from behind. A furled umbrella leans against the stool. It is a burglary scene with no guilt in it, painted with salon polish and signed at lower right.
context: The painting was reproduced as a full-page wood engraving in the German family magazine Die Gartenlaube in 1884 (issue 42, p. 697), captioned 'Vorbereitungen zur Reise. Nach dem Oelgemälde von Henriette Ronner', so it was finished by that year. By then Ronner-Knip, Amsterdam-born and Brussels-based since 1850, was famous for long-haired, playful cats in bourgeois interiors. The magazine's accompanying note is the fun part. It counts the culprits ('one, two, four young kittens and an old one'), pities the owner who will come back to a squashed hat, and closes with a moral for readers: lids and room doors are useless unless they are kept shut.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://kykolnik.livejournal.com/369784.html

title: Cat
description: One long-haired cat lies curled on a pale cushion, plumed tail swept round in front, and turns its head to fix us with two yellow-green eyes. Ronner-Knip gives it the attention a portrait painter would give a sitter. Wikimedia files it under paintings of red cats, and the coat is a warm brown-and-orange tabby, darker stripes running through the fur, with a white chin and pink nose. It is oil on panel, 32 by 46.5 cm, a smooth support that suits her fine, feathery strokes for fur. A faint monogram and date sit at lower right, which is how the auction house dated it.
context: In 1897 Ronner-Knip was 76 and living in Ixelles, on the edge of Brussels, still painting the cats that had made her name. She had been honoured with the Order of Leopold in 1887 and would join the Dutch Order of Orange-Nassau in 1901. The picture's known history is commercial: the photograph comes from a Düsseldorf auction house, and its present owner is not recorded. Ronner-Knip had become famous enough as a cat specialist that the French critic Henry Havard published a monograph on her in 1892 with the blunt title 'Un peintre de chats', a painter of cats.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Düsseldorfer Auktionshaus

title: Cats and the Cockatoo
description: Four kittens tilt their heads back at a pink-crested cockatoo that leans down from a brass hoop high above them, wings half open. The bird has the high ground. A white kitten with a pink bow sits on a plant stand at the centre, a grey tabby rears up on its hind legs at the right, a tabby-and-white kitten crouches in front, and a larger striped cat stands at the left. The panel is upright, 47.5 by 30.5 cm, with a palm and a gold curtain. Reichert signs it 'C. Reichert 98' at lower left. A predator facing a bird that is too big and too loud to be prey.
context: Carl Reichert (1836–1918) was born in Vienna, the son of a history painter and lithographer, and trained from 1850/51 at the drawing academy of the Styrian estates in Graz under Josef Kuwasseg. He started as a painter of Styrian castles and town views and turned to animals after painting the two pointers of a Count Hügel, which led to recommendations at the imperial court. His output is hard to count: one tally gives about 675 landscapes and 583 animal pictures, and he also painted around 600 animal pictures, mostly horses and dogs, under the pseudonym J. Hartung. This 1898 panel passed through Christie's and is in a private collection.
image_credit: Carl Reichert · Christie's , LotFinder: entry 5121305

title: The Busybody
collection: Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp (KMSKA)
description: A calico mother cat crouches on a stack of old folios and leans forward, nose out, to inspect four kittens sprawled across a heap of drawings below. The museum calls it 'De moeial', The Busybody, so the cats are minding something that is none of their business. A black-and-white kitten perches beside her, a grey one bats at the papers, and a ginger-and-white one stares at nothing in particular. A terracotta pot of brushes and a dried bouquet suggest a painter's studio. It is a sizeable canvas, 66.2 by 92.8 cm, signed and dated at lower left, 'Ch. Van den Eycken/ 1911'.
context: Charles van den Eycken (1859–1923) was born and died in Brussels, the son of a landscape painter. He studied with the animal painter Joseph Stevens at the Brussels Académie, exhibited from 1881 at salons in Brussels, Liège, Ghent and Antwerp, and painted several pictures for Queen Marie-Henriette of Belgium. His speciality was dogs and cats doing all sorts of things. The Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp bought this canvas straight from the artist at the Antwerp Triennial of 1911, where it hung as no. 250 (inv. 1707). A small oddity: he occasionally signed his work with a different name altogether, Charles Duchêne.
image_credit: Charles van den Eycken · https://kmska.be/nl/meesterwerk/de-moeial

title: The Bachelor Party
description: Five cats line up behind a white tablecloth like a frieze, and the big brown tabby in the middle grins open-mouthed with paws planted on the table, clearly the groom. Two of his friends puff cigars, the grey one at right squints through a monocle, and the one at the far right has a cigarette going. Bottles labelled 'Old Tom' and 'Catsup' stand among the glasses, with a cigar box and ashtrays in front. Wain's favourite device: animals that stay unmistakably feline while behaving like men about town. It is oil on canvas, a long strip 29.5 by 60 cm, signed 'Louis Wain' at lower right.
context: Louis Wain (1860–1939) made his name drawing cats acting as humans, beginning with A Kitten's Christmas Party in The Illustrated London News in 1886. His cats went to tea parties, restaurants and the seaside and celebrated Christmas, often ending in mayhem; his most popular years were before the First World War, and more than 1,100 of his images appeared as postcards between 1900 and 1940. He sold pictures and copyrights cheaply, which left him poor later in life. This canvas surfaced at Bonhams; it carries no date, and Wikimedia files it only as painted 'by 1939'.
image_credit: Louis Wain · Bonhams

title: Brita, a Cat and a Sandwich (Brita, en katt och en smörgås)
description: A black-and-white cat crouches in the grass at the front, head down over something on the ground, while little Brita stands on the path behind it in a blue smock and bonnet, sandwich held up to her mouth. The title is a full inventory, and the order is probably the cat's. Behind them stand a red-boarded house with two white-framed windows full of potted flowers, sunflowers and a bed of red blooms, and a green gate swung open at the left. Larsson draws every shape in firm line and fills it with clear washes. The sheet is 47.5 by 68.5 cm, initialled 'CL' at lower left.
context: Brita, born in 1893, was the fifth of Carl and Karin Larsson's eight children, so she was about five here. The family lived at Lilla Hyttnäs in Sundborn, near Falun, a house given to them in 1888 by Karin's father and decorated by the couple; Karin designed many of the interiors Carl painted. Larsson's watercolours of this family life became famous through colour books, first Ett hem (A Home, 1899) from Bonniers. The real bestseller came later: a German selection, Das Haus in der Sonne (1909), sold 40,000 copies in three months.
title_eng: Brita, a Cat and a Sandwich
title_original: Brita, en katt och en smörgås
submovement: Swedish Arts and Crafts domestic watercolour (Sundborn)
image_credit: Carl Larsson (Swedish, 1853-1919) · https://blog.daum.net/kmozzart/17177

title: Man with the Cat (Henry Sturgis Drinker)
collection: Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.
description: A ginger tabby sleeps flat out across Henry Sturgis Drinker's lap, eyes shut and paws tucked, while his long hand rests beside it without quite touching. He sits back in a Windsor chair in a cream linen suit and purple tie, whiskers sweeping into a grey moustache, and looks at the painter steadily and a little warily. Beaux paints the suit in broad, fast strokes, all lilac and yellow shadows. The canvas is nearly life-size, 121.9 by 87.8 cm, signed at lower right. SAAM's label reads the relaxed pose and the suit as signs of a man sure of himself; the cat simply agrees.
context: Cecilia Beaux (1855–1942) painted her brother-in-law Henry Sturgis Drinker in 1898. He was a railroad executive and later president of Lehigh University, one of the East Coast men whose tastes shaped public life for decades. Beaux built a career as a portraitist at a time when few women could, and was thought to rival John Singer Sargent; Wikipedia calls this probably her finest portrait. It reached the Smithsonian American Art Museum as a bequest of Henry Ward Ranger through the National Academy of Design. Beaux had form with cats: her earlier Sita and Sarita put a black kitten on a woman's shoulder, and when the press kept asking what it meant, her sister replied that it was 'only an idea to put the black kitten on her cousin's shoulder. Nothing deeper.'
title_original: Man with the Cat (Henry Sturgis Drinker)
image_credit: Cecilia Beaux · -AGOOmzCCu5cNg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Celebrated Cats of the Fancy (Harmsworth Magazine)
description: Nine celebrities, all of them cats, each in its own roundel under the heading 'Some Costly Pets', with a price tag in the caption. Wain's plate for The Harmsworth London Magazine names its sitters like a team sheet: Xenophon, Ameer, Patrick Blue, Blue Boy, Rynda, Zaida, Banjo, Jemmy and Satan. There are Persians, British Shorthairs and two Siamese, one striding across the centre with its tail up. Each animal is drawn to be recognised by its owner. Look for number 1, 'Champion Zenophon', the striped tabby walking across the top left, valued at £100.
context: Wain, president of the National Cat Club and a working show judge, was the obvious man to draw the stars of the British cat fancy for a popular monthly in 1898. Several of these cats were famous in their own right. Xenophon, a blotched brown tabby shorthair reportedly found as a wild kitten in 1892, was among the most decorated short-haired cats of the decade and in 1898 was bought by Lady Decies, who renamed him Fulmer Xenophon; he died at her cattery in Birchington in 1903, and the cat paper Our Cats announced his death. Zaida also appears in Wain's Illustrated London News page of 1896.
title_eng: Celebrated Cats of the Fancy (Harmsworth Magazine)
title_original: Affiche pour The Harmsworth London Magazine: Les Chats Célèbres
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Harmsworth London Magazine

title: Two Cats on a Cushion (Deux chats sur un coussin)
description: Two cats sleep curled into each other: a striped tabby in front, nose tucked under a white paw and banded tail wrapped round, and a black cat behind with only its ears and one half-shut eye showing. In this impression there is very nearly nothing else. The BnF's catalogue title spells out the state: first state, 'with the cats alone', before the background curtain, the cushions and the date were added. So the cushion of the title is not here yet. The pair float on a pale plate tone crossed by stray scratches, 22.8 by 15.2 cm, with a pencil 'Steinlen' in the margin below.
context: Steinlen made the print in 1898, the same year Flammarion published his wordless cat album Des chats. The Bibliothèque nationale de France keeps this early-state impression in its reserve collection of his work (Crauzat 29). Collectors of the period prized such working states because they show a print being built: here the later states add a curtain behind, cushions beneath and the artist's signature, and the first state is the moment before any of that, when the cats were the whole idea.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cats: Tsching, Batzar, and Blanc-Blanc (Les Chats: Tsching, Batzar et Blanc-Blanc)
title_original: Les Chats: Tsching, Batzar et Blanc-Blanc
collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.
description: Three cats with names, Tsching, Batzar and Blanc-Blanc, sleep wound together into one round heap, seen from above, heads buried in each other's flanks. Steinlen writes their names along the bottom left and adds 'vu de haut' under his signature at lower right. The drawing is in charcoal, 22.6 by 29 cm, and the National Gallery's cataloguing notes the sleeping. Charcoal lets him move from a hard contour to a soft smudge with the same stick, and the background is scrubbed in with fast horizontal strokes. The pale cat at front left, left mostly as bare paper, must be Blanc-Blanc.
context: Steinlen, Swiss-born and settled in Montmartre, drew cats all his life and published a whole album of them, Des chats, in 1898. This sheet belongs to the Rosenwald Collection at the National Gallery of Art in Washington (1943.3.8031). The names make it a portrait of a household rather than a study of 'cats' in general. Tsching and Batzar are odd, cheerful names; Blanc-Blanc ('White-White') is the sort of name you give a white cat when you have run out of patience with naming things.
title_eng: The Cats: Tsching, Batzar, and Blanc-Blanc
image_credit: Théophile Alexandre Steinlen · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Cats: Pictures without Words (Plate 10) — The Clambering Ascent
medium: Photorelief etching (gillotage), from the book Des chats: dessins sans paroles (Paris: Flammarion)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A black cat and a white cat rear up on their hind legs side by side, front paws flung high at a small flying insect near the top of the page. The white one has its mouth wide open; the black one is a solid silhouette with a few scratches of light on its head. This is a detail from one page of Steinlen's wordless album Des chats, filed by Wikimedia's cataloguers under both 'hunting' and 'playing', which is about right for cats. The line is Steinlen's crayon drawing transferred photomechanically to a zinc plate and printed in relief, a cheap, durable print of a drawing.
context: Des chats: dessins sans paroles was published in Paris by Ernest Flammarion around 1898. Its plates were printed by Charles Verneau, the same printer as Steinlen's Chat Noir poster, using gillotage: the design is drawn in lithographic crayon, transferred to zinc, dusted with resin and etched so it can be printed as a relief block. The Met calls the technique photorelief etching. Its copy, a folio 44.5 cm tall, was given by Mrs Edward C. Moën in 1961 (61.687.12). Other copies are at the British Museum and the Van Gogh Museum.
title_eng: Cats: Pictures without Words (Plate 10) — The Clambering Ascent
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen / Ernest Flammarion · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Cat Arching Its Back (Chat faisant le gros dos)
description: A dark cat hunches along a bare plank floor, head lowered almost to the boards and spine humped into the big back of the title, tail trailing out behind. Steinlen scratched it straight into a zinc plate with a needle rather than biting it with acid, and the fur is all fine parallel strokes, with a few loose sweeps of drapery at upper right. The printed area is small, 14.1 by 7.5 cm, and wider than it is tall. The BnF impression is the only recorded state. His signature sits at lower right, and an unknown hand has added a cursive mark and the number '1.' in the lower margin.
context: Steinlen made the plate in January 1898, the date given by Ernest de Crauzat, whose catalogue of the artist's prints also supplies its title and number (Crauzat 7). The sheet belongs to the Bibliothèque nationale de France, mounted in the volume of Steinlen's prints kept in the Département des Estampes et de la photographie (DC-385 (1)-FOL) and digitised for Gallica. It was a busy cat year: Flammarion published his wordless album Des chats in 1898 too. Oddity: the title is not Steinlen's. A cataloguer, not the artist, decided this cat was 'making the big back'.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Black Cat and Tabby Cat Grooming (Chat noir et chat tigré faisant sa toilette)
description: A striped tabby twists on its back in the foreground with one hind leg shot straight up, deep in its wash, while a black cat sits behind it almost lost in the dark hatching, only two pale eyes staring out at us. Steinlen etched the scene on zinc on a small upright plate, so the solid black coat and the barred one are both built from bitten line, with no colour to help. The printed image measures about 12 by 17.7 cm and exists in a single state. A pencil 'St.' signs it at lower right, and someone has written 'Pl. 4' in the lower left margin.
context: Crauzat dates the plate to May 1898 and lists it as number 20 in his catalogue of Steinlen's etchings and lithographs, which is also where the descriptive title comes from. The BnF keeps the impression in the mounted volume of Steinlen's prints in its Département des Estampes et de la photographie (DC-385 (1)-FOL), and it has been digitised for Gallica. Steinlen, the Lausanne-born illustrator of Montmartre, moved easily between lithography, etching and drypoint, and the same year produced a drypoint of a cat arching its back (Crauzat 7). Neither print carries a printed title, so both cats answer to their cataloguer's descriptions.
title_eng: Black Cat and Tabby Cat Grooming
title_original: Chat noir et chat tigré faisant sa toilette
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Cover for the Album 'Des chats' (Couverture de l'album Des chats)
description: Six cats mob a fair-haired girl in a checked pink dress who carries a bowl: a grey tabby stretches up her skirt on its hind legs, a black cat arches against her ankles, a striped tabby, a calico and a long-haired black cat crowd in, and a ginger cat yowls from the back. This is the wrapper for Steinlen's cat album, a colour lithograph about 44.9 by 27.5 cm. It announces 'Des chats par Steinlen' and the publisher, Ernest Flammarion, 26 rue Racine near the Odéon. The 26 plates inside were printed in black; the cover was the shop window. The BnF impression is a loose print.
context: Flammarion issued Des chats, dessins sans paroles in 1898, and Crauzat names Imprimerie Charles Verneau as printer of this cover (Crauzat 215); Verneau also printed the album plates. The BnF's impression sits in volume 4 of its mounted Steinlen collection in the Département des Estampes et de la photographie (DC-385 (4)-FOL). Steinlen had arrived in Montmartre from Lausanne and was by then a regular of the illustrated press and the Chat Noir circle. Oddity: the sheet is signed with a monogram the BnF could not identify, on a cover that already has Steinlen's name in its title.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Two Cats Side by Side (Deux chats côte à côte)
description: Two cats sit side by side on a patterned rug against a wall and door frame: a lean, short-haired cat upright in profile, chin raised, gazing left, and a darker, fluffier cat hunkered down beside it with its eyes shut. One is on duty, one is off. The plate is nearly square, 29.7 by 29.6 cm, and this etching is recorded as the seventh state, so Steinlen went back into it at least six times after his first proof. The BnF notes it is printed on calque, a thin tracing paper. Steinlen signed it in pencil at lower right, under a dedication beginning 'à E. de Crauzat'.
context: The BnF keeps this sheet in the reserve volume of its Steinlen collection (RESERVE DC-385 (A,1)-BOITE FOL) and dates it only to the nineteenth century, with no catalogue number. The impression is dedicated to Ernest de Crauzat (1866–1944), whose catalogue of Steinlen's etchings and lithographs is still the standard reference for his prints. Steinlen, a Lausanne-born illustrator who settled in Montmartre, made cats one of his constant subjects in prints, drawings and sculpture. Fun fact: a seventh state was given to the man whose job was counting Steinlen's states, so the proof presumably passed straight into the cataloguer's own files.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Crauzat, Ernest de (1866-1944). Dédicataire · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Kiribi, portrait de chatte (brooch)
description: Kiribi was a she-cat, and this small silver plaquette is her portrait, made to be worn as a brooch. She walks left in profile, long-haired, collar at her neck and plumed tail raised high, dipping her nose into a footed goblet at the left edge. Her name is cut in tall letters at upper left, with '1898' and 'Sylla Eustache' at lower right. Its maker was a medallist, and the cat gets a medal sitter's low relief. No gold, no enamel, no pearl, whatever earlier records claimed. The piece is known from a Tadema Gallery photograph; its present owner is not recorded.
context: Louis Sylla Eustache (1856–1933), born and died in Paris, began as a metal engraver for Émile Laporte, worked alongside Gabriel Guay in the Lequien workshop, and showed at the Salon des artistes français from 1891 to 1909. Medals and plaquettes were his speciality, often portraits and animals. 'Kiribi, portrait de chatte' was exhibited in 1898, and the brooch is published in Beatriz Chadour-Sampson and Sonya Newell-Smith's book on the Tadema Gallery's jewellery from the 1860s to the 1960s (Arnoldsche, 2021, p. 68). Fun fact: two decades later, in 1919, La Mode illustrée commissioned him to design fantasy jewellery for its subscribers.
collection: Location unknown (published by the Tadema Gallery, London)
image_credit: Sylla Eustache · Tadema Gallery , sales catalogue scan image

title: Cat Nap
medium: Oil on paper laid down on panel
description: A tabby-and-white cat has given up on the day: it sleeps on a pale green damask cushion, eyes shut, forepaws stretched out and one hind foot flipped so the pink pads face us, the posture of a cat that trusts the room completely. Ronner-Knip painted it in oil on paper, later laid down on a panel, 25.8 by 38.1 cm. There is no story here, no ball of wool or toppled vase, just one animal asleep, its white bib and legs set against loose, feathery green brushwork. Her signature, 'Henriette Ronner.', sits at lower left.
context: Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) was born in Amsterdam and first taught by her father, Joseph August Knip. After marrying Feico Ronner in 1850 she moved to Brussels, and from the 1870s her fame rested on playful cats, often long-haired, in comfortable interiors. Late in life she kept animals as models and made paper figures in the poses she wanted before painting. This study was lot 251 in Christie's sale 17295 of nineteenth-century European and Orientalist art, held in December 2019. Fun fact: Christie's had to issue a correction that the medium 'should read oil on paper laid down on panel', so even the saleroom first misread the support.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://www.christies.com/lotfinder/lot_details.aspx?intObjectID=6248915&lid=1

title: Making Music
description: A white-and-tabby mother cat watches four kittens who have found a guitar and are treating it as playground equipment: one pokes its face into the sound hole, one sits on the soundboard, one scrambles up a stack of music portfolios at right, and a fourth noses about behind them. A loose string curls off the instrument, sheet music spills underneath, red drapery hangs behind. Ronner-Knip painted the scene in oil on panel, about 32 by 45 cm, and signed it 'Henriette Ronner' at lower right. The joke is the title: the only music being made is the twang of a snapped string, and the performers do not look sorry.
context: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821–1909), Amsterdam-born and Brussels-based from 1850, specialised in cats from the 1870s and was honoured with the Order of Leopold in 1887. This panel passed through J.B. Bennett & Sons in Glasgow and a Dutch private collection, was bought by its then owner in 2016, and appeared as lot 250 in Christie's sale 17295 of nineteenth-century European and Orientalist art in December 2019. Fun fact: the photograph of this painting now illustrates guitar articles on some 25 language editions of Wikipedia.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://www.christies.com/lotfinder/lot_details.aspx?intObjectID=6248914&lid=1

title: Studies of an Awakening Kitten
medium: Oil on paper laid down on panel
collection: Unknown (reproduced in Simonis & Buunk catalogue 'Harmonie en Contrast')
description: Three calico kittens share one sheet, or perhaps one kitten three times: two curled asleep at left, eyes shut and paws tucked, and one at right sitting up wide awake, round blue eyes and a ginger patch over one of them. The title says studies, plural, and the sheet reads like the moment when a kitten's eyes open before the rest of the body agrees. The warm ground is brushed in loosely around each figure. Ronner-Knip painted in oil on paper, later laid on panel, 27.1 by 36.1 cm, and marked it twice at lower right: with the initials 'HR' and the full signature 'Henriette Ronner'.
context: Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) trained with her father Joseph August Knip, exhibited in Amsterdam from 1838 and became the first woman active member of Arti et Amicitiae, then moved to Brussels in 1850 and turned to cats after 1870. Oil sketches on paper like this one were her working tools; late in life she kept live models and even folded paper figures into the poses she wanted. The study is published in Harmonie en Contrast, a catalogue of the Dutch dealers Simonis & Buunk in Ede, which is the source of the reproduction. Its present owner is not recorded.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Simonis & Buunk - Harmonie en Contrast

title: The Maine Coon
description: A long-haired tabby with a white bib sits square to us on a pale blue cloth, green eyes fixed just past the viewer, its huge tail swept round in front of its feet. It fills an upright panel 40.5 by 32 cm, painted in oil. The coat is the subject: a long-haired cat lets a painter show off, and the fur here is dragged on in short, broken strokes of brown, black and grey over a mottled gold ground. The auction title calls the sitter a Maine Coon, but that is a saleroom label, not Ronner-Knip's. The inscription at upper left, 'Henriette Ronner./94', fixes the year as 1894.
context: By 1894 Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) had spent more than four decades in Brussels and two in cats; her best-known pictures are of long-haired cats in comfortable interiors, and she received the Order of Leopold in 1887. This panel came through the Amsterdam dealer Kunsthandel M. Wolff and was offered as lot 252 at Christie's sale 17295 of nineteenth-century European and Orientalist art in December 2019. Fun fact: Wikimedia Commons now files the picture under 'History of Maine Coon cats', so a painting made in Brussels, titled by an auction house, has been drafted into an American breed's family album.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://www.christies.com/lotfinder/lot_details.aspx?intObjectID=6248916&lid=1

title: Kittens with a Basket of Lobsters (Kätzchen)
description: A tabby-and-white kitten lies flat on its back on a crumpled cloth, all four paws up and mouth wide open, squaring off against a lobster whose claw dangles over the edge of a tipped wicker basket. A second kitten peers over the basket rim at upper right, hissing too, and a label with a red seal is tucked into the lid. Julius Adam painted the encounter in watercolour and gouache on paper, a small upright sheet of 26.5 by 19 cm, and signed it 'Jul. Adam.' at upper right. Soft fur against hard shell is the whole gag, and gouache lets him lay opaque highlights on both.
context: Julius Anton Adam (1852–1913) came from a Munich family that produced painters for four generations; his father, also Julius, was a lithographer and photographer. The son spent nearly six years as a photo retoucher in Rio de Janeiro before studying at the Munich Academy, mainly under Wilhelm von Diez. Settling as a painter in 1882, he turned almost entirely to cats, earning the nicknames Katzen-Adam and Katzenraffael and a strong market in the United States. This sheet surfaced through the German auction house Van Ham. Fun fact: in 1887 a dealer contract bound him to paint only for its clients for five years.
title_eng: Kittens with a Basket of Lobsters (Kätzchen)
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · http://www.van-ham.com

title: Tabbies in Hyde Park
medium: Process print (photomechanical), supplement to Hearth and Home, 6 August 1896
description: Eight cats pedal bicycles in a tight pack through Hyde Park, most of them white, grey or black rather than striped, several in baggy bloomers and one with a bow tie, while a white terrier chases a small black animal across the foreground. Rows of cat spectators line the course at both edges. Wain plays it straight, as if reporting a sporting event. The image is wide, 30.4 by 50.6 cm, and it is a process print, a photomechanical reproduction of his drawing made for mass circulation. The printed lettering names it 'Tabbies in Hyde Park' and credits it as a supplement to Hearth and Home, 6 August 1896.
context: Wain (1860–1939), born in Clerkenwell, sold his first cat drawings to The Illustrated London News in 1884 and drew his first cats in human roles in 1886. By 1890 he was president of the National Cat Club. He sold work cheaply and often gave up copyright, so supplements like this earned him no royalties. H. G. Wells later said he 'invented a cat style, a cat society, a whole cat world'. The sheet belongs to the Wellcome Collection (39628i). Fun fact: the medical library's catalogue files it under two subjects only, 'Cats' and 'Bicycle racing'.
title_original: A Group of Cats Engaged in a Cycle-Race in Hyde Park, London
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/c3/41/901eec22019691767711a4e63f9a.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/V0023074.html

title: Carol Singing Cats
medium: Watercolour, gouache, pen and pencil on paper
description: Eight cats carol in the snow outside a row of half-timbered houses, with full kit: cello, flute, trumpet, a big brass horn and a drum, one musician sprawled flat beneath it. From an upper window at left a cat empties a jug on the band while a mouse goes flying, and two cats in the distance let fly with snowballs. Wain's cats perform a human custom with complete seriousness, and get the human reception. Watercolour, gouache, pen and pencil share one sheet of about 15 by 22 inches (roughly 38 by 56 cm), an original drawing rather than one of the printed copies through which most people met his cats.
context: Louis Wain (1860–1939) made Christmas part of his cat world from the start: his first drawing of cats in human roles, 'A Kitten's Christmas Party' of 1886, packed 150 cats into eleven panels. From 1901 his Louis Wain Annual kept the seasonal market supplied. By 1890 he presided over the National Cat Club. The present sheet is known only from an auction listing reproduced on Wikimedia Commons, with no date or owner recorded. Fun fact: H. G. Wells credited him with inventing 'a cat style, a cat society, a whole cat world'.
image_credit: Louis William Wain · Liveauctioneers.com

title: Black Cats Howl as Witches Ascend into the Night (Metamorphosis)
medium: Colour process print after a lithograph
description: Three black cats in the foreground throw their heads back and howl, and more prowl the rooftops at right, while naked witches on broomsticks stream up into a grey night over a city, the leader with one arm flung high. A thin red line of light runs along the horizon. The cats stay earthbound and loud; the women do the flying. This sheet is a colour process print, a photomechanical copy of a Steinlen lithograph, signed at lower right, and laid on a mount that carries the word 'Metamorphosis' and the artist's name in pencil, plus a page number, 23. The publication line reads only '(E. & W.)'
context: Steinlen drew the original lithograph, dated 1893 by French Wikipedia, in Montmartre, where he had settled from Lausanne and worked for Gil Blas and the Chat Noir circle. The Wellcome Collection owns this later colour reproduction (17285i) and catalogues it under witchcraft, folklore, cats and France. Neither the reproduction's date nor its publisher is recorded. Fun fact: French Wikipedia uses the image to illustrate the 'sabbat des chats', a belief strongest in central and western France that local cats gathered at night at the Devil's call, often between Mardi Gras and Ash Wednesday, and that anyone who saw them came to grief.
title_eng: Black Cats Howl as Witches Ascend into the Night (Metamorphosis)
feline_symbolism: In French folklore cats held their own nocturnal sabbath at the Devil's summons, mirroring the witches'; Steinlen's howling black cats draw on that picture of the cat as the witch's companion and double.
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/0a/30/0003636e99003d3329dc4999eaa3.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/V0011894.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-23): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/bfdtqqhy

title: Sleeping Cat
medium: Cast bronze relief plaque, brown patina, signed 'Steinlen' lower left
description: A cat sleeps curled into a tight ball on a small rectangular bronze plaque, the body swelling out of the flat ground in low relief. Its head is tucked down and turned, one forepaw folded over its face against the light, tail wrapped round so the whole animal reads as a single loop. The modelling is soft and lumpy, closer to thumb-pressed clay than to a crisp cast, and the polished highlights catch the ribs and the curve of the back. 'Steinlen' is incised at lower left.
context: Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen (1859–1923), born in Lausanne, made Montmartre his home and cats one of his constant subjects, in prints, posters, drawings and a smaller body of sculpture, mostly small bronzes of cats. This plaque belongs to the Boston Public Library, given in memory of Louis W. Black; the record names Hyman Swetzoff and the date 5 November 1959, which the cataloguer supplied. Its date of making is not recorded, so 'c. 1900' is a guess. Fun fact: the record catalogued it as a lithograph, and only the photograph shows that it is a piece of bronze.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre, 1859-1923 · This file was contributed to Wikimedia Commons by Boston Public Library as part of a cooperation project. The donation was facilitated by the Digital Public Library of America . Record in source ca

title: Portrait of a Woman with a Cat (Portret kobiety z kotem)
description: A red-and-white cat dozes on the lap of a woman in a deep red dress, eyes shut, one white forepaw stretched across her skirt while her hand rests on its back. The cat supplies the light note in a canvas built from reds and browns, white fur and ginger patches against a dress that nearly melts into the background. The sitter looks straight out, half smiling. On a canvas 100 by 69.8 cm, Pająkówna paints the stroking hand and the animal as one gesture, so the portrait is as much about a habit of touch as about a face. The sitter is not named in the museum record.
context: Aniela Pająkówna (1862 or 1864–1912), daughter of a coachman, studied in Kraków and from 1886 in Paris at the Académie Julian and the Académie Colarossi, with time in Munich, then opened her own studio in Lwów in 1891. She showed at the Vienna Künstlerhaus in 1897 and in the first exhibition of the Association of Polish Women Artists at the Sukiennice in 1899. This portrait, dated 1898, belongs to the National Museum in Warsaw (MP 3944 MNW). Fun fact: her daughter with Stanisław Przybyszewski, born in 1901, became the writer Stanisława Przybyszewska.
title_eng: Portrait of a Woman with a Cat
image_credit: Aniela Pająkówna · National Museum in Warsaw

title: Mr. Louis Wain Gets the Election Fever
medium: Photomechanical reproduction in The Sketch, vol. XXXI, no. 403 (17 October 1900), p. 535
description: Cats swarm a street plastered with election posters, and the slogans are the best part: 'Vote for Free Cats Homes and No Lethal Chamber', 'Vote for Tibbs, He Kisses the Babies', 'Vote for More Mousetraps', 'Vote for Better Cats Meat'. A striped cat up a ladder pastes another bill while a temperance meeting holds forth at the back. The title, 'Mr. Louis Wain Gets the Election Fever', casts the artist as the patient and leaves his cats to act out the symptoms. It is a black-and-white cartoon on page 535 of The Sketch for 17 October 1900, and every cat in it is a voter, a candidate or a heckler.
context: Louis Wain (1860–1939) had been president of the National Cat Club since about 1890 and supplied a steady stream of drawings to London's illustrated papers. The Sketch printed this one in volume XXXI, issue 403. Wain sold his pictures, and their copyrights, cheaply, so the reproduction of his cats in print paid publishers far better than it paid him. Fun fact: a year later he launched the Louis Wain Annual, which appeared every year from 1901 to 1915 and once more in 1921.
title_eng: Mr. Louis Wain Gets the Election Fever
title_original: Mr. Louis Wain Gets the Election Fever (The Sketch)
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXXI, No. 403, October 17, 1900, page 535

title: Waiting Up!
medium: Cartoon printed in The Sketch, vol. XXXII, no. 413 (26 December 1900), p. 386
description: Two white cats meet late at night: one, in round spectacles, has sat up with her knitting, needles raised and the ball of wool rolled off across the floor; the other, fur on end and eyes like saucers, has plainly just crept in. The printed caption delivers the joke: 'Good Gracious, Mrs. Tabby; how you startled me!' Mrs. Tabby would not dream of going to bed and leaving the late-comer out on the tiles. 'Waiting Up!' ran in The Sketch on 26 December 1900, the day after Christmas, as a single cartoon on page 386. Domestic comedy was Wain's staple: cats behaving exactly like the families who bought the paper.
context: At the turn of the century Wain was feeding cartoons to London's illustrated weeklies, and The Sketch printed a run of them between 1900 and 1902; this one is in volume XXXII, issue 413. He was about forty and supporting his mother and five sisters, which goes some way to explaining how much he drew and how little he kept. Fun fact: his whole career as a cat artist began with a cat of his own, a black-and-white kitten called Peter, who Wain said 'laid the foundation' of it.
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXXII, No. 413, December 26, 1900, page 386

title: Picture of a Cat
title_original: Picture of a Cat (The Sketch, July 18, 1900)
medium: Illustration printed in The Sketch, vol. XXX, no. 390 (18 July 1900), p. 554
description: A long-haired cat fills the frame, head and chest only, staring straight out with big pale eyes from a dark, smoky face set above an enormous pale ruff. No costume, no punchline: the published title is simply 'Picture of a Cat', and it appeared on page 554 of The Sketch on 18 July 1900. That plainness stands out in Wain's magazine work, where cats usually play out human comedies, and the fur here is built from loose, painterly strokes rather than his cartoon outline. His signature sits at lower left. What survives online is a small scan of the printed page, in black and white.
context: In 1900 Wain was president of the National Cat Club, and he could write about cats as well as draw them: in 1901 he contributed the section on the domestic cat to Hutchinson's The Living Animals of the World. A plain portrait like this one shows the observing naturalist behind the artist best known for cats at tea parties. The Sketch printed it in volume XXX, issue 390. Fun fact: between 1900 and 1940 some 75 publishers issued more than 1,100 of Wain's images as postcards.
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXX, No. 390, July 18, 1900, page 554

title: Conversation amongst Cats
description: Three white long-haired cats hold what looks like a meeting at the edge of a patterned rug. The middle one stands with its plumed tail up and looks straight at us, as if it has the floor; the one at right sits facing it, and the third lies flat on the parquet at left, eyes half shut, taking no part. A green curtain shuts off the left side and a small upholstered stool stands behind, so this is a comfortable parlour, not a pantry or a barn. At 76 × 113 cm the canvas is generous for a cat picture, and the white coats carry the light across it.
