context: Arthur Heyer (1872–1931) was born in Haarhausen, trained in Berlin at the Kunstgewerbemuseum school (1890–95), moved to Budapest in 1896 and became a Hungarian citizen in 1900. His many Turkish Angoras earned him the nickname 'Cat-Heyer'. This canvas is undated; Commons can only say 'by 1931'. It is in a private collection, and its photograph comes from a sale at the Vienna auction house Dorotheum. Fun fact: before cats took over, Heyer placed early drawings in newspapers while still a student.
image_credit: Arthur Heyer · https://www.dorotheum.com/en/auctions/current-auctions/kataloge/list-lots-detail/auktion/12991-19th-century-paintings-and-watercolours/lotID/52/lot/2337233-arthur-heyer.html

title: Cat Study
description: Three kittens pile together on a pinkish cloth: a grey long-haired kitten in the middle looks straight at us with grey-green eyes, a white one with a ginger patch dozes behind at left, and a dark tortoiseshell-and-white kitten sleeps in front, one white paw stretched out. Oil on canvas, 15 × 20.5 cm, signed and dated 1901 at upper right. Hartlepool catalogues it simply as 'Cat Study', one of three small Ronner oils that arrived together under the numbers 1947.5.1 to 1947.5.3. Ronner was eighty when she painted it, and even at the size of a postcard her study holds a whole litter.
context: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) was born in Amsterdam, trained with her father Joseph August Knip and moved to Brussels in 1850. From around 1870 she painted cats almost exclusively, often long-haired and playful, in comfortable bourgeois interiors. In 1901, the year of this study, she was made a member of the Order of Orange-Nassau. The painting is in Hartlepool Museums and Heritage Service. Fun fact: she posed her subjects twice, first by watching the live animals in her studio, then by making paper sculptures in the poses she wanted and arranging them with furniture and fabric.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: Cat Study
description: A long-haired tabby-and-white cat lies tucked into a soft loaf on a pale cushion, eyes all but closed, chin sunk into a thick white ruff. Behind it the ground is a hot red, and the cat's own shadow climbs the wall as a big black shape, as though a second, darker cat were keeping watch. Another of the three small 'Cat Study' oils by Ronner-Knip in Hartlepool, this one 15 × 20 cm on canvas, signed and dated 1901 at lower right. At about the area of a paperback cover it was never meant for a salon wall, and the brushwork settles the animal in a few passes.
context: Ronner-Knip learned to paint from her father, the landscape painter Joseph August Knip, who went blind in 1832, and by 1838 she was exhibiting at the Exhibition of Living Masters. After marrying Feico Ronner in 1850 she moved to Brussels, where her husband, often ill, acted as her manager. Cats became her near-exclusive subject after 1870. This study belongs to Hartlepool Museums and Heritage Service (HAPMG: 1947.5.2). Fun fact: she painted the lapdogs of Marie Henriette of Austria, Queen of the Belgians, before the cats took over her studio.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: Charlie Morton's Mascot: The Persian Cat of the Palace Theatre
medium: Pen, black ink, and wash on paper
collection: Published in The Sketch, vol. XXXVI, no. 458 (6 November 1901), p. 102
description: A huge, fluffy black Persian sits at a desk with a quill in one paw and an inkwell at its elbow, grinning at us with wide white-rimmed eyes, mid-letter. Wain's title names it the mascot of the Palace Theatre and the pet of 'Charlie' Morton, the theatre's manager, and the drawing filled a near-square block on page 102 of The Sketch for 6 November 1901. The mascot has been given a part to play, correspondent, rather than drawn as a plain show-cat portrait. Wain was a natural choice for the job: as president of the National Cat Club he knew long-haired show cats better than most illustrators.
context: Charles Morton (1819–1904), called the 'Father of the Halls', managed the Palace Theatre of Varieties in London from 1893, at the invitation of Sir Augustus Harris, until he retired shortly before his death. When this appeared he was 82, and his cat was evidently famous enough for a society weekly to send for the country's best-known cat artist. The Sketch printed it in volume XXXVI, issue 458. Fun fact: Morton worked almost to the end, and died in 1904 aged 85, three years after his Persian made the papers.
title_eng: Charlie Morton's Mascot: The Persian Cat of the Palace Theatre
title_original: 'Charlie' Morton's Mascot – The Persian Cat of the Palace Theatre
feline_symbolism: A theatre mascot was a good-luck charm, and Wain's title presents the cat in exactly that role.
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXXVI, No. 458, November 6, 1901, page 102

title: Homeward-Bound from the Seaside
medium: Pen, black ink, and wash on paper
description: Half a dozen cats cram into a little cart pulled by two dogs, a shaggy one and a black-and-white terrier, galloping straight at us with dust flying off the wheel. One cat flourishes a whip, one waves a Union Jack, another a St George's cross, and the driver in the middle grins with the reins in hand. The title fixes the season: 'Homeward-Bound from the Sea-Side', printed on page 406 of The Sketch on 25 September 1901, as summer ended. A pale green tint washes road and sky. Wain's comedy works by transfer: the crowding and end-of-holiday high spirits belong to people, and he hands them to cats.
context: This is one of a run of Wain cartoons that The Sketch printed in 1900–02, and it belongs to his busiest years: the Louis Wain Annual had just started (1901), and books such as The Dandy Lion (1901) and Cats (1902) came out alongside the magazine work. It is volume XXXV, issue 452. Fun fact: six years later Wain left for New York on a contract with Hearst Newspapers, and stayed until 1910.
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXXV, No. 452, September 25, 1901, page 406

title: Hunting Picture (untitled cartoon)
medium: Pen, black ink, and wash on paper
description: Two grinning cats ride muzzled hounds across a field like jockeys, reins in paw, while a bushy-tailed animal lies flipped on its back in the grass and a soaked, wide-eyed cat sits chest-deep in a stream in the foreground. The Sketch printed it on page 364 on 18 September 1901 with no title, only a note beneath: the editor had commissioned Mr. Louis Wain to draw a Hunting Picture, and 'This is the Cataleptic result!' The joke is on the commission itself. A week later the same paper ran Wain's 'Homeward-Bound from the Sea-Side' on page 406, so for two issues running his cats followed the English calendar.
context: Louis Wain was born in Clerkenwell in 1860 and sold his first cat drawings to the Illustrated London News in 1884; 'A Kitten's Christmas Party' there in 1886 made his name. By 1901 he was a fixture in the weeklies, and this untitled cartoon is one of several in The Sketch that year (volume XXXV, issue 451). Fun fact: H. G. Wells, speaking on the radio in 1925, summed him up in one line: 'He has made the cat his own.'
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXXV, No. 451, September 18, 1901, page 364

title: Pussy Bucks Up After the Dinner to the Cat's-Meat Men
medium: Pen, black ink, and wash on paper
description: Two panels, two cats. On the left a fluffy white cat peeps coyly over an open fan; on the right a cat in an enormous bow tie struts toward us with a framed board under one arm and a small black case in the other paw. The cartoon, wider than tall, ran on page 28 of The Sketch on 23 January 1901 under one of Wain's best titles: 'Pussy Bucks Up After the Dinner to the Cat's-Meat Men'. The cat's-meat men, street sellers of meat for pets, have been given a dinner, and Pussy dresses up accordingly. The men who feed London's cats get fed, and the cats approve.
context: The cartoon appeared in volume XXXIII, issue 417, in the first month of the new century's first full year, while Wain was at the height of his popularity and president of the National Cat Club. He sold such drawings outright, along with their copyright, so he earned nothing from later reprints. Fun fact: according to Wikipedia, 75 publishers between 1900 and 1940 issued more than 1,100 of his images as postcards, which means a single title like this one could circulate far beyond the magazine.
title_eng: Pussy Bucks Up After the Dinner to the Cat's-Meat Men
title_original: Pussy Bucks Up After the Dinner to the Cat's-Meat Men
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXXIII, No. 417, January 23, 1901, page 28

title: Cat on an Armchair (Chat sur un fauteuil)
collection: Musée d'Orsay, Paris (on deposit at La Piscine – Musée d'Art et d'Industrie André Diligent, Roubaix)
description: A tabby cat lies curled on the seat of a wooden armchair, eyes shut, head up, forelegs stretched straight out in front, the pale cushion lit around it like a small stage. Steinlen, who drew cats for posters, magazines and albums for decades, here gives one the dignity of oil on canvas, 46 × 55 cm, a format wider than tall that leaves room for the curving chair-back and arm as well as the animal. The stripes on the flank go down in a few broad, dark strokes, and his signature sits at lower left. The chair is human furniture, and the cat has claimed it.
context: Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen (1859–1923), Swiss-born and Paris-based, is best known for his Montmartre cats in print. This oil belongs to the Musée d'Orsay (RF 1970 5), which received it as a bequest from Mme Roger Désormière in 1973; it is on deposit at La Piscine, the Musée d'Art et d'Industrie André Diligent in Roubaix. Fun fact: Orsay's own record dates it only 'between 1859 and 1923', the artist's lifespan, while Wikidata confidently says 1902.
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · La Piscine [1]

title: Cat Study
description: Two kittens share this little canvas, not one: a white kitten with tabby patches on its head looks straight out with clear blue-green eyes, while a darker tabby sleeps against its shoulder at left, eyes shut. This is the smallest of Hartlepool's three Ronner 'Cat Study' oils, 12.5 × 15 cm on canvas, signed and dated 1902 at upper left, when the painter was eighty-one. Ronner kept making these to the end of her life, small oil notes of cats that sit somewhere between sketchbook and finished picture. Its sister studies, 1947.5.1 and 1947.5.2, are a year earlier.
context: Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) spent most of her career in Brussels and Ixelles, and from about 1870 her finished paintings showed long-haired, often playful cats in well-off households. Small studies like this one were raw material. The three Hartlepool studies share consecutive accession numbers (HAPMG: 1947.5.1–3), so they almost certainly entered the collection together. Fun fact: she showed at the Palace of Fine Arts at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, so her cats crossed the Atlantic long before reproductions made them popular there.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: The Playwright
medium: Pen, black ink, and wash on paper
description: A white cat sits at a desk with its quill pinned to the page, glaring sideways through a monocle on a cord, mouth open as if a line has just gone badly wrong. 'The Playwright' appeared on page 258 of The Sketch on 4 June 1902, a single cartoon a little taller than wide, printed over a grey tone. The title promises literary ambition, a good joke in a weekly that lived on theatre gossip and first nights. Wain loved to give his cats a profession and the airs that come with it, and a dramatist was about as airy as professions got in Edwardian London.
context: By 1902 Wain had published Fun and Frolic (1900), The Dandy Lion (1901) and Cats (1902) as well as the first Louis Wain Annual, and his cartoons ran in The Sketch for at least three years; this one is volume XXXVIII, issue 488. Behind the productivity lay money worries: he sold work and copyrights cheaply and supported his mother and sisters. Fun fact: the 1,100-plus postcard designs issued from his images between 1900 and 1940 came from 75 different publishers.
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXXVIII, No. 488, June 4, 1902, page 258

title: The Sick Kitten
description: A kitten swaddled in a cloth gets its medicine: in this frame a child's hand brings a spoon to its mouth, close enough to fill the screen. In thirty-four seconds of film two small children nurse it, and the camera does something new for 1903: it moves in. George Albert Smith cuts from a wider view to a closer one, and he does it without the round black mask he had used in 1900 to tell audiences they were looking through a lens. The kitten is the reason the close-up exists, since the action that matters is too small to read from across the room.
context: Smith made, produced and shot the film in Hove, and Warwick Trading Company released it in February 1903. It remakes his own lost 'The Little Doctor' (1901). Smith belonged to the loose group of Sussex filmmakers that the historian Georges Sadoul later called the Brighton School, and he worked from a glass-house studio built in 1899 at St Ann's Well Garden with Charles Urban's money. Fun fact: Michael Brooke of BFI Screenonline reads the dropped mask as a vote of confidence that audiences could now understand a close-up unaided.
dimensions: 35mm motion picture film strip (approx. 24 × 18 mm frame)
image_credit: George Albert Smith · http://www.screenonline.org.uk/film/id/443164/
rights_note: UK film of 1903: films made before July 1912 were protected only as series of photographs, and photographs taken before June 1957 went out of copyright 70 years after they were taken.

title: Cat with Detail Studies (Katze mit Detailstudien)
collection: Bavarian State Painting Collections (Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen), Munich
description: Four long-haired tabby kittens tumble across this canvas, not the single cat the title 'Katze mit Detailstudien' might suggest. One lies on its back at left, paws curled, gazing straight up; two more heads tilt skyward at top right, and a fourth stares out at us from the lower right. The background is barely brushed in, so the weave shows through. It is small, 29.5 × 42.5 cm, and dated 1903: a working canvas where Adam, who painted almost nothing but cats for three decades, tried poses before committing them to a sale picture.
context: Julius Adam (1852–1913) came from a Munich dynasty of painters spanning four generations. He trained in his father's photographic studio, worked for almost six years as a retoucher in Rio de Janeiro, then studied at the Munich academy and set up as a painter in 1882. After a picture of two cats brought him his first real success, he turned almost entirely to cats, earning the nicknames 'Katzen-Adam' and 'Katzenraffael'. The study belongs to the Bavarian State Painting Collections (inv. 8795). Fun fact: in 1894 he published a little book illustrated with photographs of his own cat paintings.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/en/bookmark/artwork/ma4ddPB14r

title: Invitation Card for Steinlen's Exhibition, 32 place Saint-Georges
description: A long black cat stretches across the top of the address panel like a draught excluder, head raised, ears pricked, and its tail drops down the right edge and curls into a hook. This side is the printed envelope, 12.1 × 9.2 cm, from Th.-A. Steinlen, 73 rue Caulaincourt, addressed in ink to Monsieur Beurdeley and franked with a 15-centime stamp postmarked Paris. Inside was the invitation to his exhibition at 32 place Saint-Georges, 15 November 1903. It is catalogued as Crauzat 257, and Steinlen's red monogram sits top left.
context: Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen (1859–1923) built a career in Paris on posters, illustrated papers and cats, and an exhibition card was one more chance to show both. This copy is addressed to Beurdeley (1847–1919), who appears in the BnF record as its recipient. It is now in the Département des Estampes et de la photographie of the Bibliothèque nationale de France (DC-385 (5)-FOL). Fun fact: the card reached the national collection as part of a bound album shelved as a folio, not as a loose print.
title_eng: Invitation Card for Steinlen's Exhibition, 32 place Saint-Georges
title_original: Carton d'invitation pour l'Exposition Steinlen chez Beurdeley
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Beurdeley, Alfred (1847-1919). Destinataire de lettres · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Girl in a Birch Forest with Cat (Mädchen im Birkenwald mit Katze)
description: A white cat with black patches and pale green eyes hangs over the girl's arm, clutched to her chest while its striped tail and belly dangle below her hands. She stands in a dark green dress against a pale birch trunk, looking past us, while two small red-clad figures hover in the trees behind. The canvas is large for Modersohn-Becker, 96 × 81.5 cm, almost square, and Commons files it among her portraits. The birch stems were a Worpswede signature, and the cat's bright fur is the lightest thing in the picture.
context: Paula Modersohn-Becker (1876–1907) worked in the artists' colony at Worpswede near Bremen and kept going back to Paris, where she studied the work of Gauguin and Cézanne; around 1904 she was moving toward the simplified forms and non-naturalistic colour that make her a forerunner of Expressionism. The painting is no. 518 in her catalogue raisonné and belongs to the Paula Modersohn-Becker Museum in Bremen. Fun fact: that museum, opened in 1927 by Ludwig Roselius and designed by her Worpswede acquaintance Bernhard Hoetger, is often called the first museum devoted to a woman artist.
title_eng: Girl in a Birch Forest with Cat
image_credit: Paula Modersohn-Becker · 1. Google Arts & Culture — xAExtzAT1yfw2w (page no more available) 2. Google Arts & Culture — cQFN1uw_6RxrMQ

title: Study of Eleven Cats (Studie van elf poezen)
collection: Netherlands Open Air Museum (Nederlands Openluchtmuseum), Arnhem
description: Kittens everywhere on one mahogany panel, and not all finished to the same degree. The Netherlands Open Air Museum notes that six are painted fully in oil while five stay as sketches, and the split is easy to see: fluffy brown tabbies curled asleep along the bottom, beside ghostly outline kittens drawn in thin brown line above. One small tabby head in the middle peers up with green eyes. Ronner signed and dated it 'HR 1904' at top left. It is a sampler of poses rather than a scene, here in a heavy gilt frame.
context: Ronner-Knip painted animals all her life and concentrated on cats from about 1870. The museum explains that her many quick studies, in charcoal, pencil, pen and oil, were preparation for finished paintings, and links the demand for cat pictures to the nineteenth-century acceptance of the cat as part of family life. She was eighty-three in 1904. The panel is in the Nederlands Openluchtmuseum in Arnhem (N.883). Fun fact: the museum records that its gilded frame with scroll ornament dates from 1982, so the presentation is much younger than the painting.
feline_symbolism: The museum ties pictures like this to the nineteenth-century rise of the cat as a family pet.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Netherlands Open Air Museum

title: Sleeping Kitten (Śpiący kotek)
description: A kitten asleep, chin flat on a cushion, ears soft, a few quick strokes for the closed eyes. Malczewski draws it in ink on a scrap of paper 9.5 × 15.9 cm, smaller than a postcard, and frames it with loose diagonal hatching behind, like the back of an armchair. The great painter of Polish Symbolist allegory here does something modest: he watches an animal that is not going anywhere and gets it down. On the back is a pencil sketch of a hunter, and a pencil '103' runs up the lower left edge.
context: Jacek Malczewski (1854–1929), born in Radom and active in Kraków, was a central figure of the Young Poland movement and the founder of what became Poland's school of Symbolism. Animal studies like this sit at the private end of his output. The drawing is undated; the c. 1900–1910 bracket in the old record is a guess. It has passed through the Polish art market and is recorded on the Artinfo.pl database. Fun fact: the hunter sketch on the verso means the sheet carries two of Malczewski's subjects at once, a quiet cat on one side and a man with a gun on the other.

title: Cat
description: A cat seen from behind, reduced to a handful of faint charcoal lines on a sheet 27 × 21 cm: the long curve of the back, two vertical strokes for the front legs and a small curl of paw at the bottom. Far from a dark, smudged sheet, this is one of the barest in the group, mostly empty brown paper. Amgueddfa Cymru simply calls it 'Cat'. It belongs to a large set of Gwen John cat studies in Cardiff, from seated tortoiseshells to two cats asleep, and reads best next to them, as one frame in a long observation.
context: Gwen John (1876–1939) reached Paris in 1904 after setting out with Dorelia McNeill to walk from Bordeaux to Rome; they got as far as Toulouse. In Paris she worked as an artist's model, notably for Rodin, and lived on very little. She made many sketches of her cats, and later, in Meudon, lived alone with them. National Museum Wales bought this drawing in July 1976 (NMW A 15611), together with its neighbour NMW A 15610, another charcoal 'Cat'. Fun fact: her diet in those first Paris years is recorded as mostly figs and bread.
image_credit: Gwen John · https://museum.wales/collections/online/?field0=with_images&value0=1&field1=string&value1=%20Gwen%20&field2=category&value2=Drawing&page=1

title: Cat (Kot)
description: A cat crouches low with its paws tucked forward and its head turned to the left, eyes wide and alert, the body left as a light outline while the face gets the shading. It is pencil, 13.7 × 21 cm inside its mount, unsigned. In this scan a round ink stamp reads 'Ze zbiorów Marji Malczewskiej', from the collection of Maria Malczewska, beside an inventory number that looks like 848. That stamp ties the sheet to the painter's own household, the best guarantee an unsigned drawing can have. The wide format suits the hunched cat.
context: Jacek Malczewski (1854–1929) is remembered for crowded Symbolist allegories of Polish history and myth, and as a leading figure of Young Poland. His wife, Maria née Garlewska, was the mother of their children Julia (b. 1888) and the painter Rafał (b. 1892), and her collection stamp turns up on studio drawings like this one. The sheet is undated and has passed through the Polish auction market, where Artinfo.pl recorded it as lot 50. Fun fact: the stamp spells her name 'Marji', an older Polish spelling of Marii.

title: Young Angora Cat (Junge Angorakatze)
description: One young white Angora, as Heyer's title 'Junge Angorakatze' promises: no second cat, no basket. The kitten is caught mid-step, front paw reaching forward, rump high and plumed tail flagged straight up, its blue eyes fixed on something off to the right. Its pink-lined ears and nose are the only warm notes against a blue-green backdrop and a red-brown floor. The long white coat is the reason for the picture. It is a modest canvas, 40 × 50 cm, the kind of size suited to a painter who lived on commissioned cat portraits.
context: Arthur Heyer (1872–1931) moved from Germany to Budapest in 1896 and held his first exhibition there in 1906. In 1911 he won the Count Andrássy Prize, and in 1915 he was appointed a professor in Munich, but he stayed known as 'Cat-Heyer' for his Turkish Angoras. His work hung at the Vienna Künstlerhaus and Munich's Glaspalast. This painting is undated, and its photograph comes from a 2006 flyer about the artist by Regina Pfundt. Fun fact: Heyer received a state funeral at Kerepesi Cemetery in Budapest.
image_credit: Arthur Heyer · flyer about Arthur Heyer by Regina Pfundt, 2006

title: Dog and Cat (Hund und Katze)
description: A white long-haired cat peers out from behind a tree trunk at upper left, round-eyed and perfectly still, while a white terrier with brown patches and a leather collar barks at it with its mouth wide open. That is everything the title 'Dog and Cat' promises. Heyer built his reputation on white long-haired cats, so the dog is the outsider in his usual world, and he places it on open grass while the cat keeps the tree between them. The 50 × 70 cm canvas gives the two animals room to keep their distance. Signed 'Heyer A.' lower left.
context: Arthur Heyer (1872–1931), a German-born painter who became a Hungarian citizen in 1900, was nicknamed 'Cat-Heyer', but he also painted deer, hares, pheasants, chickens and dogs. Trained in Berlin, he settled in Budapest in 1896 and exhibited in Weimar and Gotha in 1909 and at the Vienna Künstlerhaus. This canvas is undated and privately owned; its photograph comes from a sale at the Vienna auction house Dorotheum. Fun fact: in 1919 the painter of placid Angoras also published two children's books.
image_credit: Arthur Heyer · https://www.dorotheum.com/en/auctions/current-auctions/kataloge/list-lots-detail/auktion/12881-19th-century-paintings-and-watercolours/lotID/178/lot/2308662-arthur-heyer.html?currentPage=8

title: Cat Cleaning Itself (Tortoiseshell Washing Paw)
description: A tortoiseshell cat sits hunched with its head bent right down to its chest, deep in a wash, one front paw braced on the floor. Gwen John draws it in pencil and touches it with watercolour: olive and ochre patches on the back and head, while the white legs and belly stay as bare pencil line on pale paper. Grooming is the pose every cat owner knows and few artists bother with, because the animal folds into a knot of leg, tongue and fur. A few washes over the line are enough to name the cat.
context: Gwen John (1876–1939) settled in Paris in 1904 and made many sketches of her cats in the years that followed; this sheet is usually dated c. 1904–08. It was shown in Tate Britain's Gwen John and Augustus John exhibition, where the label gave it as 'Cat Cleaning Itself. Pencil and watercolour on paper'. Tate owns three small graphite-and-watercolour 'Cat' drawings of c. 1904–08 (N05154, N05155, T00156), two bought in 1940, and this is probably one of them. Fun fact: Rodin, whose model and lover she became in 1904, used her as the muse for his unfinished monument to Whistler.
image_credit: Photo © Tate (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0) · Gwen John
rights_note: Work in public domain (artist d. 1939). Collection photography © Tate, licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 3.0.

title: The Last Move
collection: Unknown (copyright owned by Braun, Clément & Co., Paris, in 1905)
description: Four cats and a chess game. A tabby kitten pounces onto the board, scattering pieces across the tablecloth, a white kitten crouches behind it, a third peers down from the carved crest of the chair, and a big tabby-and-white cat sits at left watching like a referee. The title 'The Last Move' makes that pounce the decisive play. What survives online is the 1905 halftone plate from Women Painters of the World, page 279, headed 'Flemish School, Contemporary'. Chess pieces were a favourite Ronner prop, small enough to bat, topple and chase.
context: The plate credit reads 'reproduced from the original painting by permission of Messrs. Braun, Clément & Co., Paris, owners of the copyright', so the Paris photographic firm controlled its reproduction, a sign of how commercial her cats had become. The book, edited by Walter Shaw Sparrow and published by Hodder & Stoughton in March 1905, pairs it with her 'New Tenants'. The painting's own date, medium and location are not given. Fun fact: the same book praises her daughter Alice Ronner as 'beyond dispute the foremost painter of still-life in Belgium'.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · http://www.gutenberg.org/files/39000/39000-h/39000-h.htm

title: Reclining Cat (Liegende Katze)
collection: Private collection (sold Lempertz, Cologne, 15 May 2010, lot 1938)
description: A brown tabby lies flat with its chin pressed onto its own front paws, eyes nearly shut, its ringed tail stretched out behind on a grey-green cloth. The canvas is long and low, 25 × 46 cm, and Adam lets the animal fill it. Look at the lower left: a loose green string trails off the cloth onto the floorboards, the toy that has apparently been given up on. It is signed and dated 'Jul. Adam 1905.' at upper right. Adam's reputation rested on fur and finish, and a plain study like this leaves nothing to look at but those.
context: Julius Adam (1852–1913) turned to cats after a painting of two of them brought his first big success, and by the 1900s his cat pictures had a reputation well beyond Germany, especially in the United States. In 1905, the year of this canvas, he took a gold medal at the International Art Exhibition in Munich. The painting is privately owned; it sold at Lempertz in Cologne in May 2010 for €12,600 against an estimate of €5,000–7,000. Fun fact: the auction house notes that in his lifetime he was called 'Katzenraffael', the Raphael of cats.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · lempertz.com

title: Cat car crash (postcard)
description: A motor car, a collision and a cat who wants names taken. The little red car has nosed into a grassy bank, its black-and-orange driver has been flung into a tree, and a striped passenger dangles upside down in a bush. At right a striped cat in a bowler hat raises a paw to his mouth and delivers the printed caption: 'Stop there till my mate comes, and I'll summons you both for furious driving and assault!' The card, from the Wrench Series, went to Ted Claxton, and '4/4/05' is written in ink below Wain's signature.
context: Wain was one of the most prolific postcard artists of his day: between 1900 and 1940, 75 publishers issued more than 1,100 of his images as cards. Wikimedia Commons assigns this one to the publisher Evelyn Wrench, and the scan comes from the Claxton postcard collection, uploaded by its owner from the original card. That makes it a private, used object rather than a museum piece, with a recipient and a date attached. Fun fact: Wain sold his pictures together with their copyright, so however many of these cards were posted, he earned nothing more from them.
image_credit: Louis Wain · Scan of original postcard in my possession

title: Her Favourite
collection: Private collection (Sotheby's London, The Russian Sale, 2006, lot 54)
description: A black cat with a white bib dangles in the air, held up at arm's length by a woman lying on her back across a white bed, smiling up at it with her bare legs crossed and kicked high. That cat is the 'favourite' of the title. The canvas is a wide landscape, 75.5 by 115 cm, which gives the bed, the green coverlet and the stretched-out body room. A tea tray waits on the side table and slippers lie on the floor. Bodarevsky signed it in Cyrillic and dated it 1905 at top right. The cat looks politely unconvinced.
context: Nikolai Bodarevsky (1850-1921) was born in Odesa, trained at the Imperial Academy of Arts in St Petersburg in 1869-73, and showed with the Peredvizhniki from 1880, becoming a member in 1884. Wikipedia notes that after seeing Whistler's work he turned out many female portraits in a similar manner. Her Favourite, dated 1905, is in a private collection; it came up as lot 54 in Sotheby's Russian Sale in London in 2006 with an estimate of 40,000-60,000 pounds, and it is illustrated in Romanov and Muratov's Encyclopaedia of Russian Salon Artists (2004). The odd fact: three years later the same painter was made an Academician for sketches of church mosaics, including work for the Church of the Savior on Blood.
image_credit: Nikolai Bodarevsky · [1]

title: Clinique Chéron: Veterinary Clinic (Clinique pour chiens et chats)
description: Four cats own the top of this poster: a black-and-white one balanced on the young woman's shoulder, a black cat with yellow eyes pressing its head against her cheek, and a pale and a tabby lounging along the wall, the tabby's tail hooked over the lettering. Below them three dogs, a white borzoi, a brown hound and a terrier on its hind legs, compete for her other hand. She wears a long red dress with a small white sprig pattern. It is a colour lithograph printed by Ch. Wall, 197 by 140 cm, so the animals stood close to life-size on a Paris wall.
context: Steinlen drew this poster in 1905 to advertise the Clinique Chéron, a veterinary clinic in Paris, and Ch. Wall printed it in colour lithography. It is catalogued as Crauzat 511 in the standard catalogue of Steinlen's prints. The Rijksmuseum's impression (RP-P-1968-308) was given in 1968 by P.F. Maas of Apeldoorn. By then Steinlen, Swiss-born and long settled in Montmartre, was best known for cats, from the Chat Noir poster onward. The later life of the image is a story in itself: a lithographic re-creation printed in the United States in 1992, in eight colours and an edition of 1,000, still circulates on the market, so a 'Clinique Chéron' for sale is far more likely to be that than the 1905 sheet.
image_credit: Rijksmuseum · http://hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.COLLECT.362697

title: Sleeping Tortoiseshell Cat
collection: Private collection (formerly Davis & Langdale / Abbott and Holder)
description: A tortoiseshell cat sleeps curled into an oval, head tucked down against its front paws, tail looping round from the left to close the circle. Gwen John drew it in pencil alone on a small square of tan paper, about 12 cm a side, so the patchy coat is suggested by short dark strokes along the back rather than by colour, with the tan of the sheet as the only warm tone. Nothing else is drawn: no cushion, no floor. A studio stamp, added after her death, sits at lower left in place of a signature.
context: In 1904 Gwen John, living at 19 boulevard Edgar Quinet in Paris, acquired a tortoiseshell cat and named it after the street; Christie's and Museum Wales both suggest that her tortoiseshell studies of 1904-08 show that cat. This sheet, pencil on tan paper, came down through her nephew Edwin John, who inherited her estate, and later passed through the dealers Davis & Langdale (stock no. DLA-1256, E.J. 1072) and Abbott and Holder. It is not the Cardiff drawing the old record claimed. Edgar Quinet ran off in 1908; John, who was by then Rodin's lover, wrote a poem, 'Au Chat', about the loss and sent it to him.
submovement: Modern British drawing, Gwen John's Paris cat studies
image_credit: Gwen John · http://www.abbottandholder-thelist.co.uk/mods-2019/ - archived as https://web.archive.org/web/20190906104239/http://www.abbottandholder-thelist.co.uk/mods-2019/

title: I Am a Cat (Wagahai wa Neko de Aru): First Edition Cover and Illustration
title_original: 吾輩は猫である (初版本装幀・挿絵)
artist: Hashiguchi Goyō (binding design); Nakamura Fusetsu and Asai Chū (illustrations)
description: On the cover of volume one, Hashiguchi Goyō boxed two pale cats sitting side by side in a black panel under the stamped title, a neat emblem for a narrator who sneers at his owner in fluent prose. The scan shown here is the National Diet Library's black-and-white copy of that first volume. Inside, the first volume came with uncut pages, so the reader had to slice each fold open with a paper knife to keep reading. The illustrations are by two painters trained in Western oils, Nakamura Fusetsu and Asai Chū, and Goyō added his own cat to the half-title of the second volume. Their cats are lighter and jokier than his.
context: Natsume Sōseki serialised the novel in the magazine Hototogisu from January 1905, and Ōkura Shoten and Hattori Shoten issued it as three volumes: 6 October 1905, 4 November 1906 and 19 May 1907. Sōseki, back from London, brought Western books and magazines to the design meetings and asked for a thoroughly Western look; the commission launched the young Goyō as a book designer and, later, as a woodblock printmaker. The book sold so well that from the 15th printing the binding switched from Japanese to Western style. A fun comparison from the Ghibli Museum's curator: Goyō's cat in volume two looks remarkably like Henry J. Ford's cat in Andrew Lang's Yellow Fairy Book.
title_eng: I Am a Cat: First Edition Cover and Illustration
medium: Letterpress book with multi-color woodblock cover design and monochrome woodcut illustrations
image_credit: National Diet Library Digital Collections (scan of vol. 1, 1905, via Wikimedia Commons)

title: Jerzual Street in Dinan (with a Cat)
collection: National Museum in Warsaw (Muzeum Narodowe w Warszawie)
description: The cat is easy to miss: a small pale shape trotting across the cobbles in the lower left foreground, tail out, the one moving thing in the rue du Jerzual. The Polish title adds '(z kotem)', 'with a cat', as if you are meant to hunt for it. Pankiewicz looks down the steep medieval street in Dinan toward the river Rance, timber-framed houses leaning in on the right, dark doorways under their overhangs, a few figures far down the slope. The needle lines follow beams, cobbles and slate. 'Dinan' is etched at lower right and the sheet signed in pencil below.
context: Józef Pankiewicz (1866-1940), born in Lublin, trained in Warsaw and St Petersburg and went to Paris in 1889; in 1906 he became a professor at the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts, and later he mentored the 'Kapists'. He spent repeated summers in France and made paintings and etchings of the towns he stayed in. This etching, catalogued on Commons as 'Ulica Jerzual w Dinan (z kotem)' and dated 1906 or 1908, is known from an impression offered at a Polish auction (Nautilus, via artinfo.pl). The odd detail is the title itself: a street view whose only named inhabitant is the cat.
title_eng: Jerzual Street in Dinan (with a Cat)
image_credit: Józef Pankiewicz · http://www.artinfo.pl/files//nautilus/21_aukcja/foto/121.jpg

title: Cat
medium: Pencil and gouache on buff paper
description: A cat lies hunched in a loaf, head at the left with ears up, its whole body laid in with one soft mauve-brown wash that leaves flecks of bare buff paper showing through like highlights on fur. This is a single study by Gwen John, sold at Christie's, and it is less about line than about mass: there is hardly any drawing, just the colour pooling darker along the back. Loose grey strokes around and below suggest a cushion or blanket without describing it. Her name is written in ink at lower left.
context: Gwen John (1876-1939) moved to Paris in 1904 and that year acquired a tortoiseshell cat she named Edgar Quinet, after her street. Museum Wales notes that she 'frequently captured her adored cats in spontaneous drawings', and most of the cat sheets are dated c.1904-08 on the assumption that they show Edgar Quinet, who ran away in 1908. This drawing is known from a Christie's sold-lot record (lot 5978144); the sale date and current owner are not recorded on the Commons file. John wrote of one of her cats that 'she is very important, perhaps the most important thing but that ought not to be, n'est pas?'
submovement: Modern British drawing, Gwen John's Paris cat studies
image_credit: Gwen John · https://www.christies.com/search?entry=Gwen%20John&page=1&tab=sold_lots

title: Cat
description: A cat sits upright and tall, front legs straight as columns, haunch bulging out to the left, head dropped so the eyes look half shut. Gwen John gets it down in a few dark, decisive outlines on brown paper and leaves everything inside them bare. It is one of the run of small sheets in Cardiff she simply titled 'Cat', each around 16-22 cm across, each one cat with no setting. Like its neighbours it was drawn from life, probably in a few minutes, and left the moment the shape was down.
context: Gwen John (1876-1939) settled in Paris in 1904 and that year acquired a tortoiseshell cat she named Edgar Quinet, after the street she lived on. Museum Wales notes that she 'frequently captured her adored cats in spontaneous drawings'. Amgueddfa Cymru holds a long numbered sequence of these 'Cat' sheets (NMW A 15620 to 15640 and more), and every one checked was bought on 29 July 1976, apparently as one group. The cat disappeared in 1908. John was devastated, walked the streets at night looking for her, and wrote a poem about the loss, 'Au Chat', which she sent to Rodin.
submovement: Modern British drawing, Gwen John's Paris cat studies
image_credit: Gwen John · https://museum.wales/collections/online/?field0=with_images&value0=1&field1=string&value1=%20Gwen%20&field2=category&value2=Drawing&page=1

title: Cat (verso)
description: A cat seen from behind, a rounded hump of back with the head turned toward the upper right, sitting in a thicket of crossing diagonal strokes that could be wicker or grass. This is the back of the sheet: the front of NMW A 15632 carries a charcoal cat, and when that was done Gwen John turned the paper over and drew again. The lines are faint and the body is almost all bare paper. The sheet is small, 17.2 by 16.9 cm, nearly square. Two cats back to back on one scrap is the economy of someone drawing every day.
context: Gwen John (1876-1939) acquired her first cat in 1904 in Paris, a tortoiseshell named Edgar Quinet after her street, and spent the next four years drawing it on whatever paper was at hand. Amgueddfa Cymru bought this sheet on 29 July 1976, together with a long run of other 'Cat' drawings now numbered in the NMW A 156xx series. Using both sides of a sheet is typical of a working drawing never meant for exhibition. The cat vanished in 1908; John wrote a poem about it, 'Au Chat', and sent it to Rodin, and she later wrote of a cat that 'she is very important, perhaps the most important thing but that ought not to be, n'est pas?'
submovement: Modern British drawing, Gwen John's Paris cat studies
image_credit: Gwen John · https://museum.wales/collections/online/?field0=with_images&value0=1&field1=string&value1=%20Gwen%20&field2=category&value2=Drawing&page=1

title: Cat
description: A tabby-and-white cat curled tight into an oval, seen from above, its white face and chest tucked against its flank at the left and the ears just poking up. Gwen John draws it in graphite and then lays dark brown-black stripes over the back in confident watercolour, picking out the white fur with opaque highlights against the brown paper. The sheet is only 111 by 137 mm, smaller than a postcard. There is no setting; the sleeping cat simply occupies the paper. This is a drawing made at close quarters from a living animal that was, for once, not going anywhere.
context: Gwen John (1876-1939) moved to Paris in 1904 and that year acquired a tortoiseshell cat she named Edgar Quinet, after her address on the boulevard Edgar Quinet; it turns up in most of her cat drawings, sometimes with kittens. Tate dates this one c.1904-8, and it was presented in 1957 by Miss Mary Constance Lloyd. In 1908 the cat ran away. John wrote to her friend Ursula Tyrwhitt that 'when the cats make love I run to see if my sweet is one of them', and she sent a poem about the loss, 'Au Chat', to Rodin.
submovement: Modern British drawing, Gwen John's Paris cat studies
image_credit: Gwen John · https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artists/gwen-john-1363

title: Portrait de Monsieur X (Pierre Loti)
title_original: Portrait de Pierre Loti (Portrait de Monsieur X)
description: A striped tabby sits bolt upright on a red stool in the lower left corner, yellow eyes fixed on us, as stiff and formal as the sitter beside it. The moustached man fills the rest of the canvas at half length, square to us, in a red fez and black coat, a cigarette held up in his right hand. Rousseau paints both with the same flat frontality, as if posing for an official photograph. Behind them a landscape opens up, with a leafy tree and smoking factory chimneys: the Kunsthaus calls the picture a 'portrait-paysage', the formula Rousseau favoured in his last years.
context: The sitter's name is the puzzle. Wilhelm Uhde published the picture in 1914 as 'Portrait of Mr. X (Pierre Loti)', after the naval officer and exotic-travel novelist Julien Viaud. In 1952 a Parisian man of letters, Edmond-Achille Frank, said he recognised himself in it, and the Kunsthaus says the sitter and date are still not fully settled. The provenance is the fun part: the satirist Georges Courteline bought it from Rousseau in 1906 and hung it in his 'Musée des Horreurs', a collection of bad and Sunday paintings kept as a joke. It then went through Paul Rosenberg and the Mendelssohn-Bartholdy collection in Berlin before the Kunsthaus bought it in 1940 for 22,000 francs.
image_credit: Henri Rousseau · Artbook

title: The Story of Miss Moppet: Miss Moppet Jumps upon the Mouse
medium: Watercolor, pen, and ink on paper
collection: Published illustration (Frederick Warne, 1906); original drawings bequeathed to the National Trust
description: The moment of the pounce: 'And then all of a sudden, Miss Moppet jumps upon the Mouse!' The tabby kitten has spent the previous pictures with her head tied up in a duster, pretending to be ill so the mouse will come closer, and here the act drops. Potter draws her rump up and tail flicked high, front paws pinning a tiny mouse at lower left, the blue-and-white duster still knotted round her head and a pink cushion behind. The plates were reproduced from Potter's small watercolours, and the joke is the kitten's body turning from invalid to hunter in one page.
context: The Story of Miss Moppet came out from Frederick Warne for Christmas 1906, not as a book but as a panorama: 14 pictures on one long strip folded concertina-fashion into a grey cloth wallet, about 20,000 copies at a shilling. Booksellers hated it because the strips kept unrolling, and Warne reissued it as a normal little book in 1916. Potter drew the kitten from one borrowed from a Windermere mason, which she called 'an exasperating model', and reused the drawings for The Tale of Tom Kitten; Miss Moppet is Tom's sister. Potter left most of her original book illustrations to the National Trust. In 1976 Nicholas Garland redrew the story for the New Statesman with Margaret Thatcher as the kitten and James Callaghan as the mouse.
title_eng: The Story of Miss Moppet: Miss Moppet Jumps upon the Mouse
image_credit: Beatrix Potter · Project Gutenberg ebook of The Story of Miss Moppet , image taken from this HTML version , original text with this illustration is "And then all of a sudden—Miss Moppet jumps upon the Mouse!"

title: At the Play: An Exciting Moment
medium: Color relief process with gouache on paper
collection: Raphael Tuck & Sons postcard, set 9396 'Louis Wain's Cats' (card 3 of 6); Commons scan from a private collection
description: A theatre box crammed with cats in bows and collars, a big grey tabby in the middle staring straight out with yellow eyes, the rest gaping, grinning and clutching at each other. The caption tells you why: 'An Exciting Moment'. A pair of opera glasses has been abandoned on the blue velvet ledge beside a programme, and a cat at left hides behind a pink fan. Wain gets the comedy from treating a row of cat faces as human reactions. This is a horizontal Tuck 'Oilette' postcard; this copy carries a French stamp and a greeting beginning 'Bonne' printed across the top.
context: Raphael Tuck & Sons issued this card as no. 3 of six in set 9396, 'Louis Wain's Cats', with a recorded first use in 1906; the set appears in Tuck's postcard catalogues of 1908/09 and 1911/12. Wain (1860-1939) had made anthropomorphic cats his trade since 'A Kitten's Christmas Party' in the Illustrated London News in 1886, and some 75 publishers turned more than 1,100 of his images into postcards. He sold work cheaply and gave up copyright, so this card earned him nothing after the first fee. Ramsay MacDonald's line from 1925 fits it: 'Louis Wain was on all our walls some 15 to 20 years ago.'
title_eng: At the Play: An Exciting Moment
title_original: At the Play: An Exciting Moment (Raphael Tuck & Sons)
image_credit: Louis Wain · own scan

title: At the Play
medium: Color relief process with gouache on paper
collection: Raphael Tuck & Sons postcard; Commons scan from the Carthalia collection (Andreas Praefcke)
description: Another box at the same imaginary theatre, this time hung with red curtains, and some eighteen cats packed in tiers like a school photograph. A white cat in spectacles peers over the crowd, a ginger one hides behind a green fan, and on the red ledge lie a discarded pair of pince-nez, a programme and a box of chocolates. Look at how the faces are drawn: real cat heads, whiskers and all, on bodies that lean and gesture like Edwardian theatregoers. Like its companion, it is a horizontal Tuck 'Oilette' card, printed in colour to look like a little oil painting.
context: This is card 2 of 6 in Raphael Tuck & Sons set 9396, 'Louis Wain's Cats', with a recorded first use in 1906; the Tuck database notes that the same images were also printed as cards C132 and C133, and the set was still in Tuck's catalogues in 1911/12. The scan on Commons comes from Andreas Praefcke's Carthalia collection of theatre postcards. Wain (1860-1939) left for New York in 1907 on a Hearst contract, so cards like this were among the last things he sold in London before going. H. G. Wells said of him in 1925: 'He has made the cat his own. He invented a cat style, a cat society, a whole cat world.'
title_original: At the Play: In the Theatre Box (Raphael Tuck & Sons)
image_credit: Louis Wain · own scan, https://www.andreas-praefcke.de/carthalia/id/5259

title: Untitled cartoon (cat with love letters)
medium: Pen, black ink, watercolor, and gouache on paper
collection: Published in The Sketch, vol. XXXIII, no. 426, p. 399
description: Two white cats share a bed: the husband dozes against the pillow with a smug, sleepy grin, while his wife sits bolt upright beside him, eyes popping and mouth open in outrage. The printed caption below supplies the row: Mrs. Pussy has caught him talking in his sleep, and Mr. Pussy explains he was only quoting from the 'Love Letters of a Cat'. Wain's line drawings for the weeklies ride on outline, hatching and a black background that throws the white fur forward. The magazine printed it without a title, and his signature sits at lower left.
context: The drawing appeared, untitled, in The Sketch, vol. XXXIII, no. 426, on 27 March 1901, page 399, so the date 'c. 1905' and the British Library attribution in the old record do not hold. The Sketch was a London illustrated weekly, and Wain (1860-1939) was by then the best-known cat artist in Britain, president of the National Cat Club and about to launch the first Louis Wain Annual (1901). He had dated his career as a cat artist from Peter, a black-and-white kitten who joined his household in 1884 and kept his dying wife Emily company.
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Sketch, Vol. XXXIII, No. 426, March 27, 1901, page 399

title: Cat and Plum Blossoms (梅に猫)
collection: Adachi Museum of Art, Yasugi, Shimane
description: A white cat with black patches on its head, back and tail crouches beneath an old plum tree, paws tucked, eyes half shut, losing a fight with sleep: the Adachi Museum's own phrase is that the soft sun tempts the cat but 'sleep seems to be prevailing'. Shunsō splits his methods. The trunk is built by letting ink bleed into damp silk, all soft blotted edges, while the cat's fur is laid in with fine hair strokes. The scroll is tall and narrow, 118 by 49.8 cm, and the cat sits low at bottom left under thin branches dotted with white blossom.
context: Hishida Shunsō (1874-1911) trained under Hashimoto Gahō at the Tokyo School of Fine Arts and in 1898 helped Okakura Tenshin found the Nihon Bijutsuin. His habit of building forms from graded colour instead of line got him mocked as mōrōtai, the 'vague style'. He painted Cat and Plum Blossoms in 1906 (Meiji 39); the Adachi Museum of Art in Yasugi, Shimane, holds it, and the museum sees in it his effort to marry realism and decoration. The diffusion technique for the cat is thought to have reached its peak four years later in Black Cat (1910), now an Important Cultural Property. Shunsō died of nephritis in 1911, just short of 37, fearing blindness to the end.
image_credit: Hishida shunso (1874 - 1911) – Painter (Japanese) Born in Nagano. Died in Tokyo. Details on Google Art Project · BwGvjDB8VLU0zQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Sara Holding a Cat (Sara tenant un chat)
collection: Private Collection / National Gallery of Art, Washington study
description: A ginger cat is hugged against a little girl's chest, and it stares out at us with round dark eyes while she gazes down at it with her lids lowered. She is strawberry-blonde, seen at half length in a white dress with pink sleeves and a pink ribbon bow in her hair, against a loosely brushed green ground. Cassatt puts the cat's orange coat right next to her hair and pink arms, so the warm colours almost run together and the cat has to be found by its shape. It is a portrait of a child, but the cat gets almost as much of the picture. Signed top right.
context: Mary Cassatt (1844-1926), born in Pittsburgh and settled in France, spent her last working decade on mothers and children, many of them local children who sat for her repeatedly; 'Sara' is the name attached to one such model in titles of around 1901-08. This picture is dated 1908. Its present location is not established: the Commons file, uploaded in 2005, gives 'unknown gallery' and 'unknown source', and Wikidata records only the date and artist. That gap is the oddity here: a signed late Cassatt with a cat, reproduced widely online, whose owner and medium are not on any record we could open.
image_credit: Mary Cassatt · Unknown source Unknown source

title: The Tale of Tom Kitten: On the Garden Wall
medium: Watercolor, pen, and ink on paper
collection: Published illustration (Frederick Warne, 1907); V&A holding unverified
description: Tom Kitten pushes up through a bank of ferns in his tight blue suit and straw hat, wide-eyed and tail flailing out behind for balance, with a clump of pink flowers at his feet. This plate belongs to the garden-wall episode and follows the line 'Moppet's white tucker fell down into the road', when the kittens, dressed for their mother's tea party, scramble up the rockery and their clothes start to come apart. Potter keeps Tom small inside a real garden, with ferns and blossoms given as much care as fur. The joke is in the clothes: they are visibly the wrong garments for climbing.
context: Frederick Warne published The Tale of Tom Kitten in September 1907. Potter based the cat family's house and garden on Hill Top, her own farmhouse in the Lake District, and the dedication reads: 'Dedicated to all Pickles, especially to those that get upon my garden wall', which is exactly where this picture puts them. Her word 'pickles' meant naughty kittens, and some of the kitten drawings came from the borrowed, 'exasperating' model she had used for Miss Moppet a year earlier. Moppet's lost tucker is about to be claimed by the Puddle-Ducks, who march up the road in the next pages and walk off wearing the kittens' clothes.
title_eng: The Tale of Tom Kitten: On the Garden Wall
title_original: The Tale of Tom Kitten - Illustration from p. 38
image_credit: Beatrix Potter · Project Gutenburg ebook of The Tale of Tom Kitten

title: The Tale of Tom Kitten: illustration facing 'another, larger, book'
medium: Watercolor, pen, and ink on paper
collection: Published illustration (Frederick Warne, 1907); V&A holding unverified
description: Mrs Tabitha Twitchit leans round the bedroom door, paw raised, while her kittens go to ground: two pairs of ears poke up from behind the four-poster's crimson curtains and footboard, and a grey tabby in a blue bonnet sits with its back to us on the floor. This is one of the closing plates, facing Potter's aside: 'And I think that some day I shall have to make another, larger, book, to tell you more about Tom Kitten!' The kittens have lost their clothes to the Puddle-Ducks and been sent upstairs, and the wreckage is all here: frocks, a cap and a picture frame heaped on the floorboards.
context: Frederick Warne published The Tale of Tom Kitten in September 1907, after The Story of Miss Moppet and before The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck; one of the ducks here walks straight into that next book. Mrs Tabitha Twitchit had already appeared as a shopkeeper in The Tale of the Pie and the Patty-Pan. The 'larger book' promised on this page did arrive in a sense: the whole cat family returns in The Tale of Samuel Whiskers. Wikipedia notes the small moral oddity of the ending: Tabitha lies to her guests about the measles, and the narrator says so plainly ('I am sorry to say').
title_eng: The Tale of Tom Kitten: illustration facing 'another, larger, book'
title_original: The Tale of Tom Kitten - Illustration from p. 77
image_credit: Beatrix Potter · Project Gutenburg ebook of The Tale of Tom Kitten

title: The Tale of Tom Kitten: 'Now keep your frocks clean, children!'
medium: Watercolor, pen, and ink on paper
collection: Published illustration (Frederick Warne, 1907); V&A holding unverified
description: Three kittens step out of a grey wooden porch into a garden of roses, snapdragons and hollyhocks, with Mrs Tabitha Twitchit watching from the doorway in a pink dress. This is the plate for her parting order, 'Now keep your frocks clean, children!', before she goes back to making buttered toast. Moppet and Mittens, in white pinafores, hold paws on the left; Tom stands in front in a tight blue suit with his back to us, arms held stiffly out. Everything is still clean, which is the point: next they fall on the path and Tom bursts his buttons. A small orange butterfly at right is already a distraction.
context: Frederick Warne published The Tale of Tom Kitten in September 1907. The cat family's house and garden are modelled on Hill Top, the Lake District farm Potter had bought in 1905, so the borders and path in these plates are her own. Several of the kitten studies were recycled from The Story of Miss Moppet of 1906, drawn from a borrowed kitten she called 'an exasperating model'. Tabitha's warning lists the dangers in order: the ash-pit, the pig-sty and the Puddle-Ducks. The kittens avoid the first two.
title_eng: The Tale of Tom Kitten: 'Now keep your frocks clean, children!'
title_original: The Tale of Tom Kitten - Illustration from p. 29
image_credit: Beatrix Potter · Project Gutenburg ebook of The Tale of Tom Kitten

title: 'Cats' Choker (Collier de chien aux chats)
medium: Rock crystal, gold, diamonds and enamel
description: Cats prowl through branches in rock crystal, engraved on small squares linked by a gold mesh into a band about 34 cm long and only 5.4 cm high, sized to sit close around the throat. Laid on its side and curving gently, it shows three rows of plaques, and the engraving reads frosted white against the clear stone, so the cats and sprays of foliage seem to float. Tiny diamonds hide the joints between the plaques, and white-enamelled gold runs along top and bottom. The grid of gold edges keeps everything rigid and rectilinear, and the cats repeat like a frieze.
context: René Lalique made the choker around 1906-08, at the height of his career as a jeweller, before he turned almost entirely to glass. Calouste Gulbenkian, the oil magnate and his most devoted patron, bought it directly from Lalique in 1920, and it is now in the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon. The museum's own point is the surprise: in an Art Nouveau world of whiplash curves, this is one of Lalique's most straight-edged pieces, all squares and horizontals, and the museum counts it among the most elegant in the collection.

title: Children Playing with a Cat
collection: Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Los Angeles
description: A grey-and-white cat dozes in the lap of a girl in a huge flower-trimmed blue hat, eyes shut, while a naked baby on its mother's knee reaches over to pat it. The canvas is big for a late Cassatt, 81.3 by 100.3 cm, and wide enough for the group to spread sideways. The colour is the thing to notice: high-keyed lilac walls, a cobalt vase, a yellow dress laced with orange, so bright that one writer has wondered whether Fauvism had got under her skin. The cat is the still centre of all that handling. Signed 'Mary Cassatt' at lower right.
context: Mary Cassatt (1844-1926) painted this in 1907-08, in France, late in a career spent largely on women and children. It sold at Sotheby's in 2020 for $2,198,000 and has since surfaced in the collection of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, which revealed it quietly through a website update rather than an announcement. A blogger tracking the collection calls it the most significant Impressionist work the museum owns. The irony behind the Fauvism theory: Cassatt herself called Matisse's art 'dreadful'.
image_credit: Mary Cassatt · https://www.marycassatt.org/the-complete-works.html?q=&ps=96

title: Three Cats (Drei Katzen)
description: Three cats gather round a white saucer of milk: a long-haired black-and-white cat sits upright at left, one drinks with its head down in the foreground, and a third lies at the back, watching the drinker. The canvas is 50 by 64 cm, signed 'Fr. Marc' at lower left. This is Marc before the blue horses, and the interest is in how three animal bodies fit together as one shape around that bright oval of saucer. Marc returned to cats again and again over the next four years, and this is one of the earliest canvases in that run.
context: Franz Marc (1880-1916) trained at the Munich Academy and went to Paris in 1903 and 1907, where he felt a strong affinity with Van Gogh. Around 1908-09 he was still working out his animal painting; the bright primary colour and near-Cubist forms that made his name came only from the winter of 1910-11, when, in Morgan Meis's phrase, he 'became an artist'. This canvas is catalogued in Hoberg and Jansen's catalogue raisonné (2004) and its present whereabouts are unknown, which is not unusual for Marc's early oils.
submovement: Early Franz Marc animal painting (Munich, pre-Blaue Reiter)
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.pubhist.com/person/2580/franz-marc-1880-1916-german-painter-and-printmaker

title: Manor House in Jankówka (Meeting of the Cats)
title_eng: Manor House in Jankówka (Meeting of the Cats)
collection: Muzeum Narodowe w Kielcach (National Museum in Kielce)
description: Two cats meet on a sandy path in the bottom right corner: a grey tabby walking in from the left and a black cat arching its back and lifting its tail, the classic stand-off. The painting's original title is about them, not the house. Behind them a low white manor with a dark shingled roof sits in full summer, its porch smothered in creeper, fronted by a riot of pink and dark red dahlias, red flowers and tall sunflowers at upper left. The canvas is modest, 41 by 58 cm, and the cats are tiny in it, a family joke slipped into a landscape.
context: Józef Mehoffer bought the Jankówka estate, between Dobczyce and Wieliczka in the Wieliczka Foothills, in autumn 1907, nudged by his friend the Wieliczka bookseller Jan Czarnecki. He restored the eighteenth-century wooden house, designed its interiors and laid out the terraced flower garden that appears in many of his pictures. The Muzeum Narodowe w Kielcach (inv. MNKi/M/1916) dates this oil 'after 1907'. Jadwiga Mehofferowa's notes give its first title, 'Spotkanie kotów' ('Meeting of the Cats'), and name the cats as Maciek and Czarcik, who turn up in family photographs too. Mehoffer sold the estate in 1917; the manor was pulled down in 1946.

title: Summer: Cat on a Balustrade (L'Été: Chat sur une balustrade)
medium: Lithograph (brush, crayon and spatter with scraper) in pink/mauve, violet black and brown on cream wove paper
description: A striped tabby lies the full length of a wooden balustrade, chin on folded paws, eyes narrowed to two slits of yellow, while one hind leg and the long tail drop off the rail into thin air. Steinlen drew it on the stone with brush and crayon, then roughened it with spatter and scraped back to let highlights through. In this impression the whole sheet glows gold and brown, leaves printed behind, so the summer is in the warmth of tone rather than green leaves or blue sky. The image is about 49 by 60 cm, big enough to hang like a painting, which was the point.
context: Steinlen (1859-1923), Swiss-born and long a Montmartre fixture, issued Summer and Winter as a pair of large colour lithographs in 1909, decorative prints meant for the wall rather than for books or posters. The Art Institute of Chicago's impression (1927.6372, Crauzat 292, Cate and Gill 53) came with the Charles Deering Collection; the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston has another, a gift of the Virginia and Ira Jackson Collection. The technical surprise is in the AIC's medium line: this is not a crayon drawing transferred to stone but a mix of brush, crayon and spatter, with lights scraped out of the stone afterwards.
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · YgEQQ3J1MY30yw at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

title: Winter: Cat on a Cushion (L'Hiver: Chat sur un coussin)
medium: Lithograph in 6 colours (red, ochre, yellow, black, gray-brown, brown) from two stones, with scraping on stone, on ivory wove paper
collection: The Art Institute of Chicago / National Gallery of Art, Washington
description: A tabby lies sprawled across a big pink-red cushion, front paws crossed and one paw hooked over the edge, yellow eyes half shut and ears flicked back, with two pale pink paw pads turned toward us. This is the indoor half of Steinlen's pair of seasons. Six colours from two stones (red, ochre, yellow, black, grey-brown and brown) make the winter about the warm room, set against a plain grey wall. Steinlen also scraped into the stone, which is how the fur gets its sharp little lights. His monogram sits beside the cat's head and 'Steinlen' is signed lower right. The image measures about 49 by 59 cm.
context: Steinlen published Winter: Cat on a Cushion in 1909 as the pendant to Summer: Cat on a Balustrade. The Art Institute of Chicago holds an impression (1927.6371, Crauzat 293, Cate and Gill 54) from the Charles Deering Collection, and the National Gallery of Art in Washington has another (1986.4.1), given by Lesley Hughes. The technical surprise is in the AIC's own medium line: six colours were printed from only two stones, so each stone had to carry more than one colour.
image_credit: Théophile Alexandre Steinlen · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Two Friends (Zwei Freunde)
collection: Sold at Dorotheum, Vienna (lot 7201720); present owner unknown
description: A white long-haired cat with pale green eyes crouches on a striped red rug and stares straight at us, while a fawn pug sits upright beside it, looking off to the left with a worried black face. The two friends of the title are a cat and a dog, not two cats. Ronner-Knip painted them in oil on a wood panel, 48 by 62 cm, signed 'Henriette Ronner' at lower right. A panel takes paint smoothly, which suits the fine work that long white fur demands, and the dark carved table leg behind them makes the white glow. The friendship is the joke: two supposed enemies, settled shoulder to shoulder.
context: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821-1909) was born in Amsterdam, took her first lessons from her father, the painter Joseph August Knip, and supported the family once he went blind. After her marriage in 1850 she moved to Brussels and narrowed her subjects to dogs and cats; from the 1870s she was best known for long-haired cats in bourgeois interiors. She painted royal lapdogs and kept animals at home as models, and in later years she made paper sculptures in the poses she wanted and set them among furniture and fabric. The panel was offered at the Dorotheum in Vienna; its date is only fixed as before her death in February 1909.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Dorotheum : Info about artwork

title: A Christmas Ball at Catville
medium: Color relief process on newsprint (Sunday comic section)
collection: Newspaper Sunday supplement (US), via Origins of the Sunday Comics
description: A ballroom crammed with dancing cats: couples pair off across the floor on their hind legs in tailcoats and long gowns, under two holly wreaths tied with red bows. A cat band saws and blows away in the gallery at upper right, beside a sign for ICES, and at lower left one dancer has gone flat on the floor while another sprawls over her. Wain fills the sheet edge to edge, so the eye moves from one grinning face to the next like a guest scanning the room. Made for newspaper printing, the outlines are firm. Nobody in the room seems to notice that they are all cats.
context: Dated 5 December 1909, the page comes from Wain's American years: he went to New York in 1907 on a contract with Hearst Newspapers and returned to England in 1910 after his mother died. The image on Commons comes from the Origins of the Sunday Comics project, which collects early American newspaper comic supplements, so this was almost certainly printed in a Sunday colour section for Christmas. The odd fact: Wain, who had invented the cat Christmas party in the Illustrated London News in 1886, was still selling the same idea, now to American readers, twenty-three years later.
title_original: A Christmas Ball at Catville (Sunday Comics)
image_credit: Louis Wain · Origins of the Sunday Comics

title: Second Exhibition of Animal Artists (2e Exposition des artistes animaliers)
description: A tabby lolls across a pink cushion, one paw hanging over the edge and a pale pad turned up, and the cushion itself becomes the billboard: the lettering for the second exhibition of animal artists at the Cercle International des Arts, 97 boulevard Raspail, is printed straight onto it. Steinlen signs only with his monogram, beside the cat's head, and the dates run in red at upper left. It is a colour lithograph, 50 by 64 cm, small for a poster and printed by the Paris firm Affiches G. Frichot. The wide format lets the cat stretch the whole length of the sheet, its tail trailing off the bottom.
context: Steinlen (1859-1923) was the obvious choice for an animaliers' poster in 1909: by then his cats, from the Chat Noir cabaret poster onward, were the best-known in Paris. The Bibliothèque nationale de France holds this impression in its Estampes et photographie department (FT 5-DC-385). The provenance is a neat loop: the BnF copy came from the collection of Ernest de Crauzat (1866-1944), the man who compiled the standard catalogue of Steinlen's prints, where this poster is number 517.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Lithographe · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b10510621w

title: Cats on a Red Cloth (Katzen auf rotem Tuch)
description: Two cats sleep in one heap: a black-and-white cat curled at lower left with its head tucked out of sight, and an orange-and-white cat draped over the back of it, chin on its paws, one foreleg stretched across its sleeping partner. Oil on canvas, about 50.5 by 60.5 cm. The red cloth is the event, a hot slab of colour wedged under the pair and dragged on in long stripes, while the floor around them churns in yellow straw strokes. The cats read as pattern as much as animals, Marc moving toward the unmixed colour of his next two years. Signed 'Marc' lower right.
context: Franz Marc (1880-1916) painted this in 1909-10, the moment just before the change in winter 1910-11 when, in Morgan Meis's phrase, he 'became an artist' and turned to bright primary colour. He had gone to Paris in 1903 and 1907 and felt a strong affinity with Van Gogh, and in 2007 this canvas was duly shown as plate 31 in the catalogue Van Gogh and Expressionism. PubHist places it in the Deutsche Bank art collection and lists it as Hoberg/Jansen 109. Later, red would become a loaded colour for Marc, standing for violence; here it is still just a cloth.
submovement: Early Franz Marc animal painting (Munich, pre-Blaue Reiter)
image_credit: Franz Marc · Franz Marc

title: Cat Basket
description: Two cats, not one: a calico curled tight inside a woven basket, green eyes just open over its own flank, and a tortoiseshell in the foreground, seen from behind, reaching up toward a green toy dangling on a stick among scattered yellow leaves. Oil on canvas, 58 by 69 cm, from 1909. The basket is a gift to a painter, a ready-made oval that frames one body inside the frame, and its pale weave sets off the patched fur. Read together, the pair is a little before-and-after of cat life, one asleep and one at play, treated at full easel size by a painter taking animals seriously.
context: Franz Marc (1880-1916) studied at the Munich Academy from 1900 and visited Paris in 1903 and 1907; his animal painting was still developing in 1909, and the bright primary colour and almost Cubist forms of his famous work came after the winter of 1910-11. Cat Basket is recorded in Hoberg and Jansen's 2004 catalogue raisonné of his paintings, and PubHist lists its present whereabouts as unknown. Cats run all through his work of 1909-12, from this basket to Cats on a Red Cloth and The White Cat of 1912.
submovement: Early Franz Marc animal painting (Munich, pre-Blaue Reiter)
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.pubhist.com/person/2580/franz-marc-1880-1916-german-painter-and-printmaker

title: Still Life with Cat (Der Geist im Hausgestühl: Stillleben mit Katze)
title_original: Der Geist im Hausgestühl: Stillleben mit Katze
description: A tortoiseshell-and-white cat stretches along the bottom edge of a still life, eyes shut and chin lifted, its curled tail flicking up at the far left like a question mark. Above it the set-up is all Macke: a pale turquoise tabletop with two oranges and a lemon on a white cloth, a potted geranium with one red flower, a blue-striped stoneware jug, a green ginger jar. Pinned on the wall at upper left is a picture of costumed musicians with harp and cello. The cat is the only thing in the room not posed for the sitting, and it looks as though it wandered in to bask.
context: August Macke painted the picture in 1910, at the start of the short career that ended when he was killed in Champagne in September 1914. He gave it to his mother-in-law, Sophie Gerhardt, with a dedication dated 18 February 1910: "Seiner lieben Mutter diesen Geist in unserem Hausgestühl" (to his dear mother, this spirit in our household furniture). The painting now belongs to the Lenbachhaus in Munich, inventory FH 557, and measures 69 × 74 cm. Fun fact: according to a published account of the dedication, Sophie Gerhardt did not much care for pure still lifes, so Macke added the cat to make the gift more to her taste. The title's household "ghost" is, in other words, a concession to family opinion.
title_eng: Still Life with Cat on a Garden Bench
feline_symbolism: The dedication turns the cat into a playful household spirit, a joke on the domestic setting rather than a coded symbol.
image_credit: August Macke · https://sammlungonline.lenbachhaus.de/objekt/der-geist-im-hausgestuehl-stillleben-mit-katze-30036173.html

title: Melvin Vaniman with the airship America's cat mascot Kiddo, aboard the steamship Trent
artist: Bain News Service (George Grantham Bain Collection)
description: Kiddo, a short-haired tabby with a collar and bell, peers out of the bottom right corner of the frame, ears up and eyes level with the lens, held against the chest of Melvin Vaniman, chief engineer of the airship America. Vaniman, in a tweed cap and heavy turtleneck, gives the camera a tired, satisfied half-smile. The cat was a stowaway who had just survived 71 hours aloft over the Atlantic and a lifeboat transfer to a steamer, and he looks about as impressed as cats usually do. The image survives as a 5 × 7 inch glass-plate negative, the standard format of a news agency that needed sharp pictures fast.
context: On 15 October 1910 Walter Wellman's hydrogen airship America left Atlantic City to try for the first air crossing of the Atlantic. Kiddo was discovered in the lifeboat at take-off. After engine trouble, storms and just over 1,300 miles, the crew and cat abandoned ship and were picked up by the Royal Mail steamer Trent, where this photograph was made. The George Grantham Bain news agency's negative is now in the Library of Congress. Fun fact: the America was the first airship fitted with radio, and the Smithsonian notes that the first message sent from an aircraft in flight was about this cat: "Roy, come and get this ---damn cat." Kiddo later spent time in a gilded cage in a New York department store.
title_eng: Melvin Vaniman with the airship America's cat mascot Kiddo, aboard the steamship Trent
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
feline_symbolism: The crew treated Kiddo as a mascot and credited his nine lives with their survival.
image_credit: unknown / * MVcatontrent.jpg : George Grantham Bain derivative work: DreamGuy ( talk ) · MVcatontrent.jpg

title: Marguerite with a Black Cat (Marguerite au chat noir)
collection: Centre Pompidou, Musée national d'art moderne, Paris
description: A black cat sprawls across Marguerite Matisse's lap, a heavy dark lump draped over her right hand, one white-tipped paw showing at the edge. Marguerite, fifteen, faces us head-on in a blue pinafore over a white blouse. The pose is upright and hieratic, almost an icon's, and Matisse cuts the background down to two flat bands, sea green above and pink below, so nothing competes with her almond-eyed stare. The cat is the one soft, shapeless mass in a picture built from flat colour and firm outline. The canvas is 94 × 64 cm, signed and dated lower right, "Henri Matisse 1910".
context: Matisse painted his daughter about thirty times; the Centre Pompidou counts this as one of the most stylised. Marguerite (1894–1982) had a life-saving tracheotomy as a child, and the collar and brooch here hide the scar, as a black ribbon does in other portraits. The canvas stayed in the family: Marguerite married the critic Georges Duthuit, who compared it to Byzantine art and to Coptic frescoes from Bawit, and Barbara Duthuit gave it to the Musée national d'art moderne in 2013 in memory of Claude Duthuit (inv. AM 2013-544). Fun fact: it crossed the Atlantic early, shown at the 1913 Armory Show in New York under the plainer title "Portrait de Marguerite".
image_credit: Henri Matisse · https://images.navigart.fr/1000/4N/64/4N64871.jpg

title: Black Cat (Kuroki neko, 黒き猫)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
description: A black cat crouches on a lichen-spotted oak bough near the bottom of the scroll, claws just showing on the bark, tail hanging off the far side, and stares back at us with pale yellow-green eyes. Hishida builds the body with ink washes alone, no outlines for the fur: the black thickens and thins so the coat looks soft and the body has weight. Above it the oak leaves are something else entirely, flat ochre-gold shapes with patches of green, closer to a lacquer pattern than a botanical study, though a few are nibbled with insect holes. One leaf has already fallen near the bottom edge. Real cat, decorative tree.
context: Hishida Shunsō (1874–1911) painted this in 1910, aged 36, for the fourth Bunten government exhibition, a year before his death. He had been working on a folding screen for the show, gave up on it, and produced Black Cat instead in roughly five or six days.
