The first owner was his friend and patron Akimoto Shatei; in the Taishō period it passed to Hosokawa Moritatsu, founder of the Eisei Bunko in Tokyo, who collected more than twenty Shunsō works. It is an Important Cultural Property, and it recently received its first full restoration, part-funded by crowdfunding. Fun fact: Shunsō reportedly disliked cats, yet left more than twenty cat paintings.
image_credit: Hishida Shunsō · Eisei Bunko (now at Kumamoto Prefectural Art Museum, Japan)

title: Catland: Dragging the Yule Log
medium: Gouache, watercolor, and pen and ink on board
collection: Raphael Tuck & Sons Archive / Private Collection
description: A gang of Wain's cats hauls a Yule log home through the snow on a rope at lower left, while the rest of Catland has given up work for tobogganing: cats pile onto sledges, tumble off them, wave their paws and go head over heels down the slope. One black cat has landed upside down in a drift. This is the parallel world that Wain's public called Catland, and the joke depends on the haulers doing their human job with complete seriousness while everyone else plays. The image here is a sepia print captioned 'Bringing Home the Yule Log at Christmas Time in Catland.'
context: Louis Wain (1860–1939) was the cat artist of Edwardian Britain. Between 1900 and 1940 some 75 publishers, Raphael Tuck & Sons and Valentine & Sons among them, issued over 1,100 of his designs as postcards, and his Louis Wain's Annual ran from 1901. This Yule log card is dated about 1910, the year Wain came home from three years in New York, where Hearst newspapers had hired him, after his mother's death. He sold work cheaply and gave up his copyrights, which is one reason the cards are so common and he was so often broke. Fun fact: H. G. Wells said in 1925 that Wain "invented a cat style, a cat society, a whole cat world."
image_credit: Louis Wain · http://1893victorianfarmhouse.blogspot.com/2010/06/louis-wain-artist-cats-playing-in.html

title: Girl with Cat I (Mädchen mit Katze I)
description: A dark cat arches in the girl's arms, back curved into a crescent and head turned up toward her, while she looks down at it with half-closed eyes and a small smile, one hand cupped over its body. The two lock together into one block on a nearly square canvas, 71 × 67.5 cm, the format Marc liked for exactly this. A pale shawl wraps the group like a frame. This is the first of two versions; Marc came back to the subject in 1912 with Girl with Cat II, almost the same size. Already the cat is a simple dark silhouette rather than fur and whiskers.
context: Franz Marc (1880–1916) painted the first version in 1910/11, after moving to the village of Sindelsdorf in Upper Bavaria with Maria Franck in 1910, and in the months when he was working out a theory of colour. In a letter to August Macke of 12 December 1910 he called blue the male principle, yellow the female principle and red matter, to be overcome by the other two. Within a year he and Kandinsky had founded Der Blaue Reiter. The canvas is in a private collection. Fun fact: catalogue citations of this picture as "Hoberg/Jansen 134" refer to a page in the 2004 catalogue raisonné, not to a work number.
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.pubhist.com/person/2580/franz-marc-1880-1916-german-painter-and-printmaker

title: Cat and Dog (Kot i piesek)
description: A grey-and-white cat curls up with its pointed ears tucked against a much bigger dark sleeper, the two bodies fitted together into a single low oval on a muddy ochre ground. The pairing is announced plainly in the Polish title, Kot i piesek, cat and little dog, but the picture is all truce and no standoff: nobody is awake. Oil on card was the cheap, quick support of the period, good for studies and small saleable pictures, and the brushwork stays visible here, thick and creamy in the white fur, scrubbed thin in the background. The signature, 'Leona Bierkowska', runs along the top left edge.
context: Leona Bierkowska is an obscure Polish painter, and this picture is known from the art market rather than from a museum: the image on Wikimedia Commons comes from an Artnet auction record, which gives it as oil on cardboard, dated before 1910. Pictures like this, small domestic animal scenes, were a steady line for painters who needed to sell. I could not find a reliable biography of the artist, so her training and career are not stated here. Fun fact: the cat-and-dog pairing was such a stock subject in the period that auction databases list dozens of pictures under nearly identical titles.
submovement: Polish animal genre painting (Young Poland period)
image_credit: Leona Bierkowska · https://www.artnet.com/artists/leona-bierkowska/kot-i-piesek-AW-R62oji_svlu2k0Jd7pQ2

title: Kinderbild (Cat behind a Tree)
collection: Private collection (restituted to the heirs of Alfred and Thekla Hess 2009; sold Christie's London, 24 June 2014)
description: An orange cat sleeps curled around the back of a blue tree trunk, its white-muzzled face peeking out on the left, eyes shut, and its round haunch and tail bulging out on the right, as if the tree were a screen it chose on purpose. Around it the landscape breaks into flat zones of green, yellow and blue. Nothing is shaded in the academic way; colour does the modelling and the cat is mostly a warm shape held by a cool one. It is 70.2 × 50 cm, oil on canvas, and its German title, Kinderbild, marks it as a picture with children in mind.
context: Marc painted this in 1910–11 in Sindelsdorf. It was shown at the Neue Künstlervereinigung München in March 1911 and bought by the painter Adolf Ahlers. It later belonged to Alfred and Thekla Hess of Erfurt, Jewish collectors forced to sell under Nazi persecution; it passed through the Berlin dealers Nierendorf and Thannhauser around 1935 and was acquired in 1936 by Günther Wagner of the Pelikan company. From 1950 it hung on loan in Hanover, later at the Sprengel Museum. Fun fact: in 2009 it was restituted to the Hess heirs, and in June 2014 it sold at Christie's London for £6,242,500.
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.christies.com/search?entry=marc%2C%20franz%20%281880-1916%29&page=1&tab=sold_lots

title: Two Cats (Zwei Katzen)
description: Two black-and-white cats lie curled one above the other, heads down and backs rounded, their patched coats echoed by the swelling dark and light shapes of the ground around them. They fill a tall 98 × 74 cm surface, a substantial size for an animal picture with no people and no story. Marc signed it at upper left, "Marc", as he did on the larger canvases he meant to show. With no setting to speak of, the picture is about how two bodies fit against each other: the lower cat's spine runs parallel to the upper one's, and a white tail sweeps out along the bottom like a reflection.
context: Marc painted this in 1911, the year he co-founded Der Blaue Reiter with Wassily Kandinsky and began giving animals the central place that human figures held for most of his colleagues. He thought animals offered a purer way into nature than people did. The painting's present whereabouts are unknown, and the main record of it is the reproduction in the 2004 catalogue raisonné by Annegret Hoberg and Isabelle Jansen. Fun fact: in 1936–37 the Nazi regime ordered around 130 of Marc's works removed from German museums; whether this picture was among them is not stated in the sources I could open.
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.pubhist.com/person/2580/franz-marc-1880-1916-german-painter-and-printmaker

title: Cats, Red and White (Katzen, rot und weiß)
description: Two cats sit pressed together, the white one facing us with narrow amber eyes and a few quick black whiskers, the red one turned away so we see only its back, its ear and a long tail sweeping down over a dark blue shape at the bottom. Their heads overlap so closely they almost share a silhouette. The canvas is upright, 52 × 35 cm, small and tall, like a door left ajar. The red is not a ginger coat; it is Marc's red, the colour he tied to matter and weight. The contrast between the two animals, one open and one turned away, is the whole subject.
context: Marc painted the picture in 1912 in Sindelsdorf, during the busiest year of Der Blaue Reiter, whose almanac appeared that spring. His letter to August Macke of December 1910 set out the colour code he was using: blue the male principle, yellow the female, red the matter the other two must overcome. The painting is in a private collection. Fun fact: this entry's id and the record's earlier title called it "The White Cat", which is in fact a different 1912 Marc in Halle, the white tomcat on a yellow cushion.
feline_symbolism: Marc gave colours fixed meanings: red stood for matter, heavy and earthbound, which makes the red cat a deliberate counterweight to the white one.
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.pubhist.com/person/2580/franz-marc-1880-1916-german-painter-and-printmaker

title: Two Cats, Blue and Yellow (Zwei Katzen, blau und gelb)
description: A blue cat twists into a knot in the foreground, one hind leg flung up in the air as it grooms, while a yellow cat lies stretched along the top of the canvas with its chin down, watching. The 74 × 98 cm landscape format gives them room. The colours are not a joke about fur. Blue and yellow were Marc's male and female principles, so the pair reads as a little diagram of his colour theory dressed up as a pet picture. Around them float a green ball, red fruit-like shapes and, tucked into the top left corner, a small white house. Signed lower left "Marc".
context: Marc painted it in 1912 in Sindelsdorf. By 1927 it hung in the Ruhmeshalle in Barmen (now Wuppertal). On 5 July 1937 it was confiscated in the Nazi campaign against "degenerate art", under the confiscation number EK 16133, one of around 130 Marc works stripped from German museums. Fun fact: it came to the Kunstmuseum Basel in 1939, the year the Basel museum bought heavily from the regime's sales of confiscated modern art. It is inventory 1746 there.
feline_symbolism: In Marc's 1910 colour scheme blue was the male principle and yellow the female, so the two cats can be read as a paired, gendered couple.
image_credit: Franz Marc · cgfa.sunsite.dk/marc/marc2.htm

title: Three Animals: Dog, Fox, and Cat (Drei Tiere: Hund, Fuchs und Katze)
description: A dark grey cat sits upright at the right edge and looks straight out at us, the only one of the three animals paying attention. In front of it a big white dog pads across the canvas, nose down and eyes nearly shut, and behind them a red fox lies curled asleep with its white-tipped muzzle on its paws. The canvas is 80 × 105 cm. Marc reduces them to interlocking curves and shares colour among them, so the fox's red bleeds into the ground and the cat half dissolves into green and yellow. Signed lower left "Marc". Painted in oil, with tempera according to one catalogue listing.
context: Marc painted Three Animals in 1912, the year of the Blaue Reiter almanac, when he was trying to show animals as they might experience the world rather than as humans see them. The canvas belongs to the Kunsthalle Mannheim. A dog, a fox and a cat lying peacefully together is a small utopia, the sort of harmony Marc thought had been lost by humans. Fun fact: the fox is one of Marc's favourite animals, and he painted a Blue-Black Fox in 1911; here it shares space with two domestic animals that would chase it.
title_eng: Three Animals: Dog, Fox, and Cat
image_credit: Franz Marc · www.zeno.org

title: The White Cat (Cat on a Yellow Cushion)
description: A white tomcat sleeps curled into a near-perfect circle, nose buried against one forepaw and head pillowed on a lumpy yellow cushion. The German title, Kater auf gelbem Kissen, is exact: Kater means a tom, and the cushion is as much the subject as the cat. White fur on yellow is a hard pairing because there is so little contrast, so Marc pushes the body into a tight, rounded shape and lets grey shadow and outline do the separating. Behind both he lays a hot red ground scattered with yellow star shapes. Oil on cardboard, about 49 × 60 cm, signed lower right "Marc".
context: Marc painted it in 1912 at Sindelsdorf. It belongs to the Kunstmuseum Moritzburg in Halle (Saale), a museum that had collected Marc before 1933 and lost much of its modern collection to the Nazi confiscations of August 1937. Fun fact: the cushion is doing theory. In Marc's colour letter to Macke of December 1910, yellow was the female principle, gentle and cheerful, so a sleeping cat on a yellow cushion is about as calm a statement of his system as he made.
title_eng: The White Cat (Cat on a Yellow Cushion)
feline_symbolism: Yellow was Marc's colour of the gentle female principle, which suits a cat sunk in rest.
image_credit: Franz Marc · The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title: Cat with Kittens (Katze mit Kätzchen)
description: A ginger mother cat, striped in quick red strokes, curls in a loose ring around her two kittens: a solid black one clambering up her chest with its paws out, and a white one stretched along her belly at the bottom. Marc works on a small sheet of cardboard, 35 × 30 cm, in mixed media rather than straight oil, and leaves the brown card showing all round. The size and the support suggest something quicker and more private than his exhibition canvases. Instead of a row of sweet faces, the litter is one compact whorl of colour: red, black and white.
context: Marc made this in 1912, at the height of his Blaue Reiter years in Sindelsdorf, when cats, foxes, deer and horses had replaced people as his main subjects. The work belongs to the Kunstmuseum Moritzburg in Halle (Saale), which also owns his White Cat on a yellow cushion of the same year, so the Halle museum holds two of his cat pictures from 1912. Fun fact: the number "186" that travels with this picture in online records is a page reference in the 2004 Hoberg/Jansen catalogue raisonné, not a catalogue number.
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.pubhist.com/person/2580/franz-marc-1880-1916-german-painter-and-printmaker

title: Portrait of the Artist's Wife with a Cat (Portret żony z kotem)
description: A lean black cat sits bolt upright at the far end of a green sofa, ears tall and yellow eyes catching the light, claiming a whole third of the picture for itself. Michalina Krzyżanowska leans back in the opposite corner, arms folded in a shimmering pale gown, her hair piled high, looking past us with mild patience. The canvas is nearly square and big, 114 × 124 cm, a public exhibition size for a private subject. Krzyżanowski was known for dramatic light and greys and blacks in his portraits, but here the wall behind is a flat electric blue, and the cat and the dark floor carry the black.
context: Konrad Krzyżanowski (1872–1922) trained in Kyiv, at the St Petersburg Academy under the eye of Repin and Kuindzhi, and in Munich at Simon Hollósy's school, which he followed to Nagybánya. Back in Warsaw he ran a private painting school and taught at the Warsaw School of Fine Arts from 1904 to 1909. In 1906 he married Michalina Piotruszewska, a former student, whom he painted many times. This 1912 portrait is in the Muzeum Śląska Opolskiego in Opole, inventory MSO/S/228. Fun fact: Krzyżanowski was expelled from the St Petersburg Academy after clashing with the rector over its teaching system.
title_eng: Portrait of the Artist's Wife with a Cat
image_credit: Konrad Krzyżanowski · culture.pl

title: Nude Woman with a Cat (Akt kobiety z kotem)
location: Private collection (catalogued in Katalog dzieł malarskich)
description: A small white cat with dark patches rolls on its back in the lower left corner, legs in the air, while a female nude lies stretched diagonally across a dark ground with her back to us and her head turned away at upper right. Oil on canvas, from around 1912. This is early Witkacy, before the Formism and the commercial pastel portraits that made him famous, and before he settled on annotating works with codes. Nude-with-cat was a standard studio pairing, but here the cat is tiny and playful, kicking at nothing, a little white flash against the body's long pale curve.
context: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz (1885–1939), called Witkacy, grew up in Zakopane, son of the painter and critic Stanisław Witkiewicz, and studied at the Kraków Academy under Józef Mehoffer and Jan Stanisławski against his father's wishes. Around 1911–12 he was in a turbulent affair with the actress Irena Solska and writing his first novel, The 622 Downfalls of Bungo. In 1914, after the suicide of his fiancée Jadwiga Janczewska, he joined Bronisław Malinowski's expedition towards New Guinea. The painting is catalogued as I 0175 in the catalogue of his paintings. Fun fact: the catalogue number travels with the image online, but the current owner does not.
image_credit: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz · http://ineselo69.blogspot.com/2012/10/stanisaw-ignacy-witkiewicz.html

title: Woman with a Cat (La Femme au chat)
description: A white cat stands bolt upright on the dining table, front paws planted on the cloth, staring straight back at us, while the woman beside it in a dark green blouse smiles and does nothing whatsoever about it. The table is a big pale oval that tips up towards the viewer, with a plate of food left within easy reach of the cat, a bowl of green grapes and an orange in the foreground, and a hot red wall behind. Bonnard signs at upper right. Everything is soft and warm except the cat, whose narrow face and alert ears make it the sharpest thing in the room.
context: Pierre Bonnard (1867–1947) painted this domestic scene in 1912, when tables, women and pets were the core of his Intimist repertoire; the sitter is usually taken to be Marthe, his companion and later wife. The Musée d'Orsay, which holds it as RF 1977 84, also knows it as 'Le Chat exigeant', the demanding cat. Fun fact: this entry once described a pencil drawing of a cat at the Musée Bonnard, but the photograph behind it was always this Orsay oil, so the record now follows the picture.
image_credit: Pierre Bonnard · Musée d'Orsay (via Wikimedia Commons)

title: Paris Through the Window (Paris par la fenêtre)
license: © Estate of Marc Chagall / ADAGP, all rights reserved
description: A cat with a human face sits on the window ledge, haunches down, looking out at Paris while the Eiffel Tower rises pink and grey over the roofs. The cat is the hinge between the room and the city. The canvas is big and almost square, 136 × 141.9 cm, and the window frame, striped in red, yellow and blue, takes over the left half. Flowers sit in a pot by the sill, the only other domestic thing here. Bottom right, a man with a two-coloured double face looks both ways at once, and above the tower a parachutist drifts down.
context: Marc Chagall (1887–1985) painted this in 1913, during his first stay in Paris, a few years after arriving from Russia. It belongs to the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York (accession 37.438), and a collector named Franz Kluxen is recorded among its owners. It was shown in Paris again in 2016 in the Musée de l'Orangerie exhibition "Apollinaire, le regard du poète", a fitting venue because Apollinaire was one of Chagall's early champions; Chagall's Homage to Apollinaire dates from the same year. Fun fact: the French Wikipedia entry for the picture is tagged with exactly four things, a cat, a window, the Eiffel Tower and a flower, which is a fair summary of how Chagall builds a city out of a few household objects.
collection: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
image_credit: © Estate of Marc Chagall / ADAGP. Photo: Aerra Carnicom. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from upload.wikimedia.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Mother Cat with Two Kittens
description: A white mother cat sleeps flat out on a rumpled blue cloth, head down and eyes shut, while her two kittens sit up behind her wide awake: a black-and-white one with a pink tongue just showing, and a grey tabby craning towards its sibling. The canvas is modest, 34 × 50 cm, signed lower right. This is the core product of Julius Adam's studio: soft fur in thin glazes and round eyes catching light. The mother's job here is simply to be the warm pillow, and she takes it seriously.
context: Julius Adam the Younger (1852–1913) came from a Munich dynasty of painters that ran to four generations; his grandfather was the battle painter Albrecht Adam and his father a lithographer and photographer. He worked as a photographic retoucher in Rio de Janeiro as a teenager, then studied at the Munich Academy under Wilhelm von Diez. Success with a painting of two cats turned him into "Katzen-Adam", and he painted little else afterwards; in 1887 he signed a five-year contract to paint only for one dealer's clients. This canvas surfaced at the Nagel auction house in Stuttgart. Fun fact: in 1894 he published Vom Kätzchen, a small book that set reproductions of his paintings beside original photographs.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · Nagel Auktionen http://www.auction.de

title: Four Kittens
description: Four kittens divide up a garden: a ginger one dozes in the hay of a broken wicker basket, a grey-and-white one peers over its back, a black-and-white one climbs the basket wall, and another laps from a green glazed bowl in the foreground. The cardboard is small, only 20.5 × 28 cm, signed lower right, so Adam tells them apart by coat and pose rather than detail. Oil on card was quick and cheap, and pictures this size were the affordable end of his market, kittens you could hang over a writing desk.
context: Julius Adam the Younger (1852–1913), Munich's "Katzen-Adam", came from a family of painters and photographers and trained at the Munich Academy. After a picture of two cats made his name he devoted himself almost entirely to them, and his cat paintings sold widely, especially in the United States. He was made a professor in 1892, and in 1900 the Neue Pinakothek bought his Self-Portrait with Cats. This panel passed through the Munich auction house Neumeister. Fun fact: he also used photography, which he had learned in his father's studio, and his 1894 book Vom Kätzchen paired paintings with original photographs.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · neumeister.com

title: Four Kittens and a Hedgehog
collection: Private collection (sold Lempertz, Cologne, 20 May 2023, lot 2289)
description: Four kittens meet a hedgehog, and the hedgehog is the joke. Two of them stand nose to nose on a mossy path, a ginger-and-white one creeps along a fallen branch, and a fourth clings to a tree trunk at a safe height. The hedgehog trundles in from the lower left, the one thing in the garden that punishes patting. Look up at the barn roof: a fifth small cat watches from the tiles. The canvas is 25.5 × 35.4 cm, signed lower right "Jul. Adam.", and fur against spines is a neat exercise in two textures.
context: Julius Adam the Younger (1852–1913) built his career in Munich on scenes like this: kittens meeting a beetle, a crayfish, a ball of wool or, here, a hedgehog. He won a gold medal at the 1905 International Art Exhibition in Munich for five cat pictures. This canvas carries the stamp of the Munich dealer Kunsthandlung Wimmer on the back, came from a south German private collection, and sold at Lempertz in Cologne on 20 May 2023 for €11,340 against an estimate of €6,000–8,000. Fun fact: in 1885, before he became Katzen-Adam, he worked on interior decoration at Ludwig II's Herrenchiemsee Palace.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · lempertz.com

title: Two Cats Playing
collection: Private collection (sold Lempertz, Cologne, 16 November 2024, lot 2417)
description: Two kittens square off on a draped pale green cloth: a white one with dark patches and a blue silk bow stands above, tail up, peering down, while a tabby-and-white below sits back and lifts a paw to meet it. The upright wooden panel is tiny, 20.3 × 15 cm, signed upper right "Jul. Adam." Wood gives a smoother surface than canvas for the thin, soft fur Adam liked. A carved footstool and a scrap of red carpet in the corner say this is a parlour, and the kittens have claimed it.
context: Julius Adam the Younger (1852–1913) was Munich's specialist in cats, known locally as "Katzen-Adam" and "Katzenraffael". He had trained at the Munich Academy and became a professor there in 1892, and represented Munich at the 1904 St Louis World's Fair. This panel was sold at Lempertz in Cologne in May 1984, spent forty years in a Westphalian private collection, and returned to Lempertz on 16 November 2024, selling for €3,276. Fun fact: one of the artist's nicknames, Katzenraffael, cast him as the Raphael of cats.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · lempertz.com

title: Kittens and Crayfish
description: Four kittens have found a basket of crayfish tipped over on a brick floor. A ginger one crouches on the basket rim, a calico watches from the left, and a black-and-white one bends to sniff the tangle of red-brown claws while a fourth looks on. The canvas is small, 22.5 × 33.5 cm, signed "Jul. Adam." lower right. Crayfish are a good foil for kittens: hard-shelled, armed and capable of pinching a curious nose. Cabbages piled at left suggest a kitchen larder, and the kittens are clearly not supposed to be in it.
context: Julius Adam the Younger (1852–1913) painted cats in Munich for some three decades after a picture of two cats made his name, and his work sold widely, notably in the United States. Museums hold a few examples, including his Self-Portrait with Cats in the Neue Pinakothek and The Cat Family (1882) in the Münchner Stadtmuseum, but most of his small pictures, like this one, live on the art market; this canvas was photographed by the Dorotheum auction house in Vienna. Fun fact: before turning to painting he spent almost six years in Rio de Janeiro working as a photographic retoucher.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · http://www.dorotheum.com/

title: Playing Cats
medium: Watercolour and mixed media on paper
description: Four kittens pose in and around a tipped-over basket draped with a grey cloth: a white one peeks over the top, a ginger-and-white one sits upright, and a brown tabby and a grey one lie tucked together in front. Despite the title, nobody is playing yet; they all look straight out at us. The watercolour and mixed media sheet is only about 13 × 18 cm, signed lower right "J. Adam". This is the quick, light side of Adam's output, and a few strokes of body colour pick out green eyes and whiskers.
context: Julius Adam the Younger (1852–1913), Munich's "Katzen-Adam", was a painter, lithographer and photographer, which helps explain the variety of his surviving work. After training at the Munich Academy he settled in Munich as an independent painter in 1882 and soon specialised in cats. In 1886 he married his cousin Amalie, daughter of the painter Benno Adam, and the couple lived in a villa in the Gern artists' colony in Munich. This sheet was photographed by the Dorotheum's Linz branch in 2018. Fun fact: the Bavarian state gave him the Order of St Michael in 1910 for his services to Bavaria, honours for a cat painter.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · http://www.dorotheum.com/

title: Two Kittens in a Basket with a Blue Cloth
description: Two kittens rest their front paws on the edge of a basket covered with a blue cloth: a tortoiseshell-and-white one gazes up and away, and a ginger-and-white one stares straight at us with wide blue eyes. The canvas is 19 × 27 cm, signed upper right. The basket is the classic Adam stage: it frames the kittens and keeps them more or less in one place. A weathered wooden fence and wisps of hay fill the background, and the blue cloth is the colour accent, cool against warm browns and white fur.
context: Julius Adam the Younger (1852–1913) made baskets of kittens one of his signature formats, and the formula sold steadily, especially in America. He was a member of the Adam family of Munich painters, studied at the Munich Academy under Wilhelm von Diez, Sándor Wagner and Johann Leonhard Raab, and became a professor there in 1892. This small canvas passed through Hampel Fine Art Auctions in Munich. Fun fact: a photograph survives of Adam at work in his studio painting a cat, the closest thing to a behind-the-scenes shot of how these pictures were made.
title_eng: Two Kittens in a Basket with a Blue Cloth
title_original: Zwei Kätzchen im Korb mit blauem Tuch
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · Hampel Kunstauktionen

title: Reclining Kitten (Liegendes Kätzchen)
description: A kitten lies stretched along a slanting ridge, head drooped over one front paw and eyes nearly shut, with a dark stump jutting up beneath it. The sheet is just 12.5 × 20 cm, painted in watercolour, postcard size: in 1913 Marc was making small painted cards and sheets alongside his big canvases, and they let him work fast. The kitten is built from a few thin washes and pencil-like contour, and the bare paper does much of the drawing. Up top, a crescent moon and a scatter of stars turn the nap into a night scene.
context: Marc painted this in 1913, the year he married Maria Franck in Munich on 3 June and the year of his large Fate of the Animals. After meeting the poet Else Lasker-Schüler in December 1912 he began sending her hand-painted postcards, 28 in all. This watercolour is known from the art market, recorded by Artnet; there is no museum record. Fun fact: the record previously called it an oil on cardboard with a catalogue-raisonné number, but the only sourced data describe a small watercolour.
image_credit: Franz Marc · http://www.artnet.de/k%C3%BCnstler/franz-marc/liegendes-k%C3%A4tzchen-I9Yli_I0Jcd9Z5TR474wgA2

title: Four Playing Cats (Vier spielende Katzen)
description: Cats tumble across a wide, low canvas of 44.5 × 66.5 cm: a dark brown one arches over the middle, a green one coils at lower left with its tail hooked into a spiral, and pale grey-white bodies crowd in from the right, one with its eyes squeezed shut. The horizontal format suits a pile-up, and Marc strings the bodies out so the eye slides along the curves from one cat into the next. By 1913 his forms were more faceted than in his earlier cat pictures, and here the backgrounds break into blue and green wedges behind the play.
context: Marc painted the picture in 1913, his most productive and most fractured year before the war, when prismatic, Cubist- and Futurist-influenced forms entered his animal paintings. It belongs to the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. Within three years Marc was dead, killed at Verdun on 4 March 1916, aged 36. Fun fact: the number 2384 attached to the image online appears to be the Staatsgalerie's inventory number, while the catalogue raisonné page for the picture is 210.
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.staatsgalerie.de/sammlung/sammlung-digital/nc/suche/Franz%20Marc/_/_/person/werk/auflistung/record.html

title: Two Cats (Zwei Katzen)
description: Two cats circle each other so closely that they fill the sheet edge to edge: a tortoiseshell in the foreground, all dark crosshatching patched with ochre, twists to look back over its own shoulder, while a ginger-and-white cat behind lowers its head to sniff at it. Marc draws fur with fast, scribbled lithographic line and lets a few flat tones of brown and orange do the colouring. The scratchy swirls in the background are the same marks as the fur, so the cats almost dissolve into the floor. Signed in the stone 'Lit. F. Marc' at lower left.
context: Marc made this lithograph in 1909, in the years he spent drawing animals from life in and around Munich, before colour turned symbolic in his work and before the Blaue Reiter almanac of 1912. Prints like this were where he worked out how to make an animal's body and its surroundings move together. The sheet belongs to the Lenbachhaus in Munich, which holds the largest public collection of Blaue Reiter art. Fun fact: this entry used to describe a 1913 painted postcard, but its image was always this print, so the record now follows the picture.
image_credit: Franz Marc · Copied from an art book

title: Girl with a Cat (Dziewczynka z kotem)
description: A ginger-and-white cat sits in a girl's arms at the bottom of the sheet, ears up and eyes narrowed to amber slits, looking far less impressed than she does. She wears a white headscarf and looks straight out at us, with red geraniums in a pot by the window behind her. The pastel is 50 × 40 cm, a standard upright portrait sheet, signed lower right "LŁempicka". Pastel suits children and cats alike, since neither holds a pose for long, and here the chalk rubs white fur and white blouse into one soft bundle.
context: The artist is recorded as Leokadia Łempicka, a Polish painter with Kyiv and Paris connections, and the pastel is known from a sale at the Rempex auction house in Warsaw. Commons gives her dates as 1865–1913 and the work as before 1913; I could not confirm her biography from a second source. She should not be confused with Tamara de Lempicka, whose surname came from marriage. Fun fact: online records sometimes merge the two artists, which is one reason to treat this attribution with care.
image_credit: Leokadia Łempicka · Dom Aukcyjny Rempex

title: Two Cats at Rest (Deux chats au repos)
inv_number: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510756r (Crauzat: non décrit)
description: Two cats rest side by side: a black one lies curled with its eyes shut, while a lean, pale, Siamese-looking companion sits bolt upright in profile, eyes half closed, keeping the watch. No furniture, no story, just two bodies of fur in etched line casting a shared shadow to the right. The plate is almost square, about 29.3 × 29.5 cm at the platemark, leaving plenty of empty paper above them. This impression is the final state, signed in pencil at lower right with the note "pour E. de Crauzat", so the sheet doubles as a small gift.
context: Steinlen etched this around 1914, when he was in his mid-fifties and Paris's best-known draughtsman of cats. The impression he dedicated to Ernest de Crauzat, the collector who was cataloguing his prints, now sits in a mounted album of Steinlen's work in the Département des Estampes et de la photographie of the Bibliothèque nationale de France (shelfmark DC-385 (3)-FOL), which also holds a first state. Fun fact: despite the dedication, the BnF records the print as "non décrit" in Crauzat's own catalogue raisonné. Crauzat's book appeared in 1913, so the cats arrived a year too late for their own entry.
inventory_id: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510756r (Crauzat: non décrit)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Crauzat, Ernest de (1866-1944). Dédicataire · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Two Sleeping Cats (Deux chats endormis)
inv_number: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510770w (Crauzat: non décrit)
description: Two cats sleep curled into one heap on a fluffy white cushion: a black cat behind, ears up and face buried, and a pale, short-coated cat in front with its chin tucked over a paw. The horizontal plate, 15.3 × 25.3 cm, suits animals stretched out rather than sitting up. The margins carry three kinds of handwriting: Steinlen's signature and 1914 bitten into the plate at lower left, his pencil signature with "pour E. de Crauzat" at lower right, and "4e état" scribbled in the bottom left margin, the artist keeping score of his own revisions.
context: Steinlen made the plate in 1914 and kept working it; the BnF holds both a second state and this fourth state, each catalogued separately. This impression is one of several he dedicated to Ernest de Crauzat, whose catalogue of Steinlen's prints came out in 1913, and it is mounted in the Bibliothèque nationale de France's album of Steinlen's work (Estampes et photographie, DC-385 (3)-FOL). Fun fact: for all that devotion, the BnF lists the print as "non décrit" in Crauzat. A dated plate from 1914 simply came after the book.
inventory_id: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510770w (Crauzat: non décrit)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Crauzat, Ernest de (1866-1944). Dédicataire · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Two Cats on a Ledge (Deux chats sur un rebord)
inv_number: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510771b (Crauzat: non décrit)
description: Two cats share a ledge: a slim, pale cat sits upright with its tail curled along the edge, gazing down, while a black cat crouches beside it, chin forward, peering over the drop. Its shadow lands on the wall like a third cat. The etching is small and nearly square, 19 × 17.5 cm, with bitten line and white paper. The margins are busier than the image: signature and 1914 etched top right in the plate, a pencil signature and "pour E. de Crauzat" bottom right, and "4e état" bottom left in Steinlen's own hand.
context: Steinlen etched the plate in 1914, by which time his cats had long been a Montmartre trademark, from cabaret posters to the wordless picture book Des chats. This impression went to Ernest de Crauzat, the cataloguer of Steinlen's prints, and is now mounted in the Bibliothèque nationale de France's Steinlen album (Estampes et photographie, DC-385 (3)-FOL). Fun fact: the BnF notes it as "non décrit" in Crauzat's catalogue. The dedicatee owned a print that his own reference book does not mention, because the book was out a year before the plate existed.
inventory_id: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510771b (Crauzat: non décrit)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Crauzat, Ernest de (1866-1944). Dédicataire · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Lady with Panther (Dame à la panthère)
description: A black panther lies along the base of the picture at the feet of a standing woman, head raised, tail curling up at the left, and the joke is that the cat is nearly as well accessorised as she is: it wears a blue jewelled collar. She stretches long ropes of pearls between her hands, in a pale Poiret-style gown spotted in brown with a checked hem. Barbier works in watercolour with crisp outlines and flat colour, the fashion-plate manner of the Gazette du Bon Ton, and frames the pair between two red columns. "1914 George Barbier" sits lower right.
context: Louis Cartier commissioned the watercolour from George Barbier in 1914 as an invitation card for an exhibition at the firm's rue de la Paix boutique, and Cartier later reused it in advertising. It is usually counted as the first panther in the house's imagery. The same year Charles Jacqueau set black onyx spots in diamond pavé on a wristwatch, the first panther-skin jewel. Fun fact: Louis Cartier's nickname for Jeanne Toussaint, later the firm's jewellery director, was "La Panthère", reportedly for her independence and her taste for panther skins; some accounts date the commission to 1913.
submovement: Parisian fashion illustration (Gazette du Bon Ton circle)
feline_symbolism: Cartier's own story ties the panther to Jeanne Toussaint's independence, and the motif became a house emblem of untamed luxury.
image_credit: George Barbier · link

title: Portrait of Michalina Krzyżanowska with Cat
collection: National Museum in Warsaw (Muzeum Narodowe w Warszawie)
description: A brown tabby sits upright on Michalina Krzyżanowska's lap, head tipped back to look up at her, while her hand rests lightly on its flank. She sits at half length in a huge yellow fur stole and stares out at us, unbothered. Her husband paints her in oil on a canvas 87 × 78.5 cm, large enough to make the sitting feel like an occasion. Critics place him among Poland's early expressionists, a painter of charged portraits of women. Look at the acid-green wall: faint squaring lines still show through the loose paint.
context: Konrad Krzyżanowski painted his wife many times; this version dates from 1915, when war had pushed the couple out of Warsaw to her family in Volhynia. Trained in Kyiv, St Petersburg and with Simon Hollósy in Munich, he co-founded a Warsaw painting school, and Michalina had been his pupil before they married in 1906. The National Museum in Warsaw bought the canvas (MP 5 MNW). Fun fact: during the Second World War, Michalina worked for the Polish underground under the code name "Mrs Mouse", an alias that sits nicely beside this picture.
title_eng: Portrait of Michalina Krzyżanowska with Cat
image_credit: Konrad Krzyżanowski · cyfrowe.mnw.art.pl

title: Jane Cowl with Buzzer the Cat
title_eng: Jane Cowl with Buzzer the Cat
artist_dates: American (born Germany), Berlin 1869–1942 New Milford, Connecticut
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Buzzer, a striped tabby, is held up at face height in a white-gloved hand, ears pricked and staring straight into the lens, while the Broadway actress Jane Cowl tilts her head and looks down at the cat with half-closed eyes. The Library of Congress catalogue gives the cat equal billing in the title. What survives is a 5 × 7 inch glass negative, so every print is a modern positive pulled from a fragile plate. Genthe's soft, low-contrast light melts her feathered hat into the curtain behind, but keeps every whisker sharp.
context: Arnold Genthe, born in Berlin in 1869, worked as a photographer in San Francisco and then New York, where his portrait studio photographed actors, dancers and writers. The Library of Congress dates this negative to between 1912 and 1914 and files it under the subject heading "Genthe, Arnold, 1869–1942: animals and pets", which tells you Buzzer belonged to the photographer, not to Jane Cowl (1884–1950). Fun fact: the Library bought Genthe's negatives from his estate in 1942 or 1943, so his studio cat entered a national collection in the same boxes as the Broadway stars it sat with.
title_original: Cowl, Jane, Miss, with Buzzer the cat, portrait photograph
image_credit: Arnold Genthe · This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID agc.7a13339 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyrigh

title: Study of the Cat Raminou (Étude du chat Raminou)
description: Raminou, Valadon's own cat, sleeps curled into a tight oval, eyes shut and front paws tucked under, alone on a small panel, 38.1 × 32.4 cm, painted in oil on plywood. The bare wood is left showing all around him, its grain running across the picture like a rug he happens to lie on. That cheap support suits a sketch made at home, fast and for herself. The title is written below the cat with her name: "Mon Raminou / Suzanne Valadon". The possessive is the detail to look for: Valadon labelled this one as hers.
context: Valadon painted the study around 1917, during the years she shared the rue Cortot studio in Montmartre with her son Maurice Utrillo and her husband André Utter. It belonged to Dr Robert Le Masle, who bequeathed it to the Musée national d'art moderne in 1974 (AM 1974-118). Since 3 April 1975 the panel has been on deposit at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Brest, a long way from Montmartre. Fun fact: it came back for a visit in 2015 as catalogue no. 33 of the Musée de Montmartre's exhibition on the rue Cortot studio, the closest a portrait cat gets to a homecoming.
collection: Centre Pompidou, Musée national d'art moderne, Paris (on deposit at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Brest since 1975)
image_credit: Suzanne Valadon · Cette œuvre fait partie de la collection du Musée des Beaux-Arts de Brest .

title: Merchant's Wife at Tea (Купчиха за чаем)
description: A well-fed brown-and-white cat walks along the terrace railing and arches its head against the merchant's wife's shoulder, tail curled high, while she sips tea from a saucer with her little finger raised. Kustodiev slyly gave the cat's face some of the woman's own features, so the two plump, contented creatures rhyme. Around them is a feast on a square canvas, 120 × 120 cm: a copper samovar, a cut watermelon, rolls, pretzels, grapes, cups from mismatched sets. Behind the terrace, a provincial town shows a bazaar, church domes and a neighbouring couple also at tea.
context: Kustodiev painted it quickly in the summer of 1918 in hungry, cold Petrograd. A spinal tumour had left him in a wheelchair, so the abundant provincial town comes largely from memory. The model was not a merchant's wife at all but Baroness Galina Aderkas, a medical student who lived in the same building. The canvas was shown in 1919 at the Winter Palace, in Berlin in 1922 and at the Venice Biennale in 1924, and passed to the State Russian Museum in 1925. Fun fact: Mayakovsky reproduced it in Krasnaya Niva under the more ideologically comfortable title "Woman by the Samovar".
submovement: Mir iskusstva (World of Art) circle genre painting
feline_symbolism: The pampered cat doubles the sitter: its borrowed features make it a furry echo of her sleek, well-fed contentment.
image_credit: Boris Kustodiev · GgFFUJTfMEA_Xg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Seated Cat (drawing reproduced in Claude Aveline, Les Muses mêlées)
medium: Drawing reproduced in print (Paris: André Delpeuch, 1926)
collection: Original unlocated; known from Les Muses mêlées (1926)
description: A cat sits bolt upright and faces us head-on, front legs together, tail wrapped round to the left, almond eyes narrowed under a dark mask. Wikimedia's cataloguers read it as a Siamese, a breed Steinlen drew far less often than his Montmartre alley cats, and the shaded face and ears support them. It is known through its reproduction in Claude Aveline's book Les Muses mêlées, ink line printed on an octavo leaf, 19.5 × 14.5 cm for the whole volume. Below the paws sit Steinlen's monogram "St." and a handwritten dedication ending "cordialement".
context: Les Muses mêlées was published in Paris by André Delpeuch in 1926, in a first edition of 850 copies, "avec quatre dessins inédits" by Antoine Bourdelle, Steinlen and Berthold Mahn. Steinlen had died in 1923, so his contribution appeared posthumously. Claude Aveline (1901–1992) was the pen name of Evgen Avtsine, a young writer who moved in Anatole France's circle. Fun fact: one surviving copy carries Aveline's inscription to the print scholar Clément-Janin "en souvenir d'Anatole France et de Steinlen", tying book, author and cat to the same small Parisian world.
title_eng: Seated Cat (drawing reproduced in Claude Aveline, Les Muses mêlées)
image_credit: Michel-georges bernard · Own work

title: Cat on a Flowering Summer Meadow (Katt i blommande sommaräng)
description: A tabby cat peers out of a summer meadow, only its head and a bit of striped shoulder showing, eyes half closed against the light, a little right of centre on a canvas 75.5 × 91 cm. The meadow takes up most of the room: blue-green grass in thick, choppy strokes, yellow flowers scattered everywhere, white daisies piled in the top right corner. Stripes and grass are close cousins, and the tabby pattern lets the animal half dissolve into its surroundings, a hunter's camouflage set inside a quiet summer day. Liljefors signs and dates it lower left.
context: Bruno Liljefors (1860–1939), born in Uppsala and best known for animals in the Swedish landscape, painted this in 1919, when he was nearly sixty. The canvas stayed in private hands and surfaced at Uppsala Auktionskammare in 2023 as catalogue no. 381, which is where the photograph now on Wikimedia Commons was taken. Fun fact: the auction record turns the painting into a small piece of technical data too; the reproduction was shot on a Canon EOS 5D Mark III at f/11, which is why every flower in it is crisp.
title_eng: Cat on a Flowering Summer Meadow
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Uppsala Auktionskammare

title: Interior of an Egyptian Harem (Wnętrze egipskiego haremu)
collection: Private collection (sold Dorotheum, Vienna, 19 June 2018, as 'Traute Zweisamkeit')
description: A tabby cat has folded itself into a neat loaf at the end of the bed, eyes half shut, right beside the woman's hip and the most at-home creature in the room. She sits on a red-covered bed with her chin in her hand and a feather fan in her lap, looking bored, while a warm square of light from an unseen opening falls across the painted walls. The bed end is carved with two dark lion heads. Bakałowicz paints in oil on a small wood panel, 33 × 47.5 cm, with lotus flowers in a blue vase at left. Signed "St. Bakalowicz MCMXIX, Roma".
context: Stefan Bakałowicz (1857–1947), a Warsaw-born painter who signed this panel in Rome, specialised in imagined scenes of antiquity, Roman and Egyptian. He made this panel in 1919; it is in a private collection and was sold at the Dorotheum in Vienna in June 2018 under the cosier title "Traute Zweisamkeit". Valentin Boyer, writing in 2020, traces the lion-headed bed to drawings in the Cairo Museum's 1914 general catalogue and to bed supports in Turin. Fun fact: he notes that Bakałowicz avoids pyramids and other clichés, relying instead on quiet motifs such as lotus bouquets, footstools and cats to signal Egypt.
feline_symbolism: Boyer counts the cat among the discreet, recurring motifs Bakałowicz uses to make a room read as Egyptian without resorting to cliché.
image_credit: Stefan Bakałowicz · Boyer V. Entre rêverie et authenticité – une immersion dans l'Égypte ancienne avec le peintre Stefan Bakałowicz : [фр.] // Studies in Ancient Art and Civilisation. — 2020. — Vol. 24. — P. 277—298. — doi:10.12797/SAAC.24.

title: Girl with a Cat: The Fairy (Dziewczyna z kotem: Wróżka)
description: A black cat stands on the young woman's shoulder, back arched against the red wall behind, yellow eyes glinting and one front leg dangling down over her bare collarbone. It is clearly the one in charge of the seating plan. She, the "Wróżka" of the title, leans her head sideways under a gold-and-peacock turban and gives us a sly half-smile. Wasilkowski paints in oil on a modest canvas, 47.5 × 57 cm, wider than tall, signed "Kaz. Wł. Wasilkowski" lower right. Wróżka can mean fortune-teller or fairy, and a black cat at the ear suits either trade.
context: Kazimierz Władysław Wasilkowski (c. 1861–1934) trained in Warsaw under Wojciech Gerson, in Kraków, and from 1884 to 1890 at the St Petersburg Academy, then settled in Warsaw with his wife, the painter Maria Nostitz-Wasilkowska. He specialised in portraits and sensual female figures drawn from the Bible, folklore and history; one 1935 reviewer said the stated idea was often a pretext for showing the female form in new variations. This canvas, dated around 1920, is in private hands and is known from a Polswiss Art auction listing. Fun fact: his Żądze won a gold medal at the 1900 Paris Exposition.
image_credit: Kazimierz Władysław Wasilkowski (1861-1934) · www.polswissart.pl

title: Family Afternoon (Popołudnie rodzinne)
description: A small grey-and-white tabby sits on the bare floorboards at lower right, by the open door, back half turned to us and watching the family like a polite guest. The family fills the rest of a cottage room: a mother in a red headscarf holds a baby on her lap, the father puffs a long pipe on a stool, and a boy perched on a bench chews something. A red dresser of plates, a basket of greens and sunlight from the doorway complete the genre scene. The work is known from an auction photograph, so its size and support are unrecorded. Signed lower right.
context: Franciszek Teodor Ejsmond (1859–1931), born in Krogulcza Sucha, studied at the academies of Warsaw and Munich and spent his career painting genre scenes and figures such as Romanian and Dalmatian peasant girls and a hermit now in the National Museum in Warsaw. Family afternoon is dated around 1920 and is known from an image published by the auction aggregator Invaluable; its present owner is not recorded. Fun fact: two of Ejsmond's sons, Stanisław and Julian, are listed alongside him on Wikidata, and he is buried in Warsaw's Powązki Cemetery.
image_credit: Franciszek Ejsmond (1859-1931) · https://image.invaluable.com/housePhotos/Bodo/40/658540/H21547-L190951821.jpg

title: Woman with a Cat (Femme avec un chat)
description: A small black cat curls on the woman's lap, two round eyes staring out, while her tubular hand rests on an open book beneath it. She is a nude assembled from spheres, cones and tubes, grey and polished like engine parts, with a sheet of black hair and a blank oval face. The cat gets the same geometric shorthand: a dark lozenge with ears. Léger sets them in a yellow armchair against a grid of black, white and ochre panels and a yellow-and-black harlequin pattern, on a canvas 130.8 × 90.5 cm. Signed and dated lower right.
context: Léger painted two nearly identical versions of this subject in 1921, part of a run of female figures that are thought to be studies for Three Women (Le Grand Déjeuner, 1921–22). This larger version belonged to Gottlieb Reber in Switzerland until 1958, then to Samuel and Florene Marx, and came to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1994 (1994.486). Fun fact: the smaller twin, 97.5 × 70.5 cm, went the other way through the market, from the dealer Paul Rosenberg to the Hamburger Kunsthalle, which bought it in 1967.
title_eng: Woman with a Cat (Femme avec un chat)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: Fernand Léger · Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Drawing by Louis Wain (cat)
medium: Pen, black ink, and colored crayon on wove paper
collection: Wellcome Collection, London (papers of Noel Gordon Harris, PP/NGH/58)
description: A shaggy cat lunges at us with both forelegs flung out, claws spread, grinning under a huge round nose and squinting with glee. It is a Louis Wain cat drawn rather than painted, signed "Louis Wain." below, and it survives in an unlikely place: a folder of poems, notes and drawings in a psychiatrist's papers, one of two Wain cat drawings in the file. Wellcome's cautious caption is "Drawing of cat (?)". Along the bottom edge runs a handwritten line, "Keep your mouth shut, and let me open your mind for you", with "caught!" squeezed in above.
context: The drawing is in the papers of Noel Gordon Harris (1897–1963), psychiatrist and later president of the Royal Medico-Psychological Association, given to Wellcome's Contemporary Medical Archives Centre in 1985 by his daughter Joyce Griffith (PP/NGH/58, file dated c. 1930s–1940s). Harris took a post at Springfield Mental Hospital in 1923; Wain was certified and admitted to Springfield's pauper ward in 1924, before a public appeal moved him to Bethlem. Fun fact: that overlap may be how the drawing reached Harris, though the file does not say so.
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/e8/8a/eb8541ffe2fa2b205a23b10daec9.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0018572.html

title: Reclining Nude with Cat (Liegender Akt mit Katze)
submovement: German Expressionist colour woodcut (Kirchner's Davos years)
medium: Colour woodcut on folded book prospectus
collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.
description: A black cat curls at the far right end of the couch, a dark lump by the nude's feet, while she stretches out across the block with one arm behind her head. Kirchner cut the scene into a woodcut barely the size of a playing card, 6.2 × 9.4 cm, and printed it in orange, violet and maroon. The sheet it sits on is a folded book prospectus, 26.5 × 32.4 cm unfolded, headed "Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Das graphische Werk, von Gustav Schiefler", with a column of German sales text below. Every gouge that reads as a bold slash is a few millimetres long.
context: Kirchner made the woodcut in 1924. It entered the National Gallery of Art in Washington in 2007 as a gift of Ruth Cole Kainen, a major donor of German prints (accession 2007.75.2). Fun fact: this is not a grand exhibition print but a piece of publicity printed onto a prospectus, a reminder that Kirchner was closely involved in how his work was published and sold. The NGA record does not say which book the prospectus advertised, and I could not confirm it.
image_credit: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Dingo (illustrated book by Octave Mirbeau, with 55 etchings by Pierre Bonnard)
medium: Etching on laid paper (unbound book, 55 plates)
collection: Petit Palais, Musée des Beaux-Arts de la Ville de Paris
description: In Mirbeau's novel, Miche is a three-month-old kitten whom the dog Dingo more or less raises: he sleeps with her in the same basket, guards her, carries her by the tail and takes her head in his mouth while she trusts him completely. She does not appear on the wrapper, though. There Bonnard's scribbled needle gives us Dingo alone, seen from behind, sitting and looking away, under the title in red. The unbound copy in the Petit Palais holds all 55 etched plates on laid paper, published by Ambroise Vollard in 1924, in a stack 38.5 × 28.4 cm and 4 cm thick.
context: Octave Mirbeau's Dingo (1913) is a satirical fable built around his own dog, who died in 1901; Mirbeau was too ill to finish it, and Léon Werth wrote the last chapters from his notes. Ambroise Vollard later published it with 55 etchings by Pierre Bonnard. The Petit Palais copy (PPL41) came with the bequest of Dr Maurice Girardin in 1953. Fun fact: Mirbeau's narrator calls the dog-and-kitten friendship unusual because the two belong to "races ennemies", which turns the usual cat-and-dog joke on its head.
feline_symbolism: In the novel Miche is the one creature Dingo protects, a counterweight to the dog's predatory 'law of murder'.
title_eng: Dingo (illustrated book by Octave Mirbeau, with 55 etchings by Pierre Bonnard)
image_credit: Bonnard, Pierre (Fontenay-aux-Roses, 03–10–1867 - Cannet, 23–01–1947), illustrateur · https://www.parismuseescollections.paris.fr/fr/petit-palais/oeuvres/dingo#infos-principales

title: Tabby Cat (Madara Neko, Important Cultural Property of Japan)
collection: Yamatane Museum of Art, Tokyo (Important Cultural Property)
description: A white-and-brown tabby twists round to groom itself, one hind leg kicked out to the right, head bent back over its own flank and turquoise eyes glancing sideways at us. It sits alone in a field of bare honey-coloured silk, 81.9 × 101.6 cm, with nothing to compete with it. Seihō built a career on animals observed from life, and this one was a real cat he met in the street. The small seal at upper left is a celebrity too: it was carved by Kitaōji Rosanjin. On the box inscription Seihō wrote the title as 班猫, not with the usual 斑 for "spotted".
context: Takeuchi Seihō (1864–1942), the leading Kyoto painter of modern Nihonga, painted Hanbyō in 1924. While staying in Numazu he spotted the cat at the front of a greengrocer's shop and was reminded of a cat painted by the Song emperor Huizong, which set the picture in motion. The painting belongs to the Yamatane Museum of Art in Tokyo and was designated an Important Cultural Property in 1970. Fun fact: the much-repeated story that he swapped one of his own paintings for the cat is popular but did not appear in the sources I could check.
image_credit: Takeuchi Seihō · [1]

title: Panther (Panthère)
description: A panther walks along a low plinth, head dropped below the line of its shoulders, tail trailing almost to the floor in one long curve. Pompon reduces it to the forms he trusted: a continuous back, smooth flanks, no fur, no fuss. From 1905 he deliberately simplified his animals, polishing surfaces and suppressing detail, so light does the work that carved hair would do in a 19th-century animal bronze. The paws are rounded knobs, the ears two shallow bumps. In stone it looks heavier and calmer than a bronze would, a big cat made to be walked around.
context: François Pompon (1855–1933) spent decades as a praticien, the craftsman who turned other sculptors' models into marble, running Rodin's studio by 1893 and also working for Camille Claudel and Falguière. Fame arrived late, when his Ours blanc caused a stir at the 1922 Salon d'automne and he was 67. Wikimedia Commons dates this stone Panthère to 1925 and places it in the MuMa, Le Havre's museum of modern art. Fun fact: Pompon's own sources were Japanese and Egyptian art as much as the zoo.
collection: Musée d'art moderne André Malraux (MuMa), Le Havre
image_credit: François Pompon · photo by Pymouss

title: Cat and Flowers (Neko to Hana)
submovement: École de Paris Japanese Expatriate Modernism
collection: The Museum of Modern Art, Saitama (MOMAS)
description: A black cat sits on a windowsill beside a pot of flowers, back half to us, head turned so one yellow-green eye and a fan of whiskers catch the light. Behind it the window glows yellow and orange, crossed by dark mullions. Tanaka draws in pastel on a sheet 35 cm wide and 47 cm high, so the composition stands upright. The museum's tags list pencil and coloured pencil alongside the pastel, and the fur is built from dense, scribbled black strokes over tan paper. Known first for figures and nudes, Tanaka gives the cat the same close attention. Signed lower right.
context: Tanaka Yasushi (1886–1941) left Saitama Prefectural Urawa High School in 1904 and travelled alone to Seattle to study painting, where his nudes drew notice. In 1920 he moved to Paris with his wife, showed at the Salon d'Automne and elsewhere, and died there without ever returning to Japan. The Museum of Modern Art, Saitama, which holds this sheet, dates it broadly to 1920–40. Fun fact: his career runs Saitama to Seattle to Paris, and the drawing has made the return trip he never did.

title: Two Children with a Cat (Dwoje dzieci z kotem)
collection: Muzeum Narodowe w Warszawie (National Museum in Warsaw)
description: A tabby cat sits bolt upright in the bottom right corner, half hidden among long blade-like leaves, staring out with the same flat calm as the children. They fill a canvas 100 × 82.5 cm: a dark-haired toddler in a brown smock clasps his hands, a fair older child stands behind, and a white hen perches on the fence at left. Makowski's children are a recognisable cast, stiff, doll-like figures who seem carved rather than born, with something of Polish folk toys about them. The scene is outdoors, thin trees, picket fence and brick houses, in the warm, still light he admired in the old Dutch masters.
context: Tadeusz Makowski (1882–1932) read classical philology at the Jagiellonian University and studied painting at the Kraków Academy under Jan Stanisławski and Józef Mehoffer before moving to Paris in 1908, where he stayed for life. Cubists around Henri Le Fauconnier admired his early work; later he turned to carnivals, fairs and above all children. The National Museum in Warsaw holds this canvas (MPW 2700 MNW), dated around 1920. Fun fact: he kept a diary from 1912 to 1931, published in Warsaw in 1961.
submovement: École de Paris (Polish circle), folk- and Dutch-inflected figure painting
image_credit: Tadeusz Makowski · National Museum in Warsaw

title: The Falsehood of Woman: Self-Portrait with Maryla Grossmanowa (Fałsz kobiety)
title_eng: The Falsehood of Woman (Self-Portrait with Portrait of Maryla Grossmanowa)
title_original: Fałsz kobiety, z autoportretem (Portret Maryli Grossmanowej)
medium: Pastel on paper mounted on canvas
collection: Muzeum Narodowe w Warszawie (National Museum in Warsaw)
description: A long-haired grey-brown cat crouches in the lower left corner, eyes narrowed, as if it has seen this act before. Above it Witkacy, in a brown suit, grins at us while painting a grotesque grinning face on a canvas, and Maryla Grossmanowa reclines at right in a red dress and pearls, hand to cheek, against a rocky seascape. A huge pastel, 115.5 × 184 cm, on paper laid down on canvas. Top left: "Ignacy Witkiewicz 1927 I (T.A)" and coded notations; bottom right: "Witkacy / NP1 X 1922 / NP1 II 1924". Witkacy logged what he had, or had not, been taking while he painted.
context: After 1925 Witkacy ran his portrait business as "The S.I. Witkiewicz Portrait Painting Company", with grades ranging from largely representational likenesses to expressionistic ones and ones made under narcotics, and the motto "The customer must always be satisfied". This sheet, dated January 1927, is marked T.A, a Type A. The National Museum in Warsaw bought it (Rys.W.11538) and showed it in 2022 in "Witkacy. Seismograph of the Acceleration Age". Fun fact: his mnemonics were so thorough that some pictures record nothing stronger than a cup of coffee.
image_credit: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz · cyfrowe.mnw.art.pl

title: Standing Anthropomorphic Cat with Decorative Patterns
description: A cat stands up on its hind legs, and its body is not fur but pattern: a magenta face with diamond-crossed green eyes and a tiny red heart for a nose, curling yellow acanthus ears, and a blue bow-like flourish where the chest should be. The colours are mainly yellow, purple and blue, set on a green ground worked with rows of red decoration. Wain painted it in gouache on a small sheet, 18.8 × 12.6 cm. Pencilled on the back are the words "Early Greek", his label for the style of the patterns. A cat after ancient vases, by way of a wallpaper sample book.
context: Wellcome Collection dates the gouache broadly to 1925/1939, the years Wain spent in Bethlem and then, from 1930, Napsbury Hospital, after his sisters had him certified in 1924. He kept painting there, decorating wards at Christmas and making both old-style cats and abstract, patterned designs. Fun fact: the famous sequence that supposedly charts Wain's decline into schizophrenia was assembled in 1939 by the psychiatrist Walter Maclay from undated pictures bought in a shop, and critics now point out Wain was painting conventional cats and patterned ones side by side.
title_eng: Standing Anthropomorphic Cat with Decorative Patterns
title_original: A cat standing on its hind legs, formed by patterns supposed to be in the "Early Greek" style
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/1f/9f/b6cb7095a1247632a85b8738f449.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0026932.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-21): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/bvxdmx8m

title: Three Cats Performing a Song-and-Dance Act
description: Three cats in top hats perform a song-and-dance number on a green lawn. At left a white cat in a scarlet suit kicks up a leg, waving a cane and a feathery plume; a tabby in white trousers and a yellow topper follows, cane tucked to its chest; the third, in pale pink with a green waistcoat and red hat, brings up the rear with an umbrella and an open-mouthed "oh". Behind them rise bushes of blue and white blossom. Music hall transplanted to the garden, in gouache on a sheet 17.7 × 22.6 cm, signed "Louis Wain" lower left. One umbrella among the canes: someone missed the memo.
context: Wellcome Collection dates the gouache to 1925/1939, the years of Wain's confinement in Bethlem and later Napsbury Hospital, where he kept painting and decorated the wards at Christmas. Pictures like this undercut the old story that his work simply dissolved into abstraction as his illness advanced: here are the dressed-up, jolly cats that made him famous in the 1880s and 1890s, still going strong. Fun fact: H. G. Wells wrote in 1925 that Wain "invented a cat style, a cat society, a whole cat world".
title_eng: Three Cats Performing a Song-and-Dance Act
title_original: Three Cats Performing a Song and Dance Act
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/2f/45/1297a2e55598c2ba91e267c1f500.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0026312.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-04-05): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/asen9ww3

title: Kaleidoscopic Cat II
collection: Bethlem Museum of the Mind, Beckenham, Kent
description: A ginger-and-white cat stares out with enormous green-rimmed eyes, pupils slid to one side, ears up and fur bristling outward in quick red-brown strokes. The cat itself is still very much a cat; the ornament lives behind it, a green field of blue-green scrolls and small red stars crowding in around the ears. The image's own title files it under "kaleidoscope", the word that has stuck to Wain's most patterned pictures, but here the pattern is only starting to creep in. Look for the faint signature at lower left. The reproduction comes from the Bethlem Museum of the Mind.
context: Wain was certified in 1924, moved to Bethlem Hospital after a public appeal, and in 1930 went to Napsbury, painting throughout. In 1939 the psychiatrist Walter Maclay arranged undated Wain pictures bought in a Campden Hill shop into a sequence said to chart a schizophrenic decline. Critics now note Wain painted conventional and patterned cats side by side, and later commentators link these designs to 1960s psychedelic art. Fun fact: the date is still unresolved; Wikidata gives 1910, well before his hospital years.
image_credit: Louis Wain · Bethlem Museum

title: Norman
description: A turquoise cat's head fills a blue ground, and its fur has stopped behaving like fur. White lines run across the face and broad ruff in pointed arches, loops and little hooked crockets, beaded with pink and red dots, the vocabulary of a church window rather than a tabby coat. Two huge yellow eyes and a red, cross-shaped nose hold it together, and three white sprigs rise from the crown like finials. Wellcome's cataloguer saw tracery and crockets in those lines. The sheet is small, about 18.5 by 12 cm, in flat, opaque gouache, with a single pencilled word on the back: "Norman".
context: Louis Wain (1860-1939) built a career on grinning, dressed-up cats for Victorian and Edwardian papers. In June 1924 he was certified insane and admitted to Springfield Hospital in Tooting; he moved to Bethlem in 1925 and to Napsbury in Hertfordshire in May 1930, and he kept painting in all three. Wellcome Collection can only date this gouache to 1925-1939, somewhere inside those hospital years. For a long time the catalogue called it "A cat in 'Gothic' style", a title that went straight into books and on to Wikipedia. In February 2025 Wellcome retitled it "Norman", taking the name from the pencilled word on the verso, so the cat now goes by what the back of the sheet says rather than what a cataloguer thought it looked like.
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/cd/03/9030e9bf472c799c9b492cc2ba5e.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0026931.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-21): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/nww85e9p

title: Three Cats Singing
description: Three cats sing in profile, like a church trio caught mid-verse: a brown tabby at left and two blue-grey cats beside it, all with mouths open and eyes rolled up toward something out of frame. Each grips an open red-covered book in its paws. Behind them, pink daisies and red pompom flowers crowd a yellow-green background, colours the Wellcome cataloguer called "equally lurid", a fair warning for anyone expecting Victorian browns. The sheet is gouache, about 17 by 23 cm, so the paint lies thick and matt, and Wain has signed it plainly at lower right: "Louis Wain."
context: Wain's singing, card-playing and tea-drinking cats were a staple of late Victorian illustration, and he did not stop making them after his family had him certified in 1924. He spent a year at Springfield, five at Bethlem, and his last years at Napsbury, where he died in July 1939. Wellcome Collection holds this gouache with a broad date of 1925-1939, so it belongs to the hospital decades, though no record says which ward it was painted in. Curator Bryony Benge-Abbott, writing for Wellcome in 2020, argues that work like this undercuts the old story of steady psychotic decline: alongside the patterned cats, Wain went on producing exactly the comic anthropomorphic scenes that had made him famous.
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/b7/4f/26d89e691250b47be288293a4f76.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0026168.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-04-05): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/gbcecf7t

title: Cat and Bird (Katze und Vogel)
description: A cat's face takes up almost the whole canvas, broad as a full moon and built from simple shapes: almond eyes with green vertical pupils, a long thin nose ridge, whiskers drawn as fine curving lines. On its forehead, between the eyes, perches a small pink bird, as if the cat is thinking about it. The palette stays muted, warm ochres and orange-browns over chalky white with touches of green, so the one bright note is the nose, a red heart. Above the bird hangs a small dark circle, a heavenly sign Klee used again and again. Oil and ink over a gesso ground, 38 by 53 cm.
context: Paul Klee painted Cat and Bird in 1928, while teaching at the Bauhaus in Dessau. According to the provenance summarised on Wikipedia, he consigned it to Alfred Flechtheim's Berlin gallery in 1929; in 1934 it was sold to Franz Herbert Hirschland, whose daughters inherited it. MoMA acquired it in 1975 (300.1975) through the Sidney and Harriet Janis Collection Fund and a gift of Suzy Prudden and Joan H. Meijer in memory of F. H. Hirschland. The bird is the oddity. William Rubin read the picture through Gestalt psychology: the bird is not sitting on the cat but inside its head, a thought the cat is not willing to let go of. Rubin also thought the picture unusual in Klee's work, in both handling and subject.
medium: Oil and ink on gessoed canvas mounted on wood
collection: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
feline_symbolism: Following Rubin's reading, the bird is the cat's own fixation made visible, and the red heart-shaped nose has been read as a sign of desire.
image_credit: Paul Klee · Own work

title: Portrait of Ludwik Kotulski, with Patient and a Cat
title_eng: Portrait of Ludwik Kotulski, with Patient and a Cat
title_original: Portret Ludwika Kotulskiego, z pacjentką i kotem
collection: Muzeum Sztuki w Łodzi (Museum of Art in Łódź)
location: Muzeum Sztuki w Łodzi (Museum of Art in Łódź)
description: A black cat lies across Kotulski's lap and forearm, its dark body almost swallowed by his charcoal-grey coat. He sits bald and pensive, a finger at his lips, while behind him a woman's face, described as his patient, peers over his shoulder out of a sweep of white, and at left a winged, twisting yellow-and-pink creature clutches a pedestal. The sheet is brown paper nearly a metre across, in pastel, unusually wide for a portrait. The cat was hardly required for a commission, which is presumably why it earned a place in the title. Lower right runs the book-keeping: "NP 17 / T.B / 1928 III" and the signature.
context: From around 1925 Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz ran his portrait practice as a mock business, the S.I. Witkiewicz Portrait Firm, with a printed set of rules and five price-graded types from A to E. Type B, marked "T.B" here, meant an accurate likeness with a slight push on the sitter's characteristic features. Witkacy also logged his own habits on the sheets: "NP 17" means he had not smoked for seventeen days when he made this one in March 1928. The pastel was bought by the Museum of Art in Łódź in 1973 from a private collection sold through Desa, and it was shown in the museum's big Witkiewicz exhibition in 1980. It is catalogue number I 768 in the Witkacy catalogue raisonné.
image_credit: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz · https://www.digi-art.pl/pl/p/Witkacy-Portret-Ludwika-Kotulskiego/3386

title: Story of a Sick Kitten (Historia chorego kotka)
description: A sick kitten stands on a little round table at the bottom of the sheet, tail out, far too small for the crowd around it. Baron von Hahn, "a well-known hygienist" according to the pencilled caption, looms over it with a long white beard and reaches down to stroke it; his wife Eufemja hovers, very worried; Dr Rozalja Herzberg has had herself washed and prescribed a sedative draught. At left a pessimist, Robert Holt, disagrees with everyone; at right Konstancja Przepiórkowska stays indifferent. Pencil on a sheet barely 13 by 15 cm, signed and dated lower left, with the cast list written into the picture.
context: Witkacy (Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz, 1885-1939) is best known for his commissioned pastel portraits, but he also filled sheets with quick pencil drawings of invented characters, labelled with deadpan captions in the manner of a newspaper photo story. This one is signed "Witkacy / 1928 I", January 1928, and is catalogued as I 753 in the catalogue raisonné of his pictorial works. It is in a private collection and reached Wikimedia Commons by way of witkacologia.eu, a site devoted to anecdotes about the artist. The joke is in the over-staffing: one kitten, five named adults, a hygienist, a doctor and a professional pessimist, and the only figure with a sensible attitude is the woman who walks away.
image_credit: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz · https://witkacologia.eu/Witkacy%20w%20anegdocie/anegdoty2.html

title: Black Cat Hissing (Neko)
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on Japanese paper
collection: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
description: A black cat hisses, back arched, front legs stretched low, claws spread, mouth wide on a pink tongue and white fangs. A red collar with a small gold bell and a blue-and-pink tied cord are the only bright notes besides one yellow eye. In a colour woodblock print a large area of black is a technical dare: it has to be printed evenly from a carved block, by hand, with a baren rubbed over the back of the paper. So the few details, whiskers, teeth, claws, must be carved precisely or vanish. Ink and colour on Japanese paper, with a grey shadow pooling beneath.
context: Takahashi Shōtei (1871-1945), who also signed as Hiroaki and occasionally Kōmei, trained in Japanese-style painting under his uncle Matsumoto Fūko, who gave him the name Shōtei. In 1907 the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō recruited him to design souvenir prints for foreign buyers, starting with ten landscapes after Hiroshige. He designed around five hundred prints for Watanabe before the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake, whose fire destroyed Watanabe's workshop and every woodblock in it; afterwards he recut old designs and made new ones in the shin-hanga manner. Cats turn up among his later designs, including White Cat (1924) and Playing with a Cat (1930). This impression is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, whose open-access image was enhanced and circulated by rawpixel.
image_credit: Rawpixel Ltd · Black Cat Hissing 20th century print in high resolution by Hiroaki Takahashi. Original from The Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Digitally enhanced by rawpixel.

title: Radiated Kaleidoscopic Cat (Bethlem Hospital Study)
collection: Bethlem Museum of the Mind, Beckenham, Kent
description: A single white cat crouches and grins, its fur outlined in flame-like red-orange strokes, round red-brown eyes rimmed in blue, a wide pink smile. The cat stays recognisable; the pattern is around it, concentric zigzag bands of purple, blue, green, yellow and red radiating out to the edges like an electric aura. That is the manner that later earned Wain's late cats the nickname "psychedelic", the creature reading as much as an emblem as a pet. The Commons file credits the picture to Bethlem Museum of the Mind and gives no title, size or medium, so even what it is painted on goes unrecorded there.
