context: Bethlem Museum of the Mind in Beckenham holds a group of Wain's late work, including pictures from the Guttmann-Maclay Collection assembled by the psychiatrists Eric Guttmann and Walter Maclay in the 1930s. Their arrangements of Wain's cats into a supposed clinical progression, "from conventional to psychedelic" in the museum's words, shaped how these pictures were read for decades. Wain was certified in June 1924, spent a year at Springfield, five at Bethlem and the rest of his life at Napsbury, dying in July 1939. The Commons file's date of 1875 is impossible; it would have Wain painting this as a teenager, years before his first published drawings.
image_credit: Louis Wain · Bethlem Museum

title: Cat (Kot)
collection: Muzeum Górnośląskie w Bytomiu (Upper Silesian Museum, Bytom)
description: A long-haired cat sits in three-quarter view, body turned away, head swung round to face us with a dark mask, tufted ears and two orange eyes. Those eyes are the only colour on the sheet, which is the point: Goryńska's prints lean on a crisp contour, what the Bytom museum calls her "perfect, drawn line", and lay colour on chosen areas only. Fine cut lines build a white ruff, a grey flank and a huge plumed tail sweeping round the front paws. Pencilled 1930 at lower left and signed at lower right, the sheet is titled simply Kot, "Cat": no anecdote, just the animal as a problem of shape.
context: Wiktoria Goryńska (1902-1945) was born in Vienna, trained at the Kunstgewerbeschule there, and moved to Warsaw in 1918, where she studied under Tadeusz Pruszkowski and Władysław Skoczylas and joined the Ryt Association of Graphic Artists. She worked mainly in woodcut, and her early animal subjects included a whole series of cats. She was also one of the first Polish women to fence competitively and wrote about the sport. During the occupation she served as a courier in the underground under the pseudonym "Leti"; after the Warsaw Uprising she was deported and died at Ravensbrück on 29 March 1945. This impression is in the Upper Silesian Museum in Bytom.
image_credit: Wiktoria Goryńska · muzeum.bytom.pl

title: Sitting Cat (Chat assis)
medium: Colorless mold-pressed glass, partly frosted and polished
collection: Art market (Artemis Fine Arts, 19 March 2026, lot 373); another example at Corning Museum of Glass, 2011.3.413
description: A cat sits upright, tail curled flat around the base beside its haunch, head turned and tipped down as though it has spotted something on the floor. Everything is colourless glass pressed into a mould and mostly frosted, so the fur appears only as fine textured passages on the face, chest and flank that catch the light, while broad smooth planes let it slide through. At about 20.6 cm high it is a mantelpiece object, not a paperweight. This example is signed on the underside, and it has a large chip missing from the rear left paw.
context: René Lalique designed Chat assis in 1932, when his firm was producing Art Deco glass in long runs from reusable moulds rather than as unique pieces. This impression came up at Artemis Fine Arts in Louisville, Colorado, on 19 March 2026 (lot 373) from a private Colorado collection, estimated at $1,000-1,500. The auction text points to a museum example of the same model at the Corning Museum of Glass (2011.3.413). Lalique's son Marc later moved the firm from glass to crystal in the early 1950s, so a colourless glass Chat assis signed on the base belongs to the pre-war production rather than the later crystal reissues.

title: Chat (Lidded Box with Cat Head)
medium: Pressed molded glass, satin-finished and polished
description: A cat's face looks up from the lid of a small, square pressed-glass box: a relief head with long radiating whiskers, slit pupils and a fixed, level gaze. Lalique plays two finishes against each other, satin-frosted glass for the cat and clear polished glass around it, so the face appears to float above the surface. In this example the recesses of the fur hold a warm brownish tone, which makes the ears and whisker pads read almost like an engraving. The box is roughly 10 by 10 by 5, engraved "R. Lalique" underneath. Everyone who opens it pats the cat on the head.
context: René Lalique designed the box, simply called Chat, in 1932; it is number 90 in Félix Marcilhac's catalogue raisonné of Lalique glass (2011). Lidded boxes for powder, jewellery or sweets were a staple of his Art Deco output, made in series from moulds. This example was offered by the dealer Azur Antik of Mandelieu, on the Côte d'Azur, as an Art Deco period piece in excellent condition, priced at €1,550. The dealer calls it rare, which is the kind of claim that is hard to test for a moulded production object, but the model is less familiar than Lalique's cat figurines.

title: Chat Couché (Reclining Cat Statuette)
artist: Lalique France, after a 1932 model by René Lalique
description: A cat lies hunched and compact, haunches rounded high behind, front paws tucked, head pushed forward and low with half-closed eyes fixed on the floor just ahead. About 24 cm long and 10.5 cm high, it is clear and satin-finished crystal, and the two finishes do the modelling: the frosted rump is almost featureless, while fine incised fur lines gather on the face, ears and shoulders where the light catches. From behind it reduces to a smooth frosted dome. The pose is that of a cat that intends to stay put. The piece carries an engraved signature, not a moulded one.
context: René Lalique created the Chat couché model in 1932; it is number 1207 in Félix Marcilhac's catalogue raisonné. This example, though, is crystal and was sold as "Lalique France", the firm under René's son Marc, who moved production from glass to crystal in the early 1950s. So the design is Art Deco, and the object is a later edition made from it. It was handled by BG Arts, Lalique specialists at the Marché Biron in the Saint-Ouen flea market, and is listed as sold. Long-running models like this one let collectors buy a 1932 design long after 1932, which is exactly why dating any single cat needs a look at the signature and the material.

title: I Fell in Love with a Lovely Kitten
medium: Gouache, watercolor, and graphite on paper
collection: Bethlem Museum of the Mind / Private Collection
description: A brown tabby kitten, head and chest only, gazes up and sideways with huge yellow eyes and a small round "o" of a mouth, as if caught admiring something. Wain sets it on a sky-blue ground inside a painted red border and lets the caption below do half the work: "I fell in love with a lovely kitten. & that kitten was myself." The line turns a pet portrait into a joke about vanity, the cat as narrator and object of its own affection. Wain often wrote punning captions straight on to his pictures; here the brushed lettering and the signature just above it are part of the composition.
context: Wain (1860-1939) made his living from cats that behaved like people, and captions were part of the act. This picture is undated, and its whereabouts are not recorded in any source I could open: the Wikimedia Commons file was taken from a social-media account that posts Wain images, and gives only "before 1940". The entry's link to Bethlem Museum of the Mind and its date of c. 1930-1935 could not be confirmed. What can be said is that the self-regarding caption matches Wain's long habit of putting first-person jokes into a cat's mouth, a habit he kept up through his hospital years at Bethlem and Napsbury.
title_eng: I Fell in Love with a Lovely Kitten
title_original: I Fell in Love with a Lovely Kitten
image_credit: Louis Wain · https://x.com/LouisWainBot/status/1726071617896243605

title: Two Cats (Shuang Mao Tu)
description: Two cats share a rock under a leafy branch: a long-haired white cat with black patches sits up and stares straight out, while a calico companion curls asleep behind it. The hanging scroll is more than a metre high and barely half a metre wide, ink on paper with touches of blue and ochre wash, stacked vertically: leaves above, cats in the middle, the rock in broad wet ink below. The key is the inscription at upper left. Xu explains the cats are a couple, "lifelong partners", painted to mark their union. Two square seals close it: "Beihong" and a motto, "always believe it to be good".
context: Xu Beihong (1895-1953) trained in Paris from 1919 and came home determined to graft Western drawing onto Chinese brush-and-ink painting; from 1927 he taught at National Central University in Nanjing, then the capital. According to his inscription, a lady called Yishan left her cats at his "humble home" in the new capital, a friend named Tan Junwan was the first to wish the pair a happy union, and Xu painted this to commemorate the match. He signed it late in the jiaxu year, 1934. In other words, this is a wedding portrait for two cats, with a guest list. The scroll is in the CAFA Art Museum in Beijing, the museum of the Central Academy of Fine Arts that Xu himself headed from 1950.

title: The King of Cats (Le Roi des chats)
license: © Estate of Balthus, all rights reserved
description: A tabby cat leans against the painter's shin, tail up, the only soft thing in the room. Balthus stands above it in a tight jacket and a swagger pose, in a cramped space with bare walls and hard light that MCBA compares to a prison cell. The furniture amounts to a stool and a whip. Propped against the wall, a canvas carries the title in English: "A Portrait of H. M. The King of Cats, painted by Himself", with the year in Roman numerals. Oil on canvas, 78 by 49.7 cm, painted in muted colours and thick paint.
context: Balthus painted this self-portrait in Paris in 1935, aged 27. His link with cats went back to Mitsou (1921), a picture story he drew at eleven about a cat he found and lost, published with a preface by Rilke. In 1935 he also signed letters to his future wife, Antoinette de Watteville, as the King of Cats. The Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts in Lausanne received the painting in 2016 as a gift from the Fondation Balthus Klossowski de Rola (inv. 2016-048). MCBA's curators point out a borrowed source: the pose, the bare setting and the restrained palette lean heavily on Manet's Portrait of Théodore Duret (1868).
feline_symbolism: MCBA reads the cat as Balthus's alter ego and the picture as an allegory of a wild self that has to be tamed daily, hence the whip; in his memoirs he wrote of a secret, mysterious belonging to the world of cats.
image_credit: © Estate of Balthus / MCBA Lausanne. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from mcba.ch and is not stored on this site.

title: Professor Pulverstone Had a Litter of Kittens… (Profesor Pulverstone okocił się…)
title_eng: Professor Pulverstone Had a Litter of Kittens…
location: Muzeum Tatrzańskie im. Dra Tytusa Chałubińskiego w Zakopanem
description: Five kittens tumble at lower left, one of them dark, freshly delivered by Professor Pulverstone, who sprawls above them with a big four-legged body and a shaggy, bearded human head. The caption explains he "okocił się ze zdziwienia": gave birth to kittens out of sheer astonishment on seeing two of his monsters, which he believed were figments of his imagination, start to flirt coarsely. The monsters cavort on a table at top, labelled "owe potwory". His wife files a mock-Russian complaint at bottom right, and a tame seal called Rózia gets her own label. Pencil on paper, about 22 by 32.5 cm, with "Kopia N7" circled at top.
context: Witkacy dated this one with a flourish: "Witkacy 1936 / w dzień zaduszny / 2 XI", All Souls' Day, 2 November 1936, three years before his suicide in September 1939. A note at top left reads "(Kopia / N 7)", suggesting he repeated the composition. Drawings like this, populated with invented scholars and their household beasts, ran alongside the portrait business that paid his bills. The sheet belongs to the Tatra Museum in Zakopane, the town where Witkacy grew up, and it was lent to the National Museum in Warsaw for the 2022 exhibition "Witkacy. Seismograph of the Acceleration Age". The title verb okocić się is normally used only of a cat giving birth, which is the whole joke.
image_credit: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz · https://witkacykatalog.com/pl/katalog/126674

title: Cat Catching a Bird (Chat saisissant un oiseau)
description: A striped cat stands rigid on a dark ridge, tail up, claws out like white hooks, with a black bird clamped sideways in its jaws. The bird's chest is torn open in a red wound, wings splayed, and the cat's flattened head, white eyes and bared teeth look less hungry than furious. Picasso does not soften it. The title says it plainly, Chat saisissant un oiseau, and the horizontal canvas, 81 by 100 cm, gives the struggle room to spread sideways. Oil on canvas, dated twice, 22-4-39 at upper left against the grey-blue sky and again on the reverse: 22 April 1939.
context: Picasso painted this in Paris in April 1939, a few months before the outbreak of the Second World War, and the date has tempted many readers to see the cat's violence as a comment on the times, though the picture itself carries no political label. He kept it in his studio for the rest of his life. After his death in 1973 it was among the works the French state accepted in lieu of inheritance tax, entering the Musée national Picasso in Paris in 1979 (MP178). It has travelled constantly since: from Rome and Milan in 1953 and the Tate in 1960 to Houston in 2023.
image_credit: © Succession Picasso. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from uploads2.wikiart.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Cat and Rock (hanging scroll)
description: A cat crouches on all fours, white and long-haired, with black patches over one ear, across the back and down a thick black tail, and looks straight out at us with pale, wide-set eyes. Xu builds the coat from quick, feathery grey strokes and leaves most of it bare paper. The scroll is ink and colour on paper, narrow and tall at about 100 by 34 cm, and the Palace Museum titles it after the classic pairing: Cat and Rock. The image here is a cut-out detail of the cat alone, lifted from the full scroll; the rock and the rest of the composition are outside the frame.
context: Xu Beihong (1895-1953) studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris from 1919 and spent his career fusing Western observation with Chinese brushwork; he is best known for galloping horses, but cats recur in his ink paintings of the 1930s and 1940s. This scroll, catalogued as Cat and Rock (猫石图轴), belongs to the Palace Museum in Beijing, which published it in a PDF from which the Commons detail was taken. The museum gives no date in the caption I could see. From 1939 to 1941 Xu toured Singapore, Malaya and India selling his paintings to raise war-relief funds for China, and met Tagore and Gandhi along the way, but nothing ties this particular scroll to that trip.
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and colour on paper
image_credit: Xu Beihong · https://www.dpm.org.cn/Uploads/File/2022/06/08/u62a046b5637b3.pdf

title: Figaro (frame from the Pinocchio trailer, 1940)
artist: Walt Disney Productions (Animation by Eric Larson)
description: Figaro, Geppetto's black-and-white kitten, is fast asleep in this single frame from the 1940 theatrical trailer for Pinocchio, about a minute in. He wears a floppy red nightcap, eyes shut in two contented curves, white paws resting on a pale blue blanket, with a purple-and-tan patchwork quilt pulled up below. He is pure 1940 Disney character design: a round head and a body built to squash and stretch. The frame is a film still, not a drawing, so what survives is the finished, inked-and-painted cel as photographed by the studio camera, night-blue shadows and all.
context: Figaro is not in Collodi's novel. The Disney story team added him, along with Cleo the goldfish, to give Geppetto a household, and Eric Larson did most of his animation; Clarence Nash, better known as Donald Duck, supplied his noises. Pinocchio premiered at the Center Theatre in New York on 7 February 1940 and went on general release on 23 February. Audiences took to the sulky kitten fast enough that the studio put him into several shorts in the 1940s, and later recast him for good as Minnie Mouse's pet. The trailer frame is in the US public domain because the trailer was published without a copyright notice, an accident of 1940 paperwork that the feature itself did not share.
medium: Frame from the theatrical trailer for Pinocchio (1940)
collection: Walt Disney Animation Research Library, Burbank, California
image_credit: The Walt Disney Company · Theatrical trailer (1940) at 1:04

title: Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird
title_original: Autorretrato con collar de espinas y colibrí
collection: Harry Ransom Center, The University of Texas at Austin
description: Over Kahlo's left shoulder, a black cat with pale, staring eyes and pricked ears peers out of the dark leaves, its head level with her chin. It is easy to miss, because everything else is louder: Kahlo faces us head-on, a necklace of thorns cuts into her throat and trails across her chest like roots, and a dead black hummingbird hangs from it with wings spread stiff. Behind her other shoulder a spider monkey fiddles with the thorns. Two dragonflies hover above her head and two butterfly clips sit in her hair. Oil on canvas on masonite, about 61 by 47 cm.
context: Frida Kahlo painted this in 1940, after her divorce from Diego Rivera and the end of her affair with the photographer Nickolas Muray. Muray bought it shortly afterwards, which means he paid for a picture painted in the wake of their break-up. It stayed with his collection, and the University of Texas at Austin acquired it in 1966; it now belongs to the Nickolas Muray collection at the Harry Ransom Center. Readings of the symbols vary. The hummingbird is a Mexican love charm, or a nod to the Aztec war god Huitzilopochtli; the monkey was a gift from Rivera and may stand in for him, tugging the thorns until they draw blood.
title_eng: Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird
feline_symbolism: The black cat is usually read as a sign of bad luck and death, a fitting neighbour for the dead hummingbird.
image_credit: Harry Ransom Center, The University of Texas at Austin (Acc. 66.6) · © Banco de México Diego Rivera Frida Kahlo Museums Trust / ARS, New York
rights_note: Copyrighted by Banco de México Diego Rivera Frida Kahlo Museums Trust / ARS, New York. Served directly by the holding institution (Harry Ransom Center, Acc. 66.6). Hotlinked; no local reproduction stored.

title: Dora Maar with Cat (Dora Maar au chat)
collection: Private collection (sold Sotheby's New York, 3 May 2006, sale N08195, lot 14)
description: A small black cat perches behind Dora Maar on the back of a big wooden armchair, right beside her neck, in what Sotheby's called "both an amusing and menacing attitude". She sits three-quarter length, enthroned, in a hat sprouting coloured feathers, and her face is shown from two angles at once, profile and front folded into one head. Her striped green bodice and red polka-dot skirt fight for attention, and her long painted nails turn into talons on the armrests, so the cat is not the only creature in the picture with claws. Oil on canvas, about 130 by 97 cm, signed lower left.
context: Picasso painted Dora Maar, photographer, painter and poet and his lover and main model since the mid-1930s, in Paris in 1941, early in the German occupation. The picture passed to Pierre Colle in Paris in 1946 and to the Chicago collectors Leigh and Mary Block in 1947; they sold it in 1963, after which it went unseen for decades. The Gidwitz family of Chicago consigned it to Sotheby's New York, where on 3 May 2006 it sold for $95,216,000, nearly double the estimate, to an anonymous Russian-speaking bidder, widely reported to be the Georgian billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili. It remains in a private collection. Picasso is said to have described Maar as an "Afghan cat".
submovement: Picasso wartime portraiture of Dora Maar
feline_symbolism: Cats paired with women in art have long implied female cunning and sexual aggression, and Picasso's "Afghan cat" nickname for Maar makes the black cat read as her double.
image_credit: © Succession Picasso. Image: Sotheby's, Impressionist & Modern Art Evening Sale N08195 (New York, 2006), lot 14. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from Sotheby's and is not stored on this site.

title: The Cat (Le Chat)
description: A bronze cat stands four-square on a slab base, tail cranked stiffly up behind, head turned to look out past us, ears pricked. About 55 cm from end to end, only 18 cm wide and 36 cm high, the proportions are all length, the body a long low bridge between the legs. The surface is lumpy and gouged, every push and scrape of the model kept, because lost-wax casting reproduces the wax or plaster closely, surface and all. Look at the edge of the base for the foundry's stamp, "CIRE PERDUE C. VALSUANI", lost wax, C. Valsuani, the Paris foundry that cast it.
context: Picasso made the cat in Paris, and the Musée national Picasso dates this bronze to 1943, in the middle of the German occupation. The entry's older date range of 1941-1943 probably reflects the gap between modelling and casting, which the museum record does not spell out. The cast stayed in Picasso's own studio until his death in 1973. In 1979 it entered the national collection by dation, the French arrangement that lets heirs pay inheritance tax in works of art, and it is catalogued as MP324. A small legal footnote: because Picasso's rights run until 2044, the museum's own record still marks this cat as a protected work.
image_credit: © Succession Picasso. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from popcorn-prd-perf-assets.s3.gra.io.cloud.ovh.net and is not stored on this site.

title: Lt Cdr R. H. Palmer Plays with Peebles, the Ship's Cat, on HMS Western Isles
title_original: Peebles, Ship's Cat of HMS Western Isles
artist: Ministry of Information Photo Division (official photographer)
description: Peebles, the ship's cat, is caught mid-jump through a hoop made of an officer's arms, a party trick photographed for the record. He is a shaggy black cat, front paws already reaching down past the clasped hands. The man forming the hoop is Lieutenant Commander R. H. Palmer of the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, bent double in cap and braided sleeve on the deck of HMS Western Isles at Tobermory on the Isle of Mull, with water and low hills behind. The original caption adds that Peebles was clever enough to shake hands with people entering the wardroom. Black-and-white official photograph, Crown copyright.
context: The photograph was taken by a photographer of the Ministry of Information Photo Division, the wartime unit that supplied images for press and propaganda, and it is in the Ministry's Second World War Official Collection at the Imperial War Museum as D 20280. Commons's title places it in 1944. IWM files it under morale and entertainment alongside other images of daily life afloat, a reminder that a cat jumping through a hoop counted, in 1944, as useful wartime material. Read the caption closely and Palmer turns out to be the hoop, not the photographer.
title_eng: Lt Cdr R. H. Palmer Plays with Peebles, the Ship's Cat, on HMS Western Isles
collection: Imperial War Museum, London (Ministry of Information Second World War Official Collection)
submovement: British Ministry of Information official photography
image_credit: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer · http://media.iwm.org.uk/iwm/mediaLib//43/media-43850/large.jpg This photograph D 20280 comes from the collections of the Imperial War Museums .

title: Soviet Soldiers with a Cat in Stalingrad
title_original: Советские бойцы с кошкой на руках в Сталинграде
license: © Estate of Yakov Ryumkin, all rights reserved
description: A tabby-and-white cat stares straight into the lens from the arms of a smiling Soviet soldier in Stalingrad, a city being fought over street by street. A second soldier reaches across in a padded glove to stroke it, and a third grins from behind, all three in steel helmets, a submachine gun slung across the front. Behind them rises a burnt-out wreck of girders and a great wheel. The picture is a straight black-and-white press photograph by a frontline photojournalist, and the cat is the only thing in it not in uniform. The original caption simply calls it "a cat".
context: Yakov Ryumkin (1913-1986) photographed the battle of Stalingrad for the Soviet press, and this frame, captioned "Soviet soldiers with a cat in their arms in Stalingrad", is dated 1942. It circulates through the Russian war-photo archive Voennyi Albom, which credits the image to photo.may9.ru and the information to the culture ministry's portal. Online, the picture is often linked to Mourka, a Stalingrad cat said to have carried messages between Soviet positions. Nothing in the photograph's own record supports that identification, so the cat should be treated as anonymous; the Mourka story belongs to the legend, not to this negative.
title_eng: Soviet Soldiers with a Cat in Stalingrad
collection: State Historical Museum / RIA Novosti Archive, Moscow
image_credit: © Estate of Yakov Ryumkin. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from waralbum.ru and is not stored on this site.

title: Girl with a Kitten (Kitty Garman)
license: © The Lucian Freud Archive, all rights reserved
description: A tabby kitten dangles from Kitty Garman's fist, gripped by the neck, and it is hard to say which of the two looks more alarmed. Its pale green eyes echo her olive-green ones, and its striped body and white paws hang limp below her knuckles. Freud crops in close: her face and very large eyes take up much of the canvas, every strand of brown hair drawn with a fine brush and almost no showy handling. The picture is small, about 41 by 31 cm, so the hard focus feels concentrated rather than grand. Her gaze slides off to the right; the hand does the talking.
context: Freud painted it in 1947, when he was 24; the reverse is dated September 1947 and it was shown the next month at the London Gallery, in a two-man show with John Craxton. It is one of eight portraits he made of Kitty Garman, his first wife, between 1947 and 1951. The painting first belonged to Freud's elder brother Stephen, then to the collector Simon Sainsbury, who bequeathed it to Tate in 2006; it was accessioned in 2008. Fun fact: when Tate showed the Sainsbury bequest in 2008, this small picture was picked for the catalogue cover, ahead of far larger names.
submovement: Early Lucian Freud: post-war British linear realism
feline_symbolism: Commentators read the clutched kitten as a mirror of the sitter's own wariness; Freud left no statement to that effect, so treat it as interpretation.
image_credit: © The Lucian Freud Archive. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from uploads6.wikiart.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Dalí Atomicus
license: © Philippe Halsman Archive / Magnum Photos, all rights reserved
description: Three black cats fly across the frame, one arching high above the water, two tumbling below in a tangle of legs and tails, while a sheet of water from a thrown bucket arcs past them and Salvador Dalí hangs in mid-jump, brush raised, moustache waxed upward. A chair floats at left, where an assistant's arm sneaks in at the very edge of the frame. Leda Atomica hangs at right on wires, with a step stool below it. The cats are real and so is the water. Look at the easel in the middle: its frame is empty, a window onto the bare studio wall.
context: Philippe Halsman made the picture in his New York studio in 1948 with a 4x5 twin-lens camera of his own design. He counted to four: on three, assistants (his wife Yvonne and daughter Irene among them) threw the cats and the water, and on four Dalí jumped. Halsman wrote that it took 28 attempts, others say 26, over five or six hours, developing between takes while the cats were caught and dried. Life magazine published it in 1948 together with some of the failed takes. MoMA holds a gelatin silver print. Fun fact: the title nods to Dalí's Leda Atomica, which he had been working on since 1945 and which is itself about objects suspended without touching.
collection: Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), New York
submovement: Surrealist studio photography (Halsman and Dalí collaboration)
image_credit: © Philippe Halsman Archive. Photo: Library of Congress / MoMA. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from upload.wikimedia.org and is not stored on this site.
rights_note: Public domain in the United States due to non-renewal of original copyright registration (Library of Congress Prints & Photographs LC-H9- 09633); hotlinked for compliance in international jurisdictions where photographer copyright persists (Philippe Halsman d. 1979, life + 70).

title: Oscar, cat from the German battleship 'Bismarck'
title_original: Oscar, the Cat from the German Battleship Bismarck (Unsinkable Sam)
description: A black-and-white cat sits on a floating plank of wreckage with open sea around it, glancing back over its shoulder with wide green eyes. This is a pastel, so the fur is built from soft dragged strokes of chalk rather than lines, and the white bib, white toes and black coat stand out against teal water. Bare buff paper shows at the edges, and a curling wave rises in the foreground. The framed sheet measures about 78.5 by 61 cm. The plank is the point of the picture: it restages the moment the cat was supposedly fished out of the sea after the Bismarck went down, a moment nobody photographed.
context: The pastel is by Georgina Shaw Baker (1860-1951), an animal portraitist about whom little is known, and it belongs to the National Maritime Museum in Greenwich. The story goes that the cat survived the sinking of the Bismarck in May 1941, was picked off a plank by the destroyer HMS Cossack and named Oscar, then survived Cossack's torpedoing in October 1941 and Ark Royal's in November, earning the name 'Sam'. He died in a Belfast seamen's home in 1955. Fun fact: the museum itself is sceptical. Two conflicting photographs exist, and the collar tag in one reads 'HMS Amethyst 1949', which points to a different cat altogether.
title_eng: Oscar, cat from the German battleship 'Bismarck'
image_credit: Georgina Shaw Baker · https://prints.rmg.co.uk/cdn/shop/products/T0772.jpg

title: Simon the Cat, Mascot of HMS Amethyst
title_original: Able Seacat Simon of HMS Amethyst
description: Simon, a small black-and-white cat, poses with three sailors aboard HMS Amethyst in this plain gelatin silver print by an unnamed photographer. It is the kind of informal ship's snapshot that nobody expected a museum to want, and the Imperial War Museum now files it under the cat's own name. The men are the supporting cast here. Note the credit line, the PDSA, the animal charity that gave Simon his medal and kept the pictures that made him famous.
context: Simon was a stray found on the Hong Kong docks in March 1948 by a 17-year-old seaman, George Hickinbottom, who smuggled him aboard. In April 1949, during the Yangtze Incident, a shell from a PLA battery tore through the captain's cabin; Simon was treated for burns and four pieces of shrapnel and went back to killing rats. He received the PDSA Dickin Medal in August 1949 and remains the only cat to hold it. He died in quarantine in Surrey on 28 November 1949 and lies in the PDSA cemetery at Ilford. This print, credited to the PDSA, is held by the Imperial War Museum and was shown at IWM North in 'All Aboard: Stories of War at Sea' (2010-11). Fun fact: one of his kills was a rat the crew had nicknamed 'Mao Tse-tung'.
title_eng: Simon the Cat, Mascot of HMS Amethyst
collection: Imperial War Museums, London (shown at IWM North)
image_credit: Imperial War Museum North (Ref: HU 43656) · © PDSA. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com and is not stored on this site.
rights_note: Held by the Imperial War Museum under reference HU 43656 (exhibited at IWM North 2010–2011). Because IWM does not publish a dedicated online object page or open-access download, the source record is cited from Luminous-Lint. Copyright is held by PDSA; hotlinked for identification.

title: The Mediterranean Cat (Le Chat de la Méditerranée)
license: © Estate of Balthus, all rights reserved
description: A cat with a man's posture sits at a laid table, knife and fork at the ready, wine to hand, while behind him a rainbow rises from the sea and fish leap out of it towards his plate, where a fat one already lies. It is a big oil, about 127 by 185 cm, painted in flat, sign-like colour so it reads from across a room. The cat is Balthus himself, in a striped jumper with a napkin tied at his neck. Look at the face: eyes shut and mouth curled in a grin, a rare thing in an artist whose cats usually just stare.
context: Balthus painted the panel in 1949 as decoration for a Paris restaurant; the title points to La Méditerranée, the seafood restaurant opened in 1942 opposite the Théâtre de l'Odéon, though the sources opened here do not spell out the commission. He had cast himself as a cat before, in The King of Cats (1935), and as a boy had made forty ink drawings of a stray named Mitsou, published in 1921 with a preface by Rilke. The canvas is in a private collection. Fun fact: an oil study on board for the composition (46 x 61 cm, also 1949) was shown at the Met's 2013 exhibition 'Balthus: Cats and Girls' and later sold at Sotheby's.
feline_symbolism: The cat is the artist's alter ego, a role Balthus gave cats from Mitsou onward.
image_credit: © Estate of Balthus. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from www.artchive.com and is not stored on this site.

title: The Cat (Le Chat)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
license: © Succession Alberto Giacometti, all rights reserved
description: A cat walks along a single straight line of bronze: head, spine and tail are one rod about 81 cm long, held up on four legs as thin as matchsticks. The whole sculpture is only about 14 cm deep, so seen end-on the animal almost disappears. The surface keeps the pinches and gouges of the plaster it was cast from, and the rough slab of a base is as lumpy as the cat. Look at the head, a small rounded wedge with a pricked ear, and at the tail, held dead level behind like a ruler while the legs bend mid-stride.
context: Giacometti modelled the cat in plaster in 1951, prompted by a cat his brother Diego had taken in, and showed the plaster that year at the Galerie Maeght in Paris. Bronzes followed in an edition of eight; the Met dates its cast 1954 and received it in 1998 with the Jacques and Natasha Gelman Collection. Other casts are at the Fondation Maeght, the Museum Berggruen in Berlin and the Giacometti-Stiftung (on loan to Basel). Giacometti admired how the cat slipped between objects without touching them: 'A cat is narrow and can pass between two very close objects.' Fun fact: the story goes that he made the plasters for Le Chat, Le Chien and an abandoned pair of horses in a single day, and then made no more animals.
feline_symbolism: Sotheby's reads the cat, like the companion Dog, as a stand-in for Giacometti himself; that is a cataloguer's interpretation.
image_credit: © Succession Alberto Giacometti. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from www.fondation-giacometti.fr and is not stored on this site.

title: Chat Malicieux (Mischievous Cat) Clip Brooch
description: A cat winks at you from a lapel. The body is a single oval cabochon of black onyx, while the head, ears, tiny paws and big plumed tail are worked in textured yellow gold, every hair chased in. One eye is a cabochon emerald under a curved brow set with diamonds; the other is shut, a single gold slit. A ruby makes the nose, and fine gold wires fan out as whiskers. Surviving examples are around 5 cm long, small enough to wear every day, which was the whole idea. The wink is the detail: it was not in the first drawing.
context: Van Cleef & Arpels' own archive dates the design to December 1953, when the first sketch was made; the diamond eyelid that turns a stare into a wink was added a few months later. The clip belongs to the animal pieces of La Boutique, the firm's lighter daywear line launched in 1954 at Place Vendôme, and the nickname 'Chat malicieux' (mischievous cat) came afterwards. The model stayed in production for years: auction examples are dated from the mid-1950s to around 1970, and a Sotheby's lot is stamped 1959. Fun fact: the Maison reissued the winking cat in revised form, so a 'vintage' one on the market needs its date stamp checked.
medium: 18-karat textured yellow gold, carved black onyx, cabochon emeralds, round diamonds, and ruby
collection: Van Cleef & Arpels Heritage Collection, Paris

title: 25 Cats Name Sam and One Blue Pussy (Purple Sam)
medium: Offset lithograph with hand-coloring in Dr. Ph. Martin's aniline watercolor on Strathmore paper
license: © The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, all rights reserved
description: A pink-purple cat lies stretched across the sheet, tail curling under, striped in Warhol's wobbly, broken ink line, printed by offset lithography and then washed by hand with transparent colour that wanders happily outside the outlines. Its eyes are narrowed and its whiskers splay like stray pen marks. No two copies are coloured quite alike, because friends did much of the painting. The pages are small, about 23 by 15 cm. Read the title lettering at top: it is in the looping hand of Warhol's mother, Julia Warhola, who left the 'd' off 'Named', and her son liked the mistake enough to keep it.
context: Warhol made the book in the mid-1950s (usually dated 1954) as a privately printed promotion for himself as an illustrator. His friend Charles Lisanby supplied the title, which is also the only text, and said some drawings came from a book of cat photographs he owned. The edition was planned at 190 numbered copies; Warhol and friends coloured the lithographs by hand, and most copies went out as gifts to clients. Fun fact: copy no. 4, inscribed to the Bonwit Teller executive Geraldine Stutz, served as the model for the 1987 and 1988 facsimiles, boxed with Julia Warhola's own book Holy Cats.
title_eng: 25 Cats Name Sam and One Blue Pussy (Purple Sam)
title_original: 25 Cats Name Sam and One Blue Pussy
submovement: New York commercial illustration (pre-Pop Warhol artist's book)
image_credit: © The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from upload.wikimedia.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Sympathy (Simpatía / La rabia del gato)
collection: Colección Costantini / MALBA (Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires)
license: © Estate of Remedios Varo, all rights reserved
description: A cat has jumped onto the table and knocked over a glass; the spill runs off the edge and spreads across the floor into a puddle that becomes a small sea. Instead of scolding, the woman strokes it, and sparks leap from the orange fur, link up into a little electrical contraption and reach her hair, which bristles in the same flame-orange spikes. The cat twists on the red tablecloth, hind legs kicking skyward. Varo painted it in oil on Masonite, about 96 by 85 cm, using decalcomania (paint pressed and lifted) for the watery surfaces. Look under the table: three furry tails poke out from beneath the woman's dress.
context: Varo painted it in Mexico City in 1955 and showed it that summer in 'Seis pintoras' at the Galería Diana; it appeared again in her 1956 show at the Museo de Arte Moderno. Owners included the film director Albert Lewin before it went to a private collector in 1971. At Christie's New York in May 2019 it sold for about 3.1 million dollars, reportedly to Eduardo Costantini, founder of Malba in Buenos Aires. Varo described the scene herself: the cat causes chaos, and the caress sets off sparks that give the woman a permanent wave. Fun fact: the alternative title, La rabia del gato, translates as the cat's rage.
feline_symbolism: Christie's and the critic Nancy Vosburg read the cat as Varo's alter ego, noting how her own almond-eyed face resembles a cat's.
image_credit: © Estate of Remedios Varo. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from uploads4.wikiart.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Minneke Poes (Ypres Kattenstoet Giant Festival Effigy)
description: Minneke Poes is a giant: like other Flemish processional giants she is a towering costumed figure with an oversized head, here a white cat's with rouged lips and a black feathered topknot, carried through the streets of Ypres by bearers hidden inside. She wears a red ruffled jacket over a black bodice and a vast quilted white skirt, paws held out wide, a white tail curling up behind her. She walks in the Kattenstoet as the showpiece of the parade, beside the tomcat giant Cieper. Giants are made to be read from far off, so the face is simple. Watch her in motion: giants sway and turn rather than walk.
context: Frans Van Immerseel, who also designed the tomcat Cieper, designed Minneke Poes in 1960; a Dutch Wikipedia caption says the giant was made that year for Zwevegem and given to Ypres in 1971. The Kattenstoet itself began modestly in 1938, when celluloid toy cats were thrown from the belfry of the Cloth Hall, and became a full procession on 6 March 1955; it now runs every three years in May. It recalls an older custom, recorded from at least the 1590s, of throwing live cats from the tower. Fun fact: the throwing still happens, but the jester now lobs plush cats, and the crowd fights to catch one.
title_eng: Minneke Poes (Ypres Festival of the Cats Giant Effigy)
medium: Painted papier-mâché, wood, cane armature, and tailored textile gown
collection: Stad Ieper Collection / Ypres Guild of Giants, Ypres, Belgium
image_credit: Zeisterre · Own work

title: Orangey as 'Cat' with Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany's
description: A ginger tabby, the real subject of this entry, rears up on his hind legs, tail stretched straight out, reaching for whatever Audrey Hepburn holds. As Holly Golightly she kneels barefoot in a white robe, sleep mask pushed up into her hair, a bowl on the floor beside them. The image is a cropped frame from Paramount's 1961 trailer for Breakfast at Tiffany's, so what you see is soft film colour and lighting set up for a moving camera, not a posed studio portrait. Holly calls him simply Cat, a running joke about her refusal to own anything. He was played by a trained animal actor with a reputation.
context: The cat was played by Orangey, the stage name of several red tabbies owned and trained by Frank Inn, who said he paid 25 dollars for the first. Orangey won a PATSY award for Rhubarb (1951) and a second for Breakfast at Tiffany's, the only cat to win two. He also appeared in This Island Earth, The Incredible Shrinking Man and The Diary of Anne Frank. Studio publicity treated him as one cat, though he had about a dozen stand-ins. Fun fact: a studio executive called him the world's meanest cat; he scratched actors and sometimes ran off after a take, and Inn once posted guard dogs at the studio gate to stop him escaping.
title_eng: Orangey as 'Cat' with Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany's
collection: Paramount Pictures Studio Archive / Academy Film Archive, Beverly Hills
image_credit: Paramount Pictures · YouTube : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eJJvjGKhscA – View/save archived versions on archive.org

title: The Whittington Stone Cat Monument
description: A stone cat sits on top of a weathered milestone, looking out over the traffic at the foot of Highgate Hill. Jonathan Kenworthy carved it in 1964 from Kellymount limestone; in daylight it now reads as a speckled grey, barely darker than the lichen-stained Portland stone tablet below. The shapes are smooth and simplified, a cat reduced to haunches, chest and ears, its head turned sharply over one shoulder towards the road. A ring of iron railings with scrollwork and spearhead finials, red paint flaking through the black, keeps the ensemble at arm's length. The faded inscription on one face retells the legend.
context: The stone marks roughly where, in the story, the young Dick Whittington turned back after hearing Bow Bells promise he would be Lord Mayor. The present tablet was put up in 1821 and restored in 1935; a 1745 drawing shows an earlier stone as the base of a wayside cross. The real Richard Whittington (c. 1354-1423) was a mercer who served as mayor several times and left his money to charity; the cat belongs to the later legend. The monument has been Grade II listed since 1972. Fun fact: the cat arrived 143 years after the tablet, so the most photographed part of the monument is also the newest.
medium: Polished black Kellymount limestone cat (1964) on Portland stone tablet (1821)
dimensions: Life-size cat figure atop 140 cm stone milestone
feline_symbolism: In the legend the cat is the source of Whittington's fortune.
image_credit: Felipe Tofani · https://www.flickr.com/photos/gastaum/53873083708/

title: Monument to Dr. Samuel Johnson's Cat Hodge
description: Hodge sits on top of a copy of Johnson's Dictionary, upright and self-satisfied, ears pricked, a small dark bronze silhouette against the red brick of Gough Square, with a pair of empty oyster shells beside him. The cat is life-size, and he looks across the square towards the house where his owner worked. The pale stone plinth carries his name in capitals above a black plaque with the line 'a very fine cat indeed'. Look into the oyster shells: visitors drop coins in them for luck, and on special occasions someone ties a pink ribbon of the kind used on barristers' briefs around a shell or around Hodge's neck.
context: Jon Bickley made the statue, modelling it on his own cat, Thomas Henry, and it was unveiled in 1997 by Sir Roger Cook, then Lord Mayor of London. It faces 17 Gough Square, where Samuel Johnson lived and compiled much of the Dictionary, and which he shared with his servant Francis Barber. The oysters come from James Boswell's Life of Johnson (1791): Johnson bought them for Hodge himself, so that the servants would not come to resent the cat. Fun fact: the inscription flatters Hodge more than Johnson did. Boswell records him adding, 'but I have had cats whom I liked better than this'.
title_eng: Monument to Dr. Samuel Johnson's Cat Hodge
medium: Cast bronze figure on Portland stone pedestal with open oyster shells
collection: Gough Square, City of London, England
dimensions: Life-size cat figure (approx. 50 cm) on 110 cm stone plinth
submovement: British Contemporary Public Sculpture & Literary Commemoration
location: Gough Square, City of London, England
image_credit: ceridwen · From geograph.org.uk

title: Monument to the Cat of Kazan (Kot Kazansky)
license: © Estate of Igor Bashmakov, all rights reserved
description: A very fat cat settles under a little tent-shaped canopy, and on the very top of the canopy, out of reach, sits a mouse. The whole thing is cast in aluminium and toned to look like old silver, so it reads like a piece of oversized folk metalwork in the middle of a pedestrian street. The base is engraved with the cat's titles from the old popular print: 'Alabrys: Cat of Kazan, Astrakhan wits, Siberian reason'. The mouse is the joke: the cat is plainly too comfortable to bother.
context: The Kazan sculptor Igor Bashmakov made the monument, installed in 2009 on Bauman Street at the corner of Musa Jalil Street; the idea was first raised at a Kazan conference in May 2005. The 'Cat of Kazan' comes from an eighteenth-century Russian lubok (popular woodcut print) whose caption calls him 'Kot brys, also Alabrys', though Bashmakov said he worked from the legend rather than copying the print. The legend has a documented core: an imperial decree of 13 October 1745 under Empress Elizabeth sent thirty Kazan cats to St Petersburg to catch mice in the unfinished Winter Palace, where the Hermitage cats still live. Fun fact: Kazan has two more cat monuments, a sandstone one at the Raifa Monastery, also from 2009, and a bronze outside the National Museum of Tatarstan.
title_eng: Monument to the Cat of Kazan (Alabrys)
collection: Bauman Street, Kazan, Republic of Tatarstan, Russia
submovement: Contemporary Russian Public Sculpture & Urban Folklore
image_credit: © Estate of Igor Bashmakov. Photo: Vadim Indeikin, CC BY-SA 3.0. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from upload.wikimedia.org and is not stored on this site.

feline_symbolism: The cat next to Judas is read as a negative sign tied to the betrayal, though it also works as a simple observation of a cat waiting for scraps.
title: The Last Supper (Cenacolo di San Marco)
collection: Museo Nazionale di San Marco, Florence
location: Small refectory (Refettorio piccolo), Museo di San Marco, Florence
image_credit: Francesco Bini · Own work (Wikimedia Commons, Wiki Loves Monuments), CC BY-SA 4.0
description: The cat sits bolt upright on the patterned floor right next to Judas's stool, the only figure in the room looking straight at us. Judas is on the near side of the table with his back to the viewer, one arm raised as he dips his bread in Christ's dish, and the cat has positioned itself exactly where scraps are most likely to fall. Behind the long white table, with its striped Perugia-weave cloth, the apostles sit two by two in calm conversation, John asleep against Christ. Above their heads the wall opens onto a garden of orange trees, cypresses and a palm, with birds in the sky and a peacock perched at the right. The Latin line along the back wall is Christ's promise from Luke: that they will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.
context: This is the last of Ghirlandaio's three Last Suppers, after Passignano (1476) and Ognissanti (1480), and it reuses the Ognissanti layout of a horseshoe table set into a real vaulted room. The Dominicans of San Marco commissioned it around 1486 for the small refectory, where guests of the convent rather than the friars ate. Domenico was at the height of his fame and full of commissions, so he is usually thought to have supplied the design and left most of the painting to his brother Davide and his brother-in-law Sebastiano Mainardi. Italian scholarship reads the cat beside Judas both ways at once, as a sinister sign and as a plain domestic touch, a cat waiting for food. Fun fact: a few years earlier another Florentine, Cosimo Rosselli, had put a cat squaring up to a dog right by Judas in his Last Supper for the Sistine Chapel, also in this catalogue.

feline_symbolism: The lion belongs to Jerome's legend, the beast he cured of a thorn; the sleeping cat is the domestic counterpart, a sign of the quiet of the scholar's study.
title: Saint Jerome in his Study
image_credit: National Gallery, London (public-domain artwork), via Wikimedia Commons
description: The cat is curled up asleep on the edge of the raised platform that holds Jerome's study, just left of two potted plants, a small grey shape you could easily take for a cushion. Jerome himself sits in his wooden cell in the middle of a huge Gothic hall, reading, his cardinal's hat put down on the bench behind him. Everything is laid out for slow looking: books and a ceramic jar on the shelves, a towel on a peg, a crucifix, views of sunny countryside through the windows. A partridge and a peacock stand on the stone sill at the front, next to a brass basin, and down the shadowy aisle at the right Jerome's lion pads towards us. So the picture has two felids, the saint's tame lion in the gloom and an ordinary house cat asleep in the light.
context: Antonello painted the little panel around 1475, probably in Venice or just before he went there, combining Netherlandish oil technique and minute detail with Italian perspective. The National Gallery thinks it was most probably made for an important patron, and it is often seen as a showpiece of what he could do. By 1529 it belonged to Antonio Pasqualino in Venice; later it was at Stratton in the Baring collection and was bought from the Earl of Northbrook in 1894 (NG1418). The partridge stands for truth and the peacock for immortality, while the boxwood and geranium by the cat are read as faith in salvation and the Passion. Fun fact: when Marcantonio Michiel saw it in Pasqualino's house he reported that some people took it for the work of Jan van Eyck, which is about the highest compliment an Italian painter in oil could be paid.

feline_symbolism: A cat carrying off prey inside the Garden of Eden hints that violence and appetite are already present before the Fall.
title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
image_credit: Museo del Prado high-resolution image (Prado in Google Earth), via Wikimedia Commons
description: The cat is in Paradise, which in Bosch's hands does not mean it has stopped hunting. In the left wing, just below God presenting a freshly made Eve to Adam, a spotted cat strolls away with a small dark creature hanging from its jaws, something with legs and a tail that looks more like a lizard than a mouse. Around it Eden is already slightly off: birds with strange crests, odd hybrid creatures, a bird-like thing reading a book in a dark pond, and in the background a lion tearing into its prey. The centre panel fills with naked people, giant fruit and birds, and the right wing is a night-time hell of musical instruments turned into instruments of torture. Closed, the wings show the world on the third day of Creation in grey.
context: Bosch painted the triptych in 's-Hertogenbosch, probably between about 1490 and 1510; it is not dated, and the title is modern. It is usually read as a warning against the temptations of the flesh, though scholars still argue over whether the centre shows a paradise lost or a world of sin. The Eden wing is full of animals that would have been exotic to its first viewers, including a giraffe and an elephant, and Wikipedia's account singles out the cat with its lizard-like prey. The painting later belonged to Philip II of Spain, went to El Escorial, and has been in the Prado since 1939. Fun fact: even before the Fall, the predators in Bosch's Paradise are already at work, the cat and the lion included, which is one reason some writers think his Eden was never quite innocent.

title: Madonna of the Cat (Madonna della Gatta)
collection: Museo e Real Bosco di Capodimonte, Naples
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY-SA 3.0
description: The cat is in the lower right corner, a tabby-and-white cat crouched low in the shadow of the old woman's skirts and staring straight out of the picture, eyes glinting. Everyone else is busy with each other. Mary holds the Christ Child on her lap as he reaches towards the infant John the Baptist, who leans in from the left; beside her sits an elderly woman, usually named as St Elizabeth, chin on her hand. In front of them is an empty wooden cradle with a cushion, and John's reed cross lies on the floor with its scroll trailing. It is a pyramid of figures straight out of Raphael's workshop, and then that cat.
context: Giulio Romano, Raphael's chief assistant, painted the panel around 1522 to 1523, probably for Federico II Gonzaga of Mantua while he was still in Rome. Vasari saw it in Mantua in 1566 and singled out the cat as so lifelike that it seemed alive, which is why, he says, the picture was called the painting of the cat. In the later sixteenth century it belonged to Barbara Sanseverino in Parma; the Farnese took it in 1612 when they confiscated the collections of local nobles, and it reached Naples with the rest of the Farnese inheritance under Charles of Bourbon around 1737. Fun fact: Giulio liked his model enough to use the same cat again in his erotic painting The Lovers of about 1524 to 1525.

title: The Last Supper
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY 3.0
description: The cat noses in at the bottom right corner, a white cat with a tabby head slipping out from behind an apostle's bare leg, ears back, eyes on the floor. Under the table a dog lies curled asleep beside a metal basin and a glass carafe, ready for the foot-washing nobody has got to yet. Above them the supper is pure commotion: thirteen men crammed round a white cloth, John fast asleep against Christ, apostles leaning, gesturing, rubbing their faces, one with his chin in his hand. These are farmers and labourers with sunburnt faces and dirty feet, and the centre of the table holds a lamb's head on a platter.
context: Bassano painted the canvas for the Venetian Battista Erizzo, who is recorded with it in 1546; it is now usually dated about 1546 to 1548. By 1700 it was in the Borghese collection in Rome, and the Italian state bought it in 1902 with the rest of the gallery (inv. 144). The Borghese ranks it among his finest pictures and notes how, working far from the big centres in Bassano del Grappa, he still absorbed compositional ideas from Raphael, Dürer and Leonardo while refusing to idealise the apostles. Fun fact: in 1993 the picture travelled to the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth, home of Bassano's other cat-haunted supper in this catalogue, The Supper at Emmaus.

title: The Feast in the House of Levi
title_eng: The Feast in the House of Levi
submovement: Venetian High Renaissance Monumental Decorative Painting
image_credit: Photograph by Oakenchips, light correction by Paolo Villa (Wikimedia Commons), public domain
tags: feast in the house of levi
description: The cat is under the table, right in the middle of the picture, a grey cat stretched out on the floor in the shadow of the tablecloth and playing with something at its paws. A few feet away a big dog sits on the chequered floor, looking the other way, and neither of them pays attention to Christ, who sits in the central arch above them. Veronese builds a palace for the party: three huge arches, columns, balustrades and staircases, with a pale dream of a city behind. Turbaned guests, halberdiers on the stairs, servants with flagons and a steward in a striped costume fill the loggias, and the date MDLXXIII is painted on the balustrade at left.
context: Veronese painted the canvas, one of the largest of the century, for the refectory of the Dominican friary of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in Venice, to replace a Last Supper by Titian lost in a fire in 1571. In July 1573, a few months after he finished, the Holy Office summoned him to explain the buffoons, the drunken soldiers, the dwarf and the dog in a picture of the Last Supper. Rather than repaint, he changed the subject: an inscription on the balustrades now cites Luke 5, the feast Levi gave for Jesus. Fun fact: the inquisitors pressed him to replace the dog with a Mary Magdalene, and Veronese told them it would not look right, so the dog stayed; the cat under the table seems to have escaped their notice altogether.

title: The Last Supper
collection: Basilica di San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice
location: Presbytery, Basilica di San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY 3.0
description: The cat has climbed up the side of a wicker basket in the foreground and is peering in, front paws on the rim, back legs braced, one more servant raiding the kitchen. Nobody stops it: the woman kneeling next to it is busy reaching into the same basket, and the dishes are all going the other way. Tintoretto turns the Last Supper into a dark, crowded kitchen-and-dining hall, the table running away from us on a steep diagonal, Christ near the middle giving bread to an apostle in a burst of light. Above them a smoking oil lamp throws out flame, and its smoke turns into a swarm of ghostly angels. Servants carry fruit and plates on the right, unaware that a sacrament is happening behind them.
context: Tintoretto painted the canvas in 1592 to 1594 for Palladio's church of San Giorgio Maggiore, where it still hangs in the presbytery; he died in May 1594, so it is among his last works. His earlier Last Suppers, for San Marcuola (1547) and San Felice (1559), set the table across the picture in the usual way, as Leonardo had. Here he swings it into the depth of the room and lets the everyday and the miraculous share the same light. Fun fact: the monks of San Giorgio had already commissioned Veronese's Wedding at Cana for their refectory thirty years earlier, so the same monastery ended up with two famous banquets, each with a cat raiding the scene.

title: Allegorical Female Figure with Music Book, Gamba and Cat
title_original: Allegorische Frauengestalt mit Liederbuch, Gambe und Katze
title_eng: Allegory with Music Book, Gamba and Cat (Music)
image_credit: Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek München, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: The cat sits at the woman's feet, a large fluffy white cat hunched up like a loaf with its eyes shut, either asleep or pointedly ignoring the music. She stands naked against a dark wood that opens to a pale sky, reading from a small black book held up in one hand and holding a viol by its neck in the other, its body resting on the ground. Baldung paints her very simply, a long, pale, softly modelled figure on a tall narrow panel, with nothing to tell us what she means except the book, the instrument and the cat.
context: Baldung painted the panel in 1529 as a pair with an Allegorical Female Figure with Mirror, Snake, Stag and Hind, also in Munich (inv. 5376); both came from the Electoral Gallery of the Bavarian rulers. The Pinakothek says plainly that their meaning is still unsolved. They are presumed to be personifications from the humanist world of ideas, and have been read as Music and Prudence, as the temperaments, as planetary deities, as virtues or liberal arts, or in a Christian sense, and they were probably part of a series. Fun fact: the museum's own title lists the cat as one of the three clues, alongside the songbook and the gamba, so this is one of the few cats in German painting that is officially part of an unsolved puzzle.

feline_symbolism: Here the cat stands for respectable, constant love, the girl’s faithfulness to the young man painted on the other side of the panel.
title: Girl Making a Garland (reverse of Portrait of a Young Man)
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917 (Open Access, CC0)
description: The cat sits in a window, a white cat upright on the sill with its tail hanging down over the ledge, watching the girl beside it. She sits in a yellow dress at the next opening, eyes lowered, working a garland of small blue flowers, with her long hair loose and a jewelled band round her head. Behind them is a dark wooden lattice, and a white scroll twists through the air above, lettered MIT VERGIS MEIN NIT PINT ICH: I bind with forget-me-nots. The date 1508 is painted on the dark wall at the right. Turn the panel over and a young man looks out from the other side.
context: Kulmbach trained with Jacopo de' Barbari and then in Dürer's workshop in Nuremberg, and took over many of Dürer's altarpiece commissions after 1510. This small double-sided panel shows a young man on one face and this girl on the other; the Met reads the pair as a betrothal picture, with the man as a bridegroom. The forget-me-not garland is a promise of remembrance, and the cat, following Sigrid and Lothar Dittrich's reading cited by the Met, stands for respectable, constant love directed at the man on the other side. It came to the Met as a gift from J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917. Fun fact: the curator Helmut Nickel gave his 1992 article on this panel in the Metropolitan Museum Journal the irresistible title The Bride and the Cat.

title: Joseph Interpreting the Dreams of His Fellow Prisoners
title_original: Joseph legt de dromen van zijn medegevangenen uit
title_eng: Joseph Interpreting the Dreams of His Fellow Prisoners
artist: Master of the Story of Joseph
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1953 (Open Access, CC0)
tags: master of the story of joseph
description: The cat is curled up on the chequered floor under the little round table, tucked in by a prisoner's foot and paying no attention to the prophecy being delivered over its head. Joseph, in a blue doublet and a red turban, points at the two men he shares a cell with: the butler, in red with striped hose, flinging up his hand, and the baker in brown, who has more reason to look worried. Their dreams float above them in two glowing circles, the baker carrying baskets on his head while birds peck at them, and the butler standing by a vine. It is a very comfortable prison, with a bed, a jug, bread rolls and a pewter plate, and an old man looking in through the arched doorway.
context: The story comes from Genesis 40: in Pharaoh's prison Joseph tells the butler that he will be restored to office in three days, and the baker that in three days he will be hanged, and both things come true. The round panel was part of a series on the life of Joseph, and an inventory of 1613 lists six round pictures of the story; the anonymous painter is named after the set, other panels of which are in Berlin. He worked around 1500, probably in Brussels. The Met bought it in 1953 through the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund. Fun fact: the dream that predicts the baker's death is painted as birds raiding his bread basket, so the only creature in the room calmly ignoring all the omens is the cat.

feline_symbolism: The emaciated cat that leaves a mouse alone is a visual joke on ruin: the household has fallen so low that even its cat has given up.
title: Sorgheloos ("Carefree") in Poverty
medium: Colorless glass, vitreous paint and silver stain
collection: The Cloisters, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Cloisters Collection, 1999 (Open Access, CC0)
description: The cat is the clearest sign of how bad things have got: it lies stretched flat on the floor at the young man's feet, all ribs and limp legs, while a mouse sits nearby and nobody bothers to chase it. Sorgheloos, whose name means Carefree, sits on an upturned tub in a bare kitchen, warming himself at a fire of a few straws, with a pitiful dog sitting up by the wall. The shelves hold a couple of pots and a pan, a basket sits on top of the cupboard, and through the window we glimpse the world outside going on without him. The whole scene is painted in grey-brown line on clear glass, with silver stain giving the warm yellows of the tub, the fire and his cap.
context: Sorgheloos was a popular Netherlandish character, a version of the Prodigal Son: a young man who spends everything on pleasure, is abandoned by his fair-weather friends, and ends up in want. Roundels like this one told the story in a series of small panes and decorated the windows of private houses and public buildings such as taverns, where the moral would be read by the people most in need of it. This scene comes near the end of the cycle. The Cloisters bought it in 1999. Fun fact: in earlier roundels of the story Sorgheloos is seen living it up with a companion called Lichte Fortune, Easy Fortune; by this scene she is nowhere to be seen, and all he has left is a thin dog and a thinner cat.

title: Girl with a Cat
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1933 (Open Access, CC0)
description: The cat fills the bottom of the print, a big striped tabby slung in the crook of the young woman's arm, its body draped across her forearm and one paw hanging down as only a completely relaxed cat can manage. She is shown half-length in profile, wrapped in a hood and a heavy cloak, looking down and away with a calm, rather serious face. Vermeyen builds everything out of loose, fast, crisscrossing lines that sit well with the soft fur and the folds of cloth, and leaves a plain hatched background, so the only things competing for attention are her profile and the cat.
context: Vermeyen was a painter, printmaker and designer of woven wall hangings who worked for the Habsburg regents of the Netherlands, Margaret of Austria and Mary of Hungary, and travelled with Emperor Charles V on his 1535 campaign to conquer Tunis, which he later turned into a famous set of designs for the weavers. His etchings are rare, and this one, dated 1546, survives in very few impressions; the Met's came through the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund in 1933. Fun fact: Vermeyen was nicknamed Jan with the Beard and Barbalonga, for a beard said to have been a metre long.
